News.title: No daylight, censored texts & ‘Mars-like’ isolation – nerve-shattering life on Brit sub that spent 217 DAYS underwater
News.content:
Next

A CREW of 140 people have spent a record 217 days underwater without sunlight or fresh air in an “incredible feat of human endurance”.

When HMS Vengeance set sail on April 12, Sir Keir Starmer was still Prime Minister.



His letter of last resort was locked in the captain’s safe with instructions for nuclear war if all other contact with home is lost.

For exactly 31 weeks, the 140-strong crew of HMS Vengeance has been confined inside a 150m long submarine.



In that time, the UK has had yet another Prime Minister, Russell Brand has been jailed, and Prince Harry and Meghan moved back to the UK – as reported in our world exclusive.

While underwater, the crew couldn’t send messages home for fear of revealing the sub’s location.

On submarines, the only contact with loved ones arrives as a weekly text message – known as familygrams – which are read by the captain to censor any bad news.

And when the message contains news of a baby arrival it is called a baby-gram.



Conditions onboard a sub are so extreme that NASA has studied the crew to prepare for missions to Mars.

The crew are cut off from home, below the waves, working rolling eight hour shifts without natural light or fresh air.

The previous record was 205 days set by HMS Vanguard earlier this year.

The length of its patrol had raised fears it could run low on food.

No10 said several sailors’ families had “significant life milestones while their loved ones were on deployment, including four submariners who returned home to newborn children” while on the Vanguard.



Submarine crews sleep in narrow bunk beds that are a little over 6ft long, with some cabins sleeping around nine people.

The most junior hotbed with sleeping bags.

Vitamin D tablets are offered to the crew as they’re cut off from natural daylight.



Limited amounts of booze are onboard, according to Sky News.

News about deaths or illnesses is deliberately held back until the vessel’s final day at sea, which is known as the patrol’s Day Zero.

Sailors who have to face heartbreaking news are summoned to the captain’s cabin, informed about what has happened and are transferred to land immediately by boat or helicopter.

Nuclear submarines are the only Royal Navy vessels to have a full doctor on patrol with them, as medical issues must be dealt with onboard.

Vengeance was due to return last week but had to extend at the very last minute after HMS Vanguard, which was sent to replace her, aborted its patrol.



One must always be at sea to maintain the UK’s continuous deterrent, which the Navy says has been unbroken since 1969.

HMS Vengeance sailed into Clyde to a hero’s welcome on Sunday after 217 days away.

Comrades hailed the crew for an “incredible feat of human endurance” after 31 weeks almost totally cut off from home.

It is the first patrol in history to last longer than seven months due to problems maintaining the other three subs which carry the UK’s nuclear missiles.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said his admiration was “second to none” for the submariners who crew the deterrent patrols.



He said: “I am very proud of those who serve, providing what remains the cornerstone of Britain’s defence.

“We can be extremely proud of their service, we can be extremely proud of the capability.”

The Navy’s four Vanguard class submarines were designed to do 80 day patrols but six of the previous seven patrols have lasted more than 200 days.

They were also designed to serve 25 years, due to strains on the vessels and their nuclear reactors.

But the oldest, HMS Vanguard, has been in service 33 years.



HMS Vengeance, the youngest of the four, was due to retire two years ago.

In 2016, HMS Vengeance had a Trident missile misfire after a refurb.

The intercontinental ballistic missile was due to fly 9,000km from near the coast of Florida to a target south east of Ascension Island.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But it veered dangerously of course and automatically self-destructed.

Former PM Theresa May was accused of covering up the malfunction ahead of a vote in parliament on renewing the UK’s nuclear deterrent.

A WOMAN has been sexually assaulted in a “frightening” daylight attack as cops search for a hero bystander who intervened.

Nottingham Police are investigating the alleged attack on October 19 at around 10.20am on Colwick Road, Sneinton.

The woman was reportedly assaulted by a man before screaming, which scared him off, cops said.

The alleged attacker then returned and attempted to apologise to the woman.

Now, police want to speak to a woman who intervened during the incident by shouting to the victim from across the street.

Police Constable Ethan Spinks, of Nottinghamshire Police, said: “We want to speak to the woman as she could have important information about what happened.

News.title: How shady trade in mummified body parts could unleash ancient fungal spores on world & spread to UK through postboxes
News.content:
Next

WITHIN weeks of unearthing King Tutankhamun’s tomb, Lord Carnarvon was on his death bed after being struck down by a mysterious “Mummy’s Curse”.

The Brit archaeologist was feared to have been exposed to ancient fungal spores when searching King Tut’s tomb. This same terrifying phenomenon could soon spark chaos across the globe thanks to the shady trade of mummified body parts, experts warn.



Toxic fungi can survive in mummified human tissue for centuries or more with some ancient remains being found riddled with diseases or mould.

Decaying body parts can even carry traces of highly toxic chemicals, such as arsenic and mercury, which have been found in 19th- century embalming fluids.

Sofia Aziz, a biomedical Egyptologist who has been face-to-face with Tutankhamun’s mummy, has strong views on the trade.



She told The Sun: “I don’t think mummified human remains should be sold at all. Every one of these was a person, not a souvenir.”

Touching mummified remains has had deadly consequences in the past.

The “curse of Tutankhamun” was feared to have struck down British archaeological patron Lord Carnarvon in 1923.



He died shortly after entering the chamber alongside Howard Carter. His official cause of death remains sepsis and pneumonia triggered by an infected mosquito bite on his cheek while out in Cairo.

Some experts have speculated airborne fungal spores contributed to the death after he was exposed to it inside the burial chamber of the legendary Egyptian ruler.

Decades later, in 1973, 10 out of 12 scientists died after inhaling Aspergillus spores – a common mould – after opening the 15th century tomb of King Casimir the Fourth of Poland.

Kirsty Squires, a professor of human bioarchaeology at the University of Staffordshire, told The Sun these fatal lessons can’t be forgotten about all these years on.

She fears the people behind the mummified trade networks and the buyers could quickly become super spreaders of a potential outbreak.



She said: “Private collectors may be unaware that human remains can present health hazards and may be reluctant to report an illness or suspected exposure because of the potential legal, reputational or financial consequences of disclosing their acquisition.”

Global trading of body parts has massively increased over the past few decades thanks to the rise of social media.

In the past, purchasing genuine ancient Egyptian relics came at a huge cost and were mainly limited to just the rich and powerful.



But now buying an aging arm or embalmed head is far more accessible as trades can be made online on forums or the dark web.

Today, Facebook or Instagram groups are the most common places to discuss the trade or private auction houses.

Prof Squires conducted a shocking study this year published in the International Journal of Cultural Property .

Her team analysed 128 online sale posts from 2015 to 2025 showing off or advertising remains from both humans and animals.

“Mummified heads, hands and feet were very common,” she said.



Prof Squires found the majority of the images shared showed “visible signs of deterioration”.

The main cause of the ill-fated conditions was most likely poor storage conditions, she believes.

In museums, mummies are kept in optimal temperature and humidity conditions which are strictly controlled.



But most sellers will often try and hide the body parts due to the illegal activity which means they can often be stashed in boxes and hidden in basements or garages.

This creates the perfect breeding ground for bacteria and mould – increasing the risk of a dangerous fungal eruption.

Wealthy buyers who purchase the relics are often able to afford specialist handlers and protective glass cases to store the items in. This means the conditions can be kept safe and controlled at all times.

Should the items fall into less careful hands then the consequences could be dire.

One of the biggest fears for experts is how the mummified remains are being transported.



They have been known to be shipped off in parcels or boxes like ordinary online items.

If ancient fungal spores exist on the items then they could quickly spread to the packaging and everything it comes into contact with.

This would include other parcels, the delivery person and the buyer.



This could create a potential super spreader phenomenon.

Sofia explains: “The real risk is modern mould and bacteria, which grow on remains after they have left their burial and been kept somewhere damp.

“These are the same kinds of mould found in damp homes. Dried tissue also crumbles easily, so the spores can be breathed in.

“The people most exposed are the ones who don’t know what they’re handling.

“Postal workers, couriers and customs officers have no idea what’s in the box, and no protection.”



In February, a bill was introduced in the UK through the House of Commons that sought to ban the online sale of human remains.

It was later dropped which means under current UK law, it remains legal to own, buy, and sell human bones, skulls, and remains if they are part of a private collection and haven’t been acquired illegally.

India, China and South Africa are among the only nations to have country-wide bans on human remains trading.

Some US states also have restrictions including Florida, Texas and Georgia.

Prof Squires said: “This is a global issue rather than one confined to a particular region.



“The risks therefore extend beyond the location where remains originate and can follow them through international trade, private collections and online sales.”

Another major concern is how people handle the items without gloves or any PPE equipment.

Prof Squires added: “Of the social-media posts, e-commerce listings and online auction postings I have reviewed, I have yet to see warnings that adequately address potential health risks or provide appropriate guidance on the handling and storage of mummified human remains.”

“Immunocompromised individuals may be particularly vulnerable to potential biological hazards,” the professor continued.

“Although anyone who handles or comes into close contact with mummified remains could potentially be exposed, particularly where extensive biodeterioration is present and PPE is not worn.”



Despite her grave warnings, Sofia doesn’t believe ancient fungal spores are a major global issue after decades researching ancient Egypt.

She said: “The risk is small. The resins and embalming materials the Egyptians used are what preserved these bodies so well.

“Any disease these people had in life is long dead. Scientists have found traces of ancient diseases in mummified remains, but those are fragments of genetic material, not live germs that could infect anyone.”

Researchers argue that if the trade can’t be eradicated completely then it must be monitored better to ensure the safety of everyone involved.

News.title: Nato member Estonia to close border crossings with Russia in weeks after ‘clear evidence’ of sabotage attack plot
News.content:
BORDERS SHUT Nato member Estonia to close border crossings with Russia in weeks after ‘clear evidence’ of sabotage attack plot







Next

ESTONIA has declared it will shut all border crossings to Russia in just two weeks as tensions between the Kremlin and Nato flare.

PM Kristen Michal blasted the Kremlin’s relentless hybrid attacks and said the Baltic nation would “not be intimidated” by its bully neighbour.



Michal explained on X: “On the night of 14 November, GRU-ordered sabotage attempt targeted Estonian defence company Threod Systems.

“Extensive damage was averted thanks to heightened security and a swift reaction by law enforcement. The attackers have been detained.



“This is part of Russia’s broader hybrid war against Europe, with the aim of decreasing support to Ukraine and pressure on Russia.”

Michal added that the decision had been made to “reduce the risks to our people and national security”.



Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said that the border closure will come into effect on December 1.

Eight Latvian nationals were arrested in connection with the Thereod Systems break-in attempt.



The group was aiming to cause an explosion and set the company’s property in in Viimsi, north of Tallinn, on fire.

Thereod produces tech and weapons such as long-range reconnaissance and attack drones.

The UAV manufacturer bolsters Ukraine‘s strike missions deep within Russia.



Estonia’s spooks said the attack was carried out on the orders of Russia’s military intelligence service, the GRU.

It is the second attempted arson attack on an Estonian defence company since August, when Tallinn-based Milrem Robotics was targeted.

Michal said he has instructed Minister of the Interior Igor Taro to “prepare the necessary steps” for the border closure.

He said: “We know that Russian intelligence services exploit border crossings to exert influence over people and we must be prepared to reduce the risks we face.”

The PM added that Russia aiming to “make us afraid, make us hesitate and weaken our support for Ukraine,” before adding: “Estonia’s response is the opposite.”



“Estonia is safe and secure,” he continued.

“Our state institutions are vigilant, and our people and businesses know how to respond. We will not be intimidated.”

Estonia has three open border crossings with Russia in Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula, which admit pedestrians and freight.

They operate 12 hours a day from 7am to 7pm.

The Narva crossing gets particularly busy during the summer and New Year period.



It is one of the only land crossings still open from Europe to Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The government will discuss in the coming days whether the decision will be temporary or indefinite, said Taro.

Estonian residents and truck drivers who have traveled to Russia will be able to return home over the next fortnight.

News.title: Iran launches missile and drone strike on US military base in Bahrain amid rising tensions in Middle East
News.content:
Next

IRAN fired attack drones at a US military base in Bahrain overnight amid uncertainty over fruitless peace talks.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps boasted of a “decisive and crushing response to hostile US actions”, despite six drones being shot down.



Tehran had been targeting an air-defence radar at the Riffa helicopter base but the Bahraini military said it had destroyed the threats “before they reached their target.

Sirens rang out across the Gulf kingdom as authorities urged residents in the capital, Manama, to seek shelter in several social media posts.



“Danger alert…the Ministry of Interior calls on citizens and residents to remain calm,” the Bahrain ministry wrote on X.

“Head to the nearest safe location, and follow the news through official channels to ensure public safety.”

Explosions were reportedly heard around 4am local time, with a second foray coming at 6.30am.

Iran has now attacked Bahrain twice in three days, with the country’s military blasting its “systematic hostile approach” towards the kingdom.

The energy-rich nation has borne the brunt of Iranian attacks throughout the nine-month war.

Despite a relative lull in fighting, the US and Iran are still locking horns in the Strait of Hormuz .



The vitay waterway – which around a fifth of the world’s oil travels through – has been chocked off for most of the year, sending fuel costs soaring.

There has been no breakthrough in talks since the warring nations signed a flimsy memorandum of understanding in June either.

Donald Trump was said to be mulling a renewed campaign after the midterms, but talk of more strikes have died down since.



The US president reportedly told senior advisers that he might hold off if Iran and their Houthi allies refrain from launching their own strikes.

Trump’s defeat in the midterm has been blamed on the Iran war, as months of negotiations since the April ceasefire have failed to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz for trade.

He is due to discuss the war when he meets Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping for an unprecedented three-way summit in Shenzen on Thursday.

In the wake of the election bloodbath, Trump ordered vice president JD Vance to shift his attention away from securing peace with Tehran.

Trump said in a Truth Social post: “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed.



“We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Earlier in the week, the US carried out strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island in the waterway.

Officials described the attacks as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to the IRGC firing on US aircraft.

News.title: Sinister army of gun-toting robot DOGS unleashed in gang-torn El Salvador to take back stadium’s control in major op
News.content:
Next

GUN-wielding robot dogs have been unleashed in a major military operation to seize a gang-controlled stadium.

El Salvador’s military and Haitian forces deployed the cyber-canines in a joint operation to reclaim the Sylvio Cator Stadium in Haiti from gang control.



Footage shows the mechanical pups navigating hallways and traversing stairs with a automatic weapon’s strapped to their backs.

El Salvador President Nayib Bukele said “several human skulls” were found inside the stadium in the operation.



Sinister images show a human skull and cross bones found on the dusty floor.

He said: “We will now establish an operational base at the stadium so we can continue advancing deeper into territory controlled by the gangs.

“We now have the upper hand on the ground. I firmly demand that all gang members leave the area before the offensive begins.

“Those who choose to stay and fight our forces will have to face the consequences.”



The joint-forces successfully pushed gangs out of Haiti‘s national football stadium in Port-au-Prince and locked down the area.

It’s unclear exactly how the robots assisted in the operation.

Cracking down on gangs has been a feature of Bukele’s presidency in El Salvador since he took office in 2019.



Chaos has run rampant in Haiti since 2018 with widespread gang violence bringing the country to it’s knees.

A small number of Salvadoran troops had been stationed in Haiti since the beginning of 2025, in an attempt to curb gang influence.

Their military presence is sanctioned by the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) which was established to help Haitian authorities reclaim their cities.

But on October 18, Haitian gangs ambushed four Salvadoran technicians attached to the GSF and they have since not been found.

Following the incident, Bukele has expanded El Salvador’s military presence in the country, deploying over 2,000 troops within weeks.



The UN found that between July and September of this year, at least 1,167 people were killed.

The leader recently announced a separate joint taskforce win where they reportedly “destroyed” a gang HQ.

The house was blown to pieces in a devastating airstrike after Bukele crowdsourced its location on social media.

Dramatic footage shows two attack helicopters unleashing hell on the compound with a barrage of missiles, triggering a series of massive blasts.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Videos of the deadly raid were triumphantly shared on social media by Nayib Bukele, the hardline president of El Salvador and self-styled “world’s coolest dictator”.



He said: “We kept our promise…We destroyed Lanmo San Jou’s house and the 400 Mawozo gang’s headquarters.”

News.title: The world’s most extreme body modification fans – from ‘genderless reptile’ and ‘dark barbie’ to man with giant tusks
News.content:
MOD ROCKERS The world’s most extreme body modification fans – from ‘genderless reptile’ and ‘dark barbie’ to man with giant tusks







Next

THE world’s most extreme body modification fans are determined to completely transform their appearance.

From the “genderless reptile” and “dark Barbie” to a man with giant tusks, meet the people with the most extreme looks.



Tiamat Legion Medusa, 60, has spent at least £61,000 on more than 20 procedures over two decades including castration, ear removal, tongue splitting and 18 horn implants.

Their goal is to become a “human dragon” and they are far from finished – with upcoming plans to remove their six remaining teeth in order to get a full set of dental implants designed to look like dragon’s teeth.



Tiamat also has reshaped their nose, inspired by Harry Potter character Voldemort and had the whites of both eyes permanently stained green.

They said: “I believe that I am a real and true life reptoid, a half-human/half-reptilian creature.

“I can deal with being part human, just as long as I am also part reptilian because, with my being a transspecies, no longer being ‘just human’ gives me a peace that passes all understanding.”

Tiamat hopes the full transformation to be complete by 2025 as the pre-op transexual plans a penis removal, teeth removal and more tattoos to fully morph from human to reptilian.



The 60-year-old who was born Richard Hernandez, previously explained how they was abandoned in the woods as a child and survived child abuse, self-harm and AIDs before finding happiness.

Meanwhile, Orc, 41, has tattooed roughly 80 percent of his body and has also just invested £400 to get two giant fake teeth fitted into his mouth.



Rico Ledesma, from Iguatemi, Brazil admits he got his first tattoo when he was just 15, and his first modification at 35.

Orc has since gone on to get eight subdermal piercings (placed under the skin), his tongue split and his eyeballs tattooed.

Despite his unique appearance, the artist insists he is just trying to be himself.

He said: “I am trying to be myself, these are just my ideas, my inspirations coming from the heart.”

DARK BARBIE

Aydin Mod, 20, from Rome, was only 11 years old when she started body modifications by piercing her face with a needle in her bathroom.



She has now spent over $5,000 on her transformations, including tattooing her eyeballs and face, and getting labia implants – which required her vagina to be stretched.

The 20-year-old’s ultimate goal is to become a “body modification Barbie”.

She said: “I don’t think I’ll ever stop modifying myself, I want to cover my whole body with tattoos for sure, more piercings, permanent metal teeth which I’m currently working on.

“I’ll probably tattoo my eyes again to have them more black and recently I started looking for more common surgeries as well.

“The only person I have to please is myself. For example, people call me ‘ugly’ but I don’t even consider it an insult, to be honest.”



Another mod fan, Raiden Dos Caras, 24, from Colombia, South America, has undergone over 20 surgeries to change his body in an attempt to become the most modified person in Latin America.

The dad-of-one started aged just 12 years old when he had his first-ever tattoo and has had so much work done over the years that he has lost track of how much he has spent on his transformation but estimates it has cost him £12,000.

The young dad has so far had his ears and nose cut off, installed implants in his skull, and undergone scarification branding.

Of his most difficult surgery – the nose removal – Raiden said: “It was very painful and I felt a lot of discomfort.

“Since I’ve had so many surgeries, the anaesthesia doesn’t have the same strength anymore, so I feel a lot of pain.



“Despite this being one of my most painful procedures, I think the duplications of the horns in my forehead comes close.”

HUMAN SATAN

Michel Faro do Prado, 44, from Praia Grande coast, in São Paulo, Brazil has been dubbed the human “Satan” after undergoing a number of body modifications.

The 45-year-old has even chopped off one of his fingers to make himself look more like an alien.

Michel, who has worked as a tattoo artist for 25 years, said he wants to look as sinister as possible, and has even gone to a dentist to shape his teeth into arches with plans to coat them entirely in metal.

Michel claims to have a high pain tolerance and said he doesn’t mind enduring more pain to achieve the body he desires.



He said: “Actually I have good resistance to pain, I don’t think anything is so painful, I suffer a lot more in the post-procedures than at the time,

“And the truth is that there are changes that without anesthesia would be almost impossible to be done, I would love not to feel any pain.

“But if I have to feel pain, to achieve what I want, for sure I will face it!”

After more than 60 procedures, Michel has around 85 per cent of his body covered in ink and plans to win the Guinness World Record for the planet’s most modified man.

News.title: Brutal murder, warring gangs and explosive riots… the dark side of Beyonce’s favourite part of London
News.content:
Next

NORTH London is no stranger to A-listers. Harry Styles has been spotted picnicking on Hampstead Heath and Tom Hiddleston calls Kentish Town home.

But this week, it was Tottenham, a part of London that’s made headlines for riots and knife crime, that got a shout-out from Beyoncé.



The singer played six sold-out Cowboy Carter shows at Spurs’ stadium in June 2025, drawing more than 275,000 fans.

“One of my favourite things about London is the drive to Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and passing through Seven Sisters,” she told i-D.



She loves the barber shops, the restaurants and seeing families out with their kids.

And she’s put her money where her mouth is. In 2023, her BeyGOOD foundation gave £8,000 to Chuku’s, a Nigerian tapas restaurant run by a brother and sister on Tottenham High Road.

Outside the Tube, red buses crawl past pound shops, vape shops and takeaways. The old Ward’s department store still stands empty on the corner.

When we told greengrocer Sam Grainger, 31, about Beyoncé’s soft spot for Tottenham, he cracked up.



“She’s having a laugh, isn’t she? She’s telling fibs,” said the Spurs season ticket holder, packing away a customer’s oranges.

Pointing to the High Road, he added: “Along here can’t be her favourite place in London. There are definitely pockets of trouble here, like everywhere I suppose, and it has definitely changed in the last few years.”

Barista Maria Vassalo, 22, has lived in North London all her life. She was making a cappuccino when we told her what Beyoncé had said about Tottenham. She shook her head, then laughed.



“She doesn’t see the real Tottenham though, does she? I doubt she even gets out the car when she is playing these shows. There are so many problems with robberies recently and crime from gangs in the area.

“I have been moving further and further away from here because it is just getting worse. A couple of weeks ago outside the shop here I saw a bike pull up and snatch a phone out of this woman’s hand. It was in the morning, in broad daylight, and that is not uncommon.”

On November 2, just nine days before Beyoncé’s interview came out, the Met made phone snatching on Tottenham High Road a local priority. Officers had warned of a rise near Seven Sisters and said their response included bike patrols.

In September, police recorded 12 thefts from the person and 31 reports of antisocial behaviour across the Seven Sisters policing area.

Across London, phone theft and robbery fell by about a fifth in the first eight months of the year. In September, the Met arrested more than 700 people in a month-long crackdown. Commander Andy Featherstone said officers had targeted “every stage of the organised criminal chain, including street thieves, handlers and exporters”.



The Met is also targeting knife crime and antisocial behaviour on Steele Road and drug dealing around Fairweather Close.

Further up the High Road, Sheryl Wilkins, 39, was found dead behind a wall by the B&M car park in August 2025. Her killer, Simon Levy, was told this August he would spend the rest of his life in prison.

In August 2011, buildings on Tottenham High Road went up in flames hours after a peaceful protest outside the police station over the fatal police shooting of Mark Duggan. Within days, rioting had spread to other cities in England.



Shop worker Servgi Mercelli, 25, says she’s seen more officers around lately.

She said: “You do get some problems around here at night. Young people hang around outside the shop drinking and being loud, but they do move on and there is definitely a bigger police presence around here recently.

“The people see a different Tottenham when the big events are on. It’s a completely different vibe. They just come in for the day, and everyone is here for nice time.”

On a big night at Spurs, there are 60 per cent more people on the High Road, according to Haringey Council. City Hall looked at one of Beyoncé’s 2023 Renaissance shows and found that spending in the area at its busiest was about a third higher than at the peak of an afternoon NFL game.

Spurs opened their £1billion stadium in 2019. They can now stage up to 30 major non-football events a year, up from 16. In 2024/25, when the stadium hosted Beyoncé’s Cowboy Carter shows, non-football events brought in £32.5million for the club.



A study commissioned by Spurs put the club’s contribution to Haringey’s economy at £296million in 2021/22. That’s across the whole borough. In Northumberland Park, the ward around the stadium, a study by the charity Place Matters put child poverty at 27 per cent.

In September, the Haringey Greens called for Spurs to put around 0.1 per cent of their turnover into a community fund. The party said people living near the ground had to deal with road closures and disruption to public transport.



A Haringey Green Party spokesperson told City AM: “The record-breaking events it hosts seem to be a good deal for Spurs, but a bad deal for Tottenham.”

Spurs said it had invested more than £1.2billion in the stadium and surrounding area, including new affordable homes, a primary school and improvements to local infrastructure.

Servgi has noticed changes away from the stadium too. “The area has changed as well. With the developments in Tottenham Hale, there is definitely richer people starting to move in.”

The typical home in Tottenham Hale now sells for £450,000, up from £355,000 a decade ago.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

At Holcombe Market, fishmonger Jim has been trading for 35 years. He was glad to hear what Beyoncé had to say.



“There have always been bits of trouble along here but it is definitely getting better, so it is nice for a famous person to put us on the map.”

News.title: Estonia to shut Russian border with Putin 'plotting NATO attack'
News.content:
Estonia to shut Russian border with Putin 'plotting NATO attack'

Prime minister Kristen Michal also warned that 'necessary steps' should be taken to close Estonia's eastern border with Russia after an attempted arson attack

View Image The measure will come into force on December 1 (Image: Getty Images)

Estonia is set to close all of its border crossing points with Russia in days after a sabotage attack ordered by the Kremlin.

‌



The measure will come into force on December 1 and was announced this afternoon by Estonian foreign affairs minister Margus Tshanka. Prime minister Kristen Michal also warned that "necessary steps" should be taken to close Estonia's eastern border after an attempted arson attack this morning.

Foreign affairs minister Margus Tshanka warned Russia to "understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences". He explained that closing the Baltic country's borders with Russia will reduce the Kremlin's ability "to conduct hostile activities in Estonia".

The minister added that he also informed Finland, Latvia and Lithuania about the decision. Posting on X, Mr Tshanka said: "Following clear evidence that Russia’s military intelligence service GRU, ordered a sabotage attack against an Estonian defence industry company, Estonia will close all Estonian-Russian border crossing points as of 1 December. Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences.

"Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered. Closing the border crossings will reduce Russia’s ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia and strengthen our efforts to prevent sanctions circumvention.

"I have informed my Finnish, Latvian, and Lithuanian counterparts of this decision."

News.title: Top Hamas commander who oversaw October 7 massacre killed in Israeli air strike
News.content:
Top Hamas commander who oversaw October 7 massacre killed in Israeli air strike

Samir Mahmoud Abu Younis, a senior Hamas commander, who helped lead the October 7, 2023 massacre in southern Israel, has been killed by an Israeli airstrike

View 4 Images (Image: @IDF/X)

A top Hamas commander who helped carry out the October 7, 2023 massacre in Israel had been killed in an airstrike.

‌



‌



Samir Mahmoud Abu Younis, commander of the Rafah Brigade, died in Al-Mawasi in the southern Gaza Strip during an Israeli strike today (Sunday), says Hamas's Al-Qassam Brigades military wing.

‌



The Israeli military also confirmed it had killed the Hamas commander just after midnight Saturday, saying that Abu Younis had been directing plans "to advance and carry out terror attacks". Two months earlier, his predecessor in the role, Nael ⁠Abu Obeid, was also killed in an Israeli strike.

‌



View 4 Images Mourners at the funeral of Samir Abu Younis (Image: Tariq Mohammad/APAImages/Shutterstock)

Explosion rocks Christmas market in Belgium as people burned and emergency crews swarm READ MORE :

Medics in Gaza others were also injured in the strike which killed Abu Younis in the street in the Mawasi area of the city of Khan Younis.

Abu Younis joined Hamas' armed wing in 1991 and had ‌held several senior operational roles in Rafah before becoming commander of the brigade, Hamas said.

‌



A Hamas statement said a funeral would be held for him today.

View 4 Images Samir Abu Younis died in the street during an airstrike (Image: X)

‌



Al-Qassam Brigades, the military wing of Hamas, wrote on Telegram that Younis had "participated in numerous high-profile operations and resisted enemy incursions". It stated that he was "one of the most important commanders involved in planning and overseeing the 7 October attack".

The attack by Hamas in southern Israel on October 7, 2023, led to the killing of around 1,200 people and another 251 people were taken hostage, triggered the most recent war in Gaza.

‌



Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in the Gaza Strip, the health ministry says.

View 4 Images Mourners carried the body of Abu Younis during the funeral today (Image: Tariq Mohammad/APAImages/Shutterstock)

‌



A message from the Israeli Defence Force also told of Abu Younis' role in the October 7 attack in a post on X saying that he had been killed.

It stated: "ELIMINATED: Samir Mahmoud Hassan Abu Younis, Commander of Hamas’ Rafah Brigade, in a strike in southern Gaza overnight. Abu Younis was appointed commander of the brigade approximately 2 months ago, following the elimination of his predecessor.

Article continues below

"He previously served as the brigade’s deputy commander and commander of the Tel al-Sultan Battalion. He directed terror attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops and worked to restore Hamas’ military capabilities. The terrorist was eliminated in order to remove the threat he posed."

Although a ceasefire in Gaza went into effect in October 2025 and halted major fighting, Israeli strikes have continued.

News.title: ANDY BURNHAM: 'EU deal can get Britain back on positive path and cut cost of living - I will take it'
News.content:
In Makerfield, my constituency, two-thirds of people voted to leave the EU.

I understood why back then - and still do now. Westminster and Brussels combined weren’t delivering for them. Industrial decline had stripped away good jobs. Cuts were hitting harder than elsewhere. People felt ignored by the powers-that-be.

The referendum gave voters a chance to send a message and demand change. Ten years on, it is clear that the change promised by the promoters of Brexit has not materialised. Far from taking back control, we are in a weaker position on immigration. The small boats crisis has reached our shores. Household bills and business costs have been soaring.

OnlyFans livestreaming must be banned say MPs in 'e-pimps' warning READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham has said closer ties with the UK can be hugely beneficial for the UK (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

‌



The truth is Britain ended up with a much harder Brexit than the one promised at the referendum. Rather than back Theresa May’s deal, Boris Johnson burnt our bridges. His Tory Brexit deal has done more harm than good.

I am clear: the status quo is not good enough for Britain. It is my job to look honestly at the evidence and act in Britain’s national interest. I will not shirk that responsibility.

The truth is we can’t get Britain back to where we all want it to be without sorting out our relationship with our closest neighbours. The red lines set out in Labour’s manifesto will remain.

This means no return to the Customs Union, Single Market or freedom of movement in this Parliament. However, the UK-EU Summit this week is not about these issues. It is about getting closer to Europe again and working constructively to improve a bad Brexit deal.

‌



Any deal I seek to agree in Brussels must first pass what I call the Makerfield test: will it make life better for people in the parts of Britain that have felt forgotten?

On Friday, there is a chance of reaching a deal that helps ease the cost-of-living crisis. By making it easier to move food between Britain and the EU, we can cut costs for businesses and help bring down the price of food.

Don’t just take my word for it - listen to what the M&S food boss believes the proposed deal can achieve: “fresher food and fuller shelves for our customers, lifting the pressure on the price of the weekly shop.”

It will also spare our steel, car and aluminium industries extra taxes, protecting jobs and the communities that depend on them. It will open the door to greater collaboration with our EU partners on tackling illegal immigration and small boat crossings, and further talks on lower electricity prices.

‌



Does this pass the Makerfield test? Absolutely. It is also consistent with what I said at the by-election. By delivering something much closer to what was promised at the time, it respects the 2016 vote.

The Tories have already said they will scrap any deal we secure. This is proof they haven’t changed under Kemi Badenoch. How can they turn their backs on lower food prices when families are struggling so much?

I will never do that. I will provide the leadership on this issue that they never can.

I am drawing a line under a decade of drift and division after Brexit. I am putting Britain back on a positive path and working to get our economy growing. This Friday I can take the biggest step yet down that path - and I am determined to take it.

News.title: Strictly's Dianne Buswell shares 'unbearable pain' that left her fearing for dance career
News.content:
Strictly's Dianne Buswell shares 'unbearable pain' that left her fearing for dance career

Strictly Come Dancing star Dianne Buswell shared the "unbearable pain" she felt after giving birth, claiming it left her fearing "will I ever be able to dance again?"

View 4 Images Dianne Buswell opened up on "unbearable pain" (Image: diannebuswell/Instagram)

Pro dancer Dianne Buswell has opened up about the "unbearable pain" she felt that left her fearing "will I ever be able to dance again?" The Strictly Come Dancing star, who gave birth to her first baby in March this year, is dancing with TV presenter Will Best in the current series.

‌



‌



Dianne, 37, welcomed son Bowden Mark Richard Sugg with former Strictly partner, Joe Sugg. She had originally hoped for a natural birth but her plan took an unexpected turn, eventually requiring an emergency caesarean section before the child was born on March 16.

‌



The worst was yet to come, though. The professional dancer faced "unbearable pain" during her recovery, and she even feared whether she would be able to dance again.

‌



Speaking to The Human Edge podcast, Dianne said: "You've got on top of pain, on top of having this newborn and wanting to give it all your attention, but also you can't even get out of bed. To even sit up is a real mission.

View 4 Images Dianne gave birth earlier this year (Image: PA)

"There was one night I had to go to the toilet in the middle of the night and I just burst into tears because the pain of just sitting up to manoeuvre myself out of bed was just unbearable. I was like: 'How am I going to recover and will I ever be able to dance again?' That was my initial thoughts. It was like this absolutely tore through my muscles.

‌



"I'm never going to be able to dance again. I've lost all mobility in my legs. I've lost my core strength. It was it was very intense."

Dianne, whose son is now eight months old, did eventually regain her strength and was paired with TV presenter Will Best, most famous for presenting the rebooted Big Brother on ITV.

‌



View 4 Images Dianne is competing with Will Best in this year's competition (Image: Guy Levy/BBC/Press Association)

The Australian dancer joined Strictly in 2017 and has proved successful during almost a decade on the show. She famously won the coveted Glitterball with blind comedian Chris McCausland in 2024.

‌



Dianne has also come second twice - once with her now partner, YouTuber Joe Sugg, and also with actor and model Bobby Brazier.

The dancer has also had the misfortune of her celebrity partner twice pulling out through illness and injury - comedian Robert Webb and Neighbours actor Stefan Dennis, who she competed with during her pregnancy.

‌



View 4 Images Joe Sugg and Diane welcomed their son in March (Image: PA)

Dianne said that the first couple of weeks after giving birth were the toughest, then she "started to feel so much better every day".

News.title: Kidnapping suspect killed by cops in New York street after screams of 'let me go' heard
News.content:
Kidnapping suspect killed by cops in New York street after screams of 'let me go' heard

A man accused of kidnapping a small girl has been shot and killed in the middle of a grid-locked highway in Coney Island, New York

View 2 Images The shooting followed a chaotic chase on the streets of New York (Image: NBC New York)

A suspected kidnapper has been shot and killed by police in the middle of a grid-locked New York street after a dramatic chase.

‌



‌



At least two 911 calls were made to the NYPD just before 7:30pm local time in Coney Island on Saturday with witnesses saying they had heard a screaming girl inside a white van.

‌



A woman told officers she heard the girl screaming "Let me go!" several times, NYPD Assistant Chief Charles Minch, Commanding Officer of Patrol Borough Brooklyn South, said at a press conference.

‌

A male caller reported seeing a white van with "a girl kicking and screaming in there," he added. As nearby officers spotted the suspected vehicle, they approached and a chaotic chase ensued.

As nearby officers spotted the suspected vehicle, they approached and a chaotic chase ensued.

‌



View 2 Images The suspected kidnapper was shot dead on a Coney Island highway (Image: PIX 11 News)

The driver raced off, mounting a pavement and prompting officers to call for back up on their radios, cops said after the incident.

‌



"And the driver continued to ram nearby vehicles. Officers then discharged their firearms and struck the driver," Minch said.

CPR was performed at the scene and the driver was taken to hospital where he was pronounced dead.

‌



He has not been publicly identified and cops said that no child was found in the back of the vehicle. However, police said an adult woman had been screaming in the van ad had exited before officers initially approached.

As the incident remains under investigation, officials believe the pair were having a domestic dispute which prompted her screaming.

The man was wanted last month for "unlawful imprisonment" and faced allegations of domestic assault earlier this month, Minch said.

News.title: Parents of kids with childhood dementia plead for UK treatment and funding - 'We don't have time to wait'
News.content:
Parents of kids with childhood dementia plead for UK treatment and funding - 'We don't have time to wait'

EXCLUSIVE: Some families are searching for a place on a clinical trial while others face raising millions for treatment abroad. Parents told the Mirror they're urging to government to act now

View 7 Images The families of Cody, Tate, Leni and Kole are calling for better support after diagnosis and help accessing treatment (Image: Supplied)

Parents of children with childhood dementia are racing against time to save their children’s lives as they make a desperate appeal for the Government to fund research and help them access treatment in the UK.

‌



‌



Ahead of World Sanfilippo Awareness Day on 16 November, families spoke to the Mirror about why they want childhood dementia to be recognised in Government policy. They fear their children “don’t have time to wait”.

‌



Georgia Nonas, 29, launched a petition in an urgent bid for the Government to fund FAYUVI (rebisufligene etisparvovec-hopf), which was approved in the US in September. Her son Cody Carroll, 9, was three when he was diagnosed with type A Sanfilippo but was given little hope when no treatment was available. Now, with the recent news of approval, she is fighting to save her son’s life.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 7 Images Georgia launched a petition for children diagnosed with type A Sanfilippo syndrome (Image: Supplied)

David Cameron says Alzheimer's made his mother beg sister to kill her in NHS drugs plea READ MORE :

In her appeal to the Government, she told the Mirror: “The petition was a way to say please take notice of us, we’re here and we need help. These children don’t have time to wait. A lot of us parents are struggling because we have all this hope and campaigning to get it approved, but once it’s approved, you’re in limbo because no one knows how to go at it. You feel some of that hope is lost because where you live is determining if these children are going to live or die.”

‌



Sanfilippo syndrome is a rare inherited disorder that mainly affects the brain and nervous system. It is better known as childhood dementia and can gradually take away skills such as speaking, walking and eating independently. Life expectancy varies but some children aren't expected to live past their teens while people with slower-progressing forms can live into adulthood.

Researchers estimated that 204 people in the UK die from conditions that cause childhood dementia per year, similar in scale to 240 cancer deaths recorded among UK children aged 0-14.

‌



Parents' shock at lack of support

Many parents of children with Sanfilippo syndrome have spoken of their shock at how little support they were offered after diagnosis. Tammy McDaid’s son Tate Flaherty, 5, who has type A, was diagnosed aged four following what she called a “yo-yo” journey. She said: “The diagnosis meeting itself felt very unfinished because there was nothing other than ‘this is what your child has, come back when they start deteriorating’.”

Childhood dementia was first mentioned to Tammy, 34, in March 2024. She said doctors ruled out Sanfilippo syndrome 13 months later, in April 2025, but Tate was officially diagnosed in September 2025. She has since applied for several trials. She said: “One of the trials emailed me to say they only take under fives and Tate had only just turned five weeks prior. I just thought, if he had been diagnosed initially when it was mentioned, we don’t know what the position could have been with the trials.”

‌



Tammy, from Swansea, said an MDT meeting had not happened until May 2026, after she broke down in a cardiology meeting. She said: “I remember breaking down in that meeting and just saying, ‘Where is my team? I’m so worried about his eating, but I can’t get through to anyone who will talk to me.’ How long would I have been left to it if I hadn’t cried in the appointment?”

View 7 Images An author created the children's book 'Saving Leni' to help people understand childhood dementia (Image: Supplied)

‌



'We were told there's no treatment, no cure, go home and love your child'

Emily, 34, and Gus Forrester’s daughter Leni, 3, was diagnosed with type B days before her second birthday. Gus, 36, described what the healthcare providers told them at the time. He said: “We were told at the time there’s no treatment, no cure, go home and love your child. It’s pretty haunting.” Emily added: “It’s very isolating. We just felt we were completely on our own. It was a very dark time.”

Leni has type B, which currently has no approved cure or disease-modifying treatment anywhere in the world. However, clinical trials are underway in the UK and the US. Emily, from Sevenoaks, Kent, said: “I remember saying at the time, ‘You’re getting this diagnosis that your child has a terminal condition, but you might have another ten to fifteen years of watching them deteriorate.’ I can’t imagine a worse diagnosis to receive as a parent. Everything that we now do as a family is shaped around this awful condition.”

‌



View 7 Images Kole Pearson pictured with his family (Image: Supplied)

'I will never stop advocating for my child'

At the moment many parents of children with type A have set their sights on the FDA-approved gene therapy, Fayuvi. However, the cost is $3.95million (approximately £2.95million). Tammy and Georgia have started fundraising for the treatment. Among those also fundraising are parents Bethany Gordon, 33, and Daniel Pearson, 40, whose two-year-old son Kole Pearson was diagnosed with type A in April this year, making him the youngest in the UK currently diagnosed.

‌



Speaking on fundraising, Bethany, from Ellesmere Port, said: “We have raised over £100,000, but it took a lot of effort to get there and I feel like my mental health is now starting to suffer. As well as trying to be a mum-of-three, I’m now doing things that are completely out of my comfort zone. But I won’t stop and I will never ever stop when it comes to Kole, but it’s really a heavy diagnosis to carry. My life is being turned upside down because I’ve got to advocate for my child in order to save him.”

Georgia launched her fundraiser just under a year ago after years of being told there was no treatment available for Cody. She now hopes to get him to the US for treatment. She said: “I was under the impression that there was nothing we could do and then we got this spark of hope with the new treatment coming out, and then all of a sudden you’re back to square one because you can’t get there. It’s like these highs and lows that are just quite difficult to navigate.”

‌



As well as fundraiser and petition, Georgia has also wrote and illustrated a book to help explain Sanfilippo syndrome to children, with the profit going towards Cody's treatment. You can support here

View 7 Images Tate Flaherty was four when he was diagnosed with Sanfilippo syndrome type A (Image: Supplied)

‌



Tammy has since raised over £200,000 on her fundraiser for Tate to also receive the treatment. She said: “We have to raise this money now and it seems like an impossible task. I’ve probably struggled more in the last couple of months than I have in the past year. I worked out the other day that I’d need around £20,000 a day donated in order to get him treatment next summer. It just seems like an awful amount of money.”

She added: “I think I speak for most type A parents where it’s lovely seeing children receive the treatment in the US, but it’s also extremely hard knowing that where our children were born they don’t have that access.”

‌



As Leni’s parents wait to hear whether she secures a place in one of the upcoming UK clinical trials, they have fundraised endlessly and raised over £500,000. Emily said: “Leni is the perfect candidate for trial because she’s still so young, so we were like, we can either sit back and be sad or we can fight for for Leni’s life, and we decided to do the latter. We wanted to look back and know that we did literally everything we could to save our little girl, so we launched the campaign.”

'We have to go to medical appointments and explain our child's condition'

Finding a trial or treatment is only one part of what the parents have to navigate. Some parents have had to explain the syndrome to healthcare staff at their children’s appointments. Gus said: “We’re having to go to medical appointments as the expert and teach some of the clinicians about the condition, about what’s normal, what’s not normal.

‌



“It’s been hugely consuming, but we found ourselves wanting to try and drive as much impact and benefit not just for Leni but for everyone else. There are families that have been fighting for years who have maybe run out of steam.”

View 7 Images Emily and Gus describe Leni as funny, cheeky and full of energy (Image: Supplied)

‌



An NHS spokesperson said: “The NHS carries out over 300,000 tests for rare and inherited diseases, including Sanfilippo syndrome, every year, and provides specialist support at eight centres across England. We are continuing to invest in education and training for NHS staff so that rare conditions can be recognised and treated sooner, with clinicians in the eight specialist centres also supported by the British Inherited Metabolic Diseases Group.”

The UK recently formally accepted the US approved therapy to begin reviewing the medication for UK licensing. However the MPS Society confirmed with Bethany, the MHRA are set to meet in August 2027 to consider the FDA-approved drug for use in the UK. But the meeting does not mean the drug will be approved in the NHS.

‌



Bethany said: “The difference between August 11th for us and tomorrow is life or death. If we get to August and they then decide we’ll approve this treatment but Kole has regressed to the point that he can’t receive the treatment - there is going to be someone to blame and I will then be looking for someone to blame because my child shouldn’t have to wait for a year for a decision to be made whether they’re going to save his life or not.”

'We need to invest in childhood dementia - system has left my child to die'

The families are also fighting for the Government to recognise childhood dementia in its plans for dementia research. In October, the Prime Minister announced a £48million partnership to speed up dementia research, including £33million in Government funding. However, the announcement made no mention of childhood dementia.

‌



Tammy said: “If they can invest in adult dementia, they should be able to invest the same amount into childhood dementia. That would make such a difference in our world. It shouldn’t take for the parents to be shouting. Why should we as parents have to when we’re trying to enjoy the time that we do have with our children? The system is now failing my child because they are essentially leaving him to die.”

View 7 Images The family have raised more than £100,000 in the hope of securing treatment for Kole (Image: Supplied)

‌



Gus described feeling “stonewalled” by the Department of Health and Social Care. He said: “The community has been ignored for long enough. We’re not the first parents to come along and try to advocate for our children. Why are these children not being prioritised? Andy Burnham has just announced 48 million pounds to defeat dementia but childhood dementia doesn’t even feature in that campaign. Why is an adult with dementia any more important than a child with dementia? These children need research, funding, awareness and they need treatment, and they don’t have time to wait.”

Emily added: “It could take a year for approval to reach the UK, but that could cost a child their lives, or the ability to talk. We need to preserve what skills they have. It’s a race against time for all of us families.”

Article continues below

A Department of Health and Social Care Spokesperson said: “Neurodegenerative conditions such as Sanfilippo syndrome have a devastating impact. We are making sure patients with rare diseases get a definite diagnosis faster, while improving access to specialist care, treatment and drugs.”

You can support the families through the fundraisers for Cody, Tate, Leni and Kole. To sign the petition, click here.

News.title: Alan Milburn warns 'no magic wand' to solving Neets crisis ahead of 'watershed' report
News.content:
Alan Milburn warns 'no magic wand' to solving Neets crisis ahead of 'watershed' report

Former Health Secretary Alan Milburn will this week unveil his long-awaited report into tackling Britain's 'Neets' crisis - a moment Andy Burnham has branded a 'watershed'

View 2 Images Alan Milburn's long-awaited report is set to be released this week

A former Health Secretary heading a major review into Britain's 'Neets' crisis has said it is fantasy to suggest it can be solved in two or three years.

‌



‌



Alan Milburn warned there is no "magic wand" to tackle the enormous number of 18-to-24 year olds who are not in employment, education or training (Neet). Mr Milburn, whose long-awaited report will be released this week, said that under his proposals the government will have a duty to provide opportunities - while young people must take them or face sanctions.

‌



He also said young people will "of course" lose out on benefits if his proposals are implemented. Mr Milburn told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: “This is a 10-year plan, and you've just got to be candid with people about this. Everybody thinks 'wave the magic wand, snap your fingers, and you can do it in two or three years'. I'm telling you, you can't."

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

Alan Milburn says Andy Burnham must make job or training offers for young people legal guarantee READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham has described Mr Milburn's report as a watershed (Image: Annabel Lee-Ellis/Press Association)

Under his proposals, he revealed, there will be an "opportunity guarantee" - with safeguards to prevent young people suing the government if they do not feel this has been delivered. He said: "We're calling it the opportunity guarantee, so there should be a guarantee for a young person because at the moment the only guarantee they've got is to a very simple thing, to get a benefit."

‌



He added: "So, in the end, in every welfare system in the world, there's always a backstop, there's always a sanction. And my view is very straightforward on this, most young people want to work. If you're giving them more opportunities, if you're giving them more support, which we should, then their obligation is to take up those opportunities. And if they don't, what isn't tolerable either for them or for the taxpayer is that they should be living a life on benefit, that's got to change."

Other proposals include moving some young people off some health-related benefits and onto a new "youth allowance" paid at the standard rate of Universal Credit. It comes as alarming figures revealed there are nearly one million 'Neets' in the UK.

‌



Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said a complete reset of the benefits system will be needed. He vowed any measures put forward will be a "different proposition" to the ill-fated plans torpedoed by backbenchers when Keir Starmer was PM.

The Cabinet minister said: "There will be people in the future who will not get what they would get today. When people come up for reassessment, they go on to a new system but, as I say, people are reassessed today under the current system."

‌



But he refused to say how much he wants to slash from the welfare bill by the next general election, stating: "Look, I can't say that - we uprate benefits every year, and I think it's important to keep people up with the cost of living. These are some of the poorest people in the country, and the best way to get the benefits bill down is with the long-term reset that we are talking about."

Andy Burnham has called Mr Milburn's politically sensitive report - commissioned under Mr Starmer - a "watershed" moment - but stopped short of promising to accept its recommendations in full.

Article continues below

Mr McFadden told Sky News: "It's a different proposition from last year, and I hope that Parliament views it in that light. We need a complete reset of the system in terms of what it offers young people to get these numbers."

News.title: Putin 'lifts ban on killing Zelensky' amid horror warning after Ukraine attacks
News.content:
Putin 'lifts ban on killing Zelensky' amid horror warning after Ukraine attacks

Russian officials have reportedly lifted an 'unofficial ban' on killing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and his top generals, following a high-stakes meeting with Vladimir Putin

View 2 Images Putin has reportedly lifted a ban on assassinating Zelensky (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

An 'unofficial ban' on Russia assassinating Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky as reportedly been lifted. Intelligence suggests Zelensky's top military commanders may also be in the crosshairs following a crucial meeting with Vladimir Putin.

‌



‌



Kyiv's sustained strikes on Russia's oil export terminals on the Baltic Sea are understood to have triggered the policy shift, Blokot reported.

‌



Sources indicate that, during a private meeting on Thursday, Moscow's security officials cautioned that the nation was haemorrhaging defence funds trying to counter Kyiv's drone attacks. The Leningrad region alone, where St Petersburg is situated, reportedly forked out close to the equivalent of $300 million on air defence systems.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

"It is pointless to fight the endless swarm of drones - it is necessary to destroy the very chain of decision-making," one Russian official reportedly warned, according to the outlet.

The New York Post reports that security officials determined they would prefer to eliminate the current leadership, including Zelensky, citing senior government sources.

‌



View 2 Images Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy (Image: Getty)

‌



"The destruction of other people's heating does not stop attacks on our refineries, because the people who give orders feel completely safe under the protection of Moscow's unspoken 'gentlemen's agreements' with the West," a Russian source said.

Officials reportedly indicated they could deploy heavy hypersonic weaponry to strike bunkers and motorcades transporting Ukrainian leaders and senior army commanders. This follows Putin issuing an ultimatum to Britain, insisting the UK relinquish its nuclear protection of European allies as part of a proposed agreement to bring the war in Ukraine to an end.

Article continues below

A document prepared by Russian negotiators outlines a series of sweeping conditions Moscow is seeking before it will agree to peace, including compelling Britain and France to withdraw their nuclear protection from other European nations.

The extraordinary demands, which would fundamentally alter Europe's security architecture, are detailed in a paper dated November 10 and obtained by The New York Times from a person involved in the negotiations.

News.title: Staggered age of consent to be discussed after Brand case, minister says
News.content:
A discussion over a staggered age of consent is to take place, the work and pensions secretary has said, as the government faces calls to change the law following the case against Russell Brand.

Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Pat McFadden said that "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men" have emerged this week.

A woman who alleges she was raped by jailed comedian Brand when she was 16 is now campaigning to see the law changed so that relationships between 16 and 17-year-olds and adults would be illegal.

Questions over a staggered age of consent have "been raised and will be discussed" McFadden said, adding: "[I] can't tell you what the conclusion of that would be, but the last week has certainly put that up in lights."

Adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds, under UK law.

Mia Latter, who has waived her right to anonymity, told the Sunday Times that she wants the age of consent to be staggered.

Latter is one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.

She was known by the pseudonym "Alice". Brand denied the allegations at the time and none of the six women were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.

At Southwark Crown Court on Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half-years imprisonment after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, involving four women between 2004 and 2009. He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.

Latter said she was 16 when she met the comedian, then 30. She told the Sunday Times: "I think people were so struck by my story because of the age difference and the clear imbalance [in power].

"I don't want to criminalise teenagers having sex with each other.

"If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to.

"But...if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offence."

Layla Stone, founder of the campaign group Close the Consent Gap, said bringing in a staggered age of consent was about addressing a "power imbalance" in relationships involving 16 and 17 year-olds and adults. She urged ministers to commit to such a change.

Stone, a child protection social worker, told the BBC that 16 and 17 year-olds were seen as children in "every single framework of the law" and "we don't believe [they are] old enough to consent to having sex with much older adults".

Close the Consent Gap is proposing that 16 year-olds would not be able to have a sexual relationship with anyone older than 19, and that someone aged 17 would be prohibited from a relationship with anyone older than 20.

Further allegations of sexual misconduct in the entertainment industry came in the same week Brand was convicted.

ITV News and the Guardian published a story alleging that comedian David Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

One woman said she now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour when he was a judge at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.

Walliams said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

The Metropolitan Police said on Friday it has launched an investigation into Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences", after the ITV News and the Guardian story. The Met said that the allegations it is investigating are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian but that it was "also proactively reviewing that reporting".

Speaking to Sky News, the work and pensions secretary said: "I do think that between Russell Brand, David Walliams, what's been put out there, people are looking at these issues in a new light."

News.title: Man and woman die and four arrested after police pursuit crash in Leeds
News.content:
Two people have been killed after their car was hit by a vehicle fleeing from police in Leeds.

West Yorkshire Police said it happened at 00:44 GMT, when a blue BMW 123D failed to stop for officers in Gelderd Road and then crashed into a white Volkswagen Scirocco.

The driver of the Volkswagen, a 22-year-old man, died at the scene. His passenger, a woman, 23, died later in hospital. Both were from York.

The occupants of the BMW, a 39-year-old man from Harrogate, two boys aged 16 and 17 and a 16-year-old girl, have been arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.

The 39-year-old is also being held on suspicion of driving while over the prescribed limit for cannabis, the force confirmed.

The teenagers in the BMW were taken to hospital for treatment to injuries that were not considered life-threatening.

A spokesperson for West Yorkshire Police said a referral had been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which confirmed it had started an investigation.

News.title: Ex-Met Police inspector lied about wife's death in Barbados hotel room, BBC learns
News.content:
An inquest in the UK later found that Rebekah's organs had been inexplicably "chopped up" into small pieces by a pathologist in Barbados.

This served no medical purpose and destroyed vital evidence, according to a UK pathologist who examined her body after it had been repatriated.

The inquest also established that key toxicology and histology tests - to look for signs of disease, injury or other changes in the body - were not conducted.

The coroner, Andrew Harris, said this raised the prospect of "deliberate concealment or obstruction of further investigation".

He also said that while bloodstains on bedclothes may be consistent with vomiting, he could not accept the cause of death determined by Barbadian authorities, aspiration pneumonitis - inflammation of the lungs - and delivered an open verdict.

He concluded that Rebekah's death likely involved intoxication and said unlawful killing could not be ruled out.

The inquest did not, however, consider Arter's alleged sexual exploitation of several other women whose cases he had investigated, to be within its scope.

Police in Barbados have previously said no marks of violence were found on Rebekah's body and there was nothing to suggest anything untoward - adding that they did not order toxicology tests because they believed she died from natural causes.

A week after Rebekah died, Arter flew back to the UK where he was arrested at Heathrow in connection with alleged sexual offences against another woman whose case he had investigated as a police officer in 2010. He was found dead in Wandsworth prison three days later.

In response to the BBC, Metropolitan Police Commander Simon Messinger said: "Our thoughts at this time remain with Rebekah Arter's family, who understandably have questions about the circumstances of her death.

"We would urge any victim survivors of rape and sexual offences - no matter how long ago a crime may have occurred - to reach out."

Elliot says his two young children will never know their grandmother.

"My daughter, my son - they're never gonna actually have any memories of her," he says.

"For the rest of my life, I'm never going to know how she's passed away."
