Sports.title: One for the World Cup? England's new-ball switch to Baker pays dividends
Sports.content:
As England impressively levelled their three-match ODI series against Australia with a 135-run win in Adelaide, might they have stumbled upon the perfect bowling formula with one eye on the 2027 Cricket World Cup?

Tom Banton (121 off 99 balls) was rightly named Player of the Match for his second ODI hundred that helped turn things round after a dismal defeat in Perth - from 131 all out to 355-6 in the space of 48 hours - but the bowling was equally impressive.

Image: England's Tom Banton celebrates his second ODI century against Australia in Adelaide

Gus Atkinson (4-28) claimed career-best ODI figures as he and Sonny Baker (1-45) helped set the tone early on by reducing Australia to 29-4 in the opening seven overs of their run-chase as they were ultimately bowled out for 220.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Australian cricketer Chadd Sayers, who was involved in the 'sandpapergate’ Test, believes everyone knew about it, stating there were numerous conversations about it at the time. Pictures courtesy of Sports Entertainment Network.

"The way England's bowlers attacked the first 10 overs, they didn't allow [Mitch] Marsh and [Travis] Head to get away, in terms of giving them any freebies," former England captain Sir Alastair Cook said on TNT Sports.

"They knew they'd come after them - Head hit a brilliant shot for six off a decent ball - but the way Atkinson and Baker bowled, they were made to work for their runs.

"I really liked how Baker got some movement out of the ball, that's his role in the side.

"You've got Archer and Atkinson who will hit the pitch hard - Archer, in this game, serving as the enforcer in the middle overs - so Baker using his swing up front was impressive.

"The [four] wickets early on made such a difference to the game. It was pretty much done early on, unless there was an extraordinary innings from one of the Aussies.

"Full credit to England for the way they adapted and used their bowlers in the right places."

Cook added: "Australia is a really hard place to go 1-0 down in any format. They're great front-runners, so to turn that round like they did after only 48 hours is absolutely superb.

"The leadership group should take a lot of credit for managing to get those players in the right frame of mind after the drubbing they got in Perth."

Baker-Archer switch grants 'England 'two bites at the cherry'

Baker - playing in just his fifth ODI - taking the new ball over Atkinson's usual accomplice, the more experienced Archer, was a bold move but one that paid off for England.

Image: England fast bowler Gus Atkinson took ODI career-best figures of 4-28 in Adelaide

Though Atkinson was the standout, Baker arguably deserved greater reward for his own probing opening spell, in which he dismissed Marsh (2) and had Josh Inglis dropped - Joe Root taking a stunning catch to dismiss the Australian skipper before he was then the guilty party in putting down Inglis.

"Baker's enthusiasm, you can tell he just loves playing cricket for England," former England wicketkeeper Matt Prior added on TNT Sports.

"I'm with Cooky. I'm really pleased that he was given the new ball, where he bowled full and tried to swing it.

"Brook has to take some credit as captain for making that decision."

England have 14 further ODIs scheduled ahead of the start of the 2027 Cricket World Cup in Africa in 11 months' time, and so might the Baker and Archer new-ball switch something they look to run with from here?

Image: Jofra Archer took 1-26 from 8.3 overs as he operated in a new role with the ball in the middle overs

"The change in using Jofra Archer through the middle [overs], I like that move," Australia batting consultant Mike Hussey told TNT Sports.

"It gives England two bites at the cherry. They get to attack with Baker and Atkinson at the start and, if things go well, they've got Archer to come in behind that and continue to build pressure.

"Even if things don't go well at the start, it's nice to know you've got someone of world-class quality to come in to arrest some of the momentum."

As for who has the edge going into Wednesday's series decider in Hobart (3.30am UK start time), Hussey fears the worst for Australia.

"England go into the final game with momentum because they've managed to turn things around [from Perth] straight away," he added.

"I think England will certainly take a lot of confidence away from this game. If they take the right attitude again into the final match in Hobart and start well, they'll be on their way towards a series win."

Sports.title: England level ODI series with Australia as Banton and Atkinson fire
Sports.content:
Tom Banton's second ODI hundred and Gus Atkinson's sizzling new-ball burst saw England thump Australia by 135 runs in Adelaide and set up a series decider in Hobart on Wednesday.

A touring side rolled for 131 in Friday's opener at Perth posted their highest ODI total in Australia, with a score of 355-6 underpinned by Banton's 121 from 99 balls and featuring fifties for Jordan Cox (67 off 49), Joe Root (62 off 68) and Will Jacks (54no off 40).

England lost their fourth wicket in the 35th over - Banton holing out immediately after back-to-back sixes - whereas Australia lost their fourth at the end of the seventh with just 29 runs on the board, before being dismissed for 220 in 44.3 overs with Atkinson claiming 4-28 and Jofra Archer (1-26) taking the final wicket.

Score summary - Australia vs England, second ODI, Adelaide Oval England 355-6 after 50 overs (put in to bat): Tom Banton (121 off 99 balls), Jordan Cox (67 off 49), Joe Root (62 off 68), Will Jacks (54no off 40); Xavier Bartlett (3-72) Australia 220 all out in 44.3 overs (target 356): Cameron Green (64 off 82), Matt Renshaw (63 off 74); Gus Atkinson (4-28), Sam Curran (2-38), Liam Dawson (2-41)

The ODI finale at Ninja Stadium in Tasmania next week (3.30am start UK on Wednesday) is now winner-takes-all, ahead of the sides moving on to a five-match T20 international series, starting at the Melbourne Cricket Ground next Saturday (8.15am UK time).

In Sunday's match, Australia were reeling on 13-3 after three wickets for no runs in six balls as Atkinson had Travis Head (7) and Cooper Connolly (0) caught at slip in the same over before captain Mitchell Marsh (2) perished the same way off Sonny Baker (1-45).

When Josh Inglis (3) became the fourth man caught behind, off Atkinson after a successful review, Marsh's men looked to have little hope of completing their highest successful run chase at home.

Image: England's Gus Atkinson (left) bagged four wickets during the tourists' series-levelling victory

Matt Renshaw (63) and Cameron Green (64) rebuilt with a fifth-wicket stand of 98, during which Renshaw was dropped on 27 by Jacks at cover and Green inexplicably grassed on seven at deep midwicket by Liam Dawson (2-41), the player who eventually broke the partnership when he pinned Renshaw lbw on the reverse sweep.

Green went on to be stumped in bizarre fashion as a delivery from Dawson ricocheted off wicketkeeper Cox's pads and back onto the stumps, while Sam Curran (2-38) was on a hat-trick after ousting Jack Edwards (17) with a moon ball and then Xavier Bartlett (0).

With the ball, Australia missed Mahli Beardman, who ripped through the away side with 6-24 at Optus Stadium two days earlier but was rested on Sunday, with the hosts taking a cautious approach with a quick whose young career has been hit by injury.

Image: Liam Dawson bounced back from a dropped catch with two wickets

Banton continues to flourish as opener

Banton is likely to line up in the middle order in the T20 series but has seemingly cinched a long-term spot in the ODI XI as opener after yet another impressive showing.

The Somerset batter has registered two hundreds and four fifties in nine innings since replacing the injured Jacob Bethell (knee) as Ben Duckett's top-order partner at the back end of the home summer, with this latest ton coming from a brisk 85 deliveries.

Banton was struck on the grille by a sharp bouncer from Beardman's replacement Riley Meredith early in his innings but he brushed off that blow to club many of his 16 boundaries (12 fours, four sixes) leg-side off the short deliveries Australia targeted him with.

Banton put on 137 with Root from 19-1, after Duckett clothed to point, and it was somewhat of a surprise when Root, perhaps looking to up the run rate, top-edged spinner Connolly into the off-side on the pull having been typically calm before then.

Cox and Jacks dug in initially, before helping their team plunder 110 runs from the final 10 overs, a passage of play in which Curran (14 off 9) chipped in and Atkinson (13no off 4) belted Edwards for two sixes in an 18-run 50th over that concluded with a Jacks four.

Brook delighted by England bouncing back

England captain Harry Brook, speaking at the presentation:

"I think we put in a really good performance there and it was really pleasing to see us bounce back [from the heavy defeat in Perth].

"We looked in control throughout the whole batting innings, countering their bad balls and putting them under pressure when we needed to.

"Banton played an exceptional innings, sticking to his strengths, and the depth we have means we were able to go on and get 350.

"[In the field], this is the template we want to set in every game. Bar a few dropped catches, it was awesome.

"A massive discussion in the group for a year and a half has been about wanting to be one of the best fielding sides in the world, one of the fittest and strongest sides in the world."

Marsh: England showed they are 'well rounded'

Australia captain Mitchell Marsh, speaking at the presentation:

Image: Mitchell Marsh was out for two during Australia's heavy defeat

"We bowled first thinking there might be a little bit in the wicket - which sounds weird to say at Adelaide Oval - and to maximise the first 20 overs, but England batted really well.

"I thought we tried a lot with the ball, a few different plans, like Riley Meredith bowling bumpers, but we knew England are a well-rounded side and they showed that today.

"With the bat, when you are chasing 350, you are under the pump from ball one and we needed two of the top four to go big and lay a platform."

Sports.title: India fight back as New Zealand lose first home ODI series since 2019
Sports.content:
India fought back to inflict a first home ODI series defeat on New Zealand since their own victory in the country in 2019 as they won a low-scoring fifth game in Mount Maunganui by 22 runs.

The visitors slumped to 34-3 - albeit better than the 0-3 where they found themselves during a 244-run thrashing in the fourth ODI at the same venue on Friday - and later lost four wickets for 23 runs to be bowled out for 209 after losing the toss at Bay Oval.

However, the 26 runs put on in partnership between last-wicket pair Arshdeep Singh (14) and Mohammed Siraj (14) proved crucial after that duo bagged five wickets between them - Arshdeep bagging 3-30 and Siraj 2-50 - to skittle the Black Caps for 187 in reply.

New Zealand had already seen India end their streak of 11 straight home bilateral ODI series victories but would have had the consolation of a 2-2 draw had they produced a successful chase and looked poised to do that before losing 5-55 from 64-1.

India's spin-bowling all-rounder Axar Patel followed his innings of 46 - he joint top-scored in the match alongside team-mate Ishan Kishan - with figures of 2-28 from 6.1 overs as the tourists claimed the series 3-1.

Score summary - New Zealand vs India, fifth ODI, Mount Maunganui India 209 all out in 42.1 overs (put in to bat): Ishan Kishan (46), Axar Patel (46); Mitchell Santner (3-47), Jacob Duffy (3-60), Matt Fisher (2-28) New Zealand 187 all out in 48.1 overs (target 210): Dean Foxcroft (31), Mitchell Santner (24), Nick Kelly (24); Arshdeep Singh (3-30), Axar Patel (2-28), Mohammed Siraj (2-50)

The Kiwis' woes began when Will Young (22) was caught off Arshdeep by Ruturaj Gaikwad at deep square, with top-scorer Dean Foxcroft (31) sixth out when he chopped Yash Thakur (1-38) onto his stumps to hand the India debutant his maiden ODI scalp.

Thakur's strike meant India claimed two wickets in as many balls, with Auqib Nabi removing Michael Bracewell (19) from the previous delivery, caught at deep midwicket.

New Zealand captain Mitchell Santner (24) and Kristian Clarke (16) put on 39 for the seventh wicket from 119-6 but when Santner was out slog-sweeping Naman Dhir (1-4) and Clarke snicked Arshdeep behind, Axar polished off the tail.

New Zealand lost the preceding T20I series 3-2.

The Kiwis will now host India in two Tests, starting in Wellington on November 19 ahead of a second fixture in Christchurch from November 27.

Sports.title: Australia brush off New Zealand to win fourth straight Rugby League World Cup
Sports.content:
Jack Bostock and Liam Martin both starred as Australia swept away New Zealand 32-12 in the men's Rugby League World Cup final to be crowned world champions for the fourth time in a row.

Australia had begun the tournament slowly, narrowly beating New Zealand 24-22 in their World Cup curtain-raiser in October, but when it came to the business end of the World Cup, they showcased why they are the best team in the world.

It ushered in another era of dominance for Australian Rugby League, after the Jillaroos also completed a four-peat of World Cup victories, following their 34-10 victory against New Zealand's women's side earlier on Sunday.

New Zealand had been out to win their first World Cup since 2008, but James Fisher-Harris' side were errant in defence, missing 37 tackles as Reece Walsh and Bradman Best tore apart the Kiwi line.

Image: Australia won their fourth straight Rugby League World Cup after defeating New Zealand on Sunday

"I can't put it into words. It's unbelievable," player of the match, Bostock, said.

"We were written off early in the tournament, and probably didn't play our best games.

"Last week, you saw us start to turn it on, we saw glimpses of what we could do, and today we put it all together on the big stage.

"We've got 10 club captains in our team, so there's so much leadership.

"If I can just pick up stuff from them in my young career, it's only going to do me good. I'll never forget this day."

Image: Jack Bostock was crowned Player of the Match after he scored twice

The Kangaroos wasted no time in getting on the scoreboard, with Martin, carrying three New Zealand defenders, driving over inside 95 seconds of kick-off.

New Zealand have been in excellent form throughout the campaign, and despite going down early, they hit back ten minutes later with Casey McLean receiving a chest pass from Kodi Nikorima, before darting over from close range.

The hosts made them pay, with Walsh and Best showcasing their elite handling skills to flick the ball out to Bostock, who crossed over in the corner for his first of the match.

Image: Reece Walsh showcased his incredible dancing footwork to set up Tom Trbojevic

Best then added his name to the scoresheet as Australia continued to ruthlessly probe their way through the Kiwi's defensive line.

Tom Dearden sucked in multiple defenders before sending the ball out wide to Best, who wrong-footed another defender before darting through a big gap to score.

Martin and Tom Trbojevic would bookend tries either side of half-time, with the Penrith Panthers back-row again crashing over from 10m out.

Walsh then left New Zealand stunned, dancing his way around multiple defenders before popping the ball off to Trbojevic, who scored three minutes into the second half.

Image: New Zealand were blown away in the first half as Australia scored four tries

New Zealand began to grow into the match, with Ronaldo Mulitalo having a try chalked off for a knock-on in the build-up before Isaiah Papali'i gathered a grubber kick from Nikorima to get a try back with 14 minutes to go.

But Australia were ruthless, with Bostock taking a sublime back-hand offload from Best in the corner to score his second, and secure Australia's men's 13th Rugby League World Cup.

Ponga: We made too many errors

Image: There was heartbreak for New Zealand who conceded too many errors on Sunday

New Zealand full-back Kalyn Ponga explained he was gutted by the loss but accepted his side were second best.

"It's pretty disappointing," Ponga said to Channel 7.

"We set a goal at the beginning of the camp, spoke about it at length, and it was just a disappointing performance.

"Credit to them, they played a better style of footy, and we made too many errors.

"It's disappointing because we worked so hard and built throughout the weeks for this moment, but it didn't come together."

Tedesco confirms international retirement

Image: James Tedesco confirmed his international retirement on Sunday

James Tedesco had initially been named as a reserve for tonight's match, but after Latrell Mitchell was forced to pull out due to illness, the Sydney Roosters full-back was drafted into the squad.

He explained that he hadn't even expected to come off the bench during Sunday's match, before adding that he was set to retire from international rugby league.

"I didn't expect to be playing or getting any minutes, but Kevvie gave me the last five minutes; to be part of it is pretty special," Tedesco said.

"Whatever my role with this group was, I was happy with. This will be my last time wearing this jersey, so it was pretty special.

"We talked from the start about what we were building. There were a few questions asked about our group, but I think we saved our best for last."

Sports.title: Record-breaking Andy Robertson is Scotland’s finest captain
Sports.content:
Andy Robertson may not be Scotland’s greatest player, but he is indisputably their finest captain. It counts as sacrilege, even to generations who have watched Kenny Dalglish only on YouTube, to reputationally place Robertson above the Liverpool hero on the basis of a cap haul that will reach 103 in St Gallen on Monday. Dalglish’s international career ended at 102 and the curious events that meant he missed the 1986 World Cup.

There is no requirement to compare a left-back in 2026 to a forward from decades earlier. Dalglish and Robertson are men in different positions in essentially a different sport. Instead, Robertson’s march to the top of the cap pile gives cause to laud his contribution.

Those within the Scotland setup regard Robertson as the glue who holds the scene together, a decorated footballer who treats everybody the same and carries out an abundance of unseen work to make this team better. Robertson has routinely paid for squad nights from his own pocket. The 32-year-old is as dedicated to overall environment as he is to his craft. Under Robertson’s on-field guidance, Scotland have morphed from international also-rans to serial tournament participants.

Left-backs are rarely the recipients of praise. When of the status of Robertson they do, however, receive criticism when a team struggle. He has carried the heaviest load while probably unable to celebrate the highs in an appropriate manner.

Robertson’s journey sets him apart and not only from Dalglish. By March 2014, when Robertson made his debut as a 67th-minute substitute in a friendly in Warsaw, he had been rejected by Celtic’s youth system, reset his career at Queen’s Park and turned heads in Dundee United colours. Hull would come next.

“He counts as one of my best-ever signings,” says Steve Bruce, who took Robertson to Humberside. “I still remember him holding his parents’ hands when he came down.

“He could run like the wind and had such a lovely left foot. We wanted to try and sign the best young players and thought he might get a few games due to injuries but Andy went into the side and never came out, which is testament to him. I’m absolutely delighted for him.”

Robertson and Phil Bardsley replaced Alan Hutton and Barry Bannan in Poland. “He was a young boy who played with so much freedom,” Hutton says. “He had energy and aggression to go up and down the pitch all day long, he would shell crosses into the box at 100mph. For one so young, he was also amazingly good at 1 v 1 defending. I got to 50 caps. I remember thinking there would be no chance of anybody reaching 100.”

Alex McLeish, who handed Robertson the Scotland captaincy in 2018, jokes about the possible impact on Dalglish. “Kenny will want to make a comeback,” he says. “No, he will be absolutely delighted for Andy. It tells you so much about Andy’s character that someone like Kenny Dalglish is so fond of him.

“It felt to me like a new era. We were rebuilding and Andy seemed to make the most sense as being at the forefront of that. I’m pretty sure anyone else would have made the same decision. A fantastic player with a great attitude and very well liked by all his teammates. He was a natural captain. He demands high levels without being someone to blast people. He is a hard bugger; if he talks, people shut up and listen.

“When I told him [he was captain], I still remember how his eyes lit up. He loved hearing that. He gave me such a great big smile and said how honoured he would be to captain the country.”

McLeish underplays the value of his decision. Robertson has worn the armband 80 times. McLeish could easily, for example, have handed it to Kieran Tierney, Callum McGregor or John McGinn. McLeish’s faith in Robertson and convincing of Scott McTominay to commit to Scotland were huge and lasting contributions.

Robertson’s career could easily have followed an alternative path. The Scottish game is laced with players released by major clubs who spend years lurching about in its nether regions. Blair Spittal, who played with Robertson at Queen’s Park and Dundee United, believes there may be a broader lesson here.

“I’m not saying every player could do the same as Andy but within the pyramid of Scottish football there are definitely players who just need an opportunity and someone to show then belief,” he says. “Queen’s Park at the time was a great environment for that. We were then very lucky at Dundee United to have a manager [Jackie McNamara] who believed in young players. Andy took everything in his stride. Nothing ever fazed him.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

He has made instant impressions everywhere. John Rankin was a senior player at Dundee United as Robertson elevated his reputation. He recalls a pre-season friendly at Union Berlin, when he first clapped eyes on someone who would be a Champions League winner within six years. “Who is this?” Rankin said while watching from the stand. “On his first day at the training ground, Andy bypassed the first-team dressing room to get changed with the youth team. He was so unassuming, no entitlement about him at all.

“He knew what he wanted to do. On the pitch it was a case of: ‘Get out my road, I’m coming through.’ Off the pitch he was such a humble guy, who knew his life was built on the hard work of his parents. He had hunger to be the best player in every single session. It was never about being flash, it was about working his way to the top.”

During a game at Motherwell, with United 3-0 up, Rankin warned teammates to remain compact. Next came a marauding Robertson, who cracked home a fourth before Rankin chastised him for not following orders. “But I scored, didn’t I?” came the retort.

Jordan Henderson and James Milner have been hugely influential in shaping how Robertson deals with others. Robertson did not want Steve Clarke to call time on his Scotland managerial career in June, but during an emotional meeting in Charlotte it was clear the latter’s mind was made up. Clarke would not have returned to Hampden Park four months later, but for Robertson, who was receiving recognition for 100 caps.

It is fortunate Dalglish is not protective of his record. McGinn entered this international break with 93 caps. Ryan Christie and Scott McTominay have an outside chance of reaching 102. Billy Gilmour is 25, but hit 50 caps in October.

“It’s not about now holding on to the record for ever,” says Robertson. “That’s not really me.”

Modesty. A consistent and endearing Robertson trait. Whenever this international career for the ages ends, he will be a monumental loss.

Sports.title: Terry Butcher: ‘I’ve learned to live with the Hand of God goal better’
Sports.content:
“Have you made up all these on your own?” asks Terry Butcher, sitting in a London office in the week he is presented with his England legacy cap. It turns out dozens of Guardian readers want to pick the brains of a much-loved centre-back who was feted en route to a World Cup semi-final and tormented four years previously by the mercurial genius of Diego Maradona.

Did Maradona ever admit to the “Hand of God”? Butcher found himself in the post-match doping-control room alongside his nemesis at the Azteca in 1986. “I tapped my head, then my hand, and then he tapped his head,” Butcher says. “He didn’t admit to it because, if he had, I’d have been right across that room.”

The highs and lows of Sir Bobby Robson’s remarkable England tenure are chronicled in a new book co-written by Butcher: Almost Immortal: When Bobby Robson’s England Gripped The Nation.

Your name instantly brings to mind you playing on for England with a bandaged head and bloodied shirt. With hindsight, should you have left the pitch? Sian Williams

I never contemplated leaving the pitch at all. As the captain of your country, playing in a crucial World Cup qualifier against the top team in our league, in our group, there’s no way. I said to Bobby: “If you take me off, I’ll hit you.” I don’t think I would have but I said: “No, don’t do it!” Initially, I felt the blood and it seemed like a bad one, quite severe, but when I was bandaged up I could still play and it wasn’t a problem. Heading the ball wasn’t an issue because you’re really fired up, the adrenaline’s there, so it didn’t concern me. There was no way I was going to voluntarily come off unless Bobby was of a mind to do that, but he knew my pain threshold very well and knew I would battle on. I had numerous injuries before, broke my nose in 1982, five weeks in hospital and lost a lot of blood. So he knew I had great fortitude. Things have changed dramatically now. From a medical point of view it would have been right to take me off, absolutely. But that was then and I think, as a captain, you have to lead. It’s nice that people remember me through that image, but I was just doing my job.

I once stayed at the hotel that forms part of the FA’s headquarters at St George’s Park. Above the bed, and hanging over my wife and me all night long, was a giant version of the photo of you covered in blood. It was a bit disconcerting – but what’s the strangest place you stayed in or visited while on England duty? Stu Egan

I’ve actually stayed in that room as well. Stu has told us what it was like for him and I have to say it wasn’t great for me either. I’m staring up looking at me with a bloodied head and thinking: “Oh my God, this has followed me around.” At least when you close your eyes and sleep you don’t have to see it, but I’m sorry he had to stay there.

I didn’t stay in many really strange places with England. When I was manager of Motherwell we had a Scottish Cup quarter-final and were in administration at the time. I was organising our travel myself and booked a hotel near Stranraer, online. It looked great, right by a golf course. But when we got there we realised it was a residential home for the elderly. The rooms had accessibility handles and low sinks. It wasn’t a horrible place at all, quite the opposite, it was very warm and caring. But it was strange coming down for breakfast seeing people being looked after by the nurses. We won 4-0 so it can’t have been bad for us.

View image in fullscreen Terry Butcher, bloodied head and all, was a symbol of England’s defiance in their World Cup qualifier in Sweden in 1989, which finished 0-0. Photograph: David Cannon/Getty Images

Now that time has passed and Diego has left us, has your perspective on that afternoon in Mexico City softened at all, or do you feel a professional duty to history to never let the “Hand of God” be forgotten? Victor Segovia

My feelings haven’t changed and they won’t. But I’ve learned to live with it better, I’ve learned to get through it and I’m not so annoyed by the memory. You’re just disappointed it happened. It had an influence on the game because we went one down and I think a lot of the players were shocked by what happened. Half the team saw it, half didn’t. I was one of the ones who didn’t. It had a big part to play in the fact we didn’t get switched on again and conceded the second goal. I’m more disappointed because he beat me twice. You’ve got to respect the man and respect what he did for the second goal, and what he did in that game. He was the best player I’ve played against and one that I never really got near.

Maradona’s “wondergoal” – it was really an own goal by you as you did a desperate sliding tackle, wasn’t it? David

If I’d got a touch I’d have raised my hand straight away and admitted it was the best own goal I’d ever scored. He went past Peter Shilton and I managed to get back, but I couldn’t see the ball so I was kind of feeling around him with my left foot. I couldn’t get my right foot across, but I thought I could block it. I was so surprised when he made good contact and put it in the net because I thought: “I’ve got this.” You can see me afterwards on the TV, I’m banging my shinpads, I was so angry. I was more angry about that goal than I was the “Hand of God” goal. So I’d have loved to claim that one. I know it sounds bizarre but it would have been one of my greatest achievements. Would it still have been the greatest goal scored at a World Cup?

View image in fullscreen Diego Maradona was England’s nemesis in their World Cup quarter-final in 1986 and Terry Butcher said he was the only player he ‘never really got near’. Photograph: Aflo Co. Ltd./Alamy

In the early 80s you had a brilliant side at Portman Road so I wondered if you have: “If only …” or “What if …” moments about that time. It has always felt to me that Ipswich left another big trophy or two out there. Stooze

We did. The 1980-81 season was arguably the best in our history. We lost the FA Cup semi-final, lost the league title on the last day of the season and then had to play the Uefa Cup final, which thankfully we won. It’s always at the back of your mind that you missed out on what you should have got, which was the treble. We should have done it. But I think the 66-game season was just too much for us, we didn’t have a big squad and struggled with injuries towards the end. But we came really close. Look at the teams Sir Bobby built, we were in Europe for nine seasons out of 10. There’s no particular moment I sit down and dwell on, but you know it’s there, so close but so far.

What was the one quality Bobby Robson had above all others and was he the best manager you played under? Carl Parrish

His man-management was top class. He knew how to get the best from his players, knew what buttons to press and got to know them very quickly. He could wield his strength, he was a really tough guy, but when he was friendly it was lovely. His face lit up and he made you feel really good through that man-management. He always used to say to me: “Whenever I pick you, you always do well.” When someone says that you feel really good about yourself. He knew what to say. But had an abundance of things that worked really well for him. His tactical knowledge, selection of players, the network he built up for the younger players to come through, so many things. He was the most complete manager in my eyes and I still think he’s the best. Wherever he went, home or abroad, he proved himself in a way no English manager has done.

View image in fullscreen Ipswich Town manager Bobby Robson (centre) is encouraged to address the crowd by players Terry Butcher (right) and from the left, Laurie Sivell, Kevin Beattie and John Wark during the town’s civic reception for the team following their victory in the 1981 Uefa Cup final. Photograph: Bob Thomas Sports Photography/Getty Images

What was it like playing alongside Des Walker with England? And how close were England to winning the World Cup in 1990? Ahmed Kheyre

Des was the best centre-half I played alongside for England; he was unbelievable. He prolonged my international career because he was my pace. You never beat Des Walker. He was OK on the ball, it wasn’t his strength, but he used to give it to people that had great ability in that area so he was very astute. He was very young at the time, but dependable, talked well, shouted, pulled you about, was dominant. He was one of the reasons I made it to Italia 90. As for how close we were, I think the semi-final was the best we played all tournament. As I was walking out I felt so serene, comfortable, like I was in a dream state. It was never normally like that, but I could see our boys’ faces: steely, determined, but relaxed. It was the best I’d ever felt before a game. I even successfully backheeled the ball to a teammate. It was one of the best moments of our lives. We didn’t get to the very best one, the final, but we were so close. You’re talking inches, the shot that came off the post right between Lineker and Beardsley. Beating Argentina in the final would have been the ultimate redemption.

Is it true that during your time at Rangers, the top away scorer at Ibrox was Butcher (og)? Anonymous

I think I scored more goals past Chris Woods, my own goalkeeper, than any other Scottish striker. They were crackers: pick that one out Woodsy. He was my roommate as well, so he would say: “I don’t want any more going past me.” But they were all good ones, put it that way. They weren’t just ricochets or anything else like that. Wow, they were proper own goals. If you’re going to hit it, hit it hard.

I’m a massive fan of you as a player but think I’m even more impressed by your work with veterans following the death of your son. What would be the biggest thing we could do to support veterans? Jim

We’ve got to have a specific centre for veterans, like a St George’s Park, which would be dedicated to their health and that of their families. That would be the ultimate aim for me. We need more, and bigger, facilities to focus on veterans’ mental health and respite for those around them. It would be ideal to create a military community where you’re not in service, but the families are together. It would enable the veterans to relax, get treatment, get better, get the toolbox that provides the coping mechanisms so that if something happens they know what to do and where to go. My son didn’t have that unfortunately: he stayed in his room and that was his safe place.

I enjoy my work with Combat2Coffee, which supports veterans and their families. It’s doing really well and the togetherness is great. It’s getting exponentially bigger and we’re about to open a veterans’ hub in Ipswich. It’s a special thing, you can just walk in off the street and get that support. I’m doing this because my son would have loved it, and it’s what he needed.

Sports.title: Declan Rice accepts he had an ‘average World Cup’ as England gear up for Spain showdown
Sports.content:
Declan Rice has admitted he had an “average” World Cup at the end of a gruelling season and needed time out during the international window in September and October in order to return stronger.

The Arsenal midfielder believes the break has served its purpose, having produced starring performances against Bayern Munich and Liverpool in recent weeks. He is now ready to hit his best level for England in Sunday’s Nations League showdown against Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium.

Rice managed nerve pain in a hamstring that affected his lower back throughout the second half of last season and his fitness was a talking point during the World Cup. The 27-year-old had good games, most notably against the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the last 32 when he filled in towards the end as an emergency right-back.

Rice played well and scored in the third-place playoff against France. But he was typically honest when asked to reflect on his tournament as he prepared for the Spain game. England will leapfrog the world champions and finish top of their Nations League group if – and only if – they win in Madrid. It would theoretically bring an easier draw for the two-leg quarter-finals in March.

“By my standards it was an average World Cup,” Rice said. “France was probably my best game, Congo I played really well; some of the other games I didn’t play too well but you look back … I played 69 games [in the season].

“A title win with Arsenal, a Champions League final loss and into a World Cup. It’s annoying because at the World Cup you want to be at your best, you want to be totally fresh, you want to be ready. It’s annoying that I couldn’t perform how I did at Arsenal towards the back end of the season.

“But knowing if I’m not going to be at my best, just constantly give 100% for this team, for the badge and you could see that. I loved [the last-16 win in] Mexico. We had the disappointment of Argentina in the semi-final, the second group game against Ghana. It’s games you look back on and think: ‘Could I have done better?’”

View image in fullscreen Declan Rice was frustrated with his performance levels during the World Cup. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images

The playoff against France was on 18 July. After a short break, Rice reported back to Arsenal and played 45 minutes of the Community Shield against Manchester City on 16 August. When he played the 90 minutes of the defeat at Brighton on 19 September, he “did not feel right at all”, leading to a conversation with Tuchel who stood him down from England’s first four Nations League ties, the first of which was the 3-2 loss against Spain at Wembley. Rice sent a voice note to the England captain, Harry Kane, to explain his absence.

“I had an honest conversation with the boss here [Tuchel], who was really understanding,” Rice said. “He said: ‘Take some time, get yourself ready.’ It was about using that time to come back fitter and stronger. I feel really good now. It’s still like I’m building up to being 100 per cent but it’s closer to that than I was a few weeks ago, for sure. And over the last few weeks, my performances have picked up.”

Rice, who won his 81st cap in the win over Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, had only previously withdrawn from three England camps. “I know the importance of playing for England, I know the importance of showing up, being available,” he said. “It’s one of the biggest things to me. Last camp, if I didn’t speak to the manager about it, I wouldn’t have done it. But he gave me his word. So I was in a better place mentally knowing that he authorised it.”

Rice has played at least 50 club matches in each of the past five seasons. “It’s something my body has got used to,” he said. “Probably last year, I felt it more than anything in terms of the amount of games, the toll it does take and realising as you get older, you have to take the recovery side of it a lot more seriously. When you were 21, 22, 23 … you could get up and have a round of golf the next day [after a match]. Now, even though I’m young at 27, you get up after a game and you can hardly feel your legs.”

Meanwhile, Tuchel has decided to start James Trafford in goal against Spain – an eye-catching decision that will only harden the impression that Jordan Pickford is no longer his first-choice goalkeeper. Tuchel gave them two matches apiece in the September/ October window and said that he was minded to split the minutes once again this time.

View image in fullscreen James Trafford will start in goal for England against Spain. Photograph: Richard Calver/Getty Images

When he started Pickford against Croatia, it felt as though he had shelved the plan, given his insistence that the Everton player remained his No1 and Spain is plainly the bigger game. But Tuchel announced at his pre-match conference that Trafford would be given the opportunity.

“Traff will play,” Tuchel said. “We want to see how far Traff is. So he gets a highly competitive match. We had some changes in the back four in the last match [against Croatia], so we went for more stability and more experience with Pickers. And Traff gets the match tomorrow.

“Hopefully he’s not too over-excited or overly nervous because there’s no need to be. We trust him. But it is different to play for England than to play for your club. And to have the opportunity to play matches where it really matters is the best way to show up and to show that you’re ready. We know what Jordan can do for us. Jordan is, at the moment, our No1. I have a very clear picture in high-pressure moments.”

Tuchel also revealed that Ezri Konsa was back in contention after missing the Croatia game with a minor knee problem. He made it sound as though the Arsenal defender would start. “He showed up yesterday for individual work and he showed up today for training,” Tuchel said. “Ezri is back and ready to play.”

Sports.title: De la Fuente adamant there is no racism in Spain despite England reminder to players
Sports.content:
Luis de la Fuente has told Thomas Tuchel there is no racism in Spain after the England coach’s admission that he would remind his players of the anti-racism protocol prior to their meeting at the Metropolitano on Sunday night.

This will be the first time the countries play each other in Madrid since some of England’s black players were subjected to racist abuse in a match at the Santiago Bernabéu in 2004. And although England have returned to Spain three times without incident since then, twice in Seville and once in Alicante, Tuchel was asked on Friday about going back in the buildup to Sunday’s game. The England coach replied that England “will not expect anything [untoward]” but also said: “Maybe we take our five minutes to inform the players about the protocol if there is a precedent [in Madrid].”

Asked to respond to those words, and whether Spain still had work to do combating racism after being fined for discriminatory chants about Muslims during a game against Egypt in Barcelona in March, the Spain coach asked for confirmation as to whom they had come from, then said: “I can say the opposite. Tell Thomas there is no racism. As clear as that. Exactly the same as in England. We’re not racists, none of us.”

Tuchel, speaking later on Saturday night, expressed his irritation with the media, accusing journalists of manufacturing a row. “I got asked ‘what will happen if and if and if’, and I said if it happens, we have a protocol in place. That’s it … I never talked about racism in Spain, I answered politely a question about what happens. You create a lot of confusion for absolutely nothing.”

De la Fuente also described Spain versus England as “one of the best games you can see anywhere in the world right now, maybe the best”, and admitted that his team needs to exercise more control than they had been able to do during their 3-2 win at Wembley in September.

Asked to explain how the Premier League could be the richest league in the world and English players command bigger transfer fees than Spaniards despite the national team not winning anything since 1966 while the selección have won two World Cups and three Euros in this century alone, he insisted that it is a mistake to mix price and value.

View image in fullscreen Spain defeated England at Wembley in their Nations League game in September. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

“There is a song about value and price and it is exactly that,” the Spain coach said. “Someone has to pay it and that’s very welcome but it doesn’t mean it is the real value. I am surprised often when you see the prices paid for our players compared to [the fees] paid in England. I think ‘they’re so cheap’. They [Spanish players] are the best in the world. You can buy a player for half the price of what you pay in England for someone. In that world, in that market, that’s what’s spent. But I’m clear on this: we must not confuse price and value.

“Between the English model and the Spanish model, I would choose the Spanish model,” De la Fuente added. “It is recognisable and the players have the ability to express it. The English model has developed a lot and I think it is very good. But you have to have the players. We can’t play like them and they can’t play like us.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“One of the strengths England have is the ability to run into space. When the game is open, they have people who are comfortable with that space and playing that style. Last time against them we lacked control, were unable to have longer periods of possession and impose ourselves more on our opponents.

“In the last two tournaments, England have been third and finalists. I think they are a great team and they have great players. That shows you it is not easy to win. Maybe that should make us appreciate what we’re doing this century: it is marvellous and very difficult. England are always candidates to win everything [nowadays]. This is one of the best games you can see in the world.”

Sports.title: AFC Wimbledon, a failed £87m investment bid and the challenge for fan ownership
Sports.content:
When you walk up from Haydons Road train station to Plough Lane there is a blue AFC Wimbledon billboard that reads “Fan owned football”, directly opposite the site of the old Plough Lane stadium where there are now blocks of flats. There is a memorial to the old Wimbledon FC – a reminder that supporters can often have little say in the running of their club – on the same corner, just up the road from the new Cherry Red Records Stadium.

AFC Wimbledon are one of only two majority fan-owned clubs in the EFL – along with Exeter City – but that makes running a loss-making operation, as 94% of teams in England’s top five tiers are doing according to the State of the Game report, even more challenging. “In other clubs, the owner just puts their hand in their pocket, produces cash,” said Hannah Kitcher, who has been a member of the Dons Trust Board (DTB), which runs AFC Wimbledon, for seven years. “It’s harder when the owners are fans – you can only go to them so many times.”

Kitcher was speaking before kick-off in Saturday’s League One game at home to a Blackpool side dealing with a suspected norovirus outbreak in their squad. A superb arrowed strike from Alistair Smith and some vital late saves from Nathan Bishop ended Wimbledon’s winless run of 10 matches in all competitions. The 1-0 victory moved Johnnie Jackson’s side four points clear of the relegation zone and put a positive spin on a week that started with the fallout from the withdrawal of £87m of proposed investment, leaving the club’s finances even tighter.

View image in fullscreen Alistair Smith (second right) celebrates with his Wimbledon teammates after scoring the only goal in their win over Blackpool. Photograph: Jed Leicester/Shutterstock

Wimbledon made a £2.6m loss in the 2024-25 season – a figure expected to increase by £500,000 when they publish their accounts next month – which, as Kitcher pointed out, is not as loss-making as a number of other clubs in League One. Those clubs voted in the summer to reduce spending limits from 60% to 50% of turnover but now many want to go further to curb the spiralling losses at this level. “It’s an ugly way of running a sport,” said Terry Hunt, a supporter who has been attending matches with his son Billy since AFC Wimbledon were founded in 2002 following the move to Milton Keynes.

Wimbledon returned home to Plough Lane in 2020 but had to create a bond to complete the move and the club still owe £7.5m in debts. In November 2025, the DTB warned that competing in the EFL at their new stadium was “not currently sustainable” under their structure at the time.

The makeup of the club has since changed. Last April, supporters voted in favour of reducing their voting rights from 75% to 50.01% – the same 50+1 model that gives fans the final say on decisions at German clubs – and Wimbledon sought a cash injection. An £87m investment proposal from Sloane Street Capital (SSC), a venture including the sole funder, Omar Mir, and the former Chelsea and England defender Ryan Bertrand, was already being voted on by fans when Mir suddenly walked away last Sunday, citing a change in his investment priorities.

Mir passed Wimbledon’s due diligence tests, but the tech businessman was not a unifying figure. A Josimar report has detailed his “various connections to some of the most influential and controversial figures in football, technology and global security”. The 44-year-old did not attend either of the information evenings at Plough Lane after the proposal was first made in October, instead sending a two-minute video message, which meant fans could not directly ask him about his intention to purchase 90% of the economic rights of a fan-owned football club.

View image in fullscreen Dons Trust Board member Hannah Kitcher says: “It’s harder when the owners are fans – you can only go to them so many times.” Photograph: Jed Leicester/Shutterstock

“We really wanted to have some kind of knight in shining armour,” said Niall Couper, a former member of the DTB and author of three books on Wimbledon. “In this case, I personally wasn’t sure how shiny that armour was.” Couper, who raised questions about Mir’s background before his withdrawal, chose not attend the Blackpool game owing to anger from some supporters at the deal collapsing.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

But the SSC deal is not completely dead. Bertrand and his remaining SSC partners Stuart Fiertz, Oliver Ward and Hugh Rosen – who would have owned 1.25% each of Wimbledon’s economic rights in the original proposal – have renamed themselves Sloane Street Football and are talking to other potential investors.

In the meantime, the board will seek approval from fans about taking out a loan of up to £3m to “manage the club’s cash position”, but they believe they are currently able to manage it through to the end of this season and into the next. Which division Wimbledon end up in next season remains to be seen – Jackson’s side survived relegation by four points last April and the manager will probably have his hands tied in January.

“I think we’ll probably go down, but bouncing between League Two and League One is absolutely fine by me,” said Billy Hunt. “The main goal is security and making sure we have a football club.”

Sports.title: Here Manchester United go again, taking the Two Ronnies route to hiring a new boss | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
Magnusson: And your time starts … now! What is paleontology? Smithers: Yes, absolutely correct. Magnusson: What’s the name of the directory that lists members of the peerage? Smithers: A study of old fossils. Magnusson: Correct. Who are Len Murray and Sir Geoffrey Howe? Smithers: Burke’s. Magnusson: Correct. What is the difference between a donkey and an ass? Smithers: One’s a trade union leader, the other’s a member of the Cabinet …

One of the Two Ronnies’ most celebrated sketches involves a Mastermind contestant whose specialist subject is answering the previous question. History repeats itself: the first time as comedy, the second time as Manchester United, who seem continually to be answering not the question of who would be the best available manager now, but who might have been the best available manager a few years ago.

The problem with football is that it never sits still. What was true once isn’t necessarily true now. What is true now won’t necessarily be true in a season or two’s time. Almost nothing is absolute. What works once might not work in a different context. The key to good recruitment is identifying to what extent somebody’s past success was contingent on their environment, and how they may behave in different circumstances. And that is very difficult, which is why only four managers have won the English league title with more than one club.

The possibility of José Mourinho becoming manager of United was first raised as Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013. Mourinho has recently claimed he turned the job down; other versions of events have him raging in a Madrid hotel as he learned that David Moyes had been hired, seemingly because Sir Bobby Charlton, then a senior board member, was worried about his impact on the image of the club.

It’s impossible, of course, to say whether Mourinho would have been a success had he taken the job then. But he had the ego to ensure he would not have lived in Ferguson’s shadow and, although he had been bruised by the Real Madrid experience, English football still recognised his aura. He was still adept enough to win a third league title at Chelsea.

By the time Mourinho finally took the United job in 2016, though, events in his final few months at Stamford Bridge had undermined him. He seemed weary and fractious, the tactical doubts raised in his final year at Madrid had proliferated and there was a growing sense his methods did not quite work with elite modern players.

There was a lot of talk about him as a guaranteed winner, but there’s no such thing in football. Very few managers last more than a decade at the very top. Only the most driven personalities, the most fecund minds, can endure the process of constant evolution necessary to stay ahead of the pack for more than a few years.

It’s easy to see why a board would have looked at his list of honours and been impressed, but United were appointing a manager on the way down. Was that obvious at the time? Perhaps not, but there were warning signs, and it’s the job of those doing the job of recruitment to identify them.

View image in fullscreen Erik ten Hag, skilfully as he managed Cristiano Ronaldo’s exit, seemed overawed by the United job. Photograph: Vince Mignott/EPA

With every appointment there are mitigations. Given the immense power Ferguson had, it would have been hard not to appoint Moyes when he had backed him. Yet if there was ever a time when he might have been the right man for United, it was surely six or seven years earlier; modern managers tend to peak in their mid-late 40s.

Louis van Gaal was 62 when he took the reins at United, enjoying a second coming after winning the Dutch title with AZ Alkmaar and an impressive 2014 World Cup campaign with the Netherlands. Perhaps the comparison isn’t fair in that he arrived as an elder statesman; nobody, other than perhaps Van Gaal, thought he would be a long-term appointment. But the idea he would bring calm after a period of turbulence was to ignore everything he had previously done. Van Gaal is many things but he is not a calming presence.

But again, the timing felt wrong. It could never have worked given he was preparing a side for the World Cup, but had he come in to replace Ferguson in 2013, as a hugely respected figure with a robust self-belief that was never going to care about breaking Fergusonian taboos, he might have been the man to see United through the awkward transition.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim were supposed to be the coming men, managers identified on the way up. Both seemed to make sense. Ten Hag’s Ajax had played astonishing football, had beaten Juventus and Real Madrid thrillingly in the Champions League, had come within Lucas Moura’s implausible hat-trick of a Champions League final. Amorim had ended Sporting’s 19-year title drought.

But it turned out they weren’t right. Ten Hag, skilfully as he managed Cristiano Ronaldo’s exit, seemed overawed by the job; Amorim’s insistence on playing 3-4-2-1 with a squad ill-equipped to play that way was one of the reasons Dan Ashworth expressed reservations, leading to his departure as sporting director.

It is possible, of course, maybe by this point even likely, that there is no right answer, that the mess United are in is insoluble, Old Trafford a meat grinder that will keep chewing up managerial reputations in perpetuity. But United’s board’s attempts to identify the rising star have been no more successful than their habit of appointing fading legends.

View image in fullscreen José Mourinho seemed weary and fractious when the former Chelsea and Real Madrid manager arrived at Old Trafford in 2016. Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty Images

Which brings us to Mauricio Pochettino. He has done remarkable things: he may not yet have won trophies in England but he effected such an extraordinary transformation at Tottenham that it seemed not unreasonable they should be part of the Super League project. He found things difficult at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea, but most people do. A last-16 exit at a home World Cup with the USA was about par. The question, now he is 54, is whether the sense of drift about his career is an unfortunate and temporary state, or evidence that he is not quite what he was.

Perhaps the United job will revitalise him and he will revitalise them. But this feels like another appointment that would have been better made a few years ago; that United, once again, are answering the previous question.

Sports.title: Nations League roundup: Portugal mauled by Denmark as Norway sink Wales
Sports.content:
Portugal were hammered 4-1 by Denmark on Saturday, an embarrassing Nations League defeat in their first match without Cristiano Ronaldo after his retirement from international football.

Rasmus Højlund starred with a superb double as Denmark moved into second place in Group A4 and closed in on a spot in the quarter-finals with an exceptional display in Braga.

Denmark are on nine points from five fixtures, three behind Portugal who were already sure of qualification for the last eight having won all four of their previous group fixtures.

A draw against third-placed Norway on Tuesday will see Denmark through.

Before kick-off Portugal paid tribute to Ronaldo, who announced his exit from the international game last week, with the team and mascots walking out wearing Ronaldo’s No 7 and his name on their jerseys.

Denmark were the better team from the first minute and it was no surprise when the visitors took the lead from Pierre-Emile Højbjerg’s penalty in the 43rd minute.

Højlund lashed home a volley four minutes after the restart and seven minutes later the home crowd were stunned after the Napoli striker skipped past Rúben Dias before crashing home a powerful shot from the edge of the area.

Boos and whistles began to ring out at the Estadio Municipal when Joachim Andersen headed in the fourth, and Bernardo Silva’s late consolation effort barely dampened the discontent.

View image in fullscreen Rasmus Højlund races away in delight after doubling Denmark’s lead. Photograph: Luis Vieira/AP

Wales suffered a 3-1 defeat to Norway in Oslo to dent their hopes of staying in the top tier of the Nations League.

Antonio Nusa and Andreas Schjelderup struck in the space of nine second-half minutes as Norway turned the screw. Substitute David Brooks halved the deficit 11 minutes from time as Wales finished strongly.

However, Connor Roberts brought down Schjelderup and Erling Haaland converted from the penalty spot, extending his Nations League goals record to 23, as Norway avenged their October defeat in Cardiff.

It means Wales will definitely finish bottom of Group A4, irrespective of Tuesday’s result at home to Portugal.

Although they could finish on six points with Norway, they have a worse head-to-head record and could now face a playoff in March to avoid relegation to Group B.

Terry Devlin’s first international goal kept Northern Ireland top of their Nations League group as a 1-0 win over Ukraine set up a promotion decider away to Hungary on Tuesday.

The 23-year-old Devlin has been in the goals for Portsmouth this term with four, and opened his Northern Ireland account with a fine strike in the 68th minute as he left the Ukraine goalkeeper Anatoliy Trubin flat-footed with a shot from distance.

View image in fullscreen Terry Devlin jumps for joy after scoring Northern Ireland’s winner. Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/Reuters

Pierce Charles then made a superb save to deny Danylo Sikan and preserve Northern Ireland’s fifth consecutive clean sheet – the first time they have achieved that since 2017 – and ensure they remain the only side in the competition yet to concede.

The victory put Northern Ireland back on top of Group B2 after Hungary’s 2-0 win over Georgia earlier in the afternoon, and ruled Ukraine out of contention as they lost three successive matches for the first time in six years.

A draw in Budapest would be enough to elevate Michael O’Neill’s team to League A, while even in defeat they would face a playoff in March, and they have also earned a pot two place in next month’s Euro 2028 draw.

However, O’Neill will need to watch Tuesday’s match from the stands as he joined Jamie Donley – who had a first-half strike ruled out for offside – in earning a late yellow card that results in a suspension.

Sasa Kalajdzic dealt the Republic of Ireland a late blow in Linz with the only goal in Austria’s 1-0 victory at the Raiffeisen Arena.

The result ensured that, no matter how the closing contests in Group B play out, Austria sealed promotion to League A. Ireland enter Tuesday’s critical home match at the Aviva Stadium in third place, with one point fewer than their final opponents, Kosovo.

Heimir Hallgrímsson’s team were not without chances, but only Kalajdzic made one count when the former Wolves striker poked home from close range in the 79th minute.

Sports.title: Chelsea go top of WSL as Sandy Baltimore bullet sees off Manchester City
Sports.content:
Pragmatic, resolute and gutsy. Sonia Bompastor showed her ruthless side and delivered a tactical masterclass as Chelsea earned a 1-0 win over Manchester City and leapfrogged them at the top of the Women’s Super League.

Lucy Bronze credited fellow full-back Katie McCabe with firing Chelsea up pre-match, having told them they “had to be dogs” in the game, and a dogged performance followed. Sandy Baltimore’s stunning strike in added time at the end of the first half was the difference as the west London side nullified the threat of a team that had scored in each of their preceding 21 games in all competitions, inflicting their first loss of the campaign.

The task for City got even tougher when goalkeeper Ayaka Yamashita received a straight red for clattering into Alyssa Thompson, but despite their numerical disadvantage it was end to end right up until the final whistle.

“It always affects you when you go one player down,” said manager Andrée Jeglertz. “But we handled that and that’s not why we lose the game. I think it’s small details. It’s a tight game, it’s two great football teams, there’s a lot of situations, there’s a lot of battles and they managed to score on their big chance from a great finish. We also have a couple of great opportunities where we don’t manage to score.”

Momentum was with City going into the match after their 5-0 defeat of West Ham the preceding weekend and a 4-1 win against Inter in the Champions League on Tuesday night and they were able to welcome the injured duo Vivianne Miedema and Beth Mead back to the bench to bolster their matchday squad.

At Stamford Bridge the England women’s manager, Sarina Wiegman, the US women’s manager, Emma Hayes, and passionate women’s football advocate and pundit Ian Wright were in the stands. It was a fixture that promised much, and it delivered: the league’s most potent attacks, with Chelsea having scored 28 league goals before this fixture to City’s 27, while Bompastor’s side had the most solid defence, having conceded only five times before kick-off.

Quick Guide WSL roundup: United see off Palace Show Manchester United captain Maya le Tissier marked her 150th appearance for the club with a superb strike in a 2-0 victory over Crystal Palace at the Progress with Unity Stadium. Presented with a framed shirt before kick-off, Le Tissier whipped a low shot from distance into the net in the 18th minute before Elisabeth Terland confirmed United’s win after the hour mark. United moved up to fourth with the win and they kept hold of the position after Tottenham drew a blank in a goalless draw at home to Everton, whose winless run in the league stretched to five matches. In the day’s late game, Liverpool ended a five-match winless run in the WSL by easing past Brighton 3-0. Press Association Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

It was a chess match. After a thrillingly frenetic start there was a change for Chelsea just 12 minutes in, with the centre-back Kadeisha Buchanan replaced by Veerle Buurman. There was speculation over whether the withdrawal of the Canadian defender was due to injury and Bompastor unconvincingly claimed it was.

“Yesterday in training, she got a knock to her head during contact with a teammate. She was fine after the training session. She was fine in the evening. We assessed her again this morning and everything was fine,” she said. “I just felt watching her from the beginning of the game, she was not herself. Then I took the responsibility to make the substitution. But for me, I was almost forced to do that because I know my player and I know she was not in the game.”

However, if, as many believe, the defensive switch was a tactical decision, it was a stroke of genius, as Buurman was excellent at nullifying the threat of Khadija Shaw.

“She had a really good performance against a top player,” said Bompastor. “Today was positive. But again, as I’ve told you previously, when it doesn’t work it’s not so positive.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Ayaka Yamashita fouls Chelsea’s Alyssa Thompson, leading to the goalkeeper’s red card. Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/Reuters

There were chances at both ends but they were limited and it took until the fourth of five added minutes for Chelsea to draw first blood. The goal was sensational. Baltimore collected the ball just inside the box on the right, from Ellie Carpenter, lined up her shot and sent a piledriver of a strike into the roof of the net.

It was the only shot on target in the first half.

City sought an instant reply after the break but they could not find a way through and momentum ebbed and flowed. Jeglertz withdrew Sam Coffey and Mary Fowler in favour of Miedema and Laura Blindkilde Brown to help his side assert some authority in the middle and, through Miedema, to add some creative instinct.

However, as City pushed they left themselves vulnerable on the break and when Maika Hamano’s crossfield ball was met by Alyssa Thompson with just over 15 minutes remaining it was disaster for City. Yamashita raced out of her box and clattered into the Chelsea forward, conceding a free-kick and receiving a straight red card.

Despite City’s efforts, Chelsea were in control and they held strong to blow the title race wide open.

Sports.title: 'Am I supposed to answer that?': Erling Haaland breaks silence and distances himself from Man City cheating verdict as star striker insists 'I don't really know much' but is 'incredibly happy'
Sports.content:
Erling Haaland delivered a monologue of over two minutes detailing the teams he represented in the years covered by the Premier League's investigation into Man City, as the star questioned how he was meant to respond to the club's guilty verdict. Man City were found guilty of the vast majority of charges brought against them by the Premier League for financial wrongdoing when the verdict was released in September. The club have since appealed. An independent commission ruled Man City had disguised payments worth £900million in a nine-year period with ‘sham’ deals. Man City were found to have artificially inflated sponsorship agreements and pumped money into the club from its Abu Dhabi owners via disguised payments in a bid to swerve Premier League spending rules. Haaland was quizzed about the club's situation by Norwegian broadcaster TV2, after scoring in the national team's 3-1 victory over Wales on Saturday. The Man City star's initial answer lasted for two minutes and 14 seconds, as he reeled off the teams he had represented from 2009 to 2018, the years covered by the charges. Erling Haaland insisted it was difficult for him to answer a question about Man City's guilty verdict, with the club appealing against the decision of an independent commission. Source: TV2Sport Haaland stressed he remains happy at the club after being asked about his future given the potential ramificiations if Man City fail with their appeal to overturn the verdict. 'In 2009, I played for Bryne U9s. In 2010, the U10s. In 2011, the U11s. 2012, the U12s, 2013, the U13s. Shall we continue? We don't need the whole list. 2014, the U14s. 2015, the U15s and the national team,' Haaland began. 'Then the U16s, I think. In 2016, I moved up to Bryne's first team, second team and youth team. In 2017, I went to Molde. In 2018, I was with Molde. The first team, Molde 2 and a bit with the youth team. 'So this is a question I struggle to answer because it's a legal battle… 'It's a case between the Premier League and Manchester City that a panel will deal with. Am I supposed to answer that? I'm not really sure.' Haaland continued by listing fellow Norwegians who had been at Man City at the time, joking that they may be in a better place to offer insight. 'There were quite a few Norwegians at the club during that period, I think,' Haaland said. 'Abdisalam Ibrahim, Martin Samuelsen and Omar Elabdellaoui were there. Kjetil Haug was there too. I think there were a couple more but I can't remember. The forward distanced himself from the case as he listed team he played from 2009-18, the time covered by the charges. Pictured: Haaland in action for Molde in 2018

Your browser does not support iframes.

'But it's a difficult question to answer when I don't really know that much about it. 'I assume the answers will come… I don't know when. I haven't read much about it. 'To be completely honest, I'm focused on trying to perform for Manchester City. 'A club I signed a five-year deal with in 2022 and a new nine-and-a-half-year deal in late 2024. I think that says everything about the matter. I'm a City player, and I'm incredibly happy there.' Man City have continued to insist they had 'irrefutable evidence' proving their innocence, but if the club loses its appeal, the Premier League have a range of sanctions at their disposal – including relegation or expulsion. Haaland, who has won eight major honours at the club including the Treble in 2023, was asked about whether the case has affected his thoughts on his Man City future. 'I understand that you want a little headline here, but as I said, I signed a long-term contract in 2024,' Haaland responded. 'I'd say I made a pretty good choice by joining City in 2022. We can all agree on that. I won't say it myself, but look at the trophies I've won and how I've developed on and off the pitch. 'I'm standing here after winning an international 3-1 and we're top of our group in Europe. 'Things aren't going so well for City in the league, but we'll try to turn that around against Fulham. But we can't focus on that now. Now we have to focus on Denmark.' Man City have won twice and lost three times in the Premier League since the independent commission verdict was announced in September. Enzo Maresca's side have slipped to six points behind reigning champions Arsenal following their drop off in form.

Sports.title: Jarrad Branthwaite left out of England squad for Nations League decider with Spain - as James Hill and Dan Burn leapfrog defender in Thomas Tuchel's pecking order
Sports.content:
Jarrad Branthwaite has been left out of England’s matchday squad for the Nations League decider in Spain, raising questions over his future involvement under Thomas Tuchel. The Everton centre back’s omission means that two rivals who were not in the original squad but were added last week, Dan Burn and James Hill, are now seemingly ahead of him in the pecking order. There was a clue as to Tuchel’s uncertainty over Branthwaite when, ahead of last Thursday's Croatia game, he revealed concerns over his suitability to England’s way of playing. ‘Jarrad Branthwaite is doing very well but it's a very different style of play for him from Everton towards us,’ said the head coach. Tuchel then selected Burn ahead of him for the 2-1 win, and said: ‘You can see that Dan Burn is straight away a big voice in training and is more used to the style with Newcastle from the last two seasons with Eddie Howe, where they followed in a high press and man-to-man.’ It had been thought that Branthwaite, 24, could emerge as a starter at left-sided centre back, given his good club form this season. That now feels unlikely, with Burn and Marc Guehi, who is currently injured, preferred by Tuchel. Jarrad Branthwaite has been left out of the England squad for their clash against Spain James Hill and Dan Burn, who were both added to the England squad last week, appear to have jumped above Branthwaite in the pecking order Branthwaite has made two substitute appearances under the German, totalling 28 minutes. Also left out of the matchday squad for Sunday’s game in Madrid are Josh King and James Garner. Everton midfielder Garner came off the bench against Croatia at Wembley and thought he had scored his first England goal, only for VAR to rule it out for offside. He now misses the chance to build on that cameo against the world champions. For King, 19, the wait for a senior debut continues after his maiden call-up, a reward for an impressive start to the season with Fulham. Tuchel was forced to trim three players from his 26-man travelling squad, with the return to fitness of defenders Ezri Konsa and Djed Spence increasing competition for places.
