Sports.title: Distraught Rory McIlroy breaks down in tears as he reveals his dad Gerry has been in hospital for two months after undergoing 'huge operation'
Sports.content:
A tearful Rory McIlroy revealed his father underwent a double lung transplant and has been in hospital for two months after equalling Colin Montgomerie's record of eight Race to Dubai titles on Sunday.

The world No 2 had just secured the DP World Tour's order of merit crown for a fifth straight year in Dubai when he disclosed in a post-tournament interview that Gerry McIlroy, 67, underwent a 'huge operation' in September.

He later clarified the sheer scale of the ongoing trauma by detailing that McIlroy Snr has battled his health issues for 18 months and a transplant was the 'last resort'. McIlroy added that his father is now 'recovering well' in hospital in Cleveland, having visited him before jetting to the Middle East for the end of the DP World Tour season.

McIlroy said: 'My dad is a massive part of my life, and has been my biggest supporter, is the one that got me into the game and the one that told me to follow my dreams and never give up. It's obviously been difficult.

'He's been living with this for a while, for 18 months, and it got to the point where the last resort was he needed a transplant, so he had a double-lung transplant in September. Thankfully, operation was a success and he's recovering well.

'It's been a stressful time for our family. I've been up in Cleveland a lot because that's where he is. I didn't know if I was going to go to India (last month) because I spent nine days in the ICU with him while he was recovering.

Rory McIlroy broke down in tears as he revealed his father's ongoing health issues on Sunday

Gerry McIlroy (left) has been in hospital in Cleveland for two months after a 'huge operation'

'If things were not looking as good as they were, I probably wouldn't have felt comfortable travelling or being too far away. But he's got an amazing team up there, and the doctors and nurses are absolutely incredible.

'So I felt comfortable going to India and travelling and knowing that I could obviously get back to him if I needed to, but he was obviously in wonderful hands.

'He's been making a really steady recovery. I went up to see him before I left a couple of weeks ago, and he said to me, "Rors, go and win me The Race to Dubai".

'That was in my head for the last two weeks, and I really wanted to do it for him and I know he's in hospital in his hospital bed, and he would have been watching this morning. It was nice to be able to get it done for him.'

McIlroy is extremely close to his father and often speaks about the sacrifices his father made for him to be able to reach the top of the golfing world.

Gerry has been by Rory's side throughout his life, including when he completed the Grand Slam

Gerry and Rory still maintain a healthy rivalry on the golf course and play together often

Growing up as an only child in Holywood, Northern Ireland, McIlroy's father worked multiple jobs to finance his career, with his mother Rosie doing the same.

Back in 2024, McIlroy celebrated his father's 65th birthday by playing the Old Course at St Andrews with him, and the pair still enjoy a healthy rivalry on the golf course.

McIlroy delivered on his father's wish by finishing second in the DP World Tour Championship behind Tyrrell Hatton, allowing him to pip Eugenio Chacarra on the final day of the season-long points race.

The historical significance should not be understated – matching Montgomerie's record haul is considerable in its own right, let alone for a player who spends the majority of his season on the PGA Tour.

McIlroy said: 'Winning eight Order of Merits was never really in my list of goals when I was growing up. I remember Monty being obviously a stalwart of the European Tour, going to watch him at the World Match Play at Wentworth over the years. I remember playing with him for the first time at The London Club at The European Open in 2008.

McIlroy's parents Gerry and Rosie both worked multiple jobs to be able to fund his golf career

McIlroy hugs dad Gerry and mom Rosie after winning the Masters at Augusta in April 2026

'So to pull up alongside him and to win eight of these things, yeah, it means the world to me. I'm a very proud European player. I'm proud to be a part of the DP World Tour.'

Hatton's win on the Earth Course capped a strong season, albeit a turbulent one, with the Englishman having finished third at the Masters before he went on to claim a title on the LIV circuit in June.

The 35-year-old's rebound from the demise of LIV has been impressive – this was his ninth DP World Tour crown and followed a runner-up spot in Abu Dhabi a week ago.

Hatton, whose 15-under-par total left him five clear of McIlroy, said: 'This is really special. I was really nervous today. I didn't say anything to anyone in my team, but I've had a bit of heartbreak around here, and I felt like it was going to be a difficult day. I'm just really proud. It feels so good to win here.'

Sports.title: Tom Banton makes another England statement with match-winning century in 135-run win over Australia as Harry Brook has many welcome selection headaches ahead of the World Cup - but first the tourists must triumph in Hobart, writes LAWRENCE BOOTH
Sports.content:
Tom Banton makes another England statement with match-winning century in 135-run win over Australia as Harry Brook has many welcome selection headaches ahead of the World Cup - but first the tourists must triumph in Hobart, writes LAWRENCE BOOTH

After England squared their one-day series in Australia with a thumping 135-run win at Adelaide, Daily Mail Sport examines the pressing questions ahead of Wednesday’s decider in Hobart – and beyond.

Have England now got their openers for the World Cup?

Ben Duckett has begun this series with a pair of nines, but his last two scores in the tri-series in Pakistan were 105 and 167, and it is hard to see how he misses out in southern Africa next year.

And with Jacob Bethell still recuperating from knee trouble, Tom Banton has risen to the challenge. His sparkling 121 off 99 balls in Adelaide took his record since becoming an ODI opener to 540 runs at 60, with a strike-rate of 110. He, not Bethell, is in pole position.

Will Harry ever make it Down Under?

Australians still can’t understand what all the fuss is about Harry Brook. His riotous strokeplay threatened to make him a figure of fun during last winter’s Ashes, and he began this series with a twitchy waft in Perth, where he was caught behind off Mahli Beardman for a single.

In Adelaide, where a year ago he was bowled attempting an extravagant reverse sweep off Nathan Lyon, he moved across his crease to Riley Meredith and helped a miscued scoop straight on to middle stump.

Out for just five, Brook threw back his head in anguish, but it was the kind of frivolity that doesn’t play well with Australian crowds. He could do with a score at Hobart.

Tom Banton has risen to the challenge in Jacob Bethell's absence and looks in pole position to open for England at the World Cup

Harry Brook's struggles continued in Australia with the batsman out for just five in Adelaide

Does Jordan Cox automatically make way when Jos Buttler is finally fit again?

Cox batted with characteristic swagger to make 67 off 49 balls, including an outrageous reverse sweep for four off seamer Xavier Bartlett, played a split second before he landed on both knees. It was the stroke of a player who will look back on 2026 as his breakthrough year.

But there is no room for both him and Buttler, who is still on the mend after hamstring surgery, since that would involve dropping a bowler. For all his talent, Cox may yet be in for a frustrating World Cup.

Is there any way back for Adil Rashid?

England’s best-ever white-ball spinner has now missed their last five ODIs, with Liam Dawson edging into pole position first in Pakistan and now in Australia.

The selectors felt Rashid hadn’t been at his best as he recovered from a hand injury sustained during September’s T20 series against Sri Lanka, but they also want Dawson’s extra batting to allow them to play three specialist quicks down the order, and Brook enjoys Dawson’s experience in the field – even if he did badly drop Cameron Green at deep midwicket seven runs into his eventual 64.

It’s hard to see how both spinners play in the same team, unless England leave out Sam Curran, and push Dawson up a place to No7 – which looks like too lengthy a tail.

And will they leave out Curran?

It was telling that Will Jacks, supposedly tasked with finishing the innings, batted above Curran in Adelaide. At Perth, Curran had been bounced out for a seven-ball duck by Beardman, just the latest example of his struggles against the short stuff. Now down at No7, he was caught on the fence for 14.

Jacks, by contrast, is turning into a significant white-ball cricketer, and followed his 25 in Perth with an effortless unbeaten 54 off 40 balls, helping England to 355 for six, their highest ODI total in Australia.

Increasingly, the management are wondering whether Curran – who has underwhelming ODI batting and bowling averages of 22 and 40 – is not better suited to T20 cricket. He did find himself on a hat-trick, having yorked Jack Edwards with his slower ball, but 9.50 an over made him the game’s most expensive bowler.

Jordan Cox batted with characteristic swagger to make 67 off 49 balls, but will he make way when Jos Buttler is back fit?

England's seamers will be central to their chances of winning the decider in Hobart

How important is Hobart on Wednesday?

Very. England’s failure to reach the final of the tri-series in Pakistan after throwing away two apparently unlosable matches stalled the 50-over progress they had made in 2026, with series wins over Sri Lanka (twice) and India. But victory here, even against an Australian side fielding a second-string attack, would lift spirits going into the five-match T20 series, starting in Melbourne on Saturday.

Central to their chances will be their frontline seamers. Gus Atkinson dismissed Travis Head cheaply for the second time in three days en route to a career-best four for 28, while Jofra Archer went for just three an over. Sonny Baker, meanwhile, offered more oomph than Jamie Overton had at Perth, and removed Mitchell Marsh for two thanks to a screamer in the slips by Joe Root.

Sports.title: Ashley Cole accidentally shooting a student, bare-chested Marcus Bent threatening police with a meat cleaver - and an ex-Barcelona star firing a gun in a hospital! Footballers' fascination with weapons after Amar Dedic's bow and arrows saga
Sports.content:
Amar Dedic might have fancied himself as Robin Hood – but the Newcastle United defender's latest adventure in the Northumberland countryside led to a rather less merry altercation with police last week.

The Magpies star sparked a major police operation after being spotted carrying a bow and arrows near a reservoir outside Newcastle, with at least six patrol cars joining the search for the £30million player.

After tracking down and questioning the Bosnian, officers were satisfied there was no threat to the public and that the equipment was intended for recreational use.

But Dedic's escapade was certainly not the first time a footballer has found himself in hot water over the possession, carrying or use of a weapon, with brass knuckles, meat cleavers and BB guns among the bizarre arsenal of items to have attracted the authorities' attention over the years.

Marcus Bent, with a meat cleaver, in Surrey

Former Middlesbrough and Everton forward Marcus Bent was tasered in his own home by police after threatening armed police officers with a meat cleaver and kitchen knife while under the influence of cocaine.

Bent, who avoided jail in 2016 after he pleaded guilty to possession of cocaine and affray, called Surrey Police after thinking he had discovered an intruder in his home.

Officers arrived at the scene but were initially unable to gain access to the property. Guildford Crown Court heard how the officers were about to use a battering ram to gain entry when a bare-chested Bent 'flung' open the door holding two chef's knives, with his 'eyes wide, jaw clenched and his body rigid'.

Bent, who was handed a 12-month sentence, suspended for two years, later said: 'I was paranoid and I was hallucinating. I felt there were people in my house. I remember thinking the door handle was moving.

'At no point was I ever going to take someone's life. I called them because I was hallucinating, paranoid, terrified.'

Marcus Bent arrives at court before pleading guilty to possession of cocaine and affray

Ashley Cole, with an air rifle, in Cobham

To most, Ashley Cole is England's all-time greatest full-back but the three-time Premier League winner also made headlines for an infamous training ground air rifle incident.

Back in 2011 while playing for Chelsea, Ashley Cole accidentally shot and injured 21-year-old student Tom Cowan, who was on work experience at the Blues' training ground in Cobham, Surrey.

The Champions League winning left-back was reportedly 'larking about' with a .22 air rifle and accidentally shot Cowan from just five feet away.

The student had assumed he would get an invaluable experience on his brief visit to Cobham but instead had to be treated by medics and rest for the remainder of the day after the shot was fired.

Cole accidentally shot a 21-year-old on work experience at Chelsea's training ground

Darren Bent, with a BB Gun, in Kesgrave

Ex-England star Darren Bent ran into trouble early in his career when he was questioned over the alleged shooting of a 12-year-old boy with a ball-bearing gun.

While starring for his boyhood club Ipswich at the age of 20 in May 2004, Bent was arrested on suspicion of possession of an imitation firearm with intent to cause violence, before he was placed on bail and eventually released without charge pending further investigations.

According to a Suffolk Police statement at the time, a 12-year-old boy at a play area in Kesgrave had been struck in the back by a pellet from a ball-bearing gun (BB Gun). The incident was reported to authorities by his mother.

Bent, who was given a formal caution for his actions, went on to enjoy a fruitful career in the Premier League, representing the likes of Charlton, Tottenham, Sunderland and Aston Villa while also winning 13 caps for the Three Lions.

Early on his career Premier League legend Darren Bent was arrested on suspicion of possession of an imitation firearm

Karim Adeyemi, with brass knuckles, in Germany

The only member of this list to still be playing is Germany and Barcelona's Karim Adeyemi who was fined £396,000 in 2025 for possessing a pair of brass knuckles.

The former Borussia Dortmund forward was caught with the knuckles back in 2024, at the age of 22, but had to wait until the following year to receive his punishment.

Under German law the possession, procurement and use of brass knuckles is prohibited. The young winger avoided a public trial and a criminal record and was given a fine consisting of 60 daily payments of £6,600.

Although he never used the weapon, the German was in hot water as he briefly lost his starting place in the German national team and at Borussia Dortmund.

The Westphalia giants released a statement saying: 'BVB always takes criminal allegations seriously and uses them as an opportunity to discuss them with its employees while respecting confidentiality obligations.'

Adeyemi was lucky to dodge prison time after being charged with the possession of brass knuckles

Diego Maradona, with an air rifle, in Buenos Aires

Argentina icon Diego Maradona caused injuries to four people when he fired an air rifle at journalists and photographers while hiding behind a parked Mercedes outside his Buenos Aires home in February 1994.

Four years later, Maradona was found guilty of assault with a weapon and given a suspended prison sentence of two years and ten months, which was later reduced to an even two years.

To many he is the best of all time but Diego Maradona is hardly infallible off the pitch

Despite appealing against the sentence which they claimed was 'too light', the journalists injured by Maradona said the verdict at least demonstrated there was 'justice for all' in Argentina.

'At least this exemplary case does show that there is justice for all,' said Daniel Talamoni, one of the four reporters who sued the World Cup winner.

'When the case began four years ago, everyone said it was impossible. They would sentence a man idolised in Argentina and forgive everything.'

Arda Turan, with an unlicensed gun, in a Turkish hospital

Keen fans of European football will not need to be reminded of who Arda Turan is. But they may be surprised to learn that the former Atletico Madrid and Barcelona star has had some serious trouble with the law.

Turan somehow avoided a jail sentence after discharging an unlicensed firearm in a hospital

In 2018 while on loan from Barcelona in his home country of Turkey at Istanbul Basaksehir, Turan got into an altercation with Turkish singer Berkay Sahin, who ended in hospital with a broken nose.

Then Turan turned up at the hospital that was treating Sahin with an unlicensed firearm, and fired a shot into the floor.

He was eventually sentenced to two years and eight months behind bars for firing a gun to cause panic, illegal possession of weapons and intentional injury but the sentence was suspended for five years. Basaksehir also fined the midfielder £350,000 over the incident.

Nearly a decade after the incident, Turan now manages Ukrainian powerhouse Shakhtar Donetsk, joining the club in May of last year.

Sports.title: Merab Dvalishvili calls for attackers to be released during his victory speech - as UFC star wins Abu Dhabi event days after being bloodied in hotel brawl
Sports.content:
Merab Dvalishvili calls for attackers to be released during his victory speech - as UFC star wins Abu Dhabi event days after being bloodied in hotel brawl

Merab Dvalishvili called for the release of Usman Nurmagomedov and his entourage in a victory speech after he was attacked in an Abu Dhabi hotel earlier this week.

Nurmagomedov set upon UFC star Merab Dvalishvili on Wednesday, slapping him in the lobby of Yas Hilton hotel in a revenge mission filmed by his friends.

The Georgian-American Dvalishvili then retaliated and fought back with his cameraman as the melee rapidly descended into complete mayhem.

Dvalishvili was left bloodied and bruised and the attackers were quickly detained by the authorities.

Six of the attackers were given six-month prison sentences and ordered to pay £61,000 each in fines. They will also be immediately deported when their sentences end.

Despite being left bloodied by the attack, Dvalishvili still competed at a RAF wrestling event on Saturday in Abu Dhabi.

Merab Dvalishvili used his victory speech to call for the release of Usman Nurmagomedov and his entourage after he was attacked in an Abu Dhabi hotel earlier this week. Source: X/@ChampRDS

Despite the attack in midweek, Dvalishvili triumphed at the RAF wrestling event on Saturday. Source: X/@ChampRDS

Dvalishvili overcame Brazil's Marlon Moraes within 90 seconds of their showdown at the Etihad Arena, before using his victory speech to call for the release of Nurmagomedov and his associates.

'If you can, Abu Dhabi Government or whoever can do it please release those guys, please let them out,' Dvalishvili said.

'Please, because we are just fighters and these things can happen, but I want them out, please.'

Dvalishvili's plea had been met by applause and cheers from a section of fans inside the venue.

He earlier shared a statement on social media, where he insisted he would not press charges over the attack.

'I want to thank everyone in Abu Dhabi for your help in resolving this matter. I love visiting Abu Dhabi and am happy to be welcomed,' Dvalishvili wrote.

'I do hope that they release everyone - I would not press charges. I want peace and the best for all. Thanks everyone for your love and support.'

Usman Nurmagomedov (left) was the one who initiated the brawl by slapping Dvalishvili - his brother Umar (right) lost a title shot against the Georgian last year

The Abu Dhabi court shared this post online confirming the punishments for the attackers earlier this week

Nurmagomedov and his entourage were punished for having caused 'panic, disturbed public security and endangered lives' in the attack on Wednesday.

Two of Nurmagomedov's associates were fined £10,000 each for 'disturbing public security and assaulting others'.

And the other two members of the group who recorded the assault were given six-month sentences, £61,000 fines and confiscation of the devices used.

They were punished 'for violating privacy by using information technology to film and publish footage of the brawl'.

Nurmagomedov and his team's violent ambush was four months in the making.

Back in July, Dvalishvili was competing in a RAF event in Georgia, which is a freestyle wrestling show the UFC allow their fighters to compete in outside of the day job.

While milling around at the event, a Dagestani wrestler and friend of Umar, Ahmed Gadzhimagomedov, confronted Dvalishvili about refusing to entertain a rematch of any kind with Umar.

'I was super relaxed, super chilled and then somebody (Gadzhimagomedov) came and grabbed my neck and pulled me over and started yelling at me in Russian language, which I hardly understand,' Dvalishvili told Ariel Helwani.

'And he mentioned Umar. It took me a couple of seconds to realize, "Who is this guy to tell me what to talk about him?"

'It’s between me and Umar… I have so much respect for all Dagestani people, especially fighters. The only guy who I don't like from Dagestan is Umar and his sneaky manager, Rizvan. The guy who was helping Umar disrespect me on X and Threads.'

After Gadzhimagomedov squared up to him, Dvalishvili shoved him in the neck, shouting: 'What's your problem, b***h!'

The situation, unlike the hotel brawl that escalated into a complete bloodbath, was quickly defused and there was a child in close proximity.

UFC star Dvalishvili, who was left bloodied after the attack in a five-star hotel in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday, has insisted he does not want to press charges

The 35-year-old was blind sided while carrying out an interview

Usman wanted to take revenge on behalf of fellow Dagestani Gadzhimagomedov and also his brother Umar, who lost against Dvalishvili in a title shot last year.

In the footage of the hotel attack, the group appeared to approach Dvalishvili, 35, from behind, before one man said a couple of words to him and slapped him in the face.

Dvalishvili was rocked, then kicked, and was held back by a man he appeared to be with.

He tried to fight back but a number of men overwhelmed him as his companion was attacked too. Eventually, the groups were separated, and Dvalishvili took to social media to respond to the incident.

He said in a video, bloody and bruised as he received treatment: 'What a sneaky way guys. Just two of us, me and my friend, came here in Abu Dhabi and Usman and his friends came like snakes from behind. What kind of fighters are you guys? What kind of man does this? If you want to fight, let's do it the real way.

'You guys came when there was two of us, you were prepared. What the f***.'

His companion then added: 'From behind? You call yourselves men? You're a little b***h.'

Dvalishvili continued: 'You are sneaky guys. You are not real men. It shows your guys' character, what the f*** guys? If you want to fight, let's fight. We are fighters. I talk straight, but you guys came from behind. I don't know how many guys, all your friends waiting for us in a sneaky way, wow.

'I knew guys, I knew what kind of guys you were. Usman, Umar and his friends came sneaky from behind, so many guys. Wow. I am fine guys. All my friends and family, I am f***ing fine. I am a fighter. This is nothing for me, but it shows what kind of people you guys are. P***ys do this bro. We are warriors.'

Sports.title: Youngsters will get their chance, Bruno Fernandes can thrive and touchline energy will be vital: Key lessons for Man United from incoming boss Mauricio Pochettino's 6-0 USA masterclass
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino enjoyed a stellar penultimate game in charge of the United States, thrashing Haiti 6-0.

The newly appointed Manchester United manager has just one game left before sinking his teeth into the job at Old Trafford.

He will link up with United on Wednesday, but first must navigate the second leg of their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final tie with Haiti on Tuesday.

Here, Pochettino cut a fairly reserved figure on the touchline as he was rewarded for trusting youth - and even saw his team score from a corner, something United don't do much of these days.

Without further ado, here are four things Manchester United fans learned from the win.

Mauricio Pochettino, dressed in a scarf, was fairly reserved as the United States beat Haiti 6-0

Youth will get a chance

Pochettino’s arrival spells good news for United’s proud tradition of promoting homegrown youth - it is glad tidings for the likes of Shea Lacey and Kobbie Mainoo. You wonder if, for a while, JJ Gabriel will look on forlornly from Real Madrid’s reserves.

The Argentinian handed out 13 debuts in the September-October international break, including to eight teenagers in one 4-1 victory over Peru.

His strategy was no different here as he started 18-year-old Julian Hall up front and Diego Kochen, 20, in goal - both players he has given debuts to this year. He was rewarded, with Hall scoring his fourth goal in just five games for the United States, while Kochen kept a clean sheet.

Despite his affinity for the stars of tomorrow, he is a hard schoolmaster. In a column for The Athletic in 2022, he revealed that he sat a young Harry Kane down for a brutal meeting where he showed him stats and clips to justify why he wasn’t playing him more.

Pochettino had known Kane’s potential from their first training session but wanted the ‘tough conversation’ to get the best out of him. Kane went on to score 169 goals under him for Tottenham, and now he’s the best player in the world.

His trust in fresh faces could inject some much-needed enthusiasm around the club, strengthen the squad's connection with the fanbase, and increase the energy levels in one of the Premier League's oldest, most lethargic teams.

The likes of Shea Lacey will be delighted at how Pochettino puts trust in younger players

Julian Hall, 18, struck his fourth goal in five games for the United States under Pochettino

The perfect manager for Bruno Fernandes?

Pochettino has a history of getting the most out of attacking midfielders such as Dele Alli, Christian Eriksen, and Adam Lallana. You can add Cole Palmer to that list too, though he was primarily a right winger under him at Chelsea.

Manchester United desperately need him to get a tune out of Bruno Fernandes, who has cut a frustrated figure this season and whose creative efficiency has declined - though he still has nine goal involvements.

If Christian Pulisic’s performance against Haiti is anything to go by, Fernandes will be happy. The attacking midfielder scored twice, playing a free role and being given penalty duty.

The 28-year-old was also asked to muck in defensively, and that’s something Fernandes is willing to do. Across the seasons, he has often covered more ground than any of his team-mates.

Pochettino and Pulisic have seemingly had a distant relationship, despite the latter’s insistence to the contrary. The manager branded it ‘b*******’ when the AC Milan star opted out of the Gold Cup last year, and left him out of his selection a couple of months ago, bringing in 16-year-old Cavan Sullivan.

Asked about Pochettino's upcoming final game, Pulisic said at full-time: 'We're treating it like any other game.' No emotion on display.

Depending on how you interpret Fernandes - either a die-for-the-badge club servant or a primadonna - Pochettino could draw the best or worst out of the Portuguese.

Pochettino often gets the best out of attacking midfielders - will he work well with Bruno Fernandes?

He has had a distant relationship with Christian Pulisic, but the AC Milan star scored twice here

Defenders to push up high?

Pochettino tends to push his defensive lines high up the pitch and his strategy with the United States has been no different.

They were almost caught out for trying to play the offside trap early on as a simple ball from midfield sent Danley Jean Jacques through one-on-one, forcing Kochen into a good save.

Meanwhile, full-backs Antonee Robinson and Alex Freeman were constantly pushing high and overlapping in his 4-2-3-1 system - although you’d obviously expect a strong level of intent when they’re favourites against Haiti.

Given his high-line tradition, Pochettino may well favour more mobile defenders such as Leny Yoro and Patrick Dorgu.

The battle for Harry Maguire will be to convince his new boss that his other qualities compensate for his lack of pace.

Pochettino takes inspiration from the frenetic football of Marcelo Bielsa, who managed him at Newell’s Old Boys in Argentina.

But he'll have to balance his philosophy with the reality of United's woeful defensive record this campaign. Just the 15 goals conceded in the last five games...

Pochettino showed an eagerness to intervene early in the game - a possible boost after Michael Carrick suffered from slow starts

How will his touchline work compare to Carrick?

Pochettino is typically seen as an animated character on the touchline, in contrast to Carrick's statesmanlike behaviour, but he spent lots of time in his seat here.

He has calmed down somewhat these days - though he did kick a crate of bottles in frustration at the World Cup - and didn’t even react much when his team scored.

A major criticism of Carrick is that he takes too long to change things in-game, often going late with substitutions. Pochettino has traditionally leaned that way, too, but he was eager to influence proceedings here.

Even three minutes in, at a break while Antonee Robinson was being treated, he called Pulisic over for what looked like an intense tactical chat.

United have been plagued by slow starts this season, so it was encouraging to see Pochettino so alert and full of ideas early into the game. He could have coasted, really, but wanted to eke out every advantage.

Sports.title: Ex-Australia Test fast bowler Chadd Sayers rejects Pat Cummins' denials over Sandpapergate scandal as he claims 'everyone knew' and a meeting of '60 to 90 minutes' was held after incident was exposed
Sports.content:
Chadd Sayers, the Australian seamer who won his only Test cap on the infamous tour of South Africa eight years ago, has backed up Usman Khawaja's version of the sandpaper controversy - and called into question Pat Cummins's vehement denial.

During an in-depth interview on SEN Radio before the second one-day international in Adelaide, Sayers insisted that Australia had used sandpaper during the second Test at Port Elizabeth, that more than three members of the team knew, and that there was a dressing-room meeting of '60 to 90 minutes' to discuss the subject after the plans were exposed in the third Test at Cape Town.

Sayers's testimony comes two days after Cummins called Khawaja's claims of team-wide collusion 'complete and utter nonsense'.

Asked what he thought of Cummins' press conference in Sydney, Sayers replied: 'To be honest, I didn't watch much of it. I saw him rock up and start talking and it just felt a bit awkward and, yeah, I just didn't want to see that.'

He added: 'I didn't like how he did go at Usman and got personal. I probably get why but I just don't think it needed to happen.'

Sayers, now 39, won his only cap in the fourth Test at Johannesburg, and said he had no axe to grind, describing himself as 'neutral in all this'.

Chadd Sayers (pictured), a member of the Australian Test touring party in South Africa in 2018, said every player knew sandpaper was being used on the ball

His comments contradict Australian Test captain Pat Cummins' (pictured) denial, and support Usman Khawaja's recollections

Khawaja's autobiography has seen the spotlight shine brightly once again on what happened

He said he was first aware of the use of sandpaper to rough up the ball and achieve reverse swing at Port Elizabeth, and went on: 'It was used in two Test matches and there was discussions in change rooms of how we were going to get the ball to reverse and what was going to be used.'

Sayers said the plan at Port Elizabeth was that 'Cameron Bancroft was going to take [the sandpaper] out, the ball was going to be dropped on the on the ground by the umpires and he was going to go about business'.

As 12th man, Sayers was then given the sandpaper to take off at a break after tea.

Asked if he felt uncomfortable about his role, he replied: 'Probably at the time, no. I was trying to fit into the Australian side, probably similar to Cam Bancroft and we were a young demographic then.

'I didn't know how big it was going to get, and I guess you probably don't think you're going to get caught doing it. Just going along with everyone else and trying to win a game of cricket.'

Cummins claimed there had been no team meeting after the plot was exposed at Cape Town, but Sayers said: 'We all sat in the change rooms after that day's play and probably for 60 to 90 minutes we talked about what had happened and I guess where to next. I guess at that stage we probably didn't know the severity back in Australia as well.'

Sayers said he was never interviewed by Cricket Australia, despite being told to stay close to the team hotel in the immediate aftermath, in case he was required to give evidence.

He said he didn't know why he wasn't summoned: 'Not really, but maybe because we were 12th man and we didn't play in the game. Maybe because we knew too much information. I'm not too sure.

'It's been hard because you've obviously got to tip-toe around and not be able to tell the truth. It's probably a relief now that it's out there in the open, because we all know it gets brought up a lot of places you go.'

Was it credible that Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc didn't know about the plans?

'I would have thought as a team, when you're trying to get the ball to reverse, that everyone would buy in, because if one little thing goes wrong in the field to the ball, it stops it from reversing straight away,' said Sayers.

'So yeah, as I said, I'm pretty confident to say that everyone knew.'

Sports.title: Kalajdzic scores late as Republic of Ireland taste defeat in Austria
Sports.content:
Sasa Kalajdzic dealt the Republic of Ireland a late blow in Linz with the only goal in Austria's 1-0 Nations League victory at the Raiffeisen Arena.

The result ensured that, no matter how the closing contests in Group B play out, Austria sealed promotion to League A.

Ireland enter Tuesday's critical home clash at the Aviva Stadium in third place, with one point fewer than their final opponents, Kosovo.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men were not without chances, but only Kalajdzic made one count when he broke the deadlock in the 79th minute.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson urges UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem

Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw

Ireland's head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has called for UEFA to keep his team and Israel separate in future

Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

Image: Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during the national anthem

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.
