World.title: The R500 000 homes of the West Rand, where it’s cheaper to buy than rent
World.content:
Tucked in Roodepoort on the West Rand, you’ll find Grobler Park.

The average sectional title in the area sells for R600 000, with more than a handful of homes on sale for under R500 000.

Are they worth it?



The perfect suburb for your first home

Young South Africans are frequently asked why they rent when they can buy. But very few areas have a bond that’s comparable to rent.

Grobler Park is an exception.

Sectional titles in the area start at R400 000.

According to the newest Grobler Park listing on Private Property, a buyer can purchase a 2-bedroom flat in a security complex for R400 000. Municipal rates on this home are R292, and levies are R742.

With a bond, the total cost of homeownership for a property like this in Grobler Park is R5 000.

But it’s not limited to one listing.



Grobler Park has more than half a dozen properties listed below R500 000.

Typically, these are 2-bedroom properties.

Occasionally, a 3-bedroom property will become available in this price range.

All have reasonable rates and levies. The average for both rates and levies is between R1 000 and R1 500.

Family homes in the area start at R770 000.

How does renting compare to owning in Grobler Park?

Rent on a 2-bedroom flat starts at R5 500, roughly 8% more than you would pay to own the same residence.

This at least offers buyers some return should they decide to move, as they can still benefit from higher rents.

But selling up when you’re ready to move on from Grobler Park won’t be easy.

In September, despite 270 residential listings, Grobler Park recorded 4 sales.

Property prices, like much of Gauteng, have also stagnated in Grobler Park.

In 2017, the average sale price was R580 000. By the end of 2025, it was R630 000.

But if your goal is to have a place you own that you call home, Grobler Park still has the perfect family vibe.

Raising a family in Grobler Park

Data from the South African Deeds Registry shows most buyers in Grobler Park are between 36 and 49, followed by buyers under 35.

The area is full of young families who can benefit from great feeder schools.

For primary schools, there’s Constantia Kloof Primary School and Laërskool Dr Havinga, where school fees start at R18 000 a year.

For high school, parents have half a dozen choices, including Hoërskool Die Adelaar and Hoërskool Roodepoort; both schools perform better than other high schools in the area.

However, traffic can become quite severe when driving east to Sandton during peak periods. A 43-kilometre trip that should take 50 minutes in light traffic conditions can take up to two hours.

World.title: Explainer : Why your child may end up in a different school
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Gauteng Education is racing against time to place pupils in schools for the 2027 Academic Year.

While some households will receive a notification of a successful placement at a selected school, others will have to adjust to a whole new school.

Gauteng Education MEC Lebogang Maile revealed that more than 77,000 applicants are yet to be placed, with Grade 8 pupils making up the largest share.

According to Maile, the department has identified more than 139,000 available spaces, but acknowledges that these are not necessarily in the schools or communities where demand is highest.

READ | Over 77,000 pupils in Gauteng remain unplaced

To date, 278 schools have reached capacity, including 174 primary schools and 104 secondary schools.

Pressure, according to Maile, remains concentrated in key urban centres, with the highest volumes recorded in districts located within the metropolitan municipalities of Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni.

This revelation by the provincial government may leave many parents, some still clinging to their phones for a notification, with one question: When and where will my child be placed?

Maile indicated that unplaced applicants who cannot be accommodated at these 278 schools are being transferred to the next closest school with available space.

“Gauteng does not experience uniform pressure across its schooling system. Some schools have available capacity, while others receive substantially more applications than they can reasonably accommodate. “Consequently, the challenge is not simply to count available spaces. It is to align those spaces with learner demand, geographical accessibility, school infrastructure and the practical circumstances of families,” Maile explained.

Maile said areas of high demand must be understood within the country's broader spatial and geo-social realities.

READ | Gauteng's 2027 school placement scramble

Not only does Gauteng have the highest population, but it also experiences a significant in-migration, with many turning to the province for employment or to improve their livelihoods.

These implications, according to the MEC, are evident in the province's schooling system.

“With an annual population growth of 1.6%, which outpaces the national average of 1.2 %, the province’s growth results in greater demand for schools, classrooms, educators, transport and associated infrastructure, "Maile added.

Maile said these pressure areas remain the primary focus for placement interventions, capacity optimisation and transfer management to maximise available spaces and reduce the number of unplaced applicants.

He said as of 13 November 2026, the Department commenced issuing transfer offers.

These offers are intended to help address outstanding placements, particularly where schools originally selected by applicants have reached capacity.

World.title: Gauteng's 2027 school placement scramble
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Parents and guardians of Grade 1 and Grade 8 pupils who have not been placed at their desired school due to capacity will be issued transfer offers to alternative schools.

They will then have seven days to accept or decline the offer.

This is according to Gauteng Education MEC Lebogang Maile, who gave an update on placement for the 2027 academic year, scholar transport as well as school funding.

Maile said the issuing of transfer offers began on 13 November and forms part of the admission process.

To date, more than 77,000 applicants are yet to be placed, with Grade 8 pupils making up the largest share.

READ | Over 77,000 pupils in Gauteng remain unplaced

The department says it has identified more than 139,000 available spaces, but acknowledges that these are not necessarily in the schools or communities where demand is highest.

“We understand that receiving an offer from a school other than a preferred institution may not be preferable. However, it is important to recognise that the Department must balance individual preferences with the available capacity of schools and the obligation to provide access to education across the province,” he said.

Parents and guardians who want to challenge placement outcomes will also be given an opportunity to raise objections and appeals through an established process.

An objection may be lodged within the prescribed seven-day period, with the Department required to consider and determine it within the applicable 14-day period.

World.title: The new Miss SA and the missing Mowana crown: Nungu Diamonds explains
World.content:
JOHANNESURG - Tiyani Makamu is South Africa's new beauty Queen.

But the 27-year-old's crowning on Saturday night was not without controversy, as social media attention turned to the crown on her head.

While many hailed the moment, others questioned why she did not wear the iconic Mowana crown by Nungu Diamonds.

Nungu Diamonds, which took note of the commentary, broke their silence on Sunday in a statement, explaining the crown and their relationship with the Miss South Africa Organisation.

READ | Miss SA 2025 | Qhawekazi Mazaleni crowned new queen

The fine jewellery company set the record straight, saying Nungu Diamonds did not design, craft, or supply the 2026 Miss South Africa crown.

This follows the non-renewal of a sponsorship agreement with the Miss South Africa Organisation for the 2026 pageant.

“Negotiations were conducted in good faith and continued into the final days before the finale; the parties were ultimately unable to reach a mutually beneficial agreement,” the statement read.

The company says its representatives had initially granted Miss South Africa permission to use the Mowana Crown at the finale on the understanding that sponsorship discussions would resume after the event.

However, it seems Miss SA opted otherwise

“The decision not to use the Mowana Crown rested solely with the Miss South Africa Organisation. We respect that decision,” Nungu Diamonds said.

The partnership between the Miss South Africa Organisation and Nungu Diamonds spans more than three years, starting in 2023.

Natasha Joubert became the first Miss South Africa to wear the Nungu Diamonds Mowana crown in 2023.

Miss South Africa 2024 Nia Le Roux and Miss South Africa 2025 Qhawe Mazaleni then wore it.

READ | WATCH | Women's month | Sign language is now official in SA

The crown, dubbed Mowana, is inspired by the baobab tree of Limpopo and stands as a symbol of strength, resilience and transformation

It features over 800 stones, including diamonds, gemstones, and cubic zirconia, with the largest weighing 15 carats.

Despite the controversy surrounding her crown, Makamu has her sights set on entrepreneurship during her reign as Miss South Africa.

READ | Makamu sets her sight on entrepreneurship during Miss South Africa

World.title: Over 77,000 pupils in Gauteng remain unplaced
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Gauteng Education says more than 77,000 applicants are yet to be placed, with Grade 8 pupils making up the largest share.

Of the total number of pupils who remain unplaced 31,277 are Grade 1 applicants while 46,187 are Grade 8 applicants.

Gauteng Education MEC Lebogang Maile revealed this during a briefing on Sunday.

During the briefing he gave an update Grade 1 and Grade 8 learners placement for the 2027 academic year, scholar transport as well as school funding.

READ | Gauteng Education MEC to update on 2027 school readiness

According to Maile the department has identified more than 139,000 available spaces but acknowledges that these are not necessarily in the schools or communities where demand is highest.

Maile said the biggest challenge is matching available capacity with pupil demand.

“The existence of available spaces, which sits at 139,024, as stated, does not necessarily mean that they are located at the schools or in the communities where demand is highest. “This distinction is important. Gauteng does not experience uniform pressure across its schooling system. Some schools have available capacity, while others receive substantially more applications than they can reasonably accommodate. “Consequently, the challenge is not simply to count available spaces. It is to align those spaces with learner demand, geographical accessibility, school infrastructure and the practical circumstances of families,”Maile explained.

To date, more than 267,000 Grade 1 and 8 pupils have been placed for the 2027 academic year.

READ | School placement | Thousands wait to go back to school

World.title: Makamu sets her sight on entrepreneurship during Miss South Africa reign
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - New Miss South Africa Tiyani Makamu looks beyond the crown with entrepreneurship taking center stage in her plans for the year ahead.

The 27-year-old from Gauteng was crowned on Saturday night, taking over from Qhawekazi Mazaleni.

She is a communications professional, entrepreneur and youth advocate.

READ | Chidimma Adetshina fights to remain in South Africa

Speaking to eNCA Makamu on Sunday she said her key focus will be on entrepreneurship alongside other various aspects.

This as she believes that Miss South Africa should be seen as a social diplomat who looks after various issues.

World.title: 'My dress, my choice': Ruto tells critics to leave his suits alone
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Online reports claimed Ruto donned a burgundy tuxedo suit during his daughter's wedding priced at about Sh195,000. [PCS]

President William Ruto has hit at the opposition politicians for allegedly criticising his dressing style.

Ruto on Sunday said he pays attention to how he dresses and what he says, and thus those criticising his suits should “keep off”.

He spoke in Narok County where he attended a church service at St Mary’s Girls School.

“I want to ask my brothers, those we are competing with, to have some respect… Punguzeni kiburi na madharau… sasa niwaulize koti yangu kwa harusi inawahusu nini,” Ruto said.

He added, “Wearing T-shirts will not win you votes…. For me, I pay attention to what I say, ideas I prosecute and how I dress… If you are casual about your dressing, and what you say, that is your problem.”

Ruto’s remarks come after his dress code during his daughter Charlene’s wedding.

Online reports claimed Ruto donned a burgundy tuxedo suit during his daughter's wedding priced at about Sh195,000.

But Ruto said his critics had exaggerated the prices.

“Those who change the world start by spreading their bed when they wake up… you are opposing everything and even exaggerating prices about what I wear,” he said.

Ruto further hit at his political enemies for misleading Kenyans about a World Bank report that exposed graft in his administration.

Ruto said although his government is in agreement with the 52-page report, it is unfair for the opposition figures to only focus on one aspect.

“Spare us the lecture and look at the entire report. It is my government that, in the push for transparency, demanded that report… It highlights so many areas on economic development while giving a good account of how we are moving the country forward,” he said.

Ruto further said the corruption being talked about touches on the Mombasa-Nairobi Standard Gauge Railway, which happened in a different regime.

“I want to ask those on the other side to exercise moderation and be mindful of what they say. That money could be the one sponsoring their activities, Ruto said.

World.title: Love under watch: How technology is fuelling intimate partner abuse
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Your enemy is closer than you think. For many Kenyan women, the person who demands a phone password, reads private messages and tracks their movements through a screen is not a faceless troll. He is the man they live with, or the one they used to.

That is the uncomfortable picture painted by the recently released 2025–2626 Kenya Mini Demographic and Health Survey (KMDHS), which measured technology-facilitated gender-based violence, abuse committed, assisted, aggravated or amplified through digital tools.

The most common form of abuse is online control, reported by 19 per cent of women, followed by hacking at 5 per cent and online sexual harassment or cyber sexual abuse at 3 per cent. Most of it happens on platforms women use every day.

“Sixty-seven per cent of women who experienced digital gender violence say it happened on social media, with Facebook cited by 59 per cent. Messaging apps follow at 47 per cent, with WhatsApp at 26 per cent. Among girls aged 15–19, 77 per cent reported abuse on social media.”

The report shows how widespread the abuse is. “Twenty-six percent of women age 15–49 have ever experienced technology-facilitated violence from any perpetrator,” the report says, and 21 per cent experienced it often or sometimes in the 12 months before the survey. Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced it at the hands of a current, most recent or previous partner.

The burden is not spread evenly, the report states that Nairobi City records the highest lifetime experience from any perpetrator at 33 per cent, followed by Murang’a and Baringo at 32 per cent each.

“For abuse by an intimate partner, Homa Bay 36 per cent and Baringo 35 per cent lead, while in the 12 months before the survey Trans Nzoia topped the list at 31 per cent. At the other end, Mandera and Wajir report just 3 per cent, a figure that may say as much about silence as about safety,” the report says

The picture is similar among young people. A 2024 rapid study by the Collaborative Centre for Gender and Development, working with the UNFPA and Women Economic Empowerment, found that nearly 90 per cent of young adults enrolled in three Nairobi tertiary institutions had witnessed TFGBV, and 39 per cent had experienced it personally.

Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced gender violence committed by a current, most recent or previous partner, and 22 per cent did so in the past year. When women were asked who was responsible, the answer was blunt. Current husbands or intimate partners accounted for 61 per cent of perpetrators, former partners for 22 per cent and strangers for just 13 per cent.

Women who have never been married or had a partner face a different threat. For them, the most common perpetrators are strangers at 45 per cent, online attackers at 23 per cent and friends or acquaintances at 20 per cent.

Warning signs

Control is the common thread. The report describes such behaviours by a male partner as “important early warning signs that may escalate into violence within a relationship.”

Sixty-one per cent of ever-partnered women say their current or most recent partner has shown at least one controlling behaviour, and 27 per cent report three or more. Half say he has been jealous or angry when they spoke to other men, and 36 per cent say he insists on knowing where they are at all times. Others describe partners who demand passwords or read messages without consent.

Age and marital status matter. Technology-based gender violence is lowest among girls aged 15–19 at 10 per cent and highest among women aged 20–24 at 37 per cent. Forty-one per cent of divorced, separated or widowed women have experienced it, compared with 27 per cent of married women and 19 per cent of the never married.

Yet the digital rights advocate Cherie Oyier, a programmes officer at the Kenya ICT Action Network (KICTANet), says the low figures in some places should not be read as safety. Much of the abuse happens where nobody can see it.

“Closed applications, meaning like WhatsApp, those are the ones that most people, intimate partners will usually use,” she says. “Even as you are scrolling the internet to look for these instances, we may not be able to catch it. But it does not mean that it is not happening or that it is at a lower level.”

Culture also silences women. “Most women are told just endure, this is what marriage is about,” Oyier says. “Sometimes they don’t know, it’s so overt, like it doesn’t come out clearly that this is abuse. So most of the times, it is not reported.”

Online, abuse has been turned into entertainment. “It has become banter,” she says. “Even the people who are experiencing it have trivialised it. It’s now ingrained to you, like this is something that happens, you should expect it actually. If you post a picture, one of the things that you are thinking about is what kind of comments am I going to get.”

A 2023 report by KICTANet found that more than 30 per cent of Kenyans have experienced some form of TFGBV, while 90 per cent have witnessed it. In 2025, KICTANet and Equality Now released survivor testimonies showing how deceptive online job offers, grooming and image-based abuse leave women exposed, and how many had never received counselling despite years of trauma.

The stakes are not only digital. The 2025 Report of the Technical Working Group on GBV Including Femicide, cited in the KMDHS, indicated that many cases of homicide of women and girls, and of sexual and physical harm directed towards them, “are preceded by online and offline harassment using digital tools.”

For survivors, the law offers little comfort. “The technology is moving at a very fast pace compared to the laws,” Oyier says. In an attempt to bolster the gaps, Kenya has many fragmented laws. “You’ll have the Data Protection Act, the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act, the Children’s Act, that to some extent touch on online issues, but they don’t really cohesively cover the different instances of TFGBV.”

The police, she says, often do not know either. “Just imagine you’re a woman who is in a village, for example, a village in Siaya, and you encounter violence. For you to even understand which law apply is very stressful.”

“You’re going through psychological stress and depression, and you’re also supposed to figure out which law applies in your situation. It causes even more problems for victims and survivors.”

Flagging abusive language

Artificial intelligence is adding a new layer. Even so, Oyier cautions against writing it off. “We should not vilify AI completely,” she says. KICTANet has built a lexicon to help flag abusive language and runs a tracker for online gender-based violence. “One person cannot sit down and look at everything on social media. When AI is able to pull every post that has this word, a human content moderator is able to look through it with local context and see is this TFGBV or not.”

The KMDHS findings further show that exposure to TFGBV varies across age groups and digital platforms.

“Younger women are particularly exposed on social media, with 77 per cent of women aged 15–19 and 72 per cent of those aged 20–24 who experienced TFGBV reporting abuse on social media platforms, compared with 50 per cent of women aged 40–49.”

However, messaging applications tell a different story. Women aged 40–49 reported the highest exposure through these platforms at 54 per cent, compared with 30 per cent among teenagers aged 15–19.

Wealth also influences where women encounter online abuse. Exposure on social media increases from 45 per cent among women in the lowest wealth quintile to 74 per cent among those in the highest. Conversely, women in the lowest wealth quintile report greater exposure through messaging applications, at 62 per cent, compared with 39 per cent among those in the highest wealth quintile.

These differences suggest that TFGBV cuts across age and economic backgrounds, although the platforms through which women experience it vary.

World.title: Not so fast: Court slams brake on ARA over wealth forfeiture
World.content:
Felix Mecha Nyakundi could not provide a plausible explanation for how he amassed his wealth.

The Court of Appeal has ruled that the government cannot go after a person’s wealth without prior investigations to establish reasonable grounds for suspecting that the property constitutes proceeds of crime.

In a landmark judgment, Justices Patrick Kiage, Jamila Mohammed and Nduma Nderi said that although it does not require a person to be charged for a crime for the Asset Recovery Agency (ARA) to come knocking, it bears the responsibility to link the wealth or cash to a crime.

World.title: Back to sender: Aisha Jumwa returns to UDA
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto welcome former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa has returned to President William Ruto’s United Democratic Alliance (UDA), ending a three-month political fallout with the ruling party that saw her join opposition outfit Wiper Patriotic Front and declare support for the one-term movement ahead of the 2027 General Election.

President Ruto welcomed Jumwa back into UDA at State House, Mombasa, on Thursday, November 12, 2026, in a political reunion that could reshape alignments in Kilifi County and the wider Coast region as parties position themselves for next year's elections.

The reunion comes barely three months after Jumwa dramatically announced her departure from UDA, accusing the party leadership of frustrating her political ambitions and failing to support her quest for the Kilifi gubernatorial seat.

On July 30, 2026, Jumwa announced her resignation during a press conference at her Kakuyuni home in Malindi, saying her attempts to have her grievances addressed by the President had repeatedly been unsuccessful.

Among her concerns was what she described as humiliation and rejection within the ruling party, including an alleged incident in which she was chased out of State House during a meeting between Ruto and Coast leaders.

She also accused sections of the ruling coalition of undermining her gubernatorial ambitions, claiming that the political arrangements being pursued in Kilifi were designed to deny her an opportunity to contest for the county's top seat.

President William Ruto recieve former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Jumwa, who was among UDA's founding members and one of Ruto's most vocal mobilisers at the Coast during the 2022 elections, said her loyalty to the people of Kilifi outweighed her allegiance to any political party.

"My loyalty to the people of Kilifi will always be greater than my loyalty to any political party. The voice of the people of Kilifi is louder than the voice of UDA," she declared during her exit announcement.

Her departure marked a significant political shift, particularly given her central role in mobilising support for Ruto in the Coast region.

In August, Jumwa turned to the opposition, where she was warmly received by Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka, who visited her at her Kakuyuni residence on August 14 alongside a delegation of party leaders, including Nyali MP Mohamed Ali, Kitui Senator Enoch Wambua and Wundanyi MP Danson Mwashako.

Kalonzo subsequently proposed Jumwa for the position of Wiper Deputy Party Leader, citing her political experience and influence, while also backing her ambition to contest the Kilifi governorship on a Wiper ticket.

Jumwa embraced the new political alliance, declaring support for the one-term movement and threatening to mobilise UDA supporters in Kilifi to deregister from the ruling party and join Wiper.

"We are the ones who registered UDA members in Kilifi, and we are embarking on a grassroots campaign to deregister them from UDA and join Wiper," she said at the time.

On September 8, she attended a meeting involving Wiper leaders and Coast gubernatorial aspirants, including Mohammed Ali and Danson Mwashako, as the party intensified efforts to expand its influence in the region.

However, the political alliance has now taken another turn, with Jumwa returning to the party she had accused of frustrating her ambitions.

Announcing her return, President Ruto welcomed the former Cabinet Secretary back into UDA, signalling renewed efforts to consolidate the ruling party's support in the Coast region.

"I look forward to working with her to advance the party’s transformation agenda at the Coast and across the country. We remain committed to uniting leaders and Kenyans around our shared vision of a united, inclusive and prosperous Kenya," the President said.

Her return comes as Ruto steps up political mobilisation in the Coast region ahead of the 2027 elections, with Kilifi emerging as an important battleground for competing political formations.

Jumwa's political journey has been characterised by shifting alliances. She previously served under the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), representing Malindi in Parliament before becoming Kilifi's first Woman Representative between 2013 and 2017.

She later became one of Ruto's key political allies and served in his Cabinet.

World.title: Buxton estate tensions escalate after county officials attacked
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

A dispute over the multibillion-shilling Buxton Point housing project in Mombasa turned violent after county officials were allegedly attacked while enforcing a government order suspending construction over outstanding contractual obligations.

The confrontation came a day after County Executive Committee Member (CECM) for Lands, Housing, and Urban Development Mohamed Hussein ordered GulfCap Real Estate to halt all construction activities pending the resolution of disputes involving the county government and hundreds of former Buxton Estate residents.

The officials were reportedly pelted with stones as they attempted to serve the developer with an enforcement notice, with allegations that individuals linked to businessman Suleiman Shahbal were involved in the confrontation.

Hussein condemned the incident, saying attempts to intimidate government officers would not derail efforts to enforce the law and protect public interests.

"Let them bring goons, machetes, and stones if they want. I am not intimidated. I will execute my duties, and nobody will threaten me. The law must be followed, regardless of who you are or how much money you have," he said.

"We are here for the people of Mombasa, and we will ensure their rights are protected. Nobody is above the law," he added.

The November 10 enforcement notice, issued by County Director of Physical Planning Qassim Ali, directed GulfCap Real Estate to stop further development activities and obtain valid construction permits.

The notice, issued under Section 72(1) of the Physical and Land Use Planning Act, cited construction under a varied development plan without county approval and an ongoing dispute involving the developer, former tenants, and the county government.

The notice was reportedly received by the project's manager, Billy Okendo.

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county government and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units and commercial spaces developed in the first and second phases.

An addendum to the agreement signed on January 15, 2020, outlines the county's entitlement, with the allocation expected to be transferred upon completion of the second phase.

In a letter dated April 30, 2025, the county demanded 10 per cent of the proposed 1,800 housing units, translating to 180 apartments. The demand was renewed in February 2026, with the county seeking details on how the allocation would be implemented.

However, in correspondence dated September 22, 2026, the Department of Lands, Urban Planning and Housing expressed concern over what it described as the developer's failure to provide substantive responses to previous demands.

The county also questioned whether GulfCap had provided performance security equivalent to 10 per cent of the total construction cost for each phase, as required under the agreement.

It further demanded proof of payment of the Project Development Fee, which is payable in instalments as the project progresses.

The county said it had also raised technical and planning concerns during a meeting with the developer on April 15, 2026, including the need to address outstanding issues and resubmit the masterplan application.

But the dispute goes beyond the county's financial and contractual entitlement, with more than 500 former residents accusing the developer of failing to honour promises made when they were displaced in 2019.

John Tsuma, Secretary-General of the Buxton Tenants Welfare Association, said former residents had waited for more than seven years to return to their homes despite assurances that they would be prioritised once construction was completed.

"We are very disappointed by what happened. We had a meeting with the CECM, and he made it clear that all construction activities should stop until the outstanding issues are resolved. We did not go there to fight anybody. We wanted the directive implemented," Tsuma said.

He accused the developer of benefiting from the project while former residents continued to struggle to secure the houses they were promised.

"The developer has benefited from A to Z. He was given land by the county government, and the houses were sold off-plan. Yet, when it comes to fulfilling the promises made to former residents, we are still being taken around in circles," he said.

Tsuma said residents were not demanding free houses but wanted the affordable tenant-purchase arrangement they were promised before leaving the estate.

"We are not asking for free houses. We want the tenant-purchase arrangement that was promised to us so that we can pay for the houses and return to our homes," he said.

He also questioned why the developer had allegedly failed to surrender the county government's 184 housing units under the joint venture arrangement.

Mohamed Mzee Rubea, chairman of the evicted Buxton residents, said the money paid to the families during their displacement was a relocation allowance and not compensation for their homes.

He said the former tenants were given Sh240,000, with assurances that they would rent alternative accommodation for 12 months and return once the houses were completed.

"What we received was relocation money, not compensation for our houses. We were told to take the money and rent houses for 12 months and that we would be the first people to return once construction was completed. But here we are, more than seven years later, still waiting," Rubea said.

He said the original agreement involved 522 former tenants who were promised priority access to houses under the redevelopment.

Rubea added that each household was also promised Sh60,000 as a deposit towards acquiring a house under the tenant-purchase scheme.

"We were promised Sh60,000 as a deposit for those who would take up the houses. The developer later said the money would only be given to those who actually acquired the units. We are still waiting, and many of us have not received anything," he said. At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

He further claimed that the county had written to the developer in 2023, 2024, and 2025 seeking engagement over the outstanding commitments.

Mutua Mutia, another former resident, said the prolonged dispute had left families frustrated, especially after they were promised they would return within a year.

"I have lived in Buxton since I was a young boy. My firstborn child is now more than 30 years old, and the history of Buxton is one that pains us. We were evicted with the promise that we would return after one year, but today it is seven years and we are still struggling," Mutia said.

The former residents are also demanding the reconstruction of an Early Childhood Development (ECD) centre demolished to pave the way for the project, as well as the construction of a promised community social centre.

Hussein said the county had yet to receive either facility or its share of the housing project.

"The county has not received its 10 per cent share to date. There was an agreement that the demolished ECD centre would be reconstructed and handed over to the county, alongside a community social centre, but we have not received either," he said.

The first phase of Buxton Point delivered 584 housing units in 2023, while the second phase is expected to provide between 1,400 and 1,500 additional apartments. Completion had been scheduled for August 2027.

However, GulfCap Real Estate Chief Executive Officer Chris Ochieng defended the developer's position, saying 492 housing units would be handed over to buyers by December.

While urging the county to stop politicising the project, Ochieng warned that the ongoing controversy risks disrupting the project’s completion and affecting hundreds of workers who depend on it for their livelihoods.

He said the county government's 10 per cent share would be transferred upon completion of the project.

He also maintained that the developer had supported displaced residents by providing Sh240,000 for relocation and offering them preferential rates to purchase apartments.

Ochieng said the continued involvement of county officials in the dispute was unfortunate, particularly at a time when 492 homeowners are expecting to take possession of their houses in December.

He noted that the controversy was not only creating uncertainty among prospective homeowners but also threatening the livelihoods of hundreds of people employed directly and indirectly through the project.

“It is very unfortunate that Mombasa County officials are bringing politics into a national project. We have 492 homeowners who expect to take possession of their units by December. Beyond the homeowners, hundreds of people depend on this project for employment and their daily livelihoods,” said Ochieng.

He called on the county leadership to allow the project to proceed without unnecessary political interference, arguing that Mombasa has previously witnessed housing projects that stalled despite significant public interest.

World.title: Sakaja defends Sh43.7b drop in Nairobi County's pending bills before Senate
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja tells Senate that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors. [File, Standard]

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has told the Senate that pending bills in the city have been reduced from Sh118.79 billion to Sh75.07 billion through verification and payment.

Sakaja revealed that internal verification established that the Sh43.73 billion reduction was not achieved solely through payments but also involved legal assessments, court-ordered adjustments and the verification of disputed claims.

The governor, who appeared before the Senate County Public Accounts Committee at Parliament Buildings in Nairobi on Monday, said addressing the inherited debt required establishment of a verification committee to scrutinise the entire outstanding amount and establish the validity of the claims.

“The reduction of Nairobi County pending bills by Sh 43.73 billion was not achieved entirely through cash payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court-ordered reductions and disputed claims,” said Sakaja.

He told the Senate Committee chaired by Homa Bay Senator Moses Kajwang that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors and that he had constituted a committee to undertake an internal verification of the entire amount before payments were done.

Sakaja explained that the verification established that the reduction was not solely through payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court decisions and disputed claims.

“I would like to inform Senators that my administration has provided a detailed schedule accounting for the Sh43.73 billion pending bills reduction through adjustments and reconciliations,” he said.

The governor said that of this amount Sh1.63 billion related to legal assessments, while Sh19.14 billion represented government-guaranteed loans whose servicing had been suspended due to a lack of supporting documentation and loan schedules.

Sakaja told Senators that Sh19.2 billion related to LAPFUND interest and penalties which the County said had been reduced following a court consent that brought the claim down to approximately Sh8.2 billion.

He said that they had provided a signed indemnity form, in accordance with County Treasury rules governing misplaced payment documents, alongside a financial memo confirming that the works had been undertaken and payment made.

“The audit further raised concerns over Sh16.04 million in receivables from non-exchange transactions, which lacked sufficient supporting documentation,” said Sakaja.

The governor told senators that beyond the verification of pending bills his administration had also strengthened the county’s legal department to reduce expenditure on external legal services and protect public resources.

Sakaja noted that through the reforms, Nairobi saved approximately Sh8.48 billion in legal costs over two financial years by expanding its in-house legal capacity, handling more litigation internally and negotiating reductions in legal fees claimed by private advocates.

According to the County Assembly’s Justice and Legal Affairs Committee, of the 174 court cases concluded during the period under review, 84 were handled by the County’s in-house legal team, with 47 determined in Nairobi’s favour, representing a 56 per cent success rate.

Kajwang, commended the County for reducing its pending bills but asked the Governor to provide additional documentation supporting the payments and processes undertaken to account for the Sh43.73 billion reductions.

“The Senate County Public Accounts Committee requires further clarification on the verification exercise and the adjustments made to the outstanding debt,” said Kajwang.

World.title: Gachagua dismisses opposition divisions as 'polygamous family' rivalry
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County on November 8, 2026. [Peterson Githaiga, Standard]

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua has dismissed claims of divisions within the Opposition, describing the disagreements among its leaders as normal sibling rivalry in a polygamous family, while insisting that the coalition remains united behind plans to field a single presidential candidate in the 2027 General Election.

Gachagua said the Opposition leaders were committed to working together to challenge President William Ruto, despite their differing opinions on the timing of selecting a joint presidential flagbearer and occasional disagreements among their political camps.

Speaking during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County, the former Deputy President likened the political differences to children from the same father competing for attention but eventually uniting whenever an external threat emerges.

“The Opposition is united to a man, and we have agreed that we will have a single presidential candidate. Everybody is committed, and we talk on a daily basis. The only challenge is normal petty problems,” he said.

He added that the disagreements should not be interpreted as a breakdown of the coalition, maintaining that such differences were healthy and expected in a broad political alliance.

“Ile shida kidogo ni ya boma, watoto wengi wa baba mmoja. Watoto huko ndani, oh, baba anakupenda kuliko mimi. Mbona ulinunua kiatu kabla mimi? Si hiyo ni kawaida kwa polygamous family?” he posed.

Gachagua said the bigger threat to Opposition unity was not necessarily disagreements among its principals but the conduct of their supporters, social media influencers and political bloggers, whom he accused of fuelling unnecessary tensions through insults and online confrontations.

He cautioned Opposition leaders against allowing overzealous supporters to dictate their political relationships, warning that unchecked political attacks could eventually weaken the coalition and undermine its common objective.

“If there is anything to separate us, it is our supporters and social media bloggers. Wanawakisha moto hakuna, watu wangu na wa Matiang'i wanatukanana na sisi tunakula breakfast pamoja,” he said.

He further claimed that some political influencers associated with his DCP party had been recruited and allegedly paid by individuals opposed to him to attack his leadership and the party.

Gachagua urged coalition principals to exercise restraint and avoid reacting to every provocation from supporters, insisting that political leaders must remain focused on the bigger picture.

“I want to ask leaders in the Opposition, be careful. Don't listen to overzealous supporters and influencers; they will lead you astray. Remain focused,” he warned.

On the question of selecting a joint presidential candidate, Gachagua revealed that differences remained over the appropriate timing, with Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka proposing that the flagbearer be identified before December, while Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna favoured February and Narc Kenya leader Martha Karua suggested May.

Gachagua, however, argued that selecting a candidate too early could expose the individual to political pressure and possible frustration from the government.

He proposed April next year as a more suitable time, maintaining that the coalition was united on the principle of having one candidate even if its leaders differed on the timing.

The DCP leader also dismissed arguments that academic qualifications, experience or political credentials should determine who becomes the coalition's presidential candidate, insisting that electoral numbers and the support of ordinary Kenyans would ultimately decide.

“As others say they have experience and an agenda in the Opposition, the deciding factor is the numbers. I'm with the people. You say you have capacity, but the person to decide is the voter,” he said.

He added: “Akili nyingi ni nzuri, but bila kura unaweza kaa nayo nyumbani.”

World.title: Mudavadi urges Western Kenya to unite, says region cannot remain on sidelines
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Prime CS Musalia Mudavadi. [File, Standard]

Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi has urged Western Kenya to unite ahead of the 2027 General Election, saying the region must strengthen its political representation to have a greater say in national decision-making.

Speaking during a UDA delegates' meeting in Shitoto village, Mumias East, Kakamega County, he said Western Kenya could not afford to remain on the sidelines while decisions affecting the country were being made.

"2027 is the moment we must change the narrative. We must make sure that we are at the table where decisions are made. We cannot afford to remain spectators when the future of our country and our region is being determined," he said.

Mudavadi said parliamentary influence depended on numbers, arguing that electing more MPs would give the region a stronger voice in key parliamentary committees, including the Budget Committee.

"Parliament exercises authority in its own right. We want more MPs so that we can have a say in the Budget Committee and other important committees. These positions are secured through numbers, and numbers matter when decisions affecting the country are being made," he said.

Turning to the opposition, Mudavadi described its leaders as divided and challenged them to present clear manifestos outlining what they would offer Kenyans.

He said the divisions within the opposition would work in President William Ruto's favour as he seeks re-election in 2027, expressing confidence that he would win in the first round.

"We want Ruto to win without a petition. We want to thrash them in the first round," he said.

World.title: Trump sank the GOP in 2026. He could do it again in 2028
World.content:
Judging by their choices since this month’s Democratic sweep, both the White House and congressional Republicans are vastly underestimating the party’s risk in 2028 if President Donald Trump remains as unpopular as he is now.

Dazed Republicans picking through the wreckage of their losses may console themselves with the thought that Trump’s dire approval ratings won’t pose as large a threat to the GOP in 2028, since he will be leaving the White House. But history strongly suggests that confidence is misplaced.

Outgoing presidents have cast a larger shadow than even many political professionals assume in the election to succeed them — especially when that retiring president faces widespread public discontent, as Trump does now. While popular outgoing presidents haven’t always ensured victory for their designated successors, the inverse has almost always been true: When the outgoing president is unpopular, his party has rarely won the election to replace him.

This month’s election underscored the danger looming for Republicans if Trump remains this weak. In House, Senate and gubernatorial elections across the country, the vast majority of voters who disapproved of Trump’s job performance — usually at least 80% of them — voted against Republican candidates, according to the most recently updated numbers as of November 12 from the Voter Polls conducted for CNN and other media organizations by SRSS.

“This massive repudiation of Republican candidates is totally and completely about Donald Trump,” said longtime GOP pollster Whit Ayres.

Even big losses in a midterm don’t guarantee defeat for the party holding the White House in the next presidential election. But presidents who have recovered from a bad midterm have usually changed direction in response to the rebuke (like Harry Truman after 1946 or Bill Clinton after 1994) or benefited from changing circumstances (as Ronald Reagan did when the economy recovered after his party’s poor 1982 midterm).

Trump, by contrast, remains caught in a grinding war against Iran with no clear exit. And far from adjusting his course, he has reaffirmed it with the appointment of Stephen Miller, his most ideologically extreme senior adviser, as White House chief of staff. House Republicans have responded to their losses in a similar way by choosing pugnacious Rep. Jim Jordan as their new leader.

Rep. Jim Jordan speaks with reporters after leaving the office of Senate Majority Leader John Thune at the US Capitol on November 11. Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters White House chief of staff Stephen Miller is seen in the Presidential limousine at Palm Beach International Airport in West Palm Beach, Florida on November 6. Alex Wroblewski/AFP/AFP via Getty Images

“Donald Trump is going to double down and triple down” on the policies and style that alienated voters this year, said Steve Schmidt, a longtime GOP strategist who has become a staunch Trump critic. “Any person with any attachment to real life would look at this election and say, ‘Well, they certainly should have gotten the message and they’ll be chastened,’ but that doesn’t appreciate the physics of politics, which is that as an extreme party gets smaller, it becomes more fanatical.”

History is clear on the consequences

Novelist Leo Tolstoy famously wrote that every happy family is alike, while every unhappy family is different. The relationship of outgoing presidents to the election to succeed them inverts that maxim: The impact of every unsuccessful president has been largely the same, while the role of successful presidents has diverged.

Good feelings toward popular retiring presidents Theodore Roosevelt in 1908 and Ronald Reagan in 1988 helped each man’s designated successor win election. But despite very strong job approval ratings, both Dwight Eisenhower in 1960 and Bill Clinton in 2000 saw their vice-presidents lose nail biters (although Al Gore, Clinton’s No. 2, did win the popular vote). Barack Obama in 2016 wasn’t as popular as Eisenhower or Clinton, but he also left office with majority approval — only to see his party’s designated heir, Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, lose another tight race to Trump (despite, like Gore, winning the popular vote).

But when an outgoing president has lost the public’s support, the record is far more consistent. Since the turn of the 20th century, each time an outgoing president has been broadly unpopular, his party has lost the race to succeed him. That was true for Democrats Woodrow Wilson in 1920, Harry Truman in 1952, Lyndon Johnson in 1968 and Biden in 2024, as well as for Republican George W. Bush in 2008.

According to the exit polls conducted for CNN and other media organizations, 88% of the voters who disapproved of Reagan in 1988 and Clinton in 2000 voted for the other party’s presidential candidate. In 2016, 89% of voters who disapproved of Obama voted for Trump; in 2024, 82% of voters who disapproved of Biden voted for Trump over Vice President Kamala Harris.

Trump’s two victories help explain why a popular outgoing president is no guarantee of success for his party — while an unpopular retiring president has been a more reliable kiss of death.

In 2016, according to the exit polls, Obama’s approval remained at or just above 50% in each of six swing states he had won in 2012. But Trump still flipped all of them — Iowa, Ohio, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Florida. The reason is that Trump captured a significantly larger share among the minority of voters who disapproved of Obama than Clinton won among the majority who approved. Trump harnessed virtually all the discontent about Obama, while Clinton’s own vulnerabilities prevented her from capturing as much of his support.

In 2024, the equation for Harris proved much more straightforward — and treacherous. Between 56% to 60% of voters in the seven major swing states disapproved of Biden’s performance and between 81% to 87% of those disapprovers backed Trump, powering him to victory in all of them, the exit polls found. Harris made missteps as a candidate, but her biggest problem was that pervasive discontent with the administration in which she served.

A poster cutout of Vice President Kamala Harris sits on the ground after a demonstrators protested the administration’s stance on aid to Israel on August 19, 2024, while the Democratic National Convention was being held in Chicago. Martha Irvine/AP

In recent times, the presidential nominee who had the most success separating from an unpopular outgoing president of his own party was Republican Sen. John McCain in 2008. Running against Obama, McCain won 30% of voters nationwide who disapproved of George W. Bush, the exit polls found.

As a senator who had occasionally clashed with Bush — and ran a bitter race against him for the GOP nomination in 2000 — McCain wasn’t intrinsically tied to his predecessor as closely as Harris, Gore and George H.W. Bush (who all served as vice presidents to the retiring president) or Hillary Clinton, who worked as Obama’s secretary of state. “There were famously enmities there,” between McCain and Bush, noted Schmidt, McCain’s chief strategist in the 2008 race.

Yet Schmidt said the campaign recognized it would take dramatic, even unprecedented, actions to overcome the public’s disapproval of Bush — which reached a stunning 71% in the 2008 exit poll amid fatigue with the Iraq War and fear and anger over that year’s financial crisis.

“It drove everything as a political consideration because you knew that there was a day of reckoning where you had to disrupt that headwind and fly out of it,” Schmidt said. That impulse, he said, drove McCain’s attempt to name Democrat-turned independent Sen. Joe Lieberman as his running mate. “It was going to take something like that to arrest the trajectory,” Schmidt recalled. (When Republicans rebelled over Lieberman, McCain abruptly pivoted to choosing Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin instead.)

In the end, even McCain could not paddle nearly fast enough to escape the undertow of Bush’s capsizing presidency. Obama that year won a higher share of the popular vote than any Democratic nominee since Johnson in 1964 and flipped nine states that had voted for Bush in 2004. In all of them, at least two-thirds of voters disapproved of Bush’s performance — and at least two-thirds of those disapprovers backed Obama.

The GOP’s 2028 conundrum

Through 2026, the one discordant sign for Democrats was polling consistently showing they were not winning nearly as many voters who disapproved of Trump as during his first term.

Democrats this year didn’t fully match the benchmarks they hit among Trump disapprovers in his first term. But ultimately Democrats carried about the same share of voters who disapproved of Trump as the opposition party did among voters who disapproved of Obama in 2010, Bush in 2006 and Bill Clinton in 1994. In the 2026 CNN Voter Poll measuring preferences in the national House popular vote, 86% of voters who disapproved of Trump backed Democrats; the party also won 85% to 89% of voters who disapproved of Trump in almost all the major Senate contests.

Democratic Sens.-elect Annie Andrews, James Talarico and Troy Jackson walk toward an orientation meeting for newly elected lawmakers inside the US Capitol on November 9. Win McNamee/Getty Images

That was plenty to power a Democratic landslide. Disapproval of Trump in this election was not only deep (at 63%, his national disapproval rating was considerably higher than those other presidents in their worst midterm elections), but also broad. Across the 45 states where Voter Poll data is available, most voters approved of Trump’s job performance in only five sparsely populated deep-red states — Arkansas, Idaho, South Dakota, West Virginia, and Wyoming.

In every state where Democrats flipped a governorship, a Senate seat, or both, a substantial majority of voters disapproved of Trump’s job performance — and those disenchanted voters provided the core of the winning Democratic coalition. In Texas, for instance, 96% of the votes for Democratic Senate victor James Talarico came from people who disapproved of Trump.

One reason Republicans could not surmount the Trump discontent in 2028 was that so few displayed any independence from him. As Ayres noted, Republicans concluded that if they clashed with Trump, he would either hound them out of the party or defeat them in primaries. Yet binding themselves to Trump to avoid primary challenges created insurmountable problems in the general election where “Trump and Trumpism have become toxic,” Ayres said.

That same conundrum looms over the potential 2028 Republican presidential field, particularly Vice President JD Vance. Trump is likely to fire social media thunderbolts against any attempt from Vance or other candidates to meaningfully distance from him, and no one seeking the nomination can afford too much conflict with the president, given his durable popularity with the MAGA base. Yet if Trump remains anywhere near as unpopular with the broad public as he is today, failing to separate from him could prove fatal for the eventual GOP nominee in the general election.

Vance himself seems to be aware of this catch-22; CNN reported last week that the vice president has given serious consideration to not running for president in 2028 in the wake of the GOP’s disastrous midterm performance.

There’s little sign Republicans will change course

All this underscores the GOP’s stake in Trump mounting at least some recovery by 2028. A decisive conclusion to the Iran War that lowered gas and diesel prices might lift him somewhat.

But Democratic pollster Anna Greenberg said it will be extremely difficult for Trump to regain much of the allegiance he lost over the past two years among the new voters who moved toward him in 2024 — particularly Hispanic Americans, Black men and younger men. Most of those voters, she said, feel not only disappointed but angry at Trump for failing to alleviate their economic squeeze as he promised — while focusing so much on his own priorities, like building monuments and padding his fortune.

“Especially for the people who are less ideologically committed to him… the betrayal and the broken promises make it very hard to come back from,” Greenberg said. “It’s not just the bad job performance.”

As problematic, Trump and congressional Republicans show no sign of rethinking the course that ran the party into this electoral ditch. Instead, through the elevation of the belligerent hard-liners Miller and Jordan, the GOP has not only ignored but actively rejected the voters’ roar of discontent.

President Donald Trump takes question from the media on the South Lawn of the White House on October 21. Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images

Add the prospect of extensive congressional hearings exposing corruption and self-dealing in the administration and many analysts believe Trump’s approval rating could fall even lower by 2028. “He may not be at his lowest point,” saud Emory University political scientist Alan Abramowitz, who has extensively studied the relationship between election outcomes and presidential approval. “He is going to have a hard time clawing his way back up to anything higher than he is now, given what is likely to be happening” with investigations and the economy.

If Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio wins the GOP nomination in 2028, they might find it especially difficult to escape negative feelings about Trump, since they served so closely with him. But, as Abramowitz said, “every prominent Republican has tied themselves closely to Trump over the past two years.”

Though voters still harbor many doubts about Democrats, if Trump can’t repair his public standing, those Democratic vulnerabilities may not matter as much as Republicans hope — just as they did little to stop the massive blue tide earlier this month.

World.title: Democrats look to what’s next after Trump. But first, an actual party
World.content:
Denver — The Democrats here were told: The big midterm win wasn’t about you.

But the vibes among the hundreds of party operatives, strategists and would-be 2028 presidential candidates who gathered to ask what’s next after nearly a decade of living in President Donald Trump’s shadow?

Party on, Wayne! Party on, Garth!

Democrats arguably haven’t had such a wide-open presidential field since the “Wayne’s World” era, when a preternaturally talented Southern state governor named Bill Clinton came almost out of nowhere to win the White House in 1992.

Now, Democrats have exploded out of a Trump-imposed political wilderness to their most sweeping midterm win since Watergate. And they were ready to take a beat before they begin what’s sure to be a frenzied season of presidential campaign announcements, hiring, fundraising and knife-fighting among a dozen or more White House hopefuls.

Even the would-be candidates could barely hide their elation during donor dinners, at hotel rooftop receptions, and over drinks at the bar at the Ritz-Carlton in downtown Denver, where many mingled late into the night.

Attendees listen to speeches during the What’s Next summit at Mission Ballroom in Denver on November 13. Mark Makela/Getty Images

But on the main stage, on the first day, those gathered here were warned: Voters still aren’t all that into them.

“These voters that we lost and that we have turned away are still out there and they have not become Democrats yet,” influential Democratic data guru David Shor said as the two-day gathering kicked off. “They will be here in two years, and if we have not persuaded them by then, we might not be happy with how things turn out.”

There was no agreement about how to do that. The prescriptions coming from the stage previewed the struggle that’s beginning to emerge: Did Tuesday’s wins signal an uncompromising fighter from the party’s left wing can dominate the nominating contest and go on to win a national election?

Or is the message that to win everywhere, the party should choose someone who can appeal to the voters who rejected the woke culture-war politics of the Covid era?

“The American people cannot wait two years for change. So we must work with President Trump,” said Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico.

“The only way we’re going to fix that is by fixing it together. We can’t do it with the same warfare that brought us here,” said Rob Sand, the incoming Democratic governor of Iowa.

US Representative Ro Khanna, D-CA, speaks during the “What’s Next” post-midterm election conference by the Democratic Party in Denver, on November 13. Kevin Mohatt/Reuters

Contrast those two millennial red-state newcomers with Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna, who hails from deep-blue California, co-chaired Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaign in 2020, and is widely expected to run for president in 2028 as an unapologetic progressive.

“This is not the 1990s. We cannot cobble together a fleeting big tent through perpetual triangulating, straddling, and calculating,” Khanna said onstage. The reference to “triangulating” was an unmistakable jab at a buzzword of the Clinton era.

The gathering offered a few reminders of the anger emanating from the party’s base. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen spoke after announcing he would challenge Chuck Schumer to be the next Senate majority leader.

Likely incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries was heckled by the audience, with one person yelling Jeffries was “a f**king liar!” before being escorted from the hall.

And protesters gathered outside the security perimeter, holding signs that read, “Abolish billionaires,” “No Schumer coronation,” and “No more do-nothing Democrats.” A Denver SWAT vehicle was parked between them and the rideshare dropoff line.

Protesters demonstrate outside before the second day of programming at the What’s Next summit outside Mission Ballroom in Denver, on November 13. Mark Makela/Getty Images

A protester gestures while being escorted outside by staff members during a talk with US House of Representatives Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-NY, at the “What’s Next” post-midterm election conference by the Democratic Party in Denver, Colorado, US November 13. Kevin Mohatt/Reuters House Democratic Leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-NY, watches protesters screaming at him while participating in a question and answer event during the What’s Next summit at Mission Ballroom in Denver on November 13.. Mark Makela/Getty Images

But inside that perimeter and off the stage, all the divisions evaporated into an atmosphere of celebration bordering on elation. There were food trucks parked outside the brewery serving local craft beers on draft. There were musical acts performing in the outdoor plaza in between speeches. Both days were about 65 degrees and sunny, with the weather clear enough to see the mountains.

And it was very cozy and comfortable after hours at at the Ritz bar. The drinks started flowing Thursday night, with Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, who’s considering a presidential run, holding court. Pete Buttigieg was also spotted there Thursday night, as was Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro.

And Friday evening, the nationwide FAA ground stop stranded everyone in Denver at least for a few hours. Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin sat with Govs. Abigail Spanberger of Virginia and Mikie Sherill of New Jersey until the stop was lifted. Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock huddled off the record with reporters. Buttigieg was back too, spotted snapping a selfie or two. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker couldn’t attend the conference, but his team was at the Ritz bar too. So were operatives with ties to Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and a handful of others.

David Axelrod, senior political commentator at CNN and former senior advisor to former US President Barack Obama, from left, Mikie Sherrill, governor of New Jersey, Philip Weiser, Colorado attorney general, Abigail Spanberger, governor of Virginia, and former State Representative Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat from Alaska, during the What’s Next conference in Denver, on Friday, November 13. Chet Strange/Bloomberg/Getty Images

This was where the conference’s real business unfolded. A top priority was recruiting staff and making connections for presidential campaigns that are set to start kicking off as soon as January, if not earlier, according to conversations with over a dozen strategists and operatives with ties to presidential hopefuls.

Much of the chatter and speculation focused on possible candidates who weren’t in the room, Kamala Harris and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez chief among them. Their decisions to run or not to run for president in 2028 will fundamentally shape the rest of the field.

Wins across the South underscore the power of Black voters, already perhaps the most important single constituency in any Democratic primary, and Harris starts with an enormous advantage there, especially among Black women.

And then there’s the progressive wing, energized by victories from working-class candidates and people like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

“People are thinking there’s more room for someone on the left, and wondering if it means AOC is going to run,” said one top operative with close ties to a likely 2028 Democratic presidential candidate.

There was also widespread speculation about Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, whose been widely considered a top-tier likely 2028 contender. At the heart of his appeal had been the argument he can win big in one of the most important swing states on the map. Now, he’s got a lot of competition from newer faces in the party.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro speaks to the media outside after taking the stage during the “What’s Next” post-midterm election conference by the Democratic Party in Denver, on November 13. Kevin Mohatt/Reuters

“I’m proud to be the governor of what I think is the swingiest state in America, but we got a lot of company now,” Shapiro told me in an interview. “Look at Texas, look at South Carolina, Iowa, and a whole lot more. But I think that presents an opportunity for Democrats not to be thinking about how to get to 270 on an electoral map, but get to 370 back how Obama won and Clinton won.”

Other potential contenders, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, also didn’t appear here. Newsom, who had occupied something of frontrunner status in the invisible primary as he jabbed at Trump over the past year, seemed to have faded somewhat from the main conversation, at least in these halls.

(Newsom hasn’t faded, apparently, for Trump, who spent part of his weekend attacking Newsom for commuting the death sentences of all California inmates on death row and changing them to life without parole.)

As the hundreds of Democrats who gathered here struggled to find a way out of Denver, the airport chaos almost presaged what could be a massive post-Trump hangover for a party that’s elated but set for a bruising internal struggle over what’s next.

“If you ask the American people, there is no question about who we oppose,” said Massachusetts Rep. Jake Auchincloss. “But also no sense of what we believe. That is the question we have to answer right now.”

World.title: Rubio says more work to do and downplays election losses amid speculation about political future
World.content:
Amid speculation about his political future, Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared that there is more work to be done as he downplayed Republicans’ losses in the midterm elections.

“We have much more to do over the next two, the next six, the next 20 years. Great things that last are built in decades, not election cycles,” Rubio said in an address to the conservative Federalist Society’s National Lawyers Convention in Washington, DC, on Friday evening.

Rubio has faced mounting questions about whether he will seek the presidency in 2028, particularly in the wake of last week’s midterm elections. His speech, for which he was introduced by his daughter Daniella, could further fuel speculation.

“Though we are prepared for the twists and turns and the ups and downs of the road ahead, of this I believe with all my heart that we in this generation will leave for our children and our grandchildren what Americans always leave for their children and their grandchildren: the single greatest nation in the history of the world,” Rubio said to conclude his lengthy remarks, which were met with a standing ovation.

Rubio made direct references to his party’s defeats at the ballot boxes. He also joked to the packed ballroom of lawyers and law students at the Mayflower Hotel that “on election night there was a congressman that said we all needed to lawyer up, so here we are.” He was referencing a statement from Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia — the incoming House Oversight Committee chairman.

However, Rubio downplayed the absolute power of elections, saying, “politics requires more than simply winning elections, because the government is not the only source of political power.”

“Elections (decide) who holds office for a season. Elections … they do not decide by themselves what our institutions teach or what our lawyers believe, which ideas are treated as respectable, normal, and which are deemed beyond the pale,” he said.

The top US diplomat also cited setbacks suffered during the American Revolution, suggesting that “those who believe that one setback, one defeat, one bad election spells the end of the Republic” should look to the founding fathers.

“There will be more victories, and there will be more defeats. There will be more triumphs, and there will be more disappointments. This is the nature of all undertakings of this weight and of this magnitude. There are no great men or great causes in the pages of history that did not suffer the same,” he said.

Rubio lashed out against the “weaponization of international law” and “activist courts who seek to govern by injunction” in the US. He specifically targeted the International Criminal Court, which the Trump administration is working to dismantle.

In a question-and-answer session after the speech, Rubio reiterated, “America is exceptional, but it’s not self-perpetuating.”

“It has always required those in charge to do what it takes to keep it moving forward, and that that’s what we’re called to do, and then have confidence that we can do it. It’s an enormous undertaking, and it’s like I said in my speech, it’s something that happens over you know, years and decades, not election cycle to election cycle,” he said.

World.title: Jensen Huang resigned in disgrace from Nvidia. Many in Silicon Valley are still showering him with support
World.content:
Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia was marked by corporate scandal, but many of his own former employees and colleagues across Silicon Valley are coming out in droves to express support for the man they believe to be a legend.

Huang resigned on Thursday after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including with at least one subordinate. He had already been under scrutiny after reports of an affair with another woman, who was described by US officials as a potential Chinese intelligence asset.

Huang was so integral to Nvidia’s brand that his image — with signature black leather jacket — was often turned into marketing material, including an AI-powered hologram at the company’s annual conference, known as GTC. Known for its low turnover and flat corporate structure, with Huang managing over 50 direct reports and responding to messages at all hours, Nvidia fostered deep employee loyalty.

Following his departure, current and former staff responded with tributes on social media. Edward Liu, a director and distinguished scientist who started as an intern at the company, called it “a heartbreaking day,” in a post on X, praising Huang as an inspiring leader who taught them to “reason from first principles.” Engineer Fei Peng went even further, writing that Huang’s departure “has killed NVIDIA’s soul.”

Others, like senior research scientist Gavin Woolery, openly suggested ulterior motives and suspicions about his ousting. Woolery posted on X that he felt Huang’s ousting came too quickly before all the information emerged.

“Everyone deserves a fair trial. It’s possible he has made mistakes, I’m not sure they were ill-intentioned ones, but in either case we should know the whole truth before we judge,” Woolery said.

Other employees expressed support for Nvidia’s interim leader, CFO Colette Kress.

“I am grief-stricken that Jensen is no longer with NVIDIA,” posted Bryan Catanzaro, Nvidia’s vice president of applied deep learning research. “At the same time, I fully support NVIDIA’s board and have confidence in their decisions. I’ve worked with Colette for years and know her as an extraordinary leader. She has my full support.”

Beyond Nvidia’s walls, Huang’s influence was felt across the broader tech ecosystem. Often called the “central bank” of the booming AI industry, Nvidia not only supplied the hardware powering the technology but also financed much of the sector through investments and partnerships, with Huang serving as its biggest cheerleader. That has led to criticism and fears of “circular financing,” in which Nvidia invests in companies that fuel its own growth when those businesses turn around and use Nvidia capital to purchase Nvidia products.

Exolabs founder Alex Cheema wrote about cold emailing Huang in June about an idea to make local AI much faster on Nvidia hardware. Huang responded in seven minutes and “approved a war room for us to work on this at NVIDIA HQ,” Cheema wrote.

Cheema pointed to Huang’s long-time support and promotion of open-source technology — software or hardware built on publicly accessible source code that anyone can freely inspect, modify and distribute. Most of the major AI models, like ChatGPT and Claude, run on closed-source systems.

“I don’t believe Jensen is replaceable, he’s a 1 of 1 human, but I hope NVIDIA will continue to aggressively support Open Source AI and Local AI, and continue to take bets on small startups with crazy ideas,” Cheema said.

Huang also found support among his peers — some of the biggest names in Silicon Valley and venture capital, including his longtime friend and business partner, Elon Musk. Even before Huang was ousted, Musk posted that it would be “an honor” to hire Huang after another user on X implored him to do so.

“A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it too,” Musk later posted on Friday after Huang’s resignation.

“Dark, dark day. Horrible decision for the U.S. and the western world,” Andreessen Horowitz general partner Martin Casado posted on X. The firm’s account also posted a clip from a movie about Michael Jordan, along with the quote: “ You’re gonna be remembered forever because some things are eternal.”

Even those who have criticized his actions, like Sequoia Capital’s Shaun MaGuire, who called Huang’s actions a “dumb mistake” and “bad for America,” often come with a dose of praise. “He made huge mistakes with his infidelity, which is tragic for his family and NVDA. But simultaneously he will leave a huge void, with the loss of a: technical, aggressive, founder-CEO,” MaGuire wrote on X.

World.title: Court sentences husband of ‘Monufia Bride’ murder case to death
World.content:
The Wadi al-Natrun Appellate Criminal Court on Saturday sentenced the killer of Karima Awad to death by hanging in the “Monufia Bride” case.

Karima was murdered just four months after her wedding, having endured severe abuse at the hands of her husband.

A marriage filled with brutality, oppression, and humiliation

In its remarks accompanying the verdict, the court detailed the suffering endured by Karima Awad.

It affirmed that, throughout her brief marriage, she was subjected to “brutality, oppression, humiliation, mistreatment, and a complete deprivation of the most basic human dignity” at the hands of the defendant.

The court emphasized the severity of the crimes committed against a young woman who had only been married for a few months.

The court’s focus on the mistreatment and cruelty she faced brings back the details of the incident that took place in the village of Mit Barra, in Quesna District of Monufia Governorate.

Fatal beating

Investigations into the case revealed that the victim had been subjected to physical assaults, which resulted in severe injuries that ultimately claimed her life in December 2025.
