According to the lawyer representing Karima’s family, the defendant assaulted his wife twice on the day of the incident. The first assault caused her to lose consciousness, after which he attacked her again, striking her in the chest and head.

The family’s lawyer explained that the victim’s injuries included internal bleeding and a fracture to her sternum (breastbone)—details he cited while calling for the maximum possible sentence for the defendant.

Court’s message

The court’s statement underscored the oppression, humiliation, and mistreatment endured by Karima.

These points echoed the arguments presented by the Public Prosecution during the trial, as it sought the maximum penalty for the defendant, emphasizing a husband’s duty to protect his wife and highlighting how such a crime constitutes a profound breach of the covenant of safety upon which the marital relationship is founded.

Background of the verdict

The court of first instance had initially sentenced the defendant to 15 years in prison.

However, the Public Prosecution appealed the ruling, bringing the case before the appellate criminal court.

During the previous hearing, the court decided to refer the defendant’s case files to the Grand Mufti of Egypt to seek a religious legal opinion (Fatwa) regarding the imposition of the death penalty.

In Saturday’s session, the defendant appeared in the dock, dressed in white prison attire, amid tight security measures, before the court handed down the death sentence.

With this verdict, the case has reached a new judicial milestone following months of investigations, hearings, and legal arguments.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Four people burn to death after two-vehicle collision in Aswan
World.content:
Four people were burned to death on Saturday evening following a collision between two vehicles on al-Abbasiya road in the Kom Ombo district of Aswan Governorate.

The impact caused both vehicles to catch fire, resulting in the charring of four individuals who were inside as one of the trucks was carrying petroleum products.

The Aswan ambulance dispatch center received a report of a collision between two vehicles on al-Abbasiya road in Kom Ombo district of Aswan.

The relevant authorities and civil defense teams rushed to the scene once receiving report on the accident, which involved a collision between two pickup trucks.

A formal report of the incident has been filed, and the Public Prosecution has been notified for investigations.

World.title: MP slams Finance Ministry’s move to allocate Egyptian state lands to reduce public debt
World.content:
A member of the Egyptian Parliament’s Economic Affairs Committee and economist Mohamed Fouad on Saturday criticized the practice of allocating state-owned land for the purpose of reducing public debt.

Speaking with TV host Amr Adib on the “al-Hekaya,” (The Story) show, the MP remarked: “The issue isn’t just whether the land is being sold or not; the economic implications are what matter most. Are we actually solving the problem, or are we merely postponing it?”

Fouad said that the recent allocation of 112 million square meters of land in the Red Sea region to the Finance Ministry mirrors the earlier case of the Ras Shuqair land, which he noted implies a lack of clarity regarding the outcomes of that previous initiative.

Fouad explained that a presidential decree issued on June 4, 2025, had allocated 174 million square meters in Ras Shuqair area to the Finance Ministry, with the stated objective of reducing public debt and facilitating the issuance of sovereign “Sukuk” (Islamic bonds).

He said that 17 months have passed without the development of an operational plan, or even a preliminary framework, which raises questions about the ultimate fate of these lands and the mechanisms through which they are to be utilized.

The newly allocated area in the Red Sea spans 112 million square meters, he noted, which is equivalent to approximately 60 percent of the size of the land at Ras Shuqair.

What became of Ras Shuqair?

Fouad explained that he has submitted a formal inquiry to uncover the details surrounding the allocation of the 112 million square meters of land in the Red Sea region.

He is also seeking clarification on the status of the previously allocated land at Ras Shuqair, the nature of the arrangements made for it, the plans for its utilization, and what has actually been achieved since its initial allocation.

Fouad further demanded an accounting of the funds generated and the sources intended for settling existing obligations.

He emphasized that the House of Representatives has the authority to hold the government—and the relevant minister—accountable regarding how these lands are being managed, plans for their development, and the expected economic returns.

Funds for Repaying Sukuk

Fouad raised questions regarding the mechanism for paying returns on sovereign “Sukuk” (Islamic bonds) once they are issued.

He inquired about the source of the profits and financial flows that would be used to meet these obligations—particularly in scenarios where the land in question has not yet reached the operational stage and is not yet generating revenue.

He further questioned whether such repayments would rely on returns from investment activities linked to the land, or on the state’s general public resources.

He called for clarification on the financial engineering of the process, the entity receiving the funding, the returns generated, and how financial flows are distributed among the various parties involved.

Fouad emphasized that his objection does not concern the use of state assets or the nature of the financial and investment transactions themselves, but rather the necessity of understanding the economic returns generated thereafter—pointing specifically to the Ras el-Hekma and Alam al-Roum deals, as well as other arrangements along the Red Sea coast.

The MP underscored the importance of shifting away from financing deals aimed solely at debt repayment.

Instead he advocated for the operationalization of assets and the establishment of projects that generate sustainable revenue, thereby helping to alleviate the state’s financial burdens in the long term.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: SCZONE Chief meets high-level Indian business delegation
World.content:
Head of the Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZONE) Mostafa Sheikhoon met with a high-level Indian business delegation comprising representatives of major Indian companies, coordinated by the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), at the authority’s headquarters in Ain Sokhna.

The meeting took place on the sidelines of the Indian Minister of Commerce and Industry’s visit to Egypt, as part of SCZONE’s efforts to strengthen international economic cooperation and attract global investment.

In a statement issued on Saturday, November 14, 2026, Sheikhoon said the fruitful cooperation and strong strategic relations between Egypt and India were increasingly translating into successful and promising investment partnerships for numerous Indian companies operating within SCZONE’s industrial and logistics zones.

He noted that these companies invest in a variety of sectors, foremost among them metal industries, chemicals and petrochemicals.

“The authority offers a comprehensive and competitive package of customs and tax incentives, supported by international free trade agreements (FTAs) that facilitate access to major global markets,” he added.

Sheikhoon also highlighted the authority’s focus on specialized technical workforce training centers as a targeted sector under its strategy, given their role in meeting investors’ demand for qualified personnel trained according to the latest scientific methods and in strengthening the integrated business environment.

The delegation attended a comprehensive presentation on SCZONE, its capabilities, key investment incentives and digital services. It also watched a documentary highlighting the authority’s network of ports and integrated industrial zones, major infrastructure and utilities projects, and other competitive advantages.

For his part, the CEO of industrial developer Orascom Industrial Parks highlighted the authority’s strong network of world-class industrial developers as a key pillar of SCZONE’s success, helping turn its vision into tangible achievements.

He underscored the industrial developer’s vital role in creating an integrated business environment and providing investors with extensive facilities under SCZONE’s umbrella. He also stressed the complementary roles of the authority and the developer under their longstanding strategic partnership, aimed at attracting new high-value investments and localizing a range of targeted industrial sectors.

The meeting also featured success stories of several Indian companies operating within SCZONE under Orascom Industrial Parks, highlighting the institutional support and distinctive competitive advantages they enjoy, including reliable energy supplies, world-class infrastructure and effective integration between ports and industrial zones.

This integration provides a wide range of export options to regional and international markets, the statement noted.

At the conclusion of the visit, the Indian delegation conducted an extensive tour of the Sokhna Integrated Industrial Zone to learn firsthand about its capabilities, infrastructure readiness, industrial developers and successful Indian companies operating in the manufacturing and heavy industries sectors and assess its potential to attract further investment.

World.title: Lubinda Dares Hichilema To Rule Out Third Term As Govt Defends Term-Limit Talk
World.content:
Former Justice Minister Mr Given Lubinda has challenged President Hakainde Hichilema to publicly distance himself from any attempt to extend his presidency beyond the two terms the Constitution allows. He said Zambia’s democratic principles must take precedence over individual political ambition.

In a statement, Mr Lubinda said the Head of State’s recent call for ministers to listen to citizens and stop taking them for granted should be reflected in his own leadership. He said this applied most of all to contested constitutional questions.

“President Hichilema therefore has an opportunity to demonstrate the sincerity of his recent message about listening to citizens,” Mr Lubinda said.

“He must unequivocally distance himself from any third-term agenda, discourage attempts to undermine the existing constitutional term limits and reassure the nation that his priority is delivering on the mandate entrusted to him.”

The former minister said Zambia’s rejection of a third-term bid in 2001 should remind the nation that presidential power has constitutional limits and that no individual is above the Constitution. He said listening to citizens should be a continuous responsibility of those in government, not a message reserved for campaign season. Citizens, he added, must be free to express dissenting views without being intimidated or pushed aside.

Mr Lubinda questioned how the government had handled constitutional consultations. He pointed to Constitution of Zambia (Amendment) Bill No. 7 of 2025, which was enacted in December last year despite objections from sections of civil society, church mother bodies and the Law Association of Zambia (LAZ).

“The broader lesson is that constitutional legitimacy cannot be measured merely by whether government has the numbers to pass legislation,” he said.

“The Constitution belongs to the people, and meaningful public participation must be more than a procedural formality.”

He cautioned against treating the UPND’s parliamentary majority as the collective will of Zambians, especially on fundamental constitutional changes. Petitions before Parliament, he said, did not guarantee that citizens’ concerns would be heard and reflected in the outcome.

Mr Lubinda proposed a national referendum instead, so that citizens could state their position on term limits directly.

“If government is genuinely committed to allowing citizens to determine the country’s constitutional future, why not consider a public referendum that gives Zambians a direct opportunity to express their views on any proposed changes to presidential term limits?” he asked.

He said the will of the people should be shown, not merely declared, and that constitutional questions of national importance required real consultation and consensus. The two-term limit, he said, was a democratic safeguard that promoted leadership renewal, constitutional continuity and accountability.

He urged President Hichilema to concentrate on his second-term mandate rather than let speculation about a third term overshadow national development.

“Presidents come and go, political parties rise and fall, but the Republic of Zambia must endure,” Mr Lubinda said.

“The presidency is a temporary mandate. The Republic is permanent.”

The Government is taking a different line. Chief Government Spokesperson Mr Elvis Nkandu questioned why some civil society organisations were staging protests against members of the public who are canvassing Parliament to remove the presidential term limit. He noted that President Hichilema and the UPND had taken no stand either way.

Mr Nkandu, who is also Information and Media Minister, said it was unreasonable for the organisations to mobilise protests over a matter that neither the Head of State nor the ruling party’s leadership had proposed. He said discussion of the term limit should be allowed to continue, because freedom of expression gave every citizen the right to speak without intimidation or interference.

He said it would be undemocratic to let organisations opposed to removing the limit express themselves freely while those holding the opposite view were denied the same space. Democracy, he said, required tolerance and respect for different opinions.

Mr Nkandu said the President was not preoccupied with talk of removing the term limit. He said the Head of State remained focused on creating jobs, reducing the cost of living and increasing electricity generation to prevent power shortages. The Government, he said, was more concerned with tackling those challenges than with speculation about the President’s political direction.

Opposition voices are not convinced. Leadership Movement (LM) president Dr Richard Silumbe said Zambians were spending too much time fighting each other over politics while foreign interests mined the country’s resources and financed unpopular agendas, among them a limitless presidential term.

For now, President Hichilema has not personally addressed Mr Lubinda’s challenge, and the term-limit petitions remain before Parliament.

World.title: Kalumbila District Commissioner Brenda Sankisa And Driver Killed In Road Crash
World.content:
Kalumbila District Commissioner Brenda Sankisa And Driver Killed In Road Crash

Kalumbila District Commissioner Ms Brenda Sankisa and her driver were killed early on Sunday when their Kalumbila District Council vehicle crashed into a truck on the Mutanda-Mwinilunga Road. They died on the day Zambia joined the rest of the world in remembering people lost on the road.

The crash happened at around 05:00 hours in the Kambazhi area, about 15 kilometres south of Mutanda Security Checkpoint in Chief Mumena’s area. Zambia Police Service spokesperson Ms Chipo Kaitisha said the council’s Toyota Hilux, registration GRZ 817DF, was on its way to Lusaka when it collided with a FAW truck and trailer, registration ATB 2117 and P5050T, owned by Phillip Nduna Transport of Solwezi.

At the wheel of the Hilux was Mr Christopher Katongo, 36, of Manyama area, with Ms Sankisa and District Messenger Ms Susan Phiri as passengers. Mr Katongo and Ms Sankisa, 49, died on the spot. Ms Phiri, 35, escaped with bruises to both hands and legs and was treated as an outpatient. Police say she is in a stable condition.

Ms Kaitisha said early findings placed the blame on the truck, which was travelling towards Solwezi.

“Preliminary investigations indicate that the accident occurred when the driver of the truck and trailer cut in front of the Toyota Hilux, which had the right of way, resulting in the Toyota Hilux colliding with the rear trailer,” she said.

The truck’s driver, Mr Phillip Nduna, 33, of Zangamenu area in Solwezi District, is in police custody. He has been charged with two counts of causing death by dangerous driving, contrary to Section 161(1) of the Roads and Road Traffic Act, Chapter 464 of the Laws of Zambia, one count for each life lost.

If convicted, he faces a fine of up to 30,000 penalty units, currently K12,000, or up to five years’ imprisonment, or both, on each count.

Officers from the Road Transport and Safety Agency (RTSA) have examined both vehicles at the scene. The trailer was damaged on its right rear section. The bodies of Ms Sankisa and Mr Katongo are lying in Solwezi General Hospital Mortuary, awaiting post-mortem examinations.

Ms Kaitisha used the tragedy to appeal to motorists across the country to slow down and respect other road users.

“The Zambia Police Service urges all motorists to exercise caution, obey traffic regulations, respect the right of way and avoid reckless driving,” she said.

“Drivers are reminded that road safety is everyone’s responsibility and that careless driving can result in loss of lives. Let us all drive responsibly and save lives.”

World.title: Kabimba Warns UPND Is Courting Its Own Destruction Over Mundubile Treason Case
World.content:
Former Justice Minister Mr Wynter Kabimba has warned that the UPND risks destroying itself if the State fails to secure convictions in the treason case against opposition leader Mr Brian Mundubile and 17 others. He said the ruling party is on the same road that finished the Patriotic Front (PF) after it detained President Hakainde Hichilema in 2017.

On Prime TV’s Matters Arising programme, Mr Kabimba said the prosecution was being mishandled. Months after the 18 accused were locked up, the State was relying on technicalities, and he said that was eroding public confidence in its own case.

“It’s not being done right, in my view. The State can do better in this case,” he said.

The former PF Secretary General said treason was neither difficult to prove nor difficult to disprove. One person cannot commit it alone, firearms must be present, and there must be an intention to overthrow a legally and democratically elected government.

“You can’t commit treason alone. At least there must be two of you,” he said.

Given the drama that surrounded the arrests, Mr Kabimba said the trial should have been under way by now. In his view, the public should not still be hearing legal arguments about procedure at this stage.

“Surely by now the treason case would have started, or should have started. But to start listening now to technicalities is concerning,” he said.

The 18 accused include Mr Mundubile, the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) presidential candidate, and his running mate Mr Makebi Zulu. They have been held at Mukobeko Maximum Correctional Facility in Kabwe since they were charged in late August, after security forces raided Mr Mundubile’s residence.

Treason is not bailable. In October, a constitutional bail application by the 18 failed to proceed in the Lusaka High Court after the State said it was not ready.

For Mr Kabimba, the stakes for the ruling party reach well beyond the courtroom. He said that if the government mishandled the matter, public anger could kill the UPND in the long run. Handling the case well, he said, meant one thing: taking it to the end and winning convictions.

“Not against all the 18, but at least a few of them. To convince this country that indeed there was a plot to overthrow the government,” he said.

He warned that the alternative would be fatal. If the State tried what he called “the usual tricks” and entered a nolle prosequi, discontinuing the prosecution, “then UPND is gone.”

When the programme’s host called that a strong statement, Mr Kabimba stood by it. He said the government would have no answer for the public beyond an apology. Zambians, he said, would not accept that citizens with a democratic right to take part in elections could be detained for months, only for the State to walk away from the case.

“How are they going to explain this matter to the public? It won’t make sense,” he said.

An acquittal, he added, would bring the same reckoning, because it would mean the accused had never done anything wrong.

Mr Kabimba expected the government to point to President Hichilema’s own detention in 2017 in its defence. He said that example worked against the UPND, not for it.

Mr Hichilema, then in opposition, was arrested over a traffic offence linked to the presidential motorcade. Rather than charge him with that offence, the PF government slapped him with an unbailable treason charge, and he spent 127 days in prison. Mr Kabimba said that detention became a grievance the opposition carried all the way to the 2021 polls.

“Didn’t you see HH run with that until he won the election? He did. That’s a backlash I’m talking about. So, PF finished itself through that case,” he said.

Mr Kabimba said the UPND was now walking into the same trap from the other side of power. The 2017 case had finished the PF, and he said the present one would finish the UPND if it did not end in convictions.

“The man who said that history does not repeat itself was wrong. It does, but in different circumstances,” he said.

Asked how UPND members would take his remarks, Mr Kabimba said his warning was meant to help the ruling party, not hurt it. He urged the party to act before the matter dragged on further.

“If I were them, before this thing gets so prolonged, I would actually say, listen to what Wynter said. We may have a problem,” he said.

Mr Kabimba said he was not speaking to please anyone. He was drawing on history and the lessons it offered.

The 18 accused remain in custody at Mukobeko, and the treason trial has not yet begun.

World.title: Lindiwe Alam, Project Fame Winner And “Nalema” Star, Dies In Italy
World.content:
Lindiwe “Lindi” Alam, the Zambian vocalist who won Project Fame in 2004, has died in Italy after suffering a stroke. She was in her late forties. The Zambian-born singer, songwriter, actress and activist, known in later years as Lindiwe Bungane, passed away on Saturday, 14th November 2026. At home, she is best remembered for the enduring hit “Nalema” and for winning M-Net’s pan-African talent competition. Many in the industry regard her as one of the most gifted voices Zambia has ever produced.

Zambia Association of Musicians (ZAM) president Brian “B’Flow” Bwembya announced her death in a statement. He said details of the funeral would be communicated in due course. B’Flow said Lindiwe is best remembered for “Nalema”, a song that touched many Zambians and earned her lasting recognition in the country’s music industry. As news of her death spread on Saturday evening, musicians, producers, broadcasters and fans paid tribute on social media.

“Lindiwe was a phenomenal singer. I don’t know if we have anyone with that level of vocal dexterity on the scene right now. What a massive talent to lose,” said a veteran Zambian voice coach.

Lindiwe first came to national attention in late 1999, when Chisha Folotiya’s Mondo Music Corporation launched a search for fresh talent. At the time, Kalindula, Zambia’s homegrown sound, had been pushed aside by Congolese rumba. Her breakthrough came on Daddy Zemus’s album “Chibaba”, released under the Mondo Music label on 24th December 1999. On the track “Genuine”, she performed alongside rapper C.R.I.$.I.$, and the song quickly won over Zambian music fans. It marked the start of a career that would carry her far beyond Lusaka.

Mondo Music followed up with the Rhythm Nation Project, a compilation built to showcase a new generation of Zambian artists. Lindiwe contributed “I Need More” to Volume 1, titled “Yo Yamba”, recording the song after winning the Ngoma Award for Best Female Performer. The compilation helped shape a new contemporary Zambian sound, placing her alongside acts such as Black Muntu, Shatel, JK and Tribal Cousins. She also featured with Suke Chile and Black Muntu on the hit “Usinisabu”. By the early 2000s, hers was one of the most recognisable voices in the country.

In 2004, Lindiwe represented Zambia on Project Fame, a pan-African version of the Star Academy format produced by Endemol and screened on M-Net between June and August that year. Fellow contestants dubbed her the “African diva”, and she lived up to the name in the final at the Pyramid in Johannesburg. Aged 25 at the time, she beat South Africa’s Jonathan Ross to the title, with Nigeria’s Daré Art Alade finishing third. Her prizes included a recording contract and a Citroën C2. She said she hoped her victory would open doors for other talented Zambian musicians.

The win came barely a year after Cherise Makubale became the first winner of Big Brother Africa, giving Zambians a second continental triumph in quick succession. Some of the biggest names in local music at the time, among them JK, MC Wabwino and Danny Kaya, recorded a celebratory song in her honour. JK sang the chorus, while Danny delivered a raggamuffin verse hailing her win for Zambia and for Africa. The song captured a moment of national pride. For a generation of young Zambian singers, Lindiwe became proof that the continent was within reach.

After the competition, Lindiwe released “Nalema”, which became her biggest local hit and remains her signature song. Written by Anthony Kangwa Kapampa, popularly known as Exile, and produced by TK Romaside, the song tells the story of a woman left alone at home by her partner. Its chorus was taken up as an anthem by female fans across the country. For many listeners, “Nalema” is the song that defines her legacy. It showed that her appeal reached well beyond competition stages and into everyday Zambian life.

Throughout her rise, Lindiwe featured prominently on Radio Phoenix’s Local Rhythms countdown, a programme dedicated to promoting Zambian music. The show was founded and hosted by Kalumba “K-Smash” Chikonde, late Zachariah Chavula and Douglas Leroy Namafente, aka Selecta D, who now runs a reggae session on Hot FM. She was among the first artists to make a mark on the countdown, and her productions, “Nalema” among them, enjoyed regular airtime as they were released. Some of her recordings were made while the show was at the height of its campaign for local music, giving her work a ready platform. From the start, the trio spoke highly of her talent on air and predicted she would go far.

Lindiwe relocated to South Africa after Project Fame, where she built a career on stage as well as in the studio. She gained recognition for her role in the South African production of the hit musical Dreamgirls, produced by Hazel Feldman of Showtime Management. As a recording artist, she described herself as an urban Afro-soul singer, blending neo-soul, folk, rock, jazz and R&B. Her songs often moved between several languages, including English, her native Bemba, Nyanja, Nsenga, Zulu and Lingala. That mix of sounds and languages set her apart from many of her contemporaries.

She later settled in Italy, where she continued her work as a singer, songwriter, actress and activist until her death. Although she spent much of her adult life abroad, fans continued to count her among Zambia’s own. Through her music, Zambian languages reached audiences far from home. Her name still comes up whenever Zambians discuss the country’s greatest female vocalists.

Her death removes one of the leading voices of a generation that helped homegrown Zambian pop win back ground from foreign sounds. Her songs remain part of the soundtrack of that era for many Zambians. Funeral arrangements are yet to be announced. Lusaka Times extends its condolences to her family, friends and the wider music community.

World.title: Minister of Information Calls on Church to Contribute to the Grow Zambia Agenda
World.content:
Minister of Information and Media Elvis Nkandu has urged the church to be active contributors to the Grow Zambia Agenda

Mr Nkandu says collective responsibility is required in a bid to improve the living standards of every Zambia.

He notes that the church is well positioned to complement the government in addressing the social and economic challenges in society.

The Minister stated that the church can contribute to meaningful development by promoting productivity, entrepreneurship and self-reliance, adding that they can also explore opportunities in agriculture, livestock and other income generating activities.

Mr Nkandu was speaking when he officially opened the three-day breakthrough conference for Grace Ministries Missions International at the Exploits Centre in Lusaka, which is being held under the theme Possessing new territories through warfare.

He commended the leadership of Grace Ministries International for organising a gathering which brings together believers and church leaders to reflect on faith, spiritual growth and transformation.

“Under the leadership of President Hakainde Hichilema, the government is pursuing the growth Zambia agenda which seeks to accelerate inclusive and sustainable economic growth, improve living standards and create opportunities for all Zambians,” Mr Nkandu said.

He noted that through practical interventions, the church can also address challenges such as substance abuse, unemployment and the vulnerability of disadvantaged members of society.

And he implored the church to condemn wrong doings such as corrupt activities and provide moral guidance in an effort to build responsible communities.

The Minister highlighted the important role of the church in promoting integrity, accountability, ethical leadership and responsible citizenship.

He added that the government remains ready to work with the church among other stakeholders through partnerships to mobilize resources for sustainable community investments.

Meanwhile, Mr Nkandu urged the church to spearhead national unity and peace despite differences in political affiliation, tribe religion or social standing.

Grace Ministries International Presiding Bishop Lucky Simumba noted that the conference was not just about spiritual nourishment but also for economic empowerment and productivity.

Bishop Simumba stressed that Christian’s and believers are capable of contributing to the growth of the national economy, hence urging the church to become productive and contribute positively to society to the grow Zambia Agenda.

He encouraged congregants to take advantage of the many opportunities within the economic sphere that they can take advantage of including farming, business ventures among other productive opportunities.

“Let us become part and parcel of the Grow Zambia Agenda by getting involved in farming, establishing entrepreneurial ventures and taking advantage of the opportunities available in our country,” Bishop Simumba stated.

He added that the government is also providing opportunities for those who want to pursue further studies and develop themselves in different professional fields that support various sectors of the economy.

World.title: President Hichilema counsel’s leaders
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has urged elected and appointed leaders to remain alert to the needs of the people and prioritise service delivery in their respective positions.

Speaking during a church service at Choma Central Seventh-day Adventist Church, President Hichilema challenged mayors, councillors, council chairpersons, Members of Parliament and Ministers to discern the times, keep their ears on the ground and respond to the concerns of ordinary Zambians.

The Head of State, who was accompanied by First Lady Mutinta Hichilema, stressed that leadership must translate into tangible development and improved livelihoods, reaffirming government’s commitment to sustaining development programmes across the country.

President Hichilema said leaders must understand the prevailing circumstances and ensure their decisions and actions respond to the changing needs of citizens.

“Leaders must have their ears on the ground and understand the needs of the people they serve,” Mr Hichilema said.

He cited the Free Education Policy as one of the interventions responding to the needs of children and families, particularly those from vulnerable communities.

“Through programmes such as the Free Education Policy, we are discerning the present needs of children. By ensuring children have access to quality education and are fed at school through the School Feeding Programme, we are responding to our God-given mandate as public leaders,” he said.

President Hichilema added that such interventions were not only improving access to essential services but also strengthening communities and improving livelihoods.

Meanwhile, Mositunya Conference President Pastor Maxwell Muvwimi commended President Hichilema for his commitment to supporting vulnerable members of society.

Pastor Muvwimi acknowledged the importance of interventions aimed at uplifting disadvantaged communities and improving the welfare of citizens.

And Choma Central Seventh-day Adventist Church Resident Pastor Mungende Mukoswe urged members of the public to understand the prevailing times and seasons and adapt accordingly to safeguard their livelihoods.

“People need to understand the times and seasons we are in and respond appropriately to sustain their livelihoods,” Pastor Mukoswe said.

He cited the effects of climate change, urging communities to put in place appropriate measures to respond to changing climatic conditions and mitigate their impact.

President Hichilema also made a donation of k200 thousand kwacha towards the church’s additional infrastructure and the choirs ‘ uniform.

World.title: CHIEF CONCERNED OVER TREE CUTTING DURING CATERPILLAR HARVESTING
World.content:
Chief Chibesakunda of the Bisa people in Shiwang’andu District, Muchinga Province has expressed concern over the continued cutting down of trees by some community members during caterpillar harvesting.

The traditional leader, who spoke through his Prime Minister, Mubanga Clapperson, has urged his subjects to adopt sustainable harvesting methods and desist from destroying trees in search of caterpillars.

Chief Chibesakunda warned that the practice threatens forest conservation and could affect the availability of caterpillars in future seasons.

Meanwhile, District Forest Officer Charity Kantu said forests provide a natural habitat for caterpillars and that cutting down trees during harvesting destroys their habitat and contributes to biodiversity loss.

Ms Kantu said the practice was still occurring in several caterpillar infested areas of the district.

She said the Forestry Department had intensified awareness and sensitisation campaigns and engaged traditional leaders to educate communities on sustainable harvesting methods.

‎”Cutting down trees during caterpillar harvesting destroys their natural habitat and contributes to biodiversity loss. We are therefore encouraging communities to adopt sustainable harvesting methods that do not require cutting down trees,” she said.

Ms Kantu explained that harvesters could bend or shake branches to allow fully grown caterpillars to fall without damaging trees.

She said protecting forests was essential to ensuring that communities continued benefiting from caterpillars and other forest products for generations to come.

World.title: GOVERNMENT WARNS EMPLOYERS AGAINST ABUSING ZAMBIAN WORKERS
World.content:
Government has warned that it will deal sternly with employers abusing Zambian workers, following the discovery of appalling working conditions at Chi Farm in Lusaka District.

Minister of Labour and Social Security, Misheck Nyambose, issued the warning when he inspected the Chinese-owned pig farm, Chi Farm, located along Mungwi Road in Lusaka West.

Mr Nyambose observed that workers were forced to live in deplorable conditions near pig pens and were denied access to medical care when they fell ill.

He further noted that the workers were not permitted to leave the fenced work premises even after knocking off.

The Minister said it was disheartening to note that such things were happening despite reports that some labour officers had been visiting the farm.

Meanwhile, Mr Nyambose has also threatened to punish labour officers who compromise labour laws at the expense of Zambian workers.

“I need to know the officers who have been coming here because we can’t allow this,” Mr Nyambose said.

However, the company representative who refused to comment or disclose her name referred everything to management.

The Minister has since summoned the farm management to his office.

He further directed that the details of the labour officers who have been inspecting the company be identified.

Meanwhile, Mondengwa Ward Councillor Rudia Mpundu alleged that management at the farm once attempted to bribe her with 100,000 kwacha to stop her from disclosing conditions at the facility after she visited the premises alone.

“When I came here, they offered me K100,000 so that I could keep quiet, but I refused,” Ms Mpundu said.

World.title: Africa: Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games - After The Historic Achievement, The Challenge of a Lasting Legacy for Africa
World.content:
The first Youth Olympic Games held on the African continent, the Dakar 2026 YOG, concluded on November 13th with a record praised by leaders of the Olympic movement. Beyond the organizational success and popular enthusiasm, Senegal and its partners now face a major challenge: transforming this historic first into an engine of sporting, economic, and social development. Youth training, job creation, infrastructure development, and the emergence of new talent are the main priorities for the post-Games period.

Senegal is preparing to close a historic chapter in world sport. For two weeks, from October 31 to November 13, 2026, Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly hosted the first Youth Olympic Games (YOG) organized in Africa, placing the continent at the center of attention of the international Olympic movement.

With approximately 2,700 young athletes representing 204 National Olympic Committees, 25 competitive sports, ten engagement sports and 153 medal-winning events, this fourth edition of the Summer Youth Olympic Games was an exceptional showcase for Senegal and, beyond, for the entire African continent.

But behind the sporting performances, the ceremonies and the popular mobilization, a question now arises: how to make Dakar 2026 more than just a successful event and ensure its lasting impact on the development of Africa?

This question was a major theme of the joint press conference of the International Olympic Committee (IOC) and the Organising Committee of the Youth Olympic Games (COJOJ), held on November 12 in Diamniadio.

IOC President Kirsty Coventry hailed the event as a "100% organizational success," stating that expectations had been exceeded. She particularly encouraged the continent to build on this experience.

"My wish is that Africa and the continent become fully aware of their potential. It is now up to us to make it a reality," she said.

A message that sums up the challenge of the post-Dakar 2026 era: to transform the international recognition acquired during the Games into concrete prospects for new African generations.

An Olympic first that changes the way we see Africa

By hosting an Olympic event of this magnitude, Senegal has taken a symbolic step in the history of African sport. Long absent from the map of host countries for Olympic competitions, the continent has demonstrated its ability to mobilize infrastructure, skills, and human resources around a major international event.

For the IOC's executive director of the Olympic Games, Christophe Dubi, one of the most striking elements of this edition will remain the welcome given to foreign delegations and the enthusiasm of the Senegalese people.

From Dakar to Saly, via Diamniadio, the mobilization of the public helped to give these Games a popular dimension, beyond just the competition venues.

This success also sends a signal to other African countries that aspire to host major international sporting events.

However, this does not mean that all organizational and financial obstacles have been removed. The Senegalese experience will need to be analyzed to identify financing, governance, and infrastructure management models that could be replicated elsewhere on the continent.

The stakes thus go beyond mere symbolic recognition: it is about making Dakar 2026 a reference for the organization of future sporting events in Africa.

New talents and disciplines to develop

From a sporting perspective, the Youth Olympic Games provided an international platform for a new generation of African athletes, while also allowing the Senegalese public to discover disciplines that are still underdeveloped in the country.

The chairman of the IOC Coordination Commission for Dakar 2026, Humphrey Kayange, particularly emphasized the interest generated by the sporting activities organized on the Corniche of Dakar.

These discovery spaces have allowed many young people to try out different sports and consider new opportunities for involvement.

But this enthusiasm will need to be maintained.

For Humphrey Kayange, national sports federations now have an essential role to play in order to extend this momentum, structure emerging disciplines and facilitate their access for young people.

The issue of talent identification and support is another major challenge. Kirsty Coventry pointed out that approximately 15% of participants in the Youth Olympic Games go on to compete in the Olympic Games.

This proportion highlights the role that the Youth Olympic Games can play in preparing future generations of elite athletes.

For Africa, where many young athletes still face difficulties accessing equipment, qualified coaches and funding, the continuity of training programs will be crucial.

The true sporting success of Dakar 2026 will therefore not be measured solely by the number of medals won, but also by the ability of African countries to support the talents revealed during the Games.

Training and employment: the economic legacy takes shape

Beyond sport, one of the most promising achievements of Dakar 2026 concerns the development of professional skills.

The Dakar 2026 Learning Academy, set up to prepare young professionals for jobs related to the organization of major events, has trained more than 300 participants, from 21 African nationalities, according to information provided by the IOC.

This program is a concrete example of how an international sporting competition can contribute to strengthening human capital.

Event management, operational coordination, communication, logistics and sports organization represent all areas in which the skills acquired could be valued after the Games.

The challenge now is to transform these training programs into sustainable career opportunities.

The president of the COJOJ, Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye, notably mentioned discussions with the World Bank regarding employment prospects and integration of young people.

Presented in Washington before the Games, the Learning Academy reportedly attracted the interest of the international financial institution, particularly for its potential in terms of training and employability.

In this context, closer ties have been envisaged with the World Bank's regional SIRA program, dedicated to skills development and access to employment.

These discussions, however, have yet to be finalized. No definitive funding has been announced at this stage.

For Senegal, the sustainability of this type of program could contribute to developing a pool of African professionals capable of intervening in the organization of sporting, cultural and institutional events on an international scale.

Infrastructure to be valued beyond the Games

Another central question of the Olympic legacy: the future of the sports facilities mobilized or modernized for Dakar 2026.

Organizing the Youth Olympic Games required investments in infrastructure and reception facilities, particularly in Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly.

While this equipment has met the requirements of the competition, its future use will represent a real test for public authorities and sports federations.

International experience shows that the legacy of major sporting events largely depends on the ability of host countries to ensure the maintenance, financing and accessibility of facilities after the competitions.

For Senegal, several perspectives could be explored: development of training centers, organization of regional competitions, hosting of international internships and opening of infrastructure to schools and sports associations.

The development of these facilities could also contribute to the development of a local sports economy, by promoting training activities, event services, sports tourism and related jobs.

These potential benefits will, however, need to be accompanied by appropriate management mechanisms and a long-term financing strategy.

Sport as a response to the social challenges facing youth

Beyond infrastructure and performance, Senegalese officials also want to inscribe the legacy of the YOG in a social perspective.

Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye thus mentioned a project to create sports academies in several coastal localities, including Saint-Louis, Kayar and Rufisque.

This initiative aims to offer young people new opportunities for training, guidance and integration through sport.

It takes on a particular dimension in areas facing youth unemployment, economic insecurity and perilous departures by sea.

The ambition would be to make sport a tool for support and opening up towards professional prospects, possibly involving public actors, federations and development partners.

The project remains at a design stage and will need to specify its financing arrangements, its operating model and the target audiences.

Its success will also depend on its ability to combine sports practice with education, vocational training and access to employment.

Because while sport can play an important role in social inclusion, it cannot, on its own, address the structural difficulties faced by African youth.

A legacy to be built on a continental scale

The organization of the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games finally raises the question of African sports cooperation.

Close 

By bringing together athletes, coaches, officials and professionals from different countries, the Games have created opportunities for exchange and collaboration that can continue after the competition.

This dynamic could promote the sharing of expertise between federations, the implementation of regional training programs and the development of partnerships around emerging sports disciplines.

The participation of young professionals of several African nationalities in the Learning Academy already illustrates this continental dimension.

But to produce lasting effects, these initiatives will need to be part of coordinated sports policies, supported by long-term institutional funding and commitments.

Africa has significant demographic and sporting potential. However, its development requires regular investments in local infrastructure, coach training, athlete support, and the professionalization of sports-related jobs.

Dakar 2026 could thus serve as a starting point for a broader reflection on the place of sport in African development strategies.

After the celebration, the test of the results

As the first Youth Olympic Games held in Africa come to a close, Senegal can boast of international recognition and popular mobilization that have marked this edition.

But the Olympic legacy is not decreed at the end of a closing ceremony. It is built over time, through public policies, sustained investments and programs capable of producing measurable results.

How many young people trained by the Learning Academy will find employment? How will the sports facilities be used? Will the disciplines discovered during the Games find a place in national federations? Will the sports academy projects actually come to fruition?

These are all questions that the coming years will need to answer.

Dakar 2026 will have demonstrated that Africa can host a major international Olympic event. The next challenge will be to prove that such an event can also contribute sustainably to the economic, social, and sporting transformation of the continent.

Only under this condition will the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games be able to transcend its status as a historic first and become a true legacy for future generations.

World.title: South Africa: Africa's Waste Pickers Demand Recognition in Climate Action
World.content:
As COP31 puts zero waste on the climate agenda, waste pickers across Africa say the continent's circular-economy transition cannot succeed without the people who already recover and recycle much of what it throws away.

Waste is the third-largest source of human-caused methane emissions, accounting for nearly 20% of the global total, yet the sector remains underfunded and inadequately monitored.

The UN Environment Programme estimated that municipal solid waste reached 2.1 billion tonnes in 2023 and will be at 3.8 billion tonnes by 2050. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), improved waste management, through a circular economy and better treatment technologies, has the potential to make a substantial contribution to reductions in national GHG emissions.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Under its Global Climate Action Agenda, COP31 is championing the Zero Waste initiative, which seeks to unlock the climate potential of waste management through scalable circular economy solutions. The initiative is focused on preventing food waste, moving towards circular economy solutions that turn waste into resources, and encouraging countries to include waste-related methane reductions in their updated Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). The aim is to prevent emissions at source and make waste management an integral part of national climate strategies.

The need is greatest in low-income countries, where 97% of waste is openly dumped or burned. Uncontrolled dumpsites and open burning threaten communities, contaminate water and release climate pollutants, and without knowing where these sites are, how much waste they receive and what they emit, effective intervention is extremely difficult. As COP31 pushes countries to include waste methane in their climate plans, some African investors say the continent has a chance to turn waste into an economic resource.

Waste pickers say they must be part of that shift.

Across Africa, waste pickers and reclaimers collect, sort and recover recyclable materials that would otherwise end up in landfills, rivers or the environment. Many still work with limited formal recognition, social protection, and decent working conditions. Their inclusion is therefore emerging as a key question in discussions about Africa's zero-waste future. A transition to more sustainable waste management systems, advocates argue, must build on the knowledge and contribution of existing waste workers rather than exclude them.

For the International Alliance of Waste Pickers (IAWP), the success of such initiatives will depend in part on whether the people already driving recycling and resource recovery are recognised as essential partners in their implementation.

In an interview, Eva Mokoena of South Africa's African Reclaimers Organisation (ARO) discusses the role of waste pickers in climate action, the opportunities presented by the Zero Waste Districts initiative, and the changes needed to secure their place in Africa's transition to a circular economy.

Waste is often seen as an environmental and sanitation problem, but it is increasingly recognised as a major climate challenge. Why does tackling waste matter for the fight against climate change, and what role can zero waste play in reducing emissions?

Waste is a climate issue because what we throw away does not disappear. Organic waste buried in landfills and dumpsites rots without oxygen and releases methane, a gas that traps far more heat than carbon dioxide in the short term. Open burning of waste adds black carbon and toxic smoke to the air our communities breathe. Every item that is landfilled or burnt also means new materials must be extracted, manufactured, and transported to replace it.

Zero waste addresses all of these at once. When materials are separated at source, recovered, reused and recycled, and when organic waste is composted or turned into biogas, methane from landfills falls and the demand for virgin materials drops. This is one of the fastest and most affordable ways to reduce emissions.

The key to making it work is already on the ground. Waste pickers and reclaimers are the people removing waste from landfills, rivers, and streams every day. With proper recognition, equipment, and collaboration from governments, municipalities, and residents, they can multiply the climate impact they already deliver.

Waste is often overlooked in climate talks, yet food waste and landfills are major sources of greenhouse-gas emissions, especially methane. What practical policies and local actions would most effectively reduce food waste and keep organic waste out of landfills?

The most effective policies are the ones that recognise and include waste pickers and reclaimers. They are the frontline educators of their communities: they already teach residents to separate and recycle what they buy and eat. Governments and policymakers should write waste pickers into waste and climate legislation, so that this work is formally recognised, supported and paid for.

In practice, this means separation at source, in households, markets and businesses before it reaches the landfill, with waste pickers leading door-to-door awareness and collection.

In logistics, waste picker organisations need access to land, storage facilities and transport, so that organic material can be collected, stored and processed close to where it is generated. Local processing of food waste should be turned into compost, manure and biogas through community-run facilities, creating useful products and income instead of methane.

Investment in people is also important. Incubating reclaimer cooperatives, with full access to logistics and infrastructure, is what turns good policy into results.

If we continue to ignore the people on the ground, we will keep struggling. If we invest in them, organic waste can become a resource for our communities.

How can African governments make waste reduction and the circular economy a more central part of their national climate policies?

Governments can start by recognising who already runs Africa's circular economy. Waste pickers and reclaimers are unrecognised heroes: many spend their own time and resources recovering materials and cleaning public spaces without pay or protection. Bringing them into national climate policy means three things.

First, recognition in law. National climate plans, including Nationally Determined Contributions, and waste management legislation should name waste pickers as essential service providers and set out their rights, their role and how they will be paid.

Second, a seat at the table. Waste picker organisations should take part in designing, implementing and monitoring these policies. When waste pickers help shape the rules, the rules work on the ground, and waste pickers gain the recognition and confidence to expand their work.

Third, real support. Recognition has to come with resources: equipment, infrastructure, social protection and fair payment for the services waste pickers provide to cities and to the climate.

Looking at initiatives such as Zero Waste Districts and the 1x100 campaign, how can these programmes translate into tangible benefits for African communities, from cleaner cities and reduced landfill waste to decent jobs and better livelihoods for waste pickers?

These programmes deliver real benefits when everybody works together: governments, municipalities, residents, the private sector and waste picker organisations. Waste pickers are already on the ground, in every neighbourhood and in every landfill. What makes the difference is giving them space, resources and a central role.

Education is the most important key. With educational tools, training and empowerment, waste pickers can lead awareness campaigns, help households separate their waste, and recover a much wider range of materials at once. The result is cleaner streets, less waste reaching landfills and rivers, and recycling that actually works.

For waste pickers, the benefit must be decent work: formal contracts, fair payment for collection and recovery services, safe working conditions and social protection. When district programmes are built around existing waste picker cooperatives, the jobs and income they create stay in the community.

Two African nations that have joined the Zero Waste Districts programme are Ghana and Kenya. What are the biggest waste management challenges these countries are hoping to address, and what makes the district-level approach different from previous efforts?

What makes the district-level approach different is that it starts from the community and from the organisations that already exist, rather than from large, centralised projects designed far away from the people who manage waste every day. Our affiliates in both countries describe it in these terms.

In Ghana, the Green Waste Pickers Cooperative Society Limited and the Kpone Landfill Waste Pickers Association are supporting community-led circular initiatives that build on existing cooperatives. These cooperatives drive the process of diverting waste at source, adopt measures to pre-process materials, and lead environmental campaigns in their communities.

In Kenya, the Nakuru County Waste Pickers Association is advancing zero waste through waste reduction, reuse, recycling and waste picking, alongside community-led initiatives, progressive policies and the promotion of a circular economy.

In both cases, the district becomes the unit where waste pickers, residents and local authorities can work side by side, and where results can be seen and measured.

Many African cities are still grappling with poor waste collection, overflowing landfills, and very limited recycling. What kind of investment and what kind of partnerships are required to build effective waste management and recycling systems across the continent?

Close 

The investment that works is investment in the people already doing the job. Instead of expensive systems that bypass or displace waste pickers, African cities should incubate reclaimer and waste picker cooperatives and give them full access to what they need.

In infrastructure, sorting centres, storage space and land can help make the work safer. In logistics, vehicles and equipment to collect and move materials efficiently are needed. Processing capacity with facilities to recycle materials and to turn food waste into compost, manure and biogas is necessary. Fair contracts are also a key issue to provide payments from municipalities for the collection and recovery services waste pickers provide.

The partnerships that work are inclusive ones. Municipalities, national governments, producers, funders and residents should partner directly with waste picker organisations, as equals and from the design stage. If we keep ignoring the people on the ground, cities will keep struggling with the same problems. If we invest in them, Africa can build recycling systems that are effective, fair and locally owned.

Given that COP31 is placing such a strong emphasis on zero waste, what specific commitments should African countries be demanding in order to ensure that waste reduction actually becomes a measurable element of climate action rather than just another one of the international promises?

African countries should demand commitments that reach the ground, not only the negotiating rooms. In particular, direct funding for equipment and machinery that allows waste pickers and reclaimers to recover and recycle more materials, including food waste.

Educational tools must also be designed with waste pickers and be easy to use for both reclaimers and residents, so that separation at source becomes everyday practice in every household.

Formal recognition of waste pickers in national climate plans and waste policies, with a guaranteed role in their implementation and measurable targets for diverting organic and recyclable waste from landfills, monitored with the participation of waste picker organisations, are commitments that promote long-term climate solutions.

Waste pickers are good at what we do, and we make sure that everyone we work with understands our livelihoods on the streets and in the landfills, and the important role we play. Climate commitments on waste will only become real when they are built with us.

World.title: Nigeria: Index Ebola Case - Swiss Diplomat's Wife Recovers, Discharged From Hospital
World.content:
Nigeriaâs Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) issued a public health advisory following the countryâs confirmed Ebola case.

Abuja — Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has said that the Nigeria's Ebola index case- Swiss diplomat's wife has recovered and discharged from hospital in Switzerland.

The disease intervention centre had confirmed the infection on October 20, 2026 after the patient's blood samples tested positive at the Abuja Reference Laboratory.

After receiving preliminary treatment at an undisclosed private hospital in Abuja, she and her husband were subsequently medically evacuated to Switzerland with an air ambulance on October 26, 2026.

Addressing journalists in his office in Abuja on Friday, NCDC Director General, Dr. Jide Idris, said the Swiss authorities had announced the recovery and discharge of the woman after testing negative.

He said index case tested negative after receiving treatment in an isolation facility in Switzerland.
