World.title: Ethiopia: Mekelle Residents Call for Sustained Federal Govt Efforts to Advance Reforms in Tigray
World.content:
Addis Ababa — Residents of Mekelle have urged the Federal Government to sustain and accelerate reform, reconstruction and development efforts in Tigray region.

The inhabitants further emphasized the need for consolidating progress toward lasting peace, stability and prosperity in the region.

The call was made during a consultative forum of Mekelle residents, presided over by Chief of Staff of the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), Field Marshal Birhanu Jula.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Speaking at the gathering, Field Marshal Birhanu said the defunct TPLF faction had aligned itself with the so-called "Tsimdo" group, an alliance orchestrated by Ethiopia's historical adversaries to wage war against the country.

He said his engagement with residents was aimed at fostering dialogue, strengthening cooperation and encouraging collective efforts to ensure lasting peace and stability in Tigray region.

During the discussions, residents underscored their strong desire to see an end to conflict, identifying peace, security and sustainable development as their foremost priorities.

They called for the reconstruction of damaged infrastructure, expanded employment opportunities for young people and the restoration of security to enable communities to resume normal life without fear.

"Our foremost priorities are the reconstruction of critical infrastructure, the creation of meaningful employment opportunities for our youth, and the restoration of security so that citizens can go about their daily lives in peace," participants said.

Residents also welcomed the resumption of salary payments for civil servants and ongoing infrastructure rehabilitation efforts, describing them as important steps toward restoring normalcy and accelerating the region's recovery.

Concluding the forum, participants called on the Federal Government to maintain its commitment to Tigray, sustain ongoing interventions and accelerate reform, reconstruction and development initiatives to secure lasting peace and improve the livelihoods of communities across the region.

World.title: South Africa: Joburg Turns Up the Heat As Residents Wait for Relief
World.content:
Outdoor workers should take regular breaks and residents should avoid direct sunlight between 11am and 3pm.

Cooler weather and thunderstorms are expected over the weekend, offering some relief from the heat.

Johannesburg residents face another scorching day on Friday, with emergency services urging people to drink water, take breaks and stay out of the midday sun.

The City of Johannesburg's Emergency Management Services says extremely hot conditions are expected to continue across much of the city. Outdoor workers have been urged to take regular breaks and residents should avoid direct sunlight between 11am and 3pm.

The South African Weather Service's heatwave advisory issued earlier this week included southern Gauteng, with persistently high temperatures expected until Friday, 13 November.



But some relief could arrive over the weekend.

Weather service senior forecaster Tokelo Chiloane said cooler conditions, accompanied by thunderstorms and thundershowers, are expected over the weekend.

Until then, residents have been urged to protect themselves from the heat.

"Residents are urged to stay hydrated, drink lots of water, avoid direct sunlight especially between 11h00 and 15h00 in the afternoon," Johannesburg emergency services spokesperson Robert Mulaudzi said earlier this week.

For street traders, gardeners, construction workers and others spending hours outside, regular breaks in a cool or shaded place are especially important.

The World Health Organization says older people, babies, outdoor workers and people with existing medical conditions face greater risks during hot weather. Residents should also check on relatives and neighbours who live alone.

Keeping cool does not have to mean switching on an air conditioner. The organisation recommends loose, light clothing, cool showers and wetting the skin with a damp cloth. Drink water regularly and avoid alcohol.

Never leave children, dependent adults or pets alone in a parked vehicle, even while running a quick errand.

Parents have also been warned to watch children seeking somewhere to cool off.

Mulaudzi urged families to keep young children away from dams and river streams to prevent drownings.

Heat illness needs prompt attention. Dizziness, weakness, intense thirst and headaches are signs to move into a cool place and drink water.

Confusion, seizures or a loss of consciousness require urgent medical help. Move the person into shade or a cool room and use cold, wet cloths to help cool them while waiting for assistance.

Close 

For life-threatening emergencies in Johannesburg, call 011 375 5911. The city says this number connects residents to emergency assistance, including ambulance and fire services.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: DR Congo Ebola Outbreak - Armed Groups Unrest Hold Back Response
World.content:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to spread amid repeated and ongoing deadly attacks on civilians and frontline health workers by armed groups that are obstructing efforts to stop transmission, UN responders said on Friday.

In an update, the UN Senior Ebola Response Coordinator, Julien Harneis, stressed that more people are being killed by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters than by Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in recent days.

And yet the attacks on "tens of villages all across the south of Ituri and North Kivu (provinces) goes unnoticed", Mr. Harneis maintained. "People are scared, people are furious at the lack of action on this."

Up to 500 infections per week



Echoing that message, the UN World Health Organization (WHO)'s Dr Chikwe Ihekweazu, Executive Director of WHO's Health Emergencies Programme, said that despite much progress in containing transmission within eastern DRC, about 400 to 500 cases of infection are still being identified every week.

This trend is linked to the emergence of cases in rural and hard-to-reach areas.

In more positive developments, the WHO official noted that prevention efforts have led to "a significant reduction" in transmission in previous hotspots, in particular Bunia, Mongbwalu, Rampara and Nizi, all in Ituri province in eastern DRC.

Nonetheless, the violent unrest across the vast area impacted by Ebola creates huge challenges for responders.

"We've seen so many attacks on healthcare, attacks on communities as well, attacks on people providing care, and people losing their lives, nurses in burials," Dr Ihekweazu explained. "So, we need to keep working with the community, and this is very important. And working with the specific groups instigating these attacks."

Disease threats in addition to attacks

Communities are already facing outbreaks of diseases, malnutrition and displacement driven by decades of violent unrest fuelled by dozens of armed

groups that remain active in the resource-rich region.

Earlier this week, WHO condemned attacks against frontline healthcare workers and community awareness officers, including in Cantine-Aloya in North Kivu that killed 66 civilians including three health workers. Three health facilities were also looted.

Two weeks ago, a nurse was also killed and another health worker badly injured when they were attacked while responding to an Ebola alert in Tshopo province.

Tedros appeal

Other attacks have included an arson attempt on a treatment centre and stones thrown at a vehicle used for conducting safe and dignified burials, an indication of the need to continue to build trust with extremely vulnerable communities.

"We cannot focus only on Ebola. Some people in the affected communities have said told me personally that Ebola is a lesser evil compared to some of the other threats they face," WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus stressed earlier this week.

A massive humanitarian emergency

The DRC Ebola outbreak was declared in May and has since become the largest yet as it continues to spread faster than any previous outbreak in the vast country's east and northeast provinces.

To date, more than 11,000 cases have been confirmed and more than 5,000 people have died.

In a related development, the UN World Food Programme (WFP) warned that nearly 29 million people in the DRC face acute food insecurity, with most in the conflict and Ebola-affected eastern and northeastern provinces. That number is likely to continue to increase, said Jean-Martin Bauer, WFP Director of Food Security and Nutrition Analysis.

Briefing journalists via video in Geneva, Mr. Bauer stressed that conflict is driving the hunger crisis, in addition to the Ebola outbreak.

Close 

"What we need right now is access, and we need resources to avoid the situation becoming more difficult in the DRC," he said.

Hunger emergency

Latest UN-backed food insecurity expert assessments indicate that between January and June 2027, 30.3 million people will be in crisis levels of acute food insecurity or worse, with 4.2 million of this number experiencing "emergency levels" of hunger and the most acute needs in North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri provinces "driven by persistent conflict and large-scale displacement".

Mr. Bauer noted that Ebola is just one of many disease outbreaks in DRC, but that it is compounding the hunger crisis for communities already struggling to eat.

"Families are being displaced, they're being cut off from their farms, from their livelihoods," he explained. "Food prices are rising, making affording a meal quite complicated for too many households."

World.title: Rwanda: Kigali Wetlands Will Protect 220,000 People From Floods, Says PM
World.content:
Rehabilitation of five wetlands in Kigali will reduce flood risks for more than 220,000 residents while creating public green spaces, jobs and livelihood opportunities, Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva said at the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Türkiye.

ALSO READ: Prime Minister Nsengiyumva makes case for green industrialisation

With national and international partners, approximately $195 million has been invested in flood-risk reduction, informal settlement upgrading, the construction of access roads and, more recently, the rehabilitation of five urban wetlands covering nearly 500 hectares in Kigali, the Prime Minister said.

ALSO READ: VIDEO & PHOTOS: Inside Kigali Wetlands Park

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"These investments are reducing flood risks for more than 220,000 residents while creating public green spaces, jobs and livelihood opportunities. Nature-based solutions can deliver resilience at scale," he said.

Rwanda is committed to extending this model to secondary and satellite cities, in line with the third version of its climate action plan, known as NDC 3.0.

However, he said, achieving this requires financing.

"Developing countries will need more than $300 billion annually for adaptation by 2035, up to 14 times the current support," he noted.

ALSO READ: COP31: What issues are on agenda as UN climate summit begins?

Rwanda has welcomed Türkiye's Sustainable Urban Resilience Financing Facility (SURFF), an initiative introduced under the COP31 Action Agenda.

The facility is intended to help cities turn climate objectives into investable projects, secure financing and deliver investments.

Another model of climate resilience

Prime Minister Nsengiyumva also cited the Green Gicumbi project in Gicumbi District, supported by the Green Climate Fund, which aimed to strengthen the resilience of about 249,000 people, nearly two-thirds of the district's population.

ALSO READ: What's at stake for Rwanda as COP31 approaches?

"Communities terraced hillsides, protected watersheds and moved vulnerable families into climate-resilient homes. Its independent evaluation confirms that climate-smart practices have spread, food security has improved and households are better able to withstand shocks," he said.

Achieving these ambitions requires addressing the barriers that have constrained investment, he noted.

"Good plans do not automatically become bankable projects."

Reducing carbon emissions

Delivering Rwanda's statement at the high-level segment for heads of state and government at COP31, the Prime Minister said national action alone cannot deliver the transformation required.

Close 

"Under our third Nationally Determined Contribution, Rwanda has committed to reducing emissions by 53 per cent by 2035, relative to the business-as-usual scenario."

Achieving this target requires $12 billion in investment, 80 percent of which is conditional on international support, he said. Rwanda needs predictable, accessible and adequate financing for adaptation and mitigation to meet these targets.

"We must also remove the barriers that prevent capital from flowing into viable projects in developing countries. As President Kagame observed at the recent Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, the perception that 'there are higher risks for investments in the South than in the North' is misplaced. Investments should be judged on their merits, not on their location."

He said governments and the private sector must work together to make viable projects investable, deepen markets and mobilise capital on terms that developing economies can afford, without adding to unsustainable debt.

"Rwanda stands ready to cooperate with all nations. As we assume the chairmanship of the G77 and China in 2027, we reaffirm our commitment to strengthening solidarity among developing countries and completing the outstanding work under the climate negotiations, including work on Global Goal on Adaptation indicators relating to financial needs and financial provision," he said.

World.title: Nigeria: 2027 Lagos State Governorship Debate - How the Candidates Fared
World.content:
The Lagos State governorship candidates fielded questions on the economy, housing, transportation, infrastructure, health, flooding, and other areas where the state faces challenges.

The debate among the candidates of the leading political parties for the 6 February 2027 governorship election was held last Sunday. The debate, organised by the Nigeria Debate Consortium, featured Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Obafemi Hamzat of the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) who is the incumbent deputy governor of the state, Funso Doherty of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), and Adedeji Doherty of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).

The debate, broadcast live on Sunday, 8 November, was moderated by Seun Okinbaloye of Channels Television and Nifemi Oguntoye of TVC News.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The candidates were asked how they would solve challenges affecting Nigeria's economic capital and largest city by population, such as the economy, housing, transportation, infrastructure, health, and flooding. PREMIUM TIMES monitored the debate and here is our review of how each of the candidates fared at the debate.

Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour

Due to the alphabetical arrangement of the names of the candidates' political parties on the podium, Mr Rhodes-Vivour of the ADC was asked most of the questions first. Dressed in a plain while kaftan with a hat to match, Mr Rhodes-Vivour, who was the runner-up in the 2023 governorship election when he ran on the platform of the Labour Party, started by saying that his desire for Lagos was one that is better, safer, cleaner and economically viable. He explained that his desires are the same as those of every Lagosian.

He stated that the misgovernance of the ruling APC is the reason the state is bedeviled with a lot of seemingly insurmountable problems. (The political hegemony that makes up the APC in Lagos has been in power in the state since 1999, when Nigeria's incumbent president, Bola Tinubu, who is generally considered as the political godfather of the state was elected governor under the banner of the Alliance for Democracy. Since then, his political proteges have governed the state under two other political banners - Action Congress of Nigeria and currently APC.)

He claimed he has a track record of siding with the people unlike the APC, which he claimed is elite-centred. To buttress his claim that his government would be people-centred, he immediately promised to build 100,000 housing units within four years to reduce the creeping housing shortages in the state.

The Lagos State Government estimates a housing deficit of 3.3 million in the state. This acute shortage has contributed significantly to arbitrary increases in rent and other sharp practices in the real estate sector.

During debates, politicians often struggle with the "how" of implementing their promises. Mr Rhodes-Vivour appeared to have thought through his implementation strategy. He said he would achieve his housing plan from funds to be derived from a luxury tax. He, however, did not give details of the nature of said luxury tax.

He said, if elected, his government would pass a law that would require landlords to give tenants at least a six-month notice before increasing rent. He said the law would also peg the percentage rent can be increased within a given time.

He said he would develop the Eastern Foreshore area of the state - around the Ibeju-Lekki axis while decentralising development in the state.

Mr Rhodes-Vivour plan of developing the Ibeju-Lekki area of the state leaves one wondering about his claim of decentralising development in the state.

The Ibeju-Lekki area is already one of the fastest growing areas of the state with a growing residential and industrial hub championed by facilities like the Dangote Refinery, the Lekki Free Trade Zone and the Lekki Sea Port.

With the pace at which developments in Ibeju-Lekki are moving, it is near impossible for other areas of the state such as Badagry, Ojo, and the densely populated Alimosho to keep up with that axis in the nearest future.

He promised to adopt a private sector driven approach to solving some of the persistent problems of the states such as transportation. Mr Rhodes-Vivour said he would ensure that the state is safer by removing street urchins and prioritising skill acquisition.

He said he would solve the perennial flood problem of the state by adopting a wetland policy. He said instead of just sand filling wetlands, which blocks the absorption of excess water he would introduce and encourage the adoption of technology that would not hinder the right of way of water.

When asked to respond why the state appears to be rich while its residents are poor, Mr Rhodes-Vivour admonished the government for being elite-focused rather than people-focused. He said during the campaign towards the 2023 election, Mr Hamzat promised the inhabitants of Makoko, a sprawling slum in Yaba, of developing their community only to turn around to demolish their homes and forcibly evict them.

He said while Lagos is wealthy on paper, most residents are not benefiting from that wealth.

On traffic management, Mr Rhodes-Vivour said urban planning should be decentralised. He said he would depart from the approach of building long and expensive bridges to connect parts of the state and would rather use short bridges of a few kilometres to connect communities within the state. He said he would revisit the proposal of using cable cars, improve water transportation, create cycle lanes and develop inner roads within towns and local governments.

On the metro rail, he chided the government for building the project on its balance sheet rather than welcoming private sector investment for the speedy completion of the project that has been on-going for more than 20 years. He alleged that corruption and avoidance of transparency were the reasons the project is being built on the state's balance sheet rather than through private investment.

On health, he promised to create emergency rehabilitation centres across the state to reduce the travel time of patients in need to critical and urgent care.

He also said if elected, his government would depart from what he claimed is the current pick-and-drop waste disposal policy of the state, which he blamed for the foul smell in many parts of the state. He said he would encourage capable private sector participation in waste management that would prioritise recycling and creating wealth from waste.

VERDICT: Mr Rhodes-Vivour displayed a relatively deep understanding of the problem facing the state and his responses showed that he had thought through the solutions to the problems. In many cases he explained how these problems will be solved and how his approaches at tackling the problem differ from what the incumbent administration is doing. His ideas are fresh, innovative, and in many cases reasonable alternatives to the approaches of the incumbent administration.

However, his idea of decentralising Lagos appears to be contradictory and heavily focused on the provision of transportation infrastructure without considering other means of decentralisation such as expanding of commercial and industrial hubs to other parts of the state, provision of recreation centres and entertainment facilities, which will reduce the travel time and distances across the state.

SCORE CARD: 8/10.

Obafemi Hamzat

He started by saying he considered the debate a job interview and Lagosians as his employers. He said he would bring his experience as a seasoned administrator in the United States and in Nigeria (he was the state's commissioner for science and technology under the administration of the then-Governor Bola Tinubu and was retained in the position by Mr Tinubu's successor, Babatunde Fashola).

He listed the Lekki-Ikoyi Link Bridge, the first cable bridge in West Africa and the second in Africa as one of his achievements as the commissioner for science and technology. He said his plan for Lagos will be hoisted on seven pillars, which he said formed the acronym PROMISE. He said P stands for the people, R for renewal, O for opportunities, M for machinery of government, I for inclusion, S for system and E for economic development. When asked why many Lagosians are poor but the state is rich on paper, he did not answer the question directly but went ahead to reel out some of the achievements of the incumbent government and his plan if elected as the governor of the state.

Mr Hamzat said that his government would work toward completing the metro rail line therefore creating a better and hassle-free connection of parts of Lagos. He said his government would prioritise mass movement of people by providing 4,000 CNG-powered BRT buses. He said BRT lanes would be created to connect major towns in the state like Badagry. He also promised to introduce electric ferries to improve water transportation.

He listed the housing projects that are being built by the government in areas like Ajara in Badagry. He said the government already enacted a law - the Lagos Real Estate Registration Agency Law, to deal with sharp practices in the housing sector and encourage Lagosians to report erring landlords and realtors for better enforcement of the law.

He acknowledged that the housing shortage in the state is more severe in lowbrow areas of the state, saying he intends to solve that by encouraging developers to build in less desirable parts of the state as they build expensive houses in highbrow areas like Ikoyi and Lekki. He however did not explain how this will be done.

He blamed perennial flooding in the state to increase rainfall and climate change. He acknowledged that the state is demolishing structures built on wetland or obstructing the flow of water. When challenged about the flooding in communities along the coastal roads, which was blamed on the lack of environmental impact assessment before the road was constructed, he said that contrary to the claim, an environmental impact assessment was done during his tenure as commissioner for science and technology.

On healthcare, he said, the government intends to expand the Ilera Eko health insurance programme to capture more users. Mr Hamzat said the state government is building or expanding several general hospitals across the state and that it plans to establish a university of medicine.

VERDICT: As expected, Mr Hamzat put up a spirited defence of the policies of the incumbent administration, while trying to also project that he was his own man. Refreshingly, he did not use the word "continuation" as many potential successors of ruling parties in the country are wont to do. He tried earnestly to explain the policies of the current government and what has been achieved. His responses suggested that he was aware that the job is nowhere near being done and that some of the policies require fine tuning and expansion.

However, some of his responses are hard to understand and he did not bother to explain how they would be achieved. For instance, his suggestion that property developer would be made to build houses in cheaper areas of the state sounded strange as he did not explain how he would go about doing this, the incentives to make developers or private businesses whose aim is to maximise profit use resources to develop properties in poor areas where such properties would not bring the same profit as those built in highbrow areas.

His claim about the flooding along the coastal road and how helpless the state government was with demanding that a proper impact assessment was done by the federal government sounded unconvincing. There are several areas where state governments have collaborated with the federal government for a proper development of infrastructure.

SCORE CARD: 7/10

Funsho Doherty

Mr Doherty said Lagos is operating below its potential and blamed this underperformance on bad governance. He said bad governance has made life increasingly difficult for many Lagosians. He said residents of the state are not getting the worth of the taxes they pay. He said it was time to change the political hegemony that has governed the state for the past 27 years because they have had all the time to fix the problem but have failed to do so.

He said he would prioritise affordable housing and plans to build 150,000 housing units in the first four years of his tenure, if elected. He promised to create an ombudsman to deal with sharp practices and arbitrary increases in the rent in the state, saying a situation where Lagosians use a large chunk of their salaries for rent is not sustainable.

He added that the government has to be the driver of social housing. He berated the state government for stepping back and allowing the sector to be almost fully run by the private sector, a situation, he said, is bad for many Lagosians.

The NDC governorship candidate promised to focus his attention on other areas including small businesses and the environment, while also vowing to run an honest and accountable government.

He also said his government will be people-centred as he drew a connection between the wealth of the place to the wealth of the people living therein.

He stated that, if he is elected, his government would be more involved in the provision of affordable social amenities such as transportation, healthcare and education.

He promised to make education truly free and that, if elected, his government would provide one affordable meal to children in schools. He said his idea is to enable people to prosper.

On the recurrent flooding in the state, he said, the problem is a symptom of a long failure in governance. While admitting that Lagos is a coastal state thus, exposed to flooding, he said, the government should raise the bar in tackling the problem as seen elsewhere. He advocated for the protection of wetlands. He said the practice where people are allowed to build on wetland for such properties to be demolished years later is not the solution that Lagos needs.

He claimed that no environmental impact assessment was done on the coastal road before it was constructed, hence, the unprecedented flooding experienced in the corridor this year. He said even if the road was a federal road, it was the responsibility of the state government to insist that things are done properly.

He also chastised the state government for deliberately refusing to modernise its transportation system. He said the state is stuck with the old transportation system, which is mainly run by rickety buses known as danfo, because persons in the government have vested interest. By this he was suggesting that the state government has no political will to remove street urchins and touts, popularly called agbero, representing road transport unions collecting tolls from commercial motorists. He said it is an eyesore for a city like Lagos to have its transportation system still in the hands of miscreants. He said, if elected, he would modernise transportation infrastructure in the state.

He said healthcare under his government would be made totally free for the poor. He argued that the government-run health insurance scheme, Ilera Eko, was either inadequate or not the way to go and said the government has to play a more participatory role in healthcare provision.

On waste management, he said it was too centralised, and that if elected, he would encourage local governments to play more role in the collection, recycling and disposal of waste.

Close 

VERDICT: Mr Doherty easily picked holes in the shortcomings of governance in the state. He was clear-headed about what needed to be done. However, maybe due to time or the way the questions were structured, he could not explain, for instance, how he intends to fund the one free-meal for school children and his idea of a totally -free primary healthcare provision.

One would have loved to hear how he intends to modernise the transportation infrastructure and system in the state and how he plans to rid the state of agberos.

Score Card: 7/10

Adedeji Doherty

Adedeji Doherty spent the time allotted to him to introduce himself and his plan for the state, talking about how he is a man of the people and a loyal member of the PDP.

Interestingly, he used almost a minute of his allotted three minutes to pay homage to Mr Hamzat, and Musiliu Obanikoro. a former governorship candidate of his party, who has since joined the ruling APC.

He said he has a 10-point agenda but could not list all in the time remaining.

On tackling the housing shortage in the state, he said unlike the other contestant, he has no plan to build 150,000 housing units in the state, saying that he does not control the price of building materials and cannot tell developers how to sell or rent their houses. "There is no government that can control landlords," he said. He, however, mentioned that if elected he would form a research team to look into the housing problem in the state, but again could not fully explain the role of this research team before he ran out of time.

Strangely, he said to end sharp practices in the housing sector and end arbitrary rent increases, the state government will rent houses from landlords and sublet them to Lagosians. He did not explain how this idea would be achieved or how feasible it was.

When asked why Lagosians are not reaping the benefits of its seemingly wealthy government, he blamed it on the debt burden of the state government. He said the government uses N20 billion to service debt.

He, however, promised to run a small government to save up funds for other developmental projects adding that the state currently has over 160 ministries and agencies and maintaining them was not sustainable.

He said there was nothing the state government could do about flooding and blamed the yearly flooding of the state to global climate change and that flooding is experienced all over the world. He said credit should be given to the state government for what it is doing to manage flooding in the state.

On traffic management, he said, if elected, he will build long bridges connecting far-flung parts of the state like from Berger (Kara) to Lagos Island, And another to Badagry. He wondered why the government had yet to build the 4th, the 5th and the 6th mainland bridges to deal with traffic congestion.

VERDICT: Most of Mr Adedeji Doherty's responses were trained towards either excusing the inadequacies of the policies of the incumbent government or to suggest that there was little he would do to change the status quo. This leaves one wondering about his reasons for contesting for the position if all he wants to do was rehash the ways things are being done.

He also proposed some strange policies like how his government would rent houses from landlords and then sublet them to residents. His idea of solving the traffic problem of the state by building long bridges that traverse one end of the state and another appeared not to have been given a proper thought. Of all the contestants at the debate, he was clearly the least prepared.

SCORE CARD: 3/10

Matthew McConaughey and Arch Manning were too much for LSU

I had the multiview going for most of the day yesterday, but I was multitasking for much of it. Yesterday was a big day in the Joseph household. It was the day every year I get to drag out all of my wife's Christmas decorations.

Thankfully, we're extending this madness into another weekend because she decided we needed new trees. So while most of the decorations are up, not the outdoor ones quite yet, we still have the joy of putting up two trees to look forward to.

Anyway, I did see Matthew McConaughey and Arch Manning lead Texas to victory in Death Valley and hand Lane Kiffin and company loss number four, which isn't going to cut it in the SEC.

I caught some of Michigan getting steamrolled by No. 16 Oregon, which you really hate to see. I mean, couldn’t both teams lose? And, of course, I saw Penn State put another one in the win column with a 42-14 thrashing of Minnesota.

There were a few other games that I caught parts of, but the day was dominated by the operation "get out my wife's Christmas decorations." That leads me to ask my annual question, do you decorate for Christmas before or after Thanksgiving?

Mustard on Christmas tree cakes

Have you seen people putting mustard on Christmas tree cakes?

It's happening. It sounds awful, but I have yet to see a video of someone saying it's as gross as it sounds. I think I'm going to have to let this trend get me.

I'm going to move mustard on Christmas tree cakes to the top of my odd food combinations list. Assuming the trend hasn’t taken off here, and I'm able to find the snack cakes, I'll give this a try and report back.

I don't know who would try this in the first place to see if it was good, but here we are. There's a chance it's an attempt to move product. I'll at least be able to answer whether it tastes good or not.

World.title: Congress' incoming wealthiest member vows to crack down on politicians getting rich in office
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

EXCLUSIVE: Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., poised to become the wealthiest member of Congress, told Fox News Digital that he plans to crack down on politicians who enrich themselves while serving in public office when he takes office in January.

Strada, who went from working as a bowling alley mechanic to owning a nationwide HVAC company, is expected to become Congress' richest member, according to Forbes. The incoming Republican argued that public office should be about serving Americans rather than accumulating personal wealth.

"We need to make sure that we hold politicians accountable," Strada told Fox News Digital. "Nobody, and I mean nobody, should get rich in public office. We're there to serve the American people."

"If you want to get rich, stay in the private sector. I went into business to get rich, not Washington, D.C. I'm going to Washington, D.C., to serve the American people," he continued.

The congressman-elect said combating congressional insider trading and political profiteering would be among his priorities as he prepares to leave the private sector for Capitol Hill.

Strada pointed to his own rise from a blue-collar worker to a successful businessman as proof that the American Dream remains achievable, arguing that excessive government intervention has made it harder for others to follow a similar path.

"I started with nothing. I was a handyman at a bowling alley. If I can do it, other everyday Americans can. Government needs to get out of their way and help them succeed," Strada said. "It's so important to give people opportunity to succeed and achieve their version of the American dream, and now it's time to open that up."

"That's what I plan to do in Washington, D.C., give every American the opportunity they need to succeed, prosper, open a small business and start a career," he added.

"I'm living proof of it," Strada said, referring to his own success.

The incoming Republican also warned that the growing popularity of democratic socialism and proposals for expanding government programs could undermine American entrepreneurship, innovation and small-business growth.

"I think it's important to show people the opportunity. The talking points of ‘free this, free that’ sounds great, but we do not want to suppress the American people. We instead want to show them that their goals and ambitions are achievable," Strada said.

"It was achievable for me. I never went to college, the thought of college was not even in conversation with my parents. Going to college for me was unachievable," he added.

Strada said his early work experience taught him the importance of discipline and perseverance, values he believes should be emphasized to younger generations.

"I knew I had to work, and I worked hard," Strada said, adding that young Americans could benefit from a greater emphasis on work ethic. "I think if we can instill that in young people today, they'd be better off."

The congressman-elect also identified housing affordability as a major obstacle preventing Americans from achieving financial independence, pledging to pursue federal deregulation, lower construction material costs and workforce development initiatives to make homeownership more accessible.

"Housing cost is ridiculous. I have so many examples of ways we can still build a high-quality home for substantially less money, and more Americans could live out their dream of owning a home," Strada said.

As he prepares to take office in January, Strada said he hopes to secure a seat on the House Appropriations Committee, where he believes his business experience would allow him to "best serve the American people."

World.title: Loch Ness Monster sightings jump in 2026 as scientist drills into legendary mystery
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Loch Ness Monster is making waves again amid an uptick in reported sightings — but one researcher told Fox News Digital he still isn't convinced the legendary Scottish creature is real.

Reported sightings of Nessie, as the creature is popularly known, have more than doubled in 2026, climbing to 15 from six in 2025, according to the Official Loch Ness Monster Sightings Register.

The register contains eyewitness accounts from visitors and locals around Loch Ness, a freshwater lake in the Scottish Highlands, roughly 20 miles southwest of Inverness.

1,000-YEAR-OLD CHURCH MYSTERY CRACKED BY STUDENTS FROM KING CHARLES' ALMA MATER

In March, an American man said he saw "the dark-greenish gray body of what appeared to be Nessie emerge from the water."

The man wrote, according to the register, "Nessie hovered for about 5 seconds, then dipped back into the water. Her body emerged against the chop of the surf, but appeared clearly defined against the waves, leading me to believe it wasn't just the current."

In July, a local sailor said he saw a "large oversized crocodile head above the water" while he was out on his yacht.

"The head quickly disappeared before I could get a photo," the man said. "It took me a few minutes to process what I was seeing. We made it into Fort Augustus safely with no further sightings."

'SIGNIFICANT' EARLY CHRISTIAN CHURCH EMERGES BENEATH FORMER FISH MARKET IN ANCIENT CITY

One visitor from Malta said he saw a creature in August that looked like a "very large eel" moving against the current.

"He estimated that the size was at least 7 meters [about 23 feet] in length," the register stated.

Though the increase in sightings may seem significant, one expert disagrees.

Charles Paxton, a research fellow in statistical ecology at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, told Fox News Digital there was "nothing special" about the jump in reported sightings from 2025 to 2026.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER EERIE ANGLO-SAXON 'SAND BODIES' AT NUCLEAR POWER STATION SITE

"The numbers fluctuate a lot year on year," he said.

Paxton said the modern phenomenon of Loch Ness Monster sightings began in the 1930s, particularly between 1933 and 1934.

The reported sightings quickly became a major draw for tourists, bringing crowds to the area.

"In 1934, the local government slashed its tourist budget, because they felt it wasn't necessary to do any advertising for tourism whatsoever," he said. "And there were traffic jams around the loch."

ARCHAEOLOGISTS FIND ARTIFACTS OLDER THAN STONEHENGE BENEATH BRITAIN'S HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT: 'INCREDIBLY RARE'

That surge of interest fell off over the years, but was revived again in the 1960s when the Loch Ness Investigation Bureau began collecting data on Nessie sightings.

"And then, since the '70s, numbers have generally sort of dwindled, but with fluctuations" from year to year, Paxton said.

Paxton also clarified that the database used to track modern sightings is not an official record, despite its name.

"In a real sense, there isn't an official database," he said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"There are people collecting reports of the Loch Ness Monster from a variety of sources," added Paxton. "But that website has become a central location for people to [share] their reports."

"People have these exciting, strange experiences, and the question is, what caused them?"

Paxton, who is currently researching how cultural influences may contribute to reported sightings, said statistics can help researchers better understand why people report unusual experiences.

He and his colleagues have studied patterns in Loch Ness Monster sightings, "mainly for fun, I must admit," he said.

"And people have these exciting, strange experiences, and the question is, what caused them? And I think we can use statistics to kind of investigate patterns in what's going on."

Though Paxton doesn't believe there is an unknown animal lurking in the loch, he said he doesn't think those who report seeing the monster are lying.

"I don't think that's the case at all," he said.

He cited several possible explanations, including "people seeing animals in the loch, people seeing boat wakes, people seeing wind waves, floating vegetation."

World.title: DAVID MARCUS: What big tech’s weekend from hell means for the future of data centers
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The last several days have not been good for big tech. On Thursday, Microsoft Outlook, which handles most of the business email in America, suddenly shut down. Then, on Friday, the FAA grounded every flight in the country, apparently because of technical upgrades that went wrong.

These fiber-optic faceplants happen to come at a moment when much of the country, mostly at the local level, is seeing fierce opposition to data centers, not only because of environmental concerns and energy prices but also because of real concerns that tech is becoming too big a part of our lives.

In Maryland, the story of Taylor Frazier-McCollum, a community activist who helped block a $5 billion data center project planned for the site of an abandoned mall, went viral, with the left praising the power and bravery of the individual and the right mocking her alternative idea for the site: a trampoline park.

INSIDE THE FAR-LEFT'S ANTI-DATA CENTER PUSH AND WHAT EXPERTS SAY IS DRIVING IT: 'PLAYBOOK WE'VE SEEN BEFORE'

In fairness, this Maryland activist does not come across as particularly adroit or searing in her insights. On the other hand, like many Americans, she understands implicitly the advantages a trampoline park or a Topgolf location can bring to her community. The benefits of a data center seem murky by comparison.

This kind of attitude toward data centers has many very smart people pulling their hair out in frustration. For them, the economic and technological benefits, including beating China in the AI race, obviously far outweigh the concerns of nonexperts like Frazier-McCollum.

In fact, many proponents of data centers argue that China is funding propaganda to slow our growth in the sector, even as data centers start popping up all over China like umbrella salesmen in a Manhattan rainstorm.

This is true. China, the Eddie Haskell of the planet, is absolutely "giving us the business" by stoking anti-data center fervor. But it is important to remember that data centers aren’t controversial because of Chinese information operations; rather, Chinese information operations exist because data centers are controversial.

FOREIGN ADVERSARIES RUNNING 'PSYOP' TO FUEL ANTI-AI AND ANTI-DATA CENTER MOVEMENT, WAR OFFICIAL SAYS

Up until about six months ago, data centers were not a major national news story. In fact, the place one was most likely to hear about them was local talk radio in small towns across rural America, where many people care more about who the county commissioner is than who lives at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave.

The concerns you hear from callers on these shows sound downright mundane compared to the fervent calls from experts to win the new space race against China and unleash the power of AI. But for many who live there, water rights and easements mean more than geopolitical fisticuffs.

This is why, in a strange way, this week’s tech mishaps, which inconvenienced millions of Americans at work and at airports, present an opportunity for the tech industry to explain in more practical terms why we need so many data centers.

Implicit in the pro-data center argument has been the idea, often offered with a bit of disdain, that it is absurd to oppose data centers by posting about them on devices that cannot operate without data centers. And OK, point taken, but the snark doesn’t help.

8 EVERYDAY THINGS THAT WOULD QUIT WORKING WITHOUT DATA CENTERS

In fact, Democrats, one could say cynically, capitalized on the anger many Americans felt at being talked down to by the big tech set, using it to great electoral advantage, especially in traditionally right-leaning rural areas. But Democrats, no matter who leads them, cannot maintain their blanket disapproval of data centers for long, as this weekend showed.

It was safe enough to call for data center moratoriums in the races of 2026, but as they seek to govern, Democrats will need data centers. Let’s face it, nobody is going back to typewriters and fax machines, and nobody wants to sit in seat 24B for five hours on the tarmac at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport.

RED COUNTIES WITH DATA CENTER PROJECTS SWUNG AWAY FROM GOP IN MIDTERMS, ANALYSIS FINDS

At the local level, much of the data center fuss is already working itself out through the sausage-making of politics and the courts. Some communities, like the Amish, will eschew the infrastructure projects completely and lose out on the pot of gold. But most will find a happy compromise once enough concessions are pried from developers.

For now, proponents of data centers would be wise to point to events like the Outlook outage and the flight groundings, without sneering, as the very reason we need so many data centers to power the conveniences we have all grown accustomed to.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

With the midterms behind us and our tech infrastructure on thin ice, now is the time for the case to be made that, one way or another, our future lies in data centers.

World.title: Richard Sterban of The Oak Ridge Boys dead at 83
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Richard Sterban, whose unmistakable voice helped make The Oak Ridge Boys’ "Elvira" a country music classic, has died. He was 83.

The singer died Saturday, Nov. 14, in Hendersonville, Tennessee, from complications of bronchitis and pneumonia following a long battle with cancer, according to an announcement from his family and The Oak Ridge Boys.

"We appreciate all of your love, support, and prayers. Please continue to lift us up in this difficult time, we find comfort knowing that he is currently face to face with Jesus," his family said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital.

Sterban publicly announced his pancreatic cancer diagnosis in September 2025, revealing that doctors had diagnosed him that March. Despite his health struggles, the country music veteran expressed hope that his faith and medical care would help him recover and return to performing.

JOHN ANDERSON, COUNTRY MUSIC HALL OF FAMER, DEAD AT 71

"With the help of the Good Lord above, I believe I will be able to get through this," he said at the time. He also thanked fans for their prayers and said he hoped to return to the road within several months.

NEW PANCREATIC CANCER PILL COULD RESHAPE TREATMENT AS EARLY TRIAL RESULTS STUN RESEARCHERS

After stepping away from touring in May 2025, Sterban returned to the Grand Ole Opry on Jan. 30 and 31, 2026, joining his bandmates for performances of "Elvira" that brought audiences to their feet, according to the announcement.

"Having Richard on stage with us again was one of God’s greatest blessings," fellow Oak Ridge Boys singer Duane Allen said.

GEORGE STRAIT PULLS OFF INCREDIBLE CAREER ACCOMPLISHMENT WITH STUNNING CONCERT

Born April 24, 1943, in Camden, New Jersey, Sterban began singing in Sunday school at age 6. His voice transitioned from soprano to bass by eighth grade, setting him on a path that would eventually take him from gospel quartets to some of music’s biggest stages.

Before joining The Oak Ridge Boys, Sterban performed behind Elvis Presley as a member of J.D. Sumner and the Stamps Quartet. He toured and recorded with Presley and appeared in the 1972 concert film, "Elvis on Tour."

Later that year, he left the job to become The Oak Ridge Boys’ bass singer.

"I wanted to be in the best vocal group in the world," Sterban said, according to the announcement.

Alongside lead singer Allen, baritone William Lee Golden and tenor Joe Bonsall, Sterban helped transform the Southern gospel quartet into a country and pop crossover act. Their hits included "Y’all Come Back Saloon," "Bobbie Sue," and "American Made."

But it was Sterban’s booming bass refrain on the group’s 1981 recording of "Elvira" that became his musical calling card. The song reached No. 1 on the country chart and No. 5 on the pop chart and earned a Grammy Award.

OUTLAW COUNTRY SINGER DAVID ALLAN COE DEAD AT 86

"It’s the song everyone hopes to hear at our concerts," Sterban said on its 40th anniversary, according to the announcement.

The group became Grand Ole Opry members in 2011 and entered the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2015.

DOLLY PARTON DEAD AT 80

Their decades together also forged deep personal bonds.

In January 2021, Allen reflected on his relationship with Sterban, Golden and Bonsall.

"I think the four of us have grown closer than we’ve ever been in our whole career," Allen told Fox News Digital at the time.

RANDY TRAVIS’ WIFE SAYS DOCTORS GAVE COUNTRY LEGEND 1% CHANCE OF SURVIVAL BEFORE MIRACULOUS COMEBACK

The Oak Ridge Boys also developed a lasting friendship with former President George H.W. Bush. At his request, they performed "Amazing Grace" at his funeral in Houston in December 2018, taking an overnight flight after a concert in Washington state to attend.

"There’s no way we wouldn’t do it," Sterban said, according to the announcement.

Away from the stage, Sterban was a devoted baseball fan and a part owner of the Nashville Sounds minor league team for 30 years. He continued recording late in life, contributing to several tracks on The Oak Ridge Boys’ October 2026 album, "Buried Treasures."

Sterban is survived by his wife, Donna; daughters Lauren and Tori; sons Rich, Doug and Chris; eight grandchildren; and three great-grandchildren.

World.title: Judge temporarily halts Trump’s ‘Trash Island’ golf course redevelopment in D.C.
World.content:
The Trump administration cannot close East Potomac Park to the public for now, a federal judge in Washington ruled Saturday, dealing a blow to the president’s effort to renovate its golf course.

The administration had previously announced plans to close what is effectively the entire area of East Potomac and Hains Point starting Sunday. But U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes wrote that while litigation moves forward, the course, along with surrounding bike and walking paths, must remain open to the public “except for routine, temporary closures consistent with the Course’s historical operating practices, and except as needed to address articulated, imminent threats to public safety.”

Reyes wrote that closing the park would “irreparably harm” the plaintiffs — the Washington, D.C., Preservation League — who regularly use the park.

“It runs counter to the public interest in utilizing national parkland. And the Government has not plausibly identified any harm it would suffer from a temporary restraining order that preserves the status quo pending further proceedings,” Reyes wrote.

Reyes’ order does not require the administration to continue operating the golf course, including features like the concession stand or pro shop, but does specify the administration “cannot use the absence of golf operations as a reason to exclude the public from the Course.”

The administration had argued the park had to close for repairs, including a seawall that needs mending that they argued is an “imminent threat to public safety.” The judge expressed skepticism at the argument, noting the National Park Service’s speed to cut down 400 trees in the area — an action Reyes at the time called “bad faith.”

“If public safety were at risk, NPS would have taken a step—any step—to address the safety issues it knew about. Recall that within just ten days, NPS was able to plan, muster the resources and staff, and execute felling over 400 healthy trees. So NPS was not without ability or resources. And presumably would not prioritize removing healthy trees over the public’s safety,” Reyes wrote.

President Donald Trump referred to the park as “trash island” just hours before the ruling, while criticizing Reyes.

“Trash Island is currently the Worst Golf Course anywhere in the World, but the Department of the Interior is going to make it into the Best Golf Course anywhere in the World,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The ruling came after a contentious day long hearing Friday where a lawyer for the government, Adam Gustafson, said the decision to close the park on Sunday was “distinct” from President Donald Trump’s declaration on social media that the East Potomac golf course would be closing for extensive renovations — on Sunday.

The president’s Oct. 18 announcement on Truth Social that the park’s three link-style golf courses would be transformed into one 18-hole championship style course is “not the same action” as the Interior Department’s decision to shut down a large part of the park that includes the golf course, Gustafson said.

The president has adopted several pet projects during his second term in office in an effort to modify Washington landmarks. He’s faced legal battles for some of them, including the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts and a triumphal arch. Work on both has been blocked by judges.

The Supreme Court earlier this year allowed Trump to construct a ballroom on the White House grounds.

A Justice Department spokesperson, responding to Reyes’ ruling, said that the judge’s order would not stop development of a golf course.

“The Court has acknowledged that the National Park Service can limit access to its facilities where the public is at risk of harm. Nothing in the Court’s order precludes planning for the development of a world class golf course to continue. The Department of Justice will always vociferously defend the Trump Administration’s agenda in court,” the spokesperson said.

World.title: Women with autoimmune diseases often misdiagnosed for 4 years or more
World.content:
Women with autoimmune diseases such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis are more likely to be misdiagnosed or get delayed treatment compared with men, with their symptoms often dismissed as “psychological.”

An online survey by British researchers found that it took women with an autoimmune disorder about four years to get a diagnosis, while it took men around three months to less than a year.

It adds to previous research showing disparities in diagnosis between men and women with autoimmune disorders.

“Women in particular felt not listened to or not heard or not believed by their medical professionals,” said Sydnae Taylor, a doctoral researcher at the University of Oxford in the U.K. and co-author of the study published recently in eClinicalMedicine.

Autoimmune diseases — including Type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, inflammatory bowel disease and psoriasis — occur when the immune system mistakenly attacks the body. More than 23 million people in the U.S. have an autoimmune disease, and most of them are women.

Autoimmune thyroid disease, which includes Hashimoto’s, was the most common type reported by women in the survey. It typically causes fatigue, unexplained weight gain and sensitivity to cold, among other symptoms.

Autoimmune conditions can affect anyone but are more common in women than in men, according to the federal Office on Women’s Health. For example, around 90% of people with lupus are women, according to the Lupus Foundation of America.

It’s not clear why women are more at risk. Research from the Mayo Clinic has suggested differences in the microbiome, sex hormones and that women’s bodies produce higher levels of antibodies that are associated with autoimmune disorders. A 2024 Stanford Medicine study found clues in a molecule connected to the X chromosome.

Because many of the disorders share similar symptoms in the early stages — fatigue, dizziness, low-grade fever, as well as stress, anxiety and depression — they can be difficult to diagnose.

Women and men have similar symptoms, but with women specifically, “they develop over time, so it’s often hard to recognize right at the beginning,” said Dr. Saira Z. Sheikh, the director of the UNC Rheumatology Lupus Clinic in Chapel Hill, North Carolina. Symptoms can appear during childhood and last throughout adulthood.

The survey was conducted through social media, patient support groups and community groups of underserved populations such as religious groups and the homeless population. It was translated into five languages as a way to reach diverse communities.

Participants shared data about symptom onset, how many clinicians were consulted and misdiagnosis. The data was then compared between men and women. Out of the 6,607 participants, 91.2% were women and the majority of them were from the United Kingdom.

Misdiagnosis is more likely when symptoms are “invisible,” meaning they aren’t detected in a blood test or involve pain, fatigue and neurological symptoms such as tingling, Taylor said.

In these situations, accurate diagnoses rely on doctors listening and believing the patient.

“We shouldn’t assume that women’s symptoms are psychological simply because the initial investigations are inconclusive,” Sheikh said.

World.title: Bowen Yang returns to ‘SNL’ to spoof Jensen Huang amid Nvidia spy scandal
World.content:
Former “Saturday Night Live” repertory player and writer Bowen Yang returned to help open the show this weekend with his portrayal of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

In the cold open, the nation’s most prominent tech-industry CEOs, including Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg, are at a CIA gathering devised to teach them how to identify when a woman may be duping them.

“America needs you to learn the difference between a woman who would actually want to have sex with you and a woman who is clearly a spy,” said a CIA guide, portrayed by comedian John Mulaney, the night’s host.

Mulaney, a former “SNL” writer, used the story of Huang, who resigned from Nvidia on Thursday following reports that he had extramarital relationships, including one with a suspected spy for China.

“What do you think the lesson is here?” Mulaney asked.

Zuckerberg, portrayed by Andrew Dismukes, answered: “Never date a human woman.”

Mulaney dismissed the response and those of a few of the other tech titans in the room, prompting PayPal co-founder Peter Thiel, portrayed by James Austin Johnson, to defend the group.

“Show us some respect,” he said. “We do a lot for this country. Name one time technology has let us down.”

Mulaney answered by mentioning Friday’s nationwide flight ground stop and Thursday’s global Microsoft glitch.

He tried to empathize, however, noting that it’s a rare time in human history when men “as pale and as strange as you” even survive, let alone possess “all the world’s wealth and power.”

Mulaney asked the group to remember the people they dated before they were rich and famous. “Now all of a sudden someone very beautiful is interested in you. Why do you think that might be?” he said.

Zuckerberg chimed in. “Because she’s comforted by my Meta glasses recording her at all times.”

“No,” Mulaney said.

He later introduces someone “who learned this lesson the hard way.”

Enter Huang.

“It’s me, Jensen ‘Hide Your Wife’ Huang,” Yang said.

He explained that he’s into BDSM — “breakin’ da stock market” — and urged the men not to be like him.

“Women don’t like guys like us,” he said. “That’s how we became guys like us.”

"No way it’s taking less than two hours,” Bowen Yang's Mary Todd Lincoln tells prospective Lincoln Tunnel travelers. NBC

Yang appeared in a subsequent sketch, “Little Park of Horrors,” a spoof of Broadway musicals, that centered on the city outlawing horse-drawn carriages and the two men (Marcello Hernández and Kam Patterson) who want to ride in one.

Eventually realizing the dangers and limitations, the pair opt for a vehicle ride in the Lincoln Tunnel only to be confronted by Yang’s Mary Todd Lincoln, who sings about the pitfalls of such a subterranean journey.

“No way it’s taking less than two hours,” Lincoln sings. “And it won’t be for free. I’m sayin,’ I’m sayin’ that you and you and you — you’re going to pay me.”

A fan favorite, Yang started as a writer in 2018 and joined the cast the next year. He left “SNL” in December 2025, and made his Broadway debut in September as Lincoln in playwright Cole Escola’s “Oh, Mary!”

The night’s musical guest was Phoebe Bridgers.

“SNL” airs on NBC, a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.

World.title: Democrat Mary Peltola is likely to win Alaska’s Senate race, as vote counting continues
World.content:
Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola is likely to win Alaska’s Senate race, according to an NBC News Decision Desk analysis, as vote-counting continues in the state.

Peltola has expanded her narrow lead over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan with each new batch of votes reported this week. A “likely” characterization indicates that the NBC News Decision Desk has at least 95% confidence that Peltola will win the race.

See live results here.

Alaska’s is the only remaining 2026 Senate race in which the NBC News Decision Desk has not yet made a projection.

If Peltola wins, Democrats will have a 56-44 majority in the Senate next year.

The race remains uncalled a week after polls close as votes continue to be counted. Alaskans vote heavily by mail and ballots postmarked by Election Day are counted as long as they arrived by Nov. 13 — and a few days later than that for valid overseas voters.

In a race with such a narrow margin, these final votes are important, especially given Alaska’s ranked-choice rules.

If no candidate wins a majority of the vote on the first ballot, the lowest-placed candidate is eliminated and second-choice votes from that candidate’s supporters are counted. The process then repeats until someone gets a majority.

World.title: We want to hear your experience with changes to student loan repayment plans
World.content:
President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” has transformed the sprawling federal student loan system — and student borrowers are feeling the effects of the most consequential changes.

This year, the approximately 7.5 million student borrowers under the Biden-era Saving on a Valuable Education, or SAVE, plan had to select a new one. So far, about 2 million borrowers have done so, after the Education Department warned that the SAVE plan was “illegal” and would be discontinued. The remaining borrowers who did not select a new plan were set to start receiving notices this month informing them that they missed a final deadline and were automatically moved to a new plan.

The Trump administration has said ending the SAVE plan would help streamline repayment programs while ensuring borrowers are paying off what they owe to the federal government. But student advocacy groups fear lower-income borrowers who had benefited from smaller monthly payments — or even qualified to make no payments at all based on their income — will end up with significantly higher bills under the other available plans.

We want to hear from you, whether you’re in this situation or are facing another challenge related to the recent student loan changes. Please share your experience by filling out the form below.

World.title: Sen.-elect Scott Colom says investing in the South can help Democrats win ‘a durable majority’
World.content:
Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., emphasized in an interview on NBC’s “Meet the Press” that Democrats need to invest more in southern states like Mississippi, where he flipped the seat blue for the first time in decades.

“What we need to do now as a Democratic Party is understand we can’t continue to allow that lack of investment to occur,” he said on Sunday.

Colom’s projected win last week brought Democrats to a 55-seat majority in the Senate, with the Alaska Senate race yet to be called. His victory over incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican, marked a seismic political shift in a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate 44 years ago and has not had a Black senator since the Reconstruction period.

Colom has been vocal in calling for Democrats to focus more on states like Mississippi, a sentiment he emphasized again on Sunday.

“We need to put senators like myself in positions where we can deliver for the rural South, where we can be leaders in ways that show the voters in rural America that we care about them, the voters in the Deep South that we want them to be successful,” Colom said.

“And if we do that, I think we can have a competitive elections every cycle and put ourselves in positions where we can have a durable majority,” he continued.

In the same interview, Colom identified reshaping tariff policies as his top priority to reduce prices.

“We’ve got to fight for low tariffs to lower costs that helps our farmers because they lost customers as a result of these tariffs, and we need to do everything in our power to help them get those customers back,” Colom said.

He also called for raising the minimum wage. The federal minimum wage sits at $7.25 per hour, and it has not been raised since 2009.

NBC News exit polls indicated that the cost of living was a top priority for voters. NBC’s exit polls showed that 89% of voters considered the cost of living “crucial” or a “major factor” in thinking about their vote for Congress. The same exit polls found that 66% of voters believed Trump’s tariff policies hurt the national economy.

Colom was also asked on “Meet the Press” about whether he would vote to restore nationwide rights to abortion. The Mississippi sen.-elect has said he is “personally pro-life because I’m a Christian” and that he does not “believe in late-term abortions.” He also said he does not believe that victims of rape or incest should be “forced” to “have that child.”

“I’ll study what’s right for my values and for Mississippi and try to represent those values in D.C. to the best of my abilities,” he said.

One of the tasks remaining for Congress this year is for Democrats to select their party leadership. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., announced last week that he would challenge Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for the Senate majority leader position.

Asked who he planned to support, Colom said he was “in listening mode” and did not commit to either candidate.

“I don’t know either one of them that well, so I’m going to listen to what other people tell me about them, and I’m going to figure out what are the things that people are doing well in leadership, what are the things they’re not doing well, and find out how we can work together to achieve results,” Colom said.

World.title: The Reader: A new review source for book lovers
World.content:
It's become an all-too-familiar story: Earlier this year, the Washington Post put an end to Book World, its weekly book review supplement.

"Books are expensive," said bestselling author Jonathan Alter. "Readers need help to know what's good out there."

Alter says Book World's closure created a void: "Thirty years ago, there were 30 American newspapers that, as part of their Sunday newspaper, had a book review section," he said. Today, only The New York Times still maintains a separate book review section.

"So, we stepped into the breach, and we're doing something about it," said Alter, who is co-founder of The Reader, a new, general interest, online book review, to be published every weekday.

Washington Monthly

Executive editor Haley Sweetland Edwards said, "We will have mostly book reviews, but also essays about books, columns about the literary book world, and top authors like Robert Caro and Margaret Atwood and Ann Patchett will be providing recommendations of books that have slipped below the cultural radar."

The Reader is part of Washington Monthly, a non-profit magazine. Edwards says authors lined up to be part of it: "We have 31 Pulitzer Prize-winners who have agreed to be contributors over the next year. These are the crème de la crème, and they will be reviewing for us."

Alter said, "We will review books that are going to become big bestsellers, but we're also going to review those books that sometimes fly under the radar, that are really good and that just aren't getting the recognition that they deserve."

And that's where "Sunday Morning" comes in. Each weekend, we'll offer two books for your consideration – one fiction, one non-fiction – courtesy of The Reader.

November 15

World.title: Billy Evans tells his side of "You Can See Everything," Elizabeth Holmes' portrayal
World.content:
Billy Evans may be the most-talked-about person in the most-talked-about film of the year, the documentary "You Can See Everything." He sat down with "CBS Sunday Morning" for his first-ever TV interview.

Why now? "You gotta learn really painful lessons sometimes in life," he said. "And with Elizabeth going through everything she did in the press, the lesson that was ingrained in us is, 'You can't lose your voice.'"

"You Can See Everything" is a film by Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder, who shot to fame as an absurdist comedian, and who (along with cameras) moved in with Evans and his partner Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks before the disgraced Theranos founder reported to prison in 2023.

Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes in a scene from the documentary "You Can See Everything." A24

Evans, a 34-year-old MIT grad who'd also worked in high-tech, emerges as a shape-shifting central character. Asked if he is the person we saw in the film, or something else, Evans said, "I'm deeply passionate about my family and about the work that I do. But no, I am not some controlling monster who's leveraging his wife for insert-whatever-anybody-is-saying. No, I am not those things."

It's easy to understand why the genre-bending film has become a cultural phenomenon … harder to understand why Evans agreed to do it.

"I think sometimes I take too big of risks," he said. Such as? "Inviting Nathan Fielder into your home for 34 days and trusting somebody to have the right to portray you in any way, shape or form that they so choose."

In the film, Evans is portrayed as a villain – controlling and manipulative. Yet, Evans doesn't seem angry about that: "It's super-painful, but me being angry about it doesn't help change it. Look, I'm going to live my life with integrity and with who I am, and I hope people can see that over time. But if they don't, what I care about is the people that I know, people that love me."

Billy Evans talks about the documentary "You Can See Everything." CBS News

In fact, of the documentary that has gotten rave reviews, Evans says, "I love the film," despite the fact that he is made out to be a villain. "I would have preferred for that not to be the case, but it's entertainment, you know, and I didn't get to control that edit."

His goal, he said, was "to have people see Elizabeth. And when I watch that movie, I see the person that I love in exactly who she is."

In 2014 Forbes Magazine crowned Holmes the youngest self-made female billionaire. By 2017, the year she and Evans met, she was under investigation for defrauding investors for a diagnostic machine that she falsely claimed could test for hundreds of diseases with a single drop of blood.

Evans says when they first met, he did not know who she was. "I had been at her office earlier that week," he said. "I had, like, seen her the same week. But no, really, like, the first time I met her, I did not know."

Theranos co-founder and CEO Elizabeth Holmes leaves the Robert F. Peckham Federal Building with her partner Billy Evans, during her fraud trial on November 22, 2021, in San Jose, Calif. AMY OSBORNE/AFP via Getty Images

"You Can See Everything" leaves us questioning what the truth is. There are also moments that are cringe-worthy, as when Evans is filmed in the shower completely naked. [You really can see everything.]

"I did not give consent to do that," said Evans. "Now, did I know they were filming me in the shower? Yes. But we would film 16 hours a day. Like, all sorts of things were filmed with assurances made. I was just as surprised as the rest of the country to have my whole body on camera for the world to see, and it's been an awkward experience in having, like, your kids' teachers see that. It's really uncomfortable."

Billy Evans, Elizabeth Holmes and Nathan Fielder in "You Can See Everything." A24

Evans said there were "inappropriate" and "awkward" things that happened every single day, as well as requests to film things that, he said, "are not appropriate for television. All sorts of things that the details I'd rather spare the audience."

The film's production company, A24, said, "Everything that was filmed was filmed with their consent."

Some who see the film leave convinced the co-director, Nathan Fielder, had feelings for Holmes. "I think that there are bits that are played up to criticize his own bias," said Evans. "This is a film about, what can you trust? And at the end nothing is clear."

Evans says he has not spoken to Fielder since he's seen the film. "I think they're probably worried I'm gonna sue 'em," he said, adding he has no intention to do so. "Because maybe I'm a different person than most people think I am."

Evans lives with their two young children in Texas close to Holmes' prison, and carries a gun 24/7, he says, to keep his family safe. "We have threats of violence against us daily," he said. "I've got two kids. Threats of violence daily. And I would never forgive myself for having the tools, the skills, and the ability to protect my family and not doing it.

"I will give you an example: The other day, I was driving my kids to school. And a car came up behind us really, really quickly. And we stopped at the light. And the guy starts screaming next to me. And this isn't just road rage, okay? And his window is down. And he is screaming the most vile things you have ever heard about: 'I know where you live. I know who you are. I know where your kids sleep, and the things that I will do to you.' And it was terrifying."

Even given the fallout from the movie, he says he would do it all again: "With the same people, making the same film again, with everything that I know right now? 100%. Because I would also have a better understanding of what I was walking into."

Elizabeth Holmes could transfer to a halfway house next summer. Until then, Evans and their children visit her every week behind bars.

Having his children see their mother in prison, Evens said, has become "strangely normal. Like, I hate it. I absolutely hate that my daughter's first steps were in federal prison. I hate that. … But it doesn't mean that we can't find joy as we experience this. And our job, to them, is not to talk about how much it hurts and how painful it is, but to find the joy in seeing how many acorns we can collect in the prison yard and fit in a water bottle. It's finding, you know, the small, little games that we can play to make each time we go to the same place, every weekend, feel like you're going to Disneyland."

Evans said he used to count the days she was in prison, but that became too painful. "It's been since May 30th of 2023," he said. "I miss her so much. You know, I talked to her right before I came in here. And I told her, I said, 'I'm kinda nervous.' And she said, 'Just be zen. Enjoy it. Embody love. And I'll talk to you, when you're done.'"
