World.title: Min Jin Lee on "American Hagwon" and writing "social novels"
World.content:
It's been nearly a decade since Min Jin Lee's last book made her a literary phenomenon. "Pachinko," a sweeping historical epic chronicling four generations of a Korean family living in Japan, sold more than two million copies in the United States. It was adapted into a popular series on Apple TV.

But all that success didn't come easily. "When 'Pachinko' first came out as a hardcover, it was never on the bestseller lists," said Lee. "If you look at my hardcover sales, they're abysmal. So, if you start out with failure, it's really easy."

Did she consider "Pachinko" at its beginning a failure? "Oh, I think you can ask my publishers!" she laughed. "They would just say, this didn't sell!"

It wasn't until The New York Times named it one of the best books of the year, and it was selected as a National Book Award finalist, that "Pachinko" took off.

Cardinal

Lee's latest novel, "American Hagwon" (published by Cardinal), is the third in a series she calls "The Diaspora Quartet," chronicling the migration of Koreans around the world.

"Every industrial revolution had people leaving the farm to go to the city," Lee said. "And now we have environmental diaspora, where people don't have water in their communities anymore. You have economic diaspora, where certain jobs don't exist anymore, like manufacturing. I'm focusing on Koreans, because those are the people that I know about. But I'm really writing about this modern condition."

It's a deeply personal story for Lee. She came to America in 1976, when she was seven years old. The middle of three girls, her family moved to Elmhurst, Queens, where she grew up in a very blue-collar neighborhood. Her parents, a marketing executive and piano teacher in Korea, opened a newspaper stand and, later, a jewelry shop.

"As a little kid, I was so unbearably shy," Lee said. "I didn't really speak or interact with my peers very well."

Min Jin Lee (far left) and her family. Family Photo

But she tested into a highly-competitive public high school, where she found friends – and her footing.

From there it was on to the Ivy League, where she discovered something important was missing: Yale did not offer Korean language or Korean history courses – which, Lee says, was ignoring the full story.

"I think because of the Cold War and because of the Korean War in American history, I do think this is a rational thing to ask for," she said. So, Lee organized a letter-writing campaign, and convinced the university to start a Korean Studies program. "I think that it really helped the school," she said. "My mom has this whole theory that wherever you go, you should make it better than when you found it."

While at Yale, Lee was also struggling with a serious liver condition. "I learned that I would get liver cancer in my 20s or 30s; that's what the doctor said to me," she said. "I was like, 'Oh, if I have until 35, what do I want to do?' So, it gave me this sort of courage that I don't think normally I would have had."

Correspondent Jo Ling Kent with author Min Jin Lee. CBS News

Lee went to law school, then to a big firm. But before long, the hours and the stress caused her liver disease to flare up, and she decided to take a leap. "I thought, if I walk away from money and status and power, at least I'll find tremendous enrichment for me," she said.

Lee found that by writing what she describes as "social novels": "I think it's to write realistic fiction that reflects on society today, saying, this is what I think and this is the way things should be," she said.

Lee conducted thousands of interviews with people of Korean descent. In her conversations, one topic came up more than any other. And so, in "American Hagwon," she takes on education.

"A hagwon is a for-profit learning center," Lee said. "In Korea, you can go to a hagwon to become a police officer. You can go a hagwon to become a K-pop idol. And you can go to a hagwon to learn English. So, starting at the age of four or five, 80% of Koreans in South Korea send their children to hagwons."

Much of the book takes place in hagwons in Korea and the U.S., centering on a family whose life is upended when they come to America. Lee said of the father, John Koh, "John goes to the most elite school in Korea; and yet, he ends up working frying fish for somebody else."

The family's experience raises big questions about the value of education: "Sometimes someone will tell you, you go to college to get a job," said Lee. "But other people will say education should be a form of transformation and liberation. Gradually, as I worked on the book, the more I was interested in wisdom. Like, how do you obtain wisdom? How do you live a wise life?"

While "American Hagwon" is set in the 1990s, Lee says what's happening in the world today makes these questions essential. She opens her book with the line: "The rules of engagement have changed already."

"I think this is the condition of the modern person in the 21st century, and 2026 for certain, especially in the era of AI," she said. "The rules of engagement have changed already, and you didn't know. Like, we didn't get the memo. Everybody is changing the game, the paradigm, the rules. Now that we know that, what are you supposed to do? How do you educate your children? How do you retool yourself?"

Thanks to an experimental treatment in her 30s, Lee's liver disease was cured. In Harlem, where she lives with her husband and raised her son, she's already researching her fourth book, the final in her Diaspora Quartet.

Lee said, "What I would really love is if readers could feel that they have the internal resources to manage the change that feels alarming and threatening to them, and then have the internal resources and the fortitude to care for others. There's no way we're going to be able to make it through this era unless we have each other."

World.title: U2 on 50 years and their duet with Dolly Parton
World.content:
When U2 came knocking, Bono, The Edge, Adam Clayton and Larry Mullen Jr. didn't just arrive with new music; the band came bearing gifts, which they proceeded to place over a photo of Bruce Springsteen.

"We just wanna get Bruce Springsteen off your wall," Bono said. "There's some new blood coming through! But honestly Bruce, give the young people a break."

Trying to make space for U2 on the wall. CBS News

The up-and-coming Irish quartet is celebrating its 50th birthday this year – that's half a century of hits.

In September, U2 went back to the Dublin school where they first came together. Playing Mount Temple Comprehensive was "kind of amazing," said The Edge. "We used the music room in Mount Temple as our rehearsal space."

Bono said he didn't know what to expect from the students there: "I was nervous going out there."

"There were a couple of cheeky signs, like, 'When is Oasis playing?'" said The Edge. "But for the most part they really seem to get into it."

It was at Mount Temple in 1976 where Mullen pinned a note to the school bulletin board looking for bandmates. "I'd no expectations that anyone would show up, bizarrely," Mullen said.

The four got together via word of mouth. "Yeah, it's one of those funny things that the note is legendary," said Clayton. "And then when we started to talk about it, we realized none of us had seen it, and we'd been told about it by a friend or whatever."

In September, U2 performed at the Dublin school where the group formed 50 years ago. CBS News

The band has just released "Carnaval de Luz," their first album of new music in nearly nine years, created through a process that Bono called "chaotic."

The Edge reframed that as "nicely chaotic."

"Very functionally dysfunctional," Bono continued. "You would be shocked at just how raw it is and how just about to collapse."

"We're not precious in any way," The Edge said. "Until almost the record is in the store, we will try and improve and change and develop."

Won't you drive yourself nuts doing that? "Yeah. We do!" The Edge laughed.

Correspondent Anthony Mason with members of the band U2: Bono, Larry Mullen Jr., Adam Clayton and The Edge. CBS News

The new album marks the return of drummer Larry Mullen, Jr., who had to sit out the band's 2024 residency at Sphere in Las Vegas with a neck injury that threatened his career. He said he wasn't terribly confident that he would be able to come back: "I had a congenital fusion, from moving like that for over 50 years, it basically had had enough," he said. "Yeah, a lot of people were very much on the page of, you've had a great life, you know, this is not worth it."

He risked paralysis if the surgery went wrong. "But you know what? I really wanted to get back and play in any capacity," Mullen said.

Asked if they were worried that he might not play again, The Edge said, "At some point, if Larry had had to retire, we would have had to have made a very difficult call about whether U2 can go on at all."

"Maybe we could have got a better looking, more fun drummer," Bono added.

Island Records

The band calls "Carnaval de Luz" an album of "defiant joy." It includes the song "Torn," a duet with Dolly Parton that would prove to be her last recording

Bono said he approached singing with her on the track "With great trepidation."

Parton had shared the song with Bono: "She was like, 'You can take this wherever you want to go, and I might like where you want to take it,'" he said. "But you didn't know until it came back."

How generous an act is that for a songwriter? "Oh, no, not just a songwriter; one of the great songwriters who ever lived," Bono said.

U2 will be back out on the road next year, aiming for another groundbreaking live show. "That's our promise to our audience, is to try and have a shot at the best night of anybody's life," said Bono. "That's what we want out of our show."

Half a century on, U2 is still striving to be heard. "Whether it's relevant or not is really not up to us," said The Edge. "But whether we want to try and be relevant is up to us."

Asked what it means to be relevant, The Edge replied, "To be relevant is to speak of the moment. That's why we write songs. We all believe that we could next week write the best U2 song we've ever written. So, there's a lot to fight for, really."

"We think we are at our best," said Bono. "And if anyone out there thinks they're better … come and take it!"

World.title: New Mexico wanted free childcare for all. This is what's worked — and what hasn't
World.content:
New Mexico wanted free childcare for all. This is what's worked — and what hasn't

toggle caption i Nina Alexandria Riggio for NPR

Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

It's a hazy August morning, and Judyn Martinez is dropping her daughter off at Kids Campus, a sought-after childcare center in Santa Fe that is now free for any eligible family in New Mexico.

"It's an amazing school so far. She loves it. I love it," Martinez said. "Everyone's nice. She's learning, growing already."

A year ago this month, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to every family, regardless of income. To qualify, families must be residents of New Mexico and adults in the house must be working, looking for work, in school or unable to work.

Sponsor Message

Many parents, including Martinez, told NPR that it's been life-changing.

"I'm really grateful for universal childcare because I wouldn't have been able to send her," Martinez said.

There's just one drawback for families: Right now, the state doesn't have the capacity to meet the demand, which has left some families waiting without childcare. Martinez said it took her about a year and half to get off the waitlist for Kids Campus — a waitlist that, today, has nearly 700 children on it.

When she first spoke with NPR in September, Lilia Doyle said her 2-year-old son was on six different waitlists.

"I'm 97th on a multi-hundred person waitlist. I'm 75th on something. And some, I'm not even getting calls back," Doyle said.

Doyle, a children's librarian with a background in early childhood education, lives in Santa Fe. She acknowledged that she's selective when it comes to childcare. Still, she said, it should be easier.

"I have great belief in this program, but as it currently stands, I think the rollout needs a lot, a lot of help."

toggle caption i Nina Alexandria Riggio for NPR

According to the state, New Mexico has about 67,000 children 5 and under, and about 50% of them are enrolled in the universal childcare program. Some of the remaining families participate in other free public programs, like New Mexico PreK and Head Start.

Sponsor Message

But many children aren't enrolled in any public, free childcare program, and it's hard to know exactly how many are in Doyle's position, unable to access universal childcare because of limited capacity. New Mexico officials acknowledged to NPR that the program needs to expand.

In order to work for every family, the program will have to overcome both a shortage of childcare workers and childcare slots — two challenges that are also playing out at the national level.

Because of that, across the country, policymakers and childcare advocates are keeping a close eye on this Southwestern experiment.

Cynthia Osborne, who leads Vanderbilt University's Prenatal-to-3 Policy Impact Center, said New Mexico is "going to provide lessons that the rest of the states are going to have to pay attention to."

"If New Mexico can show us how to build the infrastructure, I think other states will say that's an investment that we should make."

But the challenges to building that infrastructure – and keeping costs under control – are very real.

The program has built-in safeguards in case economic downturns make it harder to pay for – and one of those safeguards was recently triggered: The annual Consumer Price Index rose above 3%, which means wealthier families – who make more than $198,000 for a household of four – will soon have to start making a copayment. According to the state's Early Childhood Education and Care Department, ECECD, that copay won't exceed $148.50 a month. The department says this change will affect about 10% of enrolled families, and will remain in effect through the fiscal year.

How it happened in New Mexico

Like many states, New Mexico previously offered childcare subsidies to low-income families, and free childcare to the lowest-income families. For a while, the state was raising the income limits for those programs.

toggle caption i Nina Alexandria Riggio for NPR

Families, providers and grassroots organizers had also been campaigning to do away with those limits entirely. One of the big sticking points was how to pay for it, and the answer came in 2022, when New Mexicans voted to dedicate a portion of the state's Land Grant Permanent Fund to early childhood education. Much of that fund consists of taxes and royalties on the state's vast oil and gas production, and it's large enough to provide hundreds of millions of dollars to support childcare every year.

Sponsor Message

Then, in September 2025, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham announced a plan for free, universal childcare and prekindergarten, which would begin Nov. 1 of that year. After it launched, the program was approved by the Democrat-majority state legislature and was officially written into law in March 2026.

Any licensed or registered childcare provider in New Mexico can participate in the program. The state offers higher reimbursements for centers that pay workers higher wages and operate a minimum of 10 hours, five days a week.

"I think childcare is a gamechanger for every single thing that a state ought to deliver for its families," Lujan Grisham told NPR.

The governor said this year is going "stunningly well."

"I can't go anywhere in New Mexico… where I don't have a parent tell me that this is life-changing and transformative," she said.

But she knows more capacity is needed.

"We need to keep growing," Lujan Grisham said. "It is not a stagnant set of opportunities."

In 2025, ECECD set a goal to create 12,000 new childcare spots in the first few years of the program, but did not share a specific deadline with NPR. According to the department, they are more than halfway there.

A nationwide childcare shortage

It was no surprise that accessibility would be an issue for a program like this.

Nearly half of all U.S. children, ages 5 and under, live in a licensed childcare desert, where demand for care outpaces availability, according to the Center for American Progress, a left-leaning think tank.

Olga Grays, a childcare provider for more than 20 years, said she fields messages every day from desperate parents who she isn't able to give slots to. That's one reason she's part of a group chat that includes over 40 childcare providers in her area.

toggle caption i Bree Lamb for NPR

"Every time somebody calls me, you know, I put their name and the age of their kids in that group. And I'm like, 'Does anybody have openings?' You know, but the sad thing is that not a lot of people have openings, especially for infants."

Grays, a single mother of five, operates out of her home in Las Cruces, in the southern part of the state.

At Mrs. Olga's Daycare, the living room has been transformed into a classroom, with cushioned, fall-safe floors. The outdoor space is part children's playground and part garden oasis.

Sponsor Message

"[The children] can play with water, with dirt, grass. They ground themselves. It makes a world of a difference," Grays said.

She wishes she didn't have to turn any children away.

toggle caption i Bree Lamb for NPR

"I think that's one of our biggest issues right now, is making sure that we have enough spots available for everybody coming in," Grays said. "And I think that's one of the flaws that perhaps other states can learn from."

According to the Center for American Progress, rural areas especially struggle with childcare deserts — and New Mexico is very rural.

"It's not a lack of funding, it's a lack of providers," the state's speaker of the house, Javier Martinez, told NPR. He's a Democrat and an advocate for universal childcare. "We have communities that are miles from any type of population center. Hundreds of miles sometimes. And so there are communities where that market isn't quite there to support a business."

The tension around providing free childcare to wealthier families

The program's current operating budget is almost $600 million.

But there's concern among some state lawmakers that it's projected to be about $50 million over budget this year.

"By calling it universal, all we've done is add the wealthier folks," said state Sen. Steve Lanier, a Republican representing the northwest corner of New Mexico.

Lanier sued to stop the governor's universal childcare initiative — a lawsuit that was ultimately unsuccessful.

He told NPR that the steep price tag for this program is why he only supports childcare assistance for some.

"My daughter's a school teacher. She has two young boys. She gets free childcare. So, from a personal view, I see where it is needed. I mean, that helps her and her family immensely," Lanier said. "But somebody that's making $450,000, $600,000, do they really need that assistance?"

Catron Allred, who oversees the early childhood center at Santa Fe Community College, doesn't see it that way.

Sponsor Message

"To me, I think it's a mentality of early childhood as a public good," she explained. "Nobody questions a wealthy family sending their kids to public school and it should be the same for early childhood."

It's not a one-size-fits-all model

While New Mexico is the only state with free, universal childcare right now, other states and cities have made progress in that direction, including Oregon, Connecticut, Washington, D.C., New York City and Vermont, which has tapped into payroll taxes for funding.

In New York City, which already has free prekindergarten for 3- and 4-year-olds, Mayor Zohran Mamdani recently rolled out free daycare for thousands of the city's 2-year-olds.

As in New Mexico, "Both the biggest challenge and opportunity in New York City is our scale," explained Emmy Liss, executive director of the Mayor's Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education.

toggle caption i Bree Lamb for NPR

"We know that every family's childcare needs are different. We know that our diverse landscape of childcare providers offer a really wide mix of services that families value," Liss added. "But to build a system that incorporates all of those different providers and meets the needs of all of our families is a complex challenge."

Liss said the goal is to have free pre-k for every 2-year-old by the end of the mayor's first term. But instead of expanding access to everyone all at once, as New Mexico has done, she said the city is growing capacity "in parallel" with access by creating more slots and matching them with families.

"We are working to build the infrastructure, the workforce, the physical capacity and the support to providers to ensure that we can continue to scale access to care here," Liss told NPR.

She said her office has been in conversation with leaders in New Mexico, and has had the chance to learn from them. But ultimately, she said, "Our realities are different."

Sponsor Message

"I think we're making slightly different choices in how we are implementing expanded access to care, which is good. I think we should be making different choices, responsive to the needs we hear from New Yorkers."

Childcare can make or break a parent's work life

Veronica Ramirez lives in Ohkay Owingeh, a federally recognized tribe and pueblo in northern New Mexico. She said she learned about universal childcare when it was in the news last year and decided to enroll her 2-year-old daughter.

"For my daughter, I think it's really opened doors for her," Ramirez told NPR.

"Just being able to be around other little human beings that are her age...I've seen her go up to other little kids in public and say hi or just start playing with them. And I'm like, 'Oh, well, she's social now. She's not clinging to mom only.' "

toggle caption i Bree Lamb for NPR

For Ramirez, having consistent childcare has enabled her to do more nonprofit work, including as an outreach coordinator at a birth center that primarily serves indigenous clients in nearby Española. It helps that her 7-year-old son is in school for the same hours as her daughter is in daycare.

"Now I'm able to work more and make more money and support my family a little bit better," Ramirez said.

The childcare help has opened other doors for her, too.

"I'm trying to get my bachelor's. I had my son when I was 19, right when I graduated high school," Ramirez said. "It's taken me a little bit longer, but I'm getting closer to getting a degree."

A new paper from Arizona State University found that lower-income mothers in New Mexico have seen significant gains since free, universal childcare was enacted, with full-time employment increasing by 23%.

toggle caption i Bree Lamb for NPR

But for Lilia Doyle, in Santa Fe, working full-time won't be an option until she gets her son off a waitlist and into consistent childcare. When she first spoke to NPR in September, she said she and her family are living on her husband's income.

Sponsor Message

"Hopefully our finances will be able to absorb it," she said. "We'll buckle down, and we'll make it through, but … it's not ideal."

Then, in October, Doyle got some news: A childcare center told her they found a spot for her son – but it wouldn't open up until August 2027.

World.title: Midterm voters ended the long-running GOP dominance in state legislatures
World.content:
Midterm voters ended the long-running GOP dominance in state legislatures

toggle caption i Sarah Kallis/GPB News

The midterm elections saw historic changes in state legislatures.

Pennsylvania voters elected a Democratic majority in the state Senate for the first time since Jimmy Carter was president. Democrats in Texas will run the state House there for the first time in 24 years . The Georgia House will have a Democratic majority for the first time in more than 20 years .

The results reversed a GOP dominance in legislatures that began in 2010 and had solidified since.

Going into the midterms, Republicans controlled legislatures in 28 states and Democrats held 18 . The remaining few were divided. Now, with some votes still being counted, it looks likely the Democrats will hold a 24-to-22 lead with others divided.

Sponsor Message

So far, Democrats have picked up seats in nearly every state that held legislative elections, according to data compiled by NPR. Democrats gained significant ground in unexpected, reliably Republican states, like Texas, Utah and Florida.

The shift could mean real change in people's lives as legislatures rewrite laws on taxes, reproductive rights, access to health care, school funding and other issues. Legislatures have also been important in promoting or blocking President Trump's agenda.

New Democratic 'trifectas,' controlling the legislature and governor's office

The Republican State Legislative Committee, which coordinates support for GOP candidates, blamed the losses on the national anti-incumbent mood and heavy spending for Democrats. "Ultimately, the results of this cycle underscore both the challenges Republicans face and the importance of maintaining a strong, sustained presence in the states," the group's president. Edith Jorge-Tuñón, wrote.

The president of their rival organization , Heather Williams of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, said their wins "proved what is possible when you put statehouses at the center of a national strategy."

Some of the biggest changes could come in states where Democrats now control both chambers of the legislature and the governor's office. They gained six new "trifectas."

In Arizona, Democrats will have the majorities in the state House and Senate and hold the governor's office — a trifecta — for the first time since 1966.

One possible policy change could be on school vouchers. Gov. Katie Hobbs has repeatedly tried to reform and limit the state's billion-dollar voucher program , which provides public money for private school tuition regardless of family income. But the Republican-run legislature had blocked her. Arizona Democrats have said they also hope to provide financial relief on rent, utilities and childcare.

Sponsor Message

In Pennsylvania, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro has promised to work with a newly Democratic legislature to raise the minimum wage to $15 an hour, strengthen abortion rights and increase affordable housing.

Democrats also won trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin and in Nevada, where they won the governor's office. They broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas.

Going into the midterms, Republicans had a few more trifectas than the Democrats. Now Democrats will likely have 22 and the Republicans 17, with 10 other states divided, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures . (That doesn't include Nebraska, with a Republican governor and a unicameral legislature controlled by Republicans.)

Democrats can break Republican momentum in some states

In some states, including Georgia, North Carolina and Texas, Democrats have turned Republican-controlled legislatures into divided legislatures.

Georgia Democrats won the House and came close in the Senate. On their agenda, they could try to win over a few GOP lawmakers and pass Medicaid expansion to provide health care to more low income residents. There could also be an effort by House Democrats to repeal that state's six-week abortion ban, but that could be a tough sell in the Senate.

Democrats won control the North Carolina state House. As for the state Senate, a Republican is leading the race for one seat by just over a couple hundred votes and it is likely headed to a recount. It will determine if Republicans have a one-seat majority or if the chamber will be tied. If it is tied, the Democratic lieutenant governor would be the tie-breaker.

North Carolina Democrats are expected to try and roll back some abortion restrictions. And Democratic Gov. Josh Stein has called on both parties to work on addressing affordability concerns once the legislature convenes.

In several states, Democrats fell short of flipping some Republican-held chambers but won enough seats to end Republican supermajorities. The Multistate government relations firm says that happened in six states that had GOP, veto-proof supermajorities.

Sponsor Message

That will matter most where there are Democratic governors, who now have leverage to veto GOP initiatives, like in North Carolina, Ohio and Kansas.

World.title: A new generation of disability rights activists carry on Judy Heumann's legacy
World.content:
A new generation of disability rights activists carry on Judy Heumann's legacy

toggle caption i Apple TV

Judy Heumann is known as the mother of the disability rights movement — yet she is lesser known than many of the other civil rights activists of her time. Now, a new film seeks to change that.

Being Heumann, the latest movie from Oscar-winning director Sian Heder, tells the story of the young woman from Brooklyn who led the movement to win the first civil rights protections in the country for people with disabilities.

Before the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) was passed in 1990, there was Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 . It was a single sentence, written into the law, promising people with disabilities the right to fair employment and access to public life without facing discrimination.

Sponsor Message

But for years, there were no rules or regulations making the federal government actually enforce those protections.

Until the spring of 1977, when a band of activists with disabilities decided to do something about it. Led by Heumann and Kitty Cone, activists took over the former Department of Health, Education and Welfare building in San Francisco for nearly a month — widely considered the longest sit-in of a federal building in U.S. history.

People across disability groups — from wheelchair users to people with intellectual and health-related disabilities — camped out, demanding, and eventually winning the passage of rules that made Section 504 enforceable. The protests paved the way for federally funded institutions like schools, libraries, city buildings and other entities to be made accessible for disabled people.

toggle caption i HolLynn D'Lil/Getty Images

"Judy always said, 'disability only becomes a tragedy for me when society fails to provide the things we need to lead our lives' — job opportunities or barrier-free buildings, for example," says former NPR correspondent Joe Shapiro, who covered disability and was a friend of Heumann's until she died in 2023.

Regarding disability rights as basic civil rights was a novel concept at the time, but has remained core to the movement today.

Shapiro says Heumann was fueled by the idea of a generation of young disabled people who would come of age under the ADA: "They see the ADA as a floor, not a ceiling, and Judy loved that there's this new generation demanding more."

Sponsor Message

With the film having opened in theaters this month and now streaming on Apple TV, NPR sat down with some members of the ADA generation to talk about Heumann's legacy, and the threats they see today to the movement she helped launch.

"It is our job to carry on her legacy and keep that fire burning all these decades later," says Kaleigh Brendle, who started a disability rights organization called Judy's League to push back against the Trump administration's efforts to roll back protections attached to Section 504.

Last month, a federal judge dealt a blow to disability rights activists by agreeing to strip out mentions of "integration" of people with disabilities from Section 504 regulations. This erased some of the very language Heumann and her movement had helped win 50 years ago.

As she watched Being Heumann, Brendle says she "felt simultaneously sad that we're here again because I know she would be hurting to see so much of what she fought for at risk. But it also strengthened my resolve."

Brendle, who is blind and has other disabilities, held a watch party of Being Heumann with four other members of Judy's League. They spoke to NPR about their impressions.

These are excerpts from that conversation, edited for length and clarity.

On what stood out most about Being Heumann:

Liam Holland, 25, Philadelphia: The very first line of the movie is Judy chanting "[Sign 504]!" That gave me chills right away, because almost 50 years later, 504 is the exact reason we founded Judy's League. Seeing her lead the chant hit home because we are still fighting those exact same battles today.

Cricket Bidleman, 27, Baltimore: Like Liam said, seeing history come full circle was not particularly encouraging. But we did it once, so we can do it again. We can save 504.

Kaleigh Brendle, 23, Berkeley, Calif.: What I loved seeing over and over on display was just the unshakable resolve that Judy showed, that fire that would not be extinguished … And I think right now we're seeing relentless challenges to our rights from this administration, from every direction. ... It really gave me hope and renewed what I feel we need to be doing right now.

Sponsor Message

Ellana Crew, 30, Baltimore: I feel I've never seen so many real disabled people on screen in one place ... They are laughing, they are swearing, they're telling dirty jokes … That was one of my favorite things, honestly, it was just like, 'OK, wow, I didn't expect that to be in this movie.' They are not shying away from disabled people as sexual and romantic beings, which is rarely something that society lets us talk about. And ... it's remarkable how many of the sentiments in the movie, based on this time in the 1970s, still feel so relevant today.

On what parts of the disability rights movement back then still feel relevant:

Ellana Crew: A lot of attitudes expressed by non-disabled people [in the film] felt fairly indistinguishable from the attitudes I hear today. Like some of the same sentiments, some of the same opinions of pity, charity-based mindsets of like, "Oh, well we feel bad for you, but we can't do anything about it, it's just too hard." I think people would be amazed how often that still happens today, or maybe they wouldn't.

Cricket Bidleman: It's amazing to see how in some ways we've made so much progress. I mean, now we have computers and technology that work for us, and autonomous vehicles and things like that. But the discrimination hasn't really changed that much.

Kaleigh Brendle: What really moved me was hearing Judy lead the "Sign 504" chant because I, along with several other people in Judy's league ... we were in Austin, Texas on the Capitol steps this July. And all these years later we were having to chant "Hands off 504."

On how the legacy of Judy Heumann and other activists has shaped the disability rights movement today:

Liam Holland: Every week, I roll a mile and back [in my wheelchair] by myself to get chicken for my dinner puree. That trip has a lot of curb cuts. Before 504, sidewalks did not have ramps, which stopped disabled people's access to sidewalks. The [1977] sit-in forced the government to mandate public access. So every curb I go over is directly tied to that fight. ... The people at the deli see me come in every week by myself. They fist-bump me, get my card from my wallet, put it back ... And then I roll home over curb cuts listening to music. So what Judy means to me, quite simply, is independence and normalcy.

Sponsor Message

Leigh White, 30, Galloway, N.J.: Unfortunately, history rhymes. And we're not right back where we started, but we are in the crucible, if you will, where we're kind of being fired at on all sides. And it's important to remember her grit and her tenacity and her true dedication ... Disabled individuals are the largest minority group in the United States. And it crosses all genders and all races and everything. So by fighting for the rights of people with disabilities, it kind of raises all boats.Kaleigh Brendle: I always say to other people that don't understand the disability experience: If you broke your arm tomorrow, you would expect that the world would accommodate you. You would expect to have the accommodations that you needed as you navigated that temporary disability. Why is it wrong for us to expect what you would expect in that situation?

Cricket Bidleman: We've made so many advancements because of people like Judy and because of … all these activists and advocates who came before us. And although I do have to struggle with people to obtain access to media or textbooks or the standardized testing to get into various education, it's still nothing compared to some of the things we saw in the movie

Leigh White: Us being part of the 'ADA generation,' we're able to reap the benefits. And with hindsight we're really able to appreciate the work that she's done and then kind of carry the torch into the future. So that the struggles we're going through right now, hopefully the next generation of disabled youth don't have to go through the same things.

World.title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from moving ahead on Washington public golf course redevelopment
World.content:
Judge temporarily blocks Trump from moving ahead on Washington public golf course redevelopment

toggle caption i Tom Brenner/AP

WASHINGTON — A federal judge on Saturday ordered a two-week delay to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House, blocking for now President Donald Trump's push to redevelop the site along the Potomac River into a championship-level venue.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months. Trump had announced work would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.

Sponsor Message

The plaintiffs argue that Trump's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the Republican president denies. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would "irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."

The president's public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the decision. Trump said on Oct. 26 that "We are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th in order to renovate and rebuild for Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons." He added that the goal was to renovate and rebuild "a World Championship Public Facility."

Reyes in her ruling Saturday noted that Trump's posts presented a problem for the government. "They indicate that the Washington National Plan is final and that NPS will close the Park to implement it," she wrote. "Both points favor granting Plaintiffs' motion for another temporary restraining order."

Reyes said her order "ENJOINS the government from closing East Potomac Park and the East Potomac Golf Course during the daily hours in which they were open as of November 14, 2026. It does not order the Government to undertake any active management of either. Further, for the avoidance of any doubt, the Government remains free, as it has since the onset of this litigation, to conduct repairs on any part of the Park and Course with any notice required by the existing Preliminary Injunction."

Sponsor Message

The judge said the order is in effect "through November 28, 2026, or further order from the Court, whichever comes first."

The Justice Department said in a statement Saturday that the judge acknowledged that the National Park Service can limit access to its facilities where the public is at risk of harm. "Nothing in the Court's order precludes planning for the development of a world class golf course to continue," it said. "The Department of Justice will always vociferously defend the Trump Administration's agenda in court."

Catherine Carroll, a senior legal adviser at Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs, praised the ruling. "We are grateful that once again, a court has intervened to prevent irreparable harm caused by the Trump-Vance administration's pursuit of another one of the president's vanity projects," she said. "The administration's inexplicable drive to destroy East Potomac Park would have taken away a treasured park that could never be replaced."

The park's redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others.

Reyes had signaled throughout a five-hour court hearing Friday that she was likely to issue some stoppage for the park closure. The only issue was how expansive it might be. Justice Department lawyer Adam Gustafson argued that the entire East Potomac Park, which includes three golf courses, a miniature course, bike riding lanes and other recreational areas, was being closed because of safety factors. He also noted that the lease between the government and the current operator, National Links Trust, was ending Sunday.

Reyes pointed out that safety had not been part of the discussion over the closure for months and that ending the lease felt more like an action that provided a premise for the closure rather than an action that led to the closure of the course about 2 miles from the White House.

toggle caption i Tom Brenner/AP

Even before the order, Trump lashed out in a social media post Saturday, contending that Reyes "doesn't want us to quickly and inexpensively fix up the Course which is, also, very dangerous." He said people who live in the Washington area would get a 50% discount on "any and all Rates charged" and that the redevelopment would "evolve into something very special, something which the Judge will be able to take great pride in seeing!"

Sponsor Message

Reyes' order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump's projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project.

Reyes, who was nominated to the court by Democratic President Joe Biden, had for months been reticent about approving the plaintiffs' requests for work stoppages. The plaintiffs had argued the administration was moving ahead with work related to the project despite the pending lawsuit.

Her reluctance to issue orders ended in October, spurred in part by a tree-cutting spree by the administration over a holiday weekend with little notification to the judge or plaintiffs.

Officials and government lawyers said the tree work was part of a 2019 plan that recommended the cutting. In response, the judge confronted the administration over what she portrayed as deceitful actions over its intentions for the project.

Reyes has repeatedly expressed frustration over the minute planning details she has been asked to adjudicate, including over the trees being cut down at the 106-year-old park. The Justice Department filed a request that Reyes be removed from the case because of what it called her "egregious behavior" and questioned her impartiality. Reyes has not recused herself.

The restraining order was one of two issues Reyes took up during Friday's hearing.

She announced plans last week to name Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, to examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Justice Department had violated ethics or misled her during the course of the case.

World.title: FAA ground stop disrupts college football
World.content:
FAA ground stop disrupts college football

toggle caption i Justin Ford/Getty Images

The Federal Aviation Administration's ground stop on Friday has led not only to travel headaches, but also schedule changes and delays in college sports.

Many college football teams were in airports Friday on their way to upcoming games when the nationwide ground stop was issued and thousands of flights were canceled. The FAA on Saturday said airports were returning to normal operations, but that delays and cancellations would continue through the day.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy acknowledged the ground stop's impact on college football. Several games on Saturday were delayed for hours.

"If you look at the cost of what happened yesterday, we're talking if you like football — I know we've had some disruptions to the college football schedule. Some games are being moved," Duffy said during a news conference Saturday. "That's not the most important thing, but we do want to move teams around the country so we can have playoffs happen."

Sponsor Message

Utah, ranked No. 2 in the College Football Playoff Rankings, will kick off against Arizona in Tucson at 8:30 p.m. local time — a three-hour delay. The Auburn vs. Mississippi State game was pushed back more than four hours to start at 3:15 p.m. local time in Mississippi because of the ground stop. The Florida Atlantic Owls were also unable to fly to Oklahoma on Friday ahead of their game against the Tulsa Golden Hurricane. Saturday's game, which was supposed to begin at 2:30 p.m. local time, was moved to 6:15 p.m. local time.

While other college teams were able to arrive at their destinations and proceed with games on Saturday, the University of Mississippi did not.

Ole Miss, ranked No. 19, was not able to fly to Oklahoma as planned on Friday for its matchup with the University of Oklahoma Sooners. The game between the two teams, which was scheduled to occur Saturday, will now take place on Sunday at 1 p.m. ET, according to the Southeastern Conference. The game will compete with several NFL games that will be televised at the same time. NFL teams were largely unaffected by the ground stop.

In order to help alleviate fans' frustration, the Sooners on Saturday announced "fan appreciation" promotions for the rescheduled game. Oklahoma students can go to the game for free with their student ID and there will be reduced prices on concession items such as $2 for popcorn or a 16-ounce beer.

World.title: Florida city cancels St. Patrick's Day parade, citing new anti-DEI law
World.content:
Florida city cancels St. Patrick's Day parade, citing new anti-DEI law

toggle caption i Alex Wong/Getty Images

One of the first casualties of a new Florida law that prohibits taxpayer dollars from going toward diversity initiatives is a St. Patrick's Day parade in a beach town that has been celebrating its Irish American community for nearly 60 years.

The city of Delray Beach announced this week that it was canceling its popular St. Patrick's Day festivities in compliance with a new law that takes effect on Jan. 1. The city will also withdraw its sponsorship of LGBTQ Pride celebrations in June, officials said.

The law, backed by Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is part of the state's ongoing crackdown on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives that the governor has called discriminatory and said have "no place" in public institutions.

Sponsor Message

The city lawyer for Delray Beach, a community in southeast Florida with picturesque beaches and a historic downtown, told the mayor that any government-sponsored celebrations of culture, ethnicity or heritage that are not a national holiday (for example: Independence Day) could run afoul of the new anti-DEI law. So, Mayor Tom Carney said, he made the difficult decision to cancel one of the city's biggest events of the year.

In past years, the parade, an annual event since 1970, wound its way through the downtown core of Delray Beach with spectators lined up several-people deep along the route. Local businesses and organizations sponsored floats and giveaways. School bands played as they marched through the streets. Participants included members of the Ancient Order of Hibernians, the largest and oldest Irish Catholic organization in the country.

"I've said it's engrained in the DNA of Delray and I do mean that. It's one of our signature events," Carney, a Republican, told NPR.

The mayor said he's hopeful that the city can find a path forward — and a way to preserve the event.

If a private sponsor were to volunteer to take over the St. Patrick's Day parade, or the June Pride celebrations, Carney said, the city would gladly hand over the reins and support the continuation of these festivities.

Sponsor Message

"These types of events we should be celebrating because in this country, people can have these events. In other countries, you can't do this. We have great freedoms here," he said. "And if the community wants something and it's not against public policy then I would support them to do it if they're using private dollars. If we can do it, we should do it."

Carney, who is of Irish descent, said the parade was privately run until about eight years ago — so returning to a private-sponsorship model would be a callback to the parade's origins. His own family, he said, was involved in keeping the parade going during the 1980s and 1990s.

Delray Beach officials said they have been inundated with emails, calls and social media messages from constituents who are angry that the community's decades-long celebration had been axed.

"It was kind of a call to action to me," Carney said. "The community really wants to have it, so we should go ahead and have it, we just need to get it privately funded."

The governor, meanwhile, has accused Delray Beach of weaponizing the new anti-DEI measure to make a political point. DeSantis said the city was "engaging in "malicious compliance" in a message he posted on X following the city's cancellation announcement.

"What they are doing is not mandated by Florida law," the governor wrote. "It's just an attempt to make a political point — a point that legacy media will no doubt try to amplify. We've seen these stunts throughout the years. Rinse and repeat."

The mayor said the city is merely trying to stay out of trouble with the law. The measure, SB1134, asserts that any official that violates the provision could face civil or legal consequences.

"The legislation has unintended consequences. The governor may genuinely believe what he believes and I take him at his word; our city attorney came up with a different conclusion," Carney said. "I'm going to leave it at that."

World.title: Maintenance gone awry caused nation-wide ground stop, says Transportation Secretary
World.content:
Maintenance gone awry caused nation-wide ground stop, says Transportation Secretary

Transcript

ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:

What caused the cascade of failures which brought the U.S. air travel system to its knees on Friday? Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's explanation - a contractor was replacing a router to upgrade the nation's outdated air traffic control equipment when something went very wrong.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

SEAN DUFFY: This was an FAA system that didn't meet the moment. Our contractor didn't meet the moment. Or the equipment didn't meet the moment and cause the outages.

SCHMITZ: The system is back online, and flights are now taking off, but travelers throughout the country are still dealing with the disruption. NPR spoke to one traveler, Andres Martinez Murillo, last night.

ANDRES MARTINEZ MURILLO: My flight keeps getting delayed further. They don't know if it's, like, a crew issue. They don't know if it's, like, a pilot issue. I don't even know if we have a plane.

SCHMITZ: Murillo told NPR he finally boarded his first flight this morning, but his second flight's been canceled, and he still does not know when he will reach his final destination. For more, we're joined by NPR transportation correspondent Joel Rose. Hey, Joel.

JOEL ROSE, BYLINE: Hey, Rob.

SCHMITZ: So many angry passengers today that still have not gotten to their destinations - what more do we know about the cause of all of this?

ROSE: We are starting to get a clearer picture. The heads of the Department of Transportation and the Federal Aviation Administration held a press conference today, and they put the blame squarely on a longtime FAA contractor, L3 Harris Technologies. They say the company was doing a routine maintenance upgrade of a server as part of a transition from older copper wire to fiber optic cable, and that is when things went sideways.

Sean Duffy and FAA leaders were asked several times why a faulty router could lead to telecom outages across such a wide part of the country. They said that is still under investigation. In a statement, L3 Harris says it is supporting the FAA's investigation into what went wrong and that it takes the impact on airlines and travelers seriously.

SCHMITZ: OK. Let's step back here just for a moment. What was happening in the air while all of this was playing out on the ground?

ROSE: Air traffic controllers were starting to see intermittent problems with radar and communication systems around 3:30 p.m. Eastern. By 3:44 p.m., the FAA declared a nationwide ground stop. Here is some of the reaction from air traffic controllers and pilots in Salt Lake City, as you can hear in archived audio from the website, liveatc.net.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: You guys got any updates from your company about what's going on?

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #2: Not at all. If you've got info, we're all ears.

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: I wish we did. We basically only know what the FAA tells us, which is not a lot.

ROSE: I talked to one air traffic controller who was working when the outage began. He is a controller at one of the en route centers that handle high altitude traffic and was not authorized to speak publicly, but he described the situation as chaos. He said, a lot of airplanes were being diverted away from their original destinations. Some of them were running out of fuel. And he emphasized just how this whole system depends on the air traffic controllers, who found a way to more than 3,000 planes onto the ground quickly and safely, even when their equipment was letting them down.

SCHMITZ: So we've got a lot of confused pilots, a lot of confused air traffic controllers. You know, I'm just curious, the air traffic controller that you spoke to - did he have any thoughts about the apparent cause of this ground stop?

ROSE: I should say that we spoke this morning before the press conference by DOT, but this controller was already beginning to think that this was probably a mistake by a contractor who was doing work to upgrade the air traffic control system, which this controller says is happening all the time. He also places some of the blame on the oversight of the FAA for not having enough redundant systems in place, you know, to prevent this kind of outage from happening. He questioned why this work was going on in the middle of a busy Friday afternoon instead...

SCHMITZ: Right.

ROSE: ...Of late at night when it would not have had as much impact if something went wrong. He said it, quote, "just screams incompetence, like, gross incompetence."

SCHMITZ: You know, it does seem quite remarkable that a single point of failure like this could have such an enormous impact. What has the FAA said about this?

ROSE: Well, they said this was considered routine maintenance work. They are still investigating why it appears to have basically broken the entire national airspace. Here is Rebecca Guy, the acting chief technology officer at the FAA.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

REBECCA GUY: What we are doing is that root cause analysis, but at this time, we do believe what occurred with that router has been worked through.

ROSE: In other words, they think they have solved the problem. The FAA administrator promised that things should be back to normal by close of business on Sunday.

SCHMITZ: That is NPR transportation correspondent, Joel Rose. Joel, thank you so much for all that reporting.

ROSE: You're welcome.

World.title: US has lost measles elimination status, global health authorities say
World.content:
US has lost measles elimination status, global health authorities say

toggle caption i Amy Maxmen/KFF Health News



The U.S. has lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, a public health triumph secured a quarter century ago.

Researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations on the country's status told KFF Health News that the Pan American Health Organization reached the conclusion this week: Measles has reestablished regular transmission in the country.

PAHO had planned a public announcement on Nov. 17.

In public health parlance, measles elimination depends on a country's sporadic outbreaks ending within a year. That's no longer happening in the United States.

"It's a very sad moment," said Anne Schuchat, an epidemiologist and a former deputy director at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention who was not involved in PAHO's decision.

Sponsor Message

"Measles causes so much unnecessary suffering, everything from a high fever and missed work and school to long-term complications like progressive degenerative nerve disease and death," Schuchat said.

Measles outbreaks are entirely preventable: Two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine prevent about 97% of infections, so when almost everyone in a community is fully vaccinated, the virus can't spread.

In the past two years, over 830 people have been hospitalized with measles in the U.S. More than 8,000 people have been sickened in outbreaks that have cost roughly $125 million in medical care, public health response, and productivity losses, Johns Hopkins University researchers estimate.

States have reported 13 measles-associated deaths, including a 7-month-old in New York and infants in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin in recent months. Babies typically aren't vaccinated before they're a year old.

PAHO, an international group that oversees health in the Americas and works with the World Health Organization, based its assessment on two analyses: one by the CDC and another by an independent group of measles experts.

Researchers anticipated this conclusion after an outbreak in Utah surpassed the one-year mark in June.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, Emily Hilliard, attributed the resurgence of measles to vaccination gaps that opened years before this administration. Indeed, rates of childhood vaccination have steadily declined since the COVID pandemic started.

Sponsor Message

But many scientists also blame the Trump administration for spreading vaccine misinformation and stifling a swift, strong response to outbreaks.

For example, the administration cut millions of dollars from children's immunization programs run by state health departments and terminated funds for research on vaccine hesitancy.

After Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. sacked CDC director Susan Monarez in August 2025, she told Congress she was fired because she would not preapprove changes to vaccine recommendations "without reviewing the evidence."

Monarez added that "we already have seen the largest measles outbreak in more than 30 years" and that, "if vaccine protections are weakened, preventable diseases will return."

Spokespeople for HHS and the White House defended the administration, and Kennedy, who led a prominent anti-vaccine organization before he took the helm at HHS. "The President and the Secretary have repeatedly encouraged measles vaccination, coordinated with states, and facilitated the deployment of vaccine doses across the country," White House spokesperson Allison Schuster wrote in an email.

Past administrations sounded alarms

For more than three decades, the federal government treated measles as a preventable tragedy, with sizable outbreaks triggering national efforts to boost vaccination and stop the virus from spreading.

That's no longer the case, said Patsy Stinchfield, executive director of the Measles Collaborative, a new initiative that educates the public about vaccines and assists health workers responding to outbreaks.

Stinchfield was a pediatric nurse at a children's hospital in Minnesota during the nation's last surge of measles before elimination, from 1989 to 1991. She recalled an entire ward devoted to children with measles and the enormous effort required to prevent the virus from spreading to kids with cancer and weakened immune systems.

Two children at the hospital died of measles. "That changed my career forever," she said.

Back then, she said, the federal government "saw the urgency." Officials held press conferences, spoke on the news about vaccines, issued clinical guidelines, and published reports in the CDC's flagship journal — the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, or MMWR — that drove policies.

Sponsor Message

When data suggested that some children weren't mounting a strong response to a single dose of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine, a CDC advisory committee recommended two doses of the shot.

When CDC analyses found that many children with measles hadn't been vaccinated due to cost, the government launched the Vaccines for Children program to make immunizations available free of charge to underinsured families.

Cases plummeted. By 2000, the CDC and PAHO determined that measles was no longer a national threat — measles transmission had been eliminated.

"Elimination" allows for occasional outbreaks, because measles is not eradicated worldwide and a small fraction of people, such as young infants, can't be protected by vaccines.

People infected abroad sparked occasional outbreaks after U.S. elimination, but — until now — those fizzled out because of herd immunity, when 95% of people within a community are immunized. In those situations, outbreaks peter out and vulnerable people are protected.

toggle caption i Amy Maxmen/KFF Health News



It would be 14 years before another significant outbreak in the U.S. Then in 2015, the virus took off among unvaccinated children at Disney parks in California, giving rise to outbreaks elsewhere. Congress saw some 125 cases as an emergency and summoned the CDC's Schuchat to testify on the situation.

"Vaccination wasn't a partisan issue," she recalled. "This was about problem-solving: What can we do about this?"

National television aired a video of then-U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy talking with Sesame Street's Elmo about vaccination. HHS officials worked with vaccine experts on strategies to boost public confidence in vaccines. California and Vermont tightened vaccine requirements.

In 2019, House and Senate committees met again about measles, as a large outbreak took hold in Orthodox Jewish communities in New York and New Jersey took hold. Congress asked HHS leaders how the administration planned to curb the rise of vaccine misinformation online.

"Internet fraudsters who claim that vaccines are not safe are preying on the unfounded fears and daily struggles of parents, and they are creating a public health hazard that is entirely preventable," Lamar Alexander, then a Republican senator from Tennessee, said at the time.

Sponsor Message

Alex Azar, health secretary during the first Trump administration, and then-CDC Director Robert Redfield held a press conference stressing the "importance of on-time vaccination."

And during the 2014, 2015, and 2019 outbreaks, the CDC's MMWR published detailed articles within weeks of data collection. Timing matters since the reports guide emergency response. "The MMWR is the voice of the CDC," Schuchat said, "alerting the nation, the media, clinicians, and public health experts to events that require action."

'The dog didn't bark'

Just after President Donald Trump took office in 2025, a measles outbreak exploded in West Texas. Within seven months, it surpassed the size of any in the U.S. since 1992, spread to Mexico and at least three other states, sickened more than 4,500 people in the two countries, and killed at least 16.

Instead of broadcasting clear, repeated messages on the importance of measles vaccines, Kennedy falsely claimed on Fox News that they lead to "deaths every year."

Congress didn't call a hearing, and HHS didn't send funds until after the emergency in West Texas had subsided. Besides an annual measles update, the MMWR didn't publish a single report on the outbreaks that year.

"A lot of this is the dog didn't bark," said Dorit Reiss, a vaccine policy researcher at the University of California Law San Francisco. "Something that normally happens isn't happening."

Political appointees have delayed or blocked several MMWR articles, according to multiple CDC officials whom KFF Health News agreed not to identify because they feared retaliation for speaking with the press. "There's a deliberate effort to downplay vaccine-preventable diseases by the administration," one official said.

"Measles reports from West Texas and New Mexico were intentionally shelved," another scientist at the agency said. In April, The Washington Post reported that Jay Bhattacharya, who temporarily led the CDC this year and remains head of the National Institutes of Health, had blocked the publication of a study in the MMWR finding that COVID vaccines halved the likelihood of emergency department visits.

Sponsor Message

"The suggestion that HHS is deliberately suppressing information about measles or other vaccine-preventable diseases is false," Hilliard, the HHS spokesperson, said in an email to KFF Health News.

Hilliard said Kennedy and the CDC have provided approximately $100 million in additional funding to respond to outbreaks. The timing of MMWR reports, she added, varies due to factors such as data analysis and scientific review.

More than a year after data was collected from Texas, a few reports came out in the CDC's journal. One study on 60 people hospitalized for measles in West Texas revealed that two required intubation and mechanical ventilation and that a baby born to a mother with measles experienced dangerous brain swelling due to the virus.

toggle caption i Amy Maxmen/KFF Health News



The MMWR still hasn't published detailed reports on massive outbreaks in South Carolina, Utah, and Pennsylvania. The CDC's national measles update hasn't appeared in the MMWR this year either. Instead, the journal has featured less urgent articles on scientific techniques that may help characterize future outbreaks.

CDC scientists told KFF Health News that they continue to analyze data but no longer expect to publish their findings in the MMWR because the process has become slow, opaque, and unpredictable. An urgent CDC report on the risks of measles to pregnant women was withheld, The Washington Post reported recently.

"We have two CDCs now," an official at the agency said. "One is staffed by CDC scientists and civil servants who are committed to public health, and the other is political appointees who go in and change the website."

The CDC's measles dashboard counts four fewer measles deaths than state health departments have reported this year. Kennedy has disputed some deaths and made unsubstantiated claims that Pennsylvania health officials misrepresented data.

Kennedy personally instructed the CDC to alter language on a webpage that said vaccines do not cause autism, he told The New York Times last year.

Sponsor Message

The page now suggests a potential link between the two and no longer lists a slew of peer-reviewed studies that rigorously searched for an association and found none. These have been replaced with speculation about a correlation and unsubstantiated accusations that the scientific establishment has buried a potential link in order "to prevent vaccine hesitancy."

The Trump administration has muddied the message on vaccines in other ways, Reiss said. Trump incorrectly said in August that the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine could be "quite lethal," and he repeated the debunked idea that vaccines may cause autism.

Stephen Miller, now Trump's White House chief of staff, has falsely said doctors "pump your kids full of shots days after birth with no understanding of the long-term consequences." Recommended vaccines and the vaccine schedule have been thoroughly studied.

Kennedy has made such claims for two decades, including as health secretary. "Having top leadership disseminating rumors, disinformation and flat-out falsehoods has been unforgivable," Schuchat said.

When pressed by journalists and Congress, Kennedy and Trump have recommended measles vaccines. But they haven't repeated the message clearly and unprompted on social media or on the podcasts and videos that Kennedy regularly appears in.

Kennedy also replaced vaccine experts on a panel advising the CDC with fringe researchers holding anti-vaccine views. And under his leadership, the CDC has laid off or forced out many vaccine specialists, including all of those in a group that partners with community organizations and pharmacies, the Immunization Services Division partnership branch.

At the same time, Kennedy has devoted resources to searching for potential harms from vaccines, including through an attempted clinical trial considered unnecessary and unethical by medical societies and the WHO.

To regain measles elimination status, the current U.S. outbreaks must end — then, future outbreaks must stop spreading within a year, said Paul Rota, a microbiologist and former CDC official. With outbreaks expanding in several states, he said, that moment isn't on the horizon.

Sponsor Message

"Bigger fires create more embers, and any one of those embers can seed another fire," he said.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. Learn more about KFF.

World.title: Canada's health-care spending tops $10,000 per person. Where is the money going?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada is spending more on health care than ever. Whether Canadians are getting more care for their money is another question.

A new report from the Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI) , an independent, non-profit organization that collects and analyzes data on Canada's health-care system, projects health-care spending will reach a record $433 billion in 2026, or $10,398 per person, an increase of 4.8 per cent over last year.

For the first time since the pandemic, inflation-adjusted spending per person is expected to surpass its previous peak, reached in 2021.

But Canada already ranks among the higher-spending countries in the developed world, while patients continue to struggle with long wait times, overcrowded hospitals and difficulty finding family doctors.

That raises a central question: Is Canada spending enough on health care, or does the problem lie in how that money is being spent?

"I believe that these records of spending are just buying us more of the same right now," said Jason Sutherland, a professor at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver and director of the Centre for Health Services and Policy Research.

He argues that without substantial changes to how health care is organized and delivered, additional spending is unlikely to produce meaningful improvements for patients.

WATCH | 1 in 10 ER patients waiting more than 14 hours for care, report finds: 1 in 10 Canadians waiting more than 14 hours in emergency rooms: report | Duration closed caption 6:56 A new report by the Canadian Institute for Health Information says that in 2024-2025, one in 10 patients in emergency departments end up spending more than 14 hours there waiting for care. Dr. Michael Herman, a spokesperson for the Canadian Association of Emergency Physicians, says the report's findings aren't a surprise.

Is $10,000 per person a lot?

The $10,398 figure represents the combined cost of publicly and privately funded health care, including hospitals, doctors, prescription drugs and services paid for through private insurance or directly by patients. It is not the amount each Canadian pays in taxes.

While the figure may seem substantial, international comparisons provide important context.

According to the CIHI report, Canada devoted 11.5 per cent of its gross domestic product to health care in 2024, compared with an OECD average of 9.3 per cent .

That placed Canada alongside other high-spending countries, including France at 11.3 per cent and Sweden at 11.2 per cent, but below Germany at 12.2 per cent and the United States at 17.2 per cent.

"We are not cheap in our health-care spending," Sutherland said.

LISTEN | Ontario doctors demand an apology over provincial letters urging reduced hours and delayed care: Here and Now Toronto 7:49 Why is the Ontario Ministry of Health asking doctors to scale back their hours and delay patient care? Some Ontario doctors are demanding an apology from the province after receiving letters from the ministry asking them to scale back their hours and delay patient care. The Ontario Medical Association is worried the letters could scare doctors into doing just that. Dr. Rebbeca Hicks is the President of the OMA. She was on Here and Now.

Sara Allin, an associate professor at the University of Toronto's Institute of Health Policy, Management and Evaluation, agreed that Canada's spending is substantial. But she said the more revealing comparison is what countries achieve with their investments.

She pointed to data showing Canada performs relatively well on some measures, including life expectancy and vaccination rates, but continues to lag in important areas of access and service delivery.

"We have very persistently long wait times," Allin said. "We have persistent challenges with care co-ordination."

She described Canada's health system as generally a middle performer among countries with similarly high expenditures.

WATCH | Soaring cancer drug prices prompt warning over patient access: His cancer drug costs $90,000/month. Doctors say it’s greed | Duration closed caption 6:17 Cancer doctors across Canada are sounding the alarm over drug prices pushing public health care past a breaking point. CBC’s Christine Birak breaks down the numbers and hears from dozens of frontline oncologists about the impact of surging costs on patients.

More money, but where is it going?

The CIHI report identifies a potentially important change in how health-care spending is growing.

Inflation-adjusted spending per person is projected to grow 2.3 per cent this year, compared with just 0.4 per cent in 2025.

More significantly, CIHI estimates public-sector spending will increase by more than $5 billion beyond what is needed to keep pace with inflation and demographic changes.

Adam Rondeau, CIHI's manager of health spending and operations analytics, said the increase could be an early indication that governments are investing in additional capacity, new technologies and innovations in health-care delivery.

But determining precisely where that money is going is more complicated.

"It's difficult to say X number of dollars is net new and related to a given program of work," Rondeau said.

He explained that the report identifies additional spending but cannot establish whether that investment is producing shorter wait times, more available services or better patient outcomes.

Meanwhile, the report states that spending on physicians is projected to increase 8.3 per cent this year, substantially faster than overall health-care spending.

Yet access to primary care remains a major challenge. CIHI's research on primary care found that 17 per cent of Canadian adults reported having no regular health-care provider in 2023.

Sara Allin, an associate professor of health policy at the University of Toronto, says Canada spends more on health care than many comparable countries, but it continues to struggle with long wait times and access to services. (Submitted by Sara Allin)

Spending more isn't necessarily spending better

For Allin, the challenge isn't simply increasing health-care budgets; it's ensuring that additional investment produces measurable improvements.

"If we're spending this much, it's more perhaps how we're spending it than the level of spending at this point in terms of driving further improvements," she said.

One important difference between Canada and some comparable countries, she said, is how health care is financed.

According to CIHI's expenditure figures, 71.4 per cent of Canada's health spending is projected to come from public sources in 2026, with the remaining 28.6 per cent financed privately.

Allin said several other wealthy countries fund a larger share of health care collectively, allowing them to cover a broader range of services, including prescription drugs, dental care and mental health supports.

She said those differences have consequences for both efficiency and equity.

Publicly financed systems can negotiate lower prices and reduce some administrative costs, she explained. They can also reduce financial barriers that prevent patients from accessing needed services.

WATCH | Health-care workers hold rally after 3.5 years without a contract: Hundreds of unionized health-care workers rally outside legislature | Duration closed caption 2:04 At least two health-care unions have gone three and a half years without a contract. On Wednesday, hundreds rallied outside the legislature demanding the government take action.

Allin said gaps in Canada's public coverage mean people without adequate private insurance can face substantial costs for necessary services, particularly prescription drugs and mental health care.

She also questioned whether Canada's health-care financing arrangements provide sufficient incentives to improve patient outcomes.

Rather than simply paying providers according to the volume of services delivered, Allin said governments could do more to link funding with measurable improvements in care.

Sutherland similarly argued that governments need to rethink where additional resources are directed.

He pointed to home care, assisted living, long-term care and other community-based services as areas where greater investment could help keep patients out of overcrowded hospitals and emergency departments.

Both experts also raised concerns about the pressure that rising health-care spending could place on other public priorities, including education, housing and social services.

Ultimately, Sutherland said, the figures should reassure Canadians that substantial resources are being devoted to health care while also prompting them to question whether those resources are being used effectively.

"I think they should be somewhat relieved that Canada is not underfunding this health-care system, but at the same time, they should be concerned that they're not getting great value for their money."
