World.title: Facing 'uncomfortable' questions, King Charles shows the 'soft power' of the Crown
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hello, royal watchers and those intrigued by what's going on inside the House of Windsor. This is your deep dive into royal news and analysis. Sign up here to get this delivered to your inbox.

As King Charles was wrapping up his recent trip to the Caribbean and South America, a palace aide let it be known via news reports that he relishes the "tough parts" of his role as monarch and would keep being used in "politically charged" deployments.

There's little doubt the nine-day sojourn was one of the tougher outings of his four-year reign, shrouded as it was in questions about whether the U.K. should apologize for its role in the transatlantic slave trade and pay reparations.

During the trip that took Charles to Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda, he spoke of the "great suffering and injustices of the past" and called the slave trade a "shameful chapter."

No apology emerged, but U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham indicated as the visit was unfolding that he was open to calls for a formal apology, a marked change in British policy on the issue.

Burnham rejected calls for financial reparations. But writing in the Guardian newspaper, he said he wanted to "launch a new drive on debt," which included helping more vulnerable countries "repay over a longer time period and with better ⁠rates."

As with trips to Canada in 2025 and the United States earlier this year, Charles was walking something of a diplomatic tightrope at a politically charged time. There seems to be an emerging pattern.

WATCH | Charles reiterates 'personal sorrow' over slavery: King Charles addresses 'shameful' history of transatlantic slave trade | Duration closed caption 1:44 Speaking at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, King Charles reiterated his 'most profound personal sorrow' over the 'monstrous injustice' of past international trade in enslaved people.

"He doesn't seem to shy away from uncomfortable historical questions," royal historian Justin Vovk said in an interview.

"By acknowledging them and navigating them, he's showing that these are real questions that matter to people. They can't be ignored. But also there is that tacit acknowledgment that his interest and recognition and engaging in those conversations does not direct policies of the British government."

Charles seems to be good at creating opportunities for dialogue "when a more overt political initiative or intervention would be counterproductive," Vovk said.

"So he really is demonstrating how effective the soft power of the Crown is for Britain's foreign relations."

Those relations were front and centre in the recent trip. Along with the calls for an apology and questions over reparations, there is republican pressure to remove the monarch as head of state in some countries.

Terrence Campbell, parliamentary leader of Guyana’s opposition group A Partnership for National Unity, holds placards during a demonstration demanding a formal British apology and reparations for slavery and colonialism in Georgetown, Guyana, on Oct. 30. (Isabel Infantes/Reuters)

" It was a very difficult, a very challenging visit," Judith Rowbotham, a social and cultural scholar and visiting research professor at the University of Plymouth in southwestern England, said in an interview.

"But he survived it, and survived it far better when you compare with the [2022] visit of the Prince and Princess of Wales to the Caribbean [that] attracted a huge amount of criticism in its aftermath, both in terms of how it was planned and how the events took place."

That trip had been seen by some as a bid to shore up ties between Britain and the Commonwealth countries on its itinerary: Belize, Jamaica and the Bahamas.

In the end, that weeklong visit drew more headlines for protests, the republican sentiment fomenting particularly in Jamaica, calls for slavery reparations and uncomfortable moments that seemed more rooted in the colonial past than looking toward the future.

This time, Rowbotham said, Charles made it clear that "as far as he was concerned, it was a matter for the Caribbean communities to make a choice about who should be their head of state."

"He was happy to continue to serve but it was something which he would not fight if they made a different decision."

Charles carried out numerous engagements in the three countries he visited, with many focusing on issues he has made a priority, including the environment and conservation, youth and sustainability.

An Indigenous child, right, presents King Charles, left, with a traditional beaded necklace during a meeting with Indigenous leaders at the National Toshaos Council at Umana Yana on Oct. 30 in Georgetown, Guyana. (Ben Stansall/Getty Images)

Any royal visit has its moments. This one had the umbrella — or initial lack thereof for the King — as the skies opened up in Antigua and Barbuda.

"He was initially clearly taken aback when there was no handy umbrella," Rowbotham said.

"He subsequently laughed it off and simply carried on," she said, calling it "the mark of a monarch who knows how to be diplomatic in a stressful situation."

WATCH | Where is the umbrella?: King Charles gets soaked in Antigua as Camilla gets only umbrella | Duration 0:45 King Charles, who was caught in heavy rain during Antigua and Barbuda's 45th Independence Day celebrations on Sunday, was captured on camera flinging his hands as he stood in the rain. (The King, who was eventually handed an umbrella, later joked about the event.)

The moment reminded Vovk of the time Charles got frustrated over a pen holder while signing documents during the ceremony confirming him as monarch in 2022.

"He has certainly gotten better at being able to laugh about those sorts of things."

Remembering the fallen

Queen Camilla, left, and Catherine, Princess of Wales, right, attend the Remembrance Sunday ceremony at the Cenotaph on Whitehall in central London on Nov. 8. (Toby Melville/AFP/Getty Images)

Members of the Royal Family honoured the memory of the fallen at annual events around London in recent days.

King Charles led the tributes on Remembrance Sunday at a ceremony attended by thousands of veterans at the Cenotaph in central London. While Charles, Prince William and others laid wreaths, Queen Camilla, Catherine, Princess of Wales, and others watched from the balcony of a nearby building.

The night before, Charles and Camilla led senior members of the Royal Family for an evening of remembrance at Royal Albert Hall.

Princess Anne, front centre, and Prince William attend the National Service of Remembrance at the Cenotaph on Nov. 8 in London, England. (Leon Neal/Getty Images)

A few days earlier, Birgitte, the Duchess of Gloucester, on behalf of Camilla, opened the 98th Field of Remembrance at Westminster Abbey.

The remembrance events are a high point of the royal ceremonial year.

The events were little changed from previous years, something that stood out to Vovk.

"This is where ritual culture becomes so important for reinforcing consistency and values across generations," he said.

"It is something that unites the Crown and the people in memory, in grief, in a sense of responsibility."

Birgitte, Duchess of Gloucester, centre, looks on during her visit to the 98th Field of Remembrance at Westminster Abbey on Nov. 5 in London. (Alberto Pezzali/Getty Images)

Meghan's father cut off monitor days after arrest, officials say

Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, was in custody this week after authorities in Florida said he cut off an ankle monitor days after his arrest on allegations of keeping child sexual abuse materials.

Meghan hasn't commented publicly in recent days, and pulled out of a speech she had been planning to give in Belgium on Tuesday. She appeared that day with her husband, Prince Harry, as he spoke at the European Parliament in Brussels.

Earlier, however, Meghan had said she was "deeply distressed" by the allegations. She also revealed that a letter containing "troubling allegations" about her father had been sent to London police in 2019.

"I was given assurances that these were being investigated," Meghan said of the letter.

"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them."

WATCH | Markle charged over child sexual abuse images: Meghan Markle's father arrested, charged over child sexual abuse images | Duration closed caption 2:01 Thomas Wayne Markle, father of Prince Harry's wife Meghan, was arrested by U.S. federal agents in Florida on Friday on charges of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs allegedly showing him with underage girls.

Media attention for several years has focused on the estrangement, and observers see the possibility recent events could influence public perceptions around Meghan, which have been polarizing in some quarters.

"I'm sure the British public and the wider public, you know, in the States and elsewhere, will have sympathy for her in regards to what's emerged about her father," royal commentator Roya Nikkah told CBC News.

Vovk sees the current situation could "dramatically shift public perception" of Meghan and could "soften public criticism and public reactions" to her.

He also wonders if it might help clear the way for some level of rapprochement between Meghan, Harry and the Royal Family.

"I don't know if I'd say a road to reconciliation, but perhaps an opportunity for some mutual support between the Sussexes and the rest of the Royal Family."

The King and the Rocket Man

Elton John, left, and King Charles pose for a photograph at Apple Music Studios, where they were recording John's Rocket Hour, in London, in October. (Apple Music/Reuters)

It's long been known that King Charles has a love of music, particularly of the classical persuasion. But his latest public musings on the overall matter have little royal precedent.

Charles sat down at a microphone opposite Elton John to take part in a special edition of the singer's show.

The episode of Elton John's Rocket Hour aired Saturday — Charles's 78th birthday — on Apple Music. It's intended to celebrate 50 years of the King's Trust — founded by Charles with his navy severance pay as the Prince's Trust in 1976 — and musicians who have supported the youth charity.

"Music has ​always been at the heart of the Prince's, and now the King's Trust," Charles said, adding that the program offered a chance to showcase performers who had supported the charity ​and newer artists it had helped launch.

In a release, Buckingham Palace said the episode also highlights artists — such as the rock band Muse — who received help from the trust at the beginning of their careers, and in some cases went on to support it as alumni.

Muse, which started out in 1994 under the name Rocket Baby Dolls, received a grant from the Prince's Trust to buy sound equipment. In 2018, the band performed a sold-out concert at the Royal Albert Hall in support of the trust.

Charles, left, meets John as he arrives for the Royal Variety Performance at the Royal Albert Hall in London, on Nov. 22, 2024. (Toby Melville/Reuters)

Charles and John shared memories of performances by musicians in support of the charity's initiatives — from rock galas at Wembley Arena to concerts in Hyde Park.

"If ⁠you champion a young artist and show you believe in them, it makes all the difference," John said. "Young people are ​our future."

Vovk saw little precedent for Charles sitting down across the table from John.

"It's potentially groundbreaking. I think this is the first time that the sovereign has done something that would be classified in this way as entertainment," he said.

"To actually sit down and have a recorded conversation with the sovereign is extraordinarily rare. Elizabeth did a few of them in her final years, but these were all about reminiscences around the Crown jewels, coronation ceremony, her father…. To have something that is so, well, mainstream, is really unheard of."

John, second from left, Charles and Tim Cook, Apple's executive chairman, pose with mentees during a music workshop for young peopleat Battersea Power Station in southwest London, on Oct. 7. (Ben Stansall/Reuters)

Royally quotable

"I was told in hospital that my recovery would not be linear. There will be good days and bad days, that it will take time. This is the same in nature."

— Catherine, Princess of Wales, regarding her recovery from cancer. She made the comment in an interview in an issue of Country Life magazine that was guest-edited by her husband, Prince William.

Royal reads

Prince William has expressed his frustration at the way women are treated in the military. The future head of the British Armed Forces has been holding under-the-radar meetings with female service personnel as part of a drive to ensure they feel "safe, respected and valued." [Daily Mail]

Prince William's Duchy of Cornwall has apologized to tenants for its handling of the sale of an estate in southwestern England and promised new valuations of their farms and homes. [The Observer]

Sophie, Duchess of Edinburgh, told Rohingya refugees in the camps at Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh "we won't walk away" after hearing about the hardships they face. [The Independent]

Prince Harry and five other prominent figures have launched a legal challenge against a judge's verdict in their unsuccessful claims against the Daily Mail's publisher, Associated Newspapers. [The Guardian]

The Princess of Wales met with families gaining extra support for their youngsters' social development at a community hospital in southern England. [ITV]

The Prince of Wales made another European away trip in support of soccer team Aston Villa as he attended a Champions League match against Barcelona. William was joined by his son, Prince George. [ESPN]

Prince George contributed a colourful drawing of a kingfisher to the edition of Country Life guest-edited by his father. [Country Life]

World.title: English was the language I built my career in. In Canada, it became something to prove
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This First Person column is written by Anusuya Datta, a writer and journalist based in Saskatoon. For more information about First Person stories, see the FAQ.

I had only been in Canada for two weeks when I got the question that would follow me around for the next few years.

I’d gone to the pharmacy to ask about medication. The woman behind the counter looked up and said, “You speak very good English . ”

By then, I had spent more than 15 years earning my living in English. Now I was being congratulated for successfully asking about a prescription.

“Thank you,” I said.

“Where did you learn it?”

“In India.”

She looked impressed.

I walked out with my prescription and a piece of information: in Canada, my English was an accomplishment.

Anusuya Datta attends a space conference, posing with a therapeutic robot seal proposed as a companion for astronauts on long missions. (Submitted by Anusuya Datta)

I had assumed I was the one immigrating. It turned out there were two of us. My English had done its paperwork. Canada makes you declare your English. That's what the international English language test is for. My English did very well. We both assumed that was the end of it. But someone had forgotten to send Saskatchewan a copy.

English wasn't the first language I learned, I admit. But it was the one I was educated in. I read novels in it and did a master's in it. Nobody in India ever congratulated me on it. It was like having elbows. You don't get complimented on elbows.

Coming face-to-face with assumptions

The pharmacist wasn’t the last. Neighbours told me I spoke English well. Doctors told me. People in shops told me, with the warmth usually reserved for someone who has parallel parked a combine. They were being kind to a newcomer, and I was grateful. I still am.

I said thank you. Every time. You don't hold up the queue to explain English isn't rocket science, and that you have, in fact, explained rocket science in it.

WATCH | Canadians share the reactions they get to their accents: I have an accent when I speak English | Duration 2:53 We asked CBC staff to talk to us about what it means to speak English with an accent, how it's impacted their lives, work and view on being in Canada.

Then my English got a job. So did I, at the same tech company in Saskatoon, which was convenient. We were both hired at a junior level. That seemed fair. We were new.

Soon my English was fine-tuning everyone's copy. Colleagues sent me their drafts the way you send a shirt to the dry cleaner, without conversation and expecting it back clean. My English had become the office Wi-Fi. Everyone used it. You don’t promote the Wi-Fi.

Eventually, I brought up a promotion on a call with my boss. I was told it was too soon. I didn't have the necessary experience.

“You need to be patient. These things take time,” he repeated, a little too slowly, as if he were weighing my English comprehension skills.

After the call, I sat for a long time. What my English lacked, I understood, was Canadian experience. It had only the other kind, where you do the work.

A year later, I joined an agriculture-technology company. I imagined data and software. The company sold agricultural chemicals in jugs.

This isn’t an attack on chemicals. Chemicals have had a long and successful career in agriculture. Jugs, for their part, have performed admirably throughout human civilization. But I couldn’t understand how the company involved technology.

The company wanted lots of content, the kind that sounds like the future of food. So I asked what the technology was. In my line of work, this is a standard opening question. It turned out to be a hostile act.

I was given a few words. Innovation. Sustainability. Transformation. None was attached to anything. My job was to expand them. I asked for details. I was told to read up.

So I read everything I could find and came back with questions. The boss came back with more keywords. Then the words started changing their meaning. One week, sustainability was the next big thing. The next, it was “woke.”

Finally, I asked why he was saying the exact opposite of what he’d said the week before. That was when he explained the problem. I wasn't understanding his feedback because English wasn't my first language.

The second half was true. I couldn’t fault his research, but it came a little late. My English had been excellent while it produced adjectives. It developed problems the moment it produced question marks.

“I’ve written for American and European organizations for over 15 years,” I told him. “My English has never been a problem. Until now.”

I was angry. Of all the things I expected to have to prove in Canada, my English wasn’t on the list.

I ended up leaving the company. My English came with me. We had been through a lot together.

It’s been more than two years since. The bitterness has aged nicely, like cheddar.

Meanwhile, my English and I went freelance. Not one client told me my English was so good. Or so bad. They asked for a redraft when one was needed and sent more work. I recommend this as a form of compliment. It’s quieter and you can invoice for it.

These days I work for a global company with people in Canada, the U.S. and Europe. People here have opinions , too. They tell me when a piece is great and when I’ve got the technology totally wrong. Not one of them has an opinion about my English. A plumber is judged on the pipes. Nobody asks where the wrench is from. I've never been so happily criticized.

English is still not my first language. It's still doing very well. It even has Canadian experience now.

Thank you for asking.

Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to us.

World.title: A man was once murdered over the pronunciation of 'Newfoundland'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Newfoundlanders and Labradorians tend to feel strongly about the right way to pronounce the name of our island, but would you kill a man over it? In 1876, someone did.

Since the release of the Netflix limited series Below, the pronunciation of “Newfoundland” has become a hot topic once again. Actors are correcting talk show hosts; online commenters are correcting actors.

While these discussions can get pretty heated, they’re nothing compared to a fight that broke out over the word exactly 150 years ago.

One Friday night in March of 1876, workers from the Hooker and Gray saw mill near Larkspur, Colorado, were chatting over supper when their landlady asked one of them, a burly New Yorker named William Atcheson, about his dog.

It was a New-FOUND-land dog, Atcheson explained. No, it wasn’t, another man interjected. It was a New-found-LAND.

The objector was John Peter Davis, a Texan teamster in his mid-thirties who was rumoured to have been a gunslinger in his youth.

The murder occurred at a backwoods lumber mill on Colorado’s Great Divide, which might have looked similar to this mill in Williamstown, New York, photographed around 1900. (Oswego County Historical Society)

This wasn’t the first time the two men had clashed. Atcheson had more formal education than many of the other men on staff, and his zeal for “proper” word use had sometimes caused him to butt heads with the workers from Texas and with Davis, who acted as their spokesman.

Tensions had been rising, and this time they boiled over. “High words and some rather hard names” were exchanged, according to a report published in The Colorado Banner.

On their way to Atcheson’s shanty to consult a dictionary — and the mere fact that he had brought a dictionary to an isolated lumber camp on the frontier may tell you something of his passion for the English language — Atcheson took a swing at Davis and landed a blow so hard it knocked the Texan to the ground.

When Davis staggered to his feet, he had a revolver in his hand, and “true to his Texan breeding and education,” as one newspaper told it, he shot Atcheson in the gut.

Atcheson remained a tough customer until the end. As he lay bleeding, he bragged about having decked Davis twice more despite the bullet lodged in his belly.

Atcheson died in the early hours of Saturday morning, and Davis fled into the woods, leaving his team of draft animals behind. Witnesses said he was distraught he’d killed someone over such a trivial argument.

A simple question about a worker’s Newfoundland dog sparked the argument. (Edwin Landseer/Victoria and Albert Museum)

A snowstorm obliterated Davis’ tracks, and, though the local sheriff led a posse in after him, he was never found.

Had the two men made it as far as the dictionary, they would have discovered it disagreed with them both.

The 1864 edition of Webster, which would have been the latest version, gave the pronunciation as NEW-fund-LAND, with primary stress on the first syllable and secondary stress on the third.

Webster’s advice is strikingly similar to the way many Newfoundlanders and Labradorians say the word today, but how did Newfoundlanders pronounce the island’s name in the 1800s?

Until the early 20th century, the official pronunciation was NEW-FOUND-LAND, where each syllable was fully articulated and equally stressed. This was the pronunciation recommended by the Broadcasting Corporation of Newfoundland in 1939, though they allowed for “a slight stressing of the final syllable.”

The Rocky Mountain News called Atcheson and Davis “chronic disputants” who “always manifested much temper in their discussions." (Colorado Historic Newspapers Collection)

It was Joey Smallwood and the Newfoundland Historical Society who, in the late 1930s, advocated for the pronunciation New-fund-LAND.

Assuming neither Atcheson nor Davis was reducing “land” to “lund,” which has always been the cardinal sin of pronunciation among Newfoundlanders, the versions both men used could probably have been heard somewhere on the island in the 19th century.

Not that either Atcheson or Davis would have known that. There’s no evidence either man had any ties to Newfoundland itself.

The story might have ended there except for a letter that arrived on the doorstep of the Castle Rock, Colo., sheriff in late 1912.

The message purported to be written by a physician in Peoria, Ore., who was treating John Peter Davis, now 70 years old.

Believing himself to be at the brink of death, Davis had apparently confessed to Atcheson’s murder. Then, either he had asked the doctor to send his statement to the Colorado authorities to unburden his soul, or the doctor had taken it upon himself to turn Davis in so he could line his pockets with any reward money that might be on offer.

Whatever the case, the letter’s description of the crime was so specific the sheriff had no doubt it was sent by someone close to the killer.

When the story of the deathbed confession leaked to the media, reporters wondered “whether justice [would] be defeated by death,” but justice was also threatened by practical details.

Calls to Peoria failed to turn up any resident by the name of John Davis. If he was indeed living there, he had probably assumed a new identity.

Thirty-six years after the crime, the sheriff of Castle Rock received a letter from a man in Peoria, Ore., confessing to the killing. (The Herald Democrat/Colorado Historic Newspapers Collection)

Meanwhile, even if Davis survived his illness, were located, and were arrested, there might not be enough evidence left to convict him.

Older Coloradans remembered the unusual killing, but no official records of it could be found among county court documents or coroner’s reports. The physician who had treated Atcheson in his final hours was dead, and the prime witness was missing.

If Davis retracted his confession, there could be no trial. It’s not clear whether he was ever brought up on charges.

The case has a final irony.

William Atcheson was a man so devoted to proper word use he died over it, but none of the news reports of his death can agree on the spelling of his name, which is recorded as Atcheson, Atchison, Atchinson and Atherson.

World.title: 'He lived and breathed it': NCAA football prospect from N.S. has died
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Nova Scotian who was set to play football at an American powerhouse college is being remembered for his exceptional talent and desire to get better on the field, but his happy-go-lucky and teddy-bear nature off it.

Marcellus Young Casario, 18, a Grade 12 student at a Georgia prep school, died Friday after a medical emergency. His father, Devin Casario, said his son hadn't been feeling well lately and had been experiencing some heart issues.

The six-foot-six, 275-pound defensive end who grew up in Halifax was set to graduate high school next month and begin attending the University of Georgia in January, a school that has produced many NFL stars.

"He lived and breathed it, and his work ethic was incredible," said Devin Casario. "He had [a] relentless motor and he was very, very coachable."

Former coaches say that while Casario's size, speed and strength were exceptional, his desire to get better is what made him stand out.

Marcellus Young Casario is shown in a photo from his time playing with Rabun Gap in Georgia. (Submitted by Devin Casario)

Chanuen Flint, a former coach and family friend, said that even at the age of six when Casario started playing football, his passion was evident.

"You just knew right away when he showed up on the field, he was all business. [He] had fun doing it, but he was there to play football," said Flint.

Early days

Colby Smith helped coach Casario when he played mites football, for kids who are seven and eight. He remembers the team playing in a halftime scrimmage at a Saint Mary's University football game. The children formed a tunnel to give the giant university players high-fives as they came out onto the field.

"I think from that very moment he knew where he wanted to be when he got older … I can remember the look on his face when they came out and he wanted to be part of that," said Smith.

Casario played minor football for teams in Halifax, Timberlea and the South Shore.

He left the province four years ago to attend a boarding school in Aurora, Ont., which played some of its games against American schools.

Marcellus Young Casario, shown wearing No. 50, always stood out for his size playing minor football in Nova Scotia. (Susanna Baard)

Marcello Lio, the head coach at St. Andrew's College, coached Casario for two years.

"Sometimes it’s easy for a young man, maybe not as passionate, to walk away from a loss, accept it and move on," said Lio. "He had struggled with that, so he always had the will to want to be better individually and want the team to win."

Overcoming adversity

Casario attended Rabun Gap-Nacoochee School, a Georgia prep school, for the past two years. He had a hip labrum injury last year that required surgery and a six-month recovery.

It wasn't clear whether he would return to full form.

In August, when training camp began, Devin Casario remembers getting a call from his son, who was in tears.

"I thought something had happened," said Devin Casa rio. "But there were tears of joy because I really think his self-belief and faith were tested after that recovery process. And I think after that first night during the conditioning test down there, he knew that he was going to be OK."

Marcellus Young Casario is shown in his senior class photo. (Rabun Gap-Nacoochee School/Facebook)

The University of Georgia wasn't Casario's only suitor. There were visits to Michigan State and Georgia Tech, all of which are well known for their football programs.

Lio said he wasn't surprised that Casario chose the University of Georgia. There were other schools where he might have been able to get on the field sooner, but the Bulldogs offered something else.

"He wanted to be pushed; there was some yearning inside him to be constantly pushed hard to be the best he can be," said Lio.

During the past two summers, when Casario returned to Nova Scotia when school was not in session, he helped coach Flint's younger son, who also plays defensive end.

Smith said Casario was always very respectful, continuing to call him "Coach" long after he was his coach.

"Even though he had these great accomplishments, he always remembered where he came from and always paid homage to all the people that helped him get where he is," said Smith.

Criminology studies

Devin Casario said his son planned to study criminology at the University of Georgia.

He said off the field, his son led a quiet life and his faith was very important to him.

"I hope something positive can come from this tragedy, and that he can serve as an inspiration to other athletes who have dreams, you know, coming out of Nova Scotia and the East Coast that through talent and hard work, perseverance, anything is possible," said Devin Casario.

"And, you know, our family is destroyed right now and trying to make sense of this, but we're so proud of him. And it's just so unfortunate that his life was cut short."

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: Carney cites her award-winning book on encampments. She's eyeing his plan to end homelessness
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

One of Canada's leading authors on homelessness says the prime minister's plan to end it is an "ambitious goal" that has potential, but won't actually go all the way.

Prime Minister Mark Carney introduced his government's second budget last week, which features a big headline promise: end homelessness in 10 years.

Governments sometimes tease big pledges in the run up to tabling a budget. That wasn't the case with this year's signature pledge, but there was an Easter egg that could have pointed to this new policy focus.

Earlier this year, Carney told the Globe and Mail that he was reading Encampment by Maggie Helwig , which won this year's Shaughnessy Cohen Prize for political writing.

Encampment tells the story of Helwig's activism and effort to keep her Toronto churchyard open to those in need. The award jury called the book "a necessary, on-the-ground view of Canada's homelessness crisis."

November's budget went on to propose a $11.2-billion cash injection to tackle homelessness, one of this year's largest line items.

Carney is not the first politician in Canada's history to set this target, but with Canadians facing an escalating affordability and housing availability crisis, the stakes are high.

Helwig gave her assessment of Carney's plan to CBC's chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton.

"I think that the commitments which have been made are serious commitments. They are constructive commitments. They are not at a scale which would end homelessness," Helwig said in an interview on Rosemary Barton Live.

"If we are able to significantly reduce levels of homelessness, especially unsheltered homelessness, that's a big deal."

Helwig says Canada faces a very difficult situation with homelessness growing exponentially.

A national homelessness count in 2025 found that more than 65,000 people were homeless on a given night in Canada, a 59 per cent increase over five years. The share of unhoused people living in unsheltered locations, including encampments, had also increased from 23 per cent to 27 per cent.

What's needed in the Liberal plan?

Helwig's broad critique of the Liberals' proposal is that it should not overlook the straightforward need for more basic housing.

"I worry that there's a bit too much emphasis on mental health and addictions, as if those were the primary drivers of homelessness," she said.

Helwig says sometimes the issue is just needing a place someone can afford to live, since long-term homelessness itself is "fantastically destructive to people's mental and physical health."

Helwig helps move a resident's belongings as Toronto city workers prepare to clear an unhoused persons encampment at St. Stephen-in-the-Fields Church, in Toronto, on Oct. 16, 2025. (The Canadian Press)

Helwig points to Dunn House in Toronto as an example of a housing program where the focus is not exclusively on mental health and addiction, but which takes a more holistic picture of what people need when coming out of chronic homelessness.

It features direct access to doctors, nurses and a host of other health professionals with the goal of improving their health and alleviating pressure on hospitals.

"No one wants to move into the crazy house for the crazy people, right?" Helwig said, referring to projects that could over-emphasize mental health language.

Helwig says the reality is that some people do need intensive mental health support but it must be provided in a way that does not stigmatize individuals.

Influence on Carney

The day after making this pledge public, Carney cited Helwig during an announcement in Winnipeg.

While downplaying Barton's questions about whether she had a direct role in motivating Carney's new ambition, Helwig said it's nice to think her book may have contributed to it.

While listening to Carney speak publicly about the goal for the first time, Helwig noted Carney's use of language emphasizing Canada becoming a community that takes care of each other — a central theme to her book.

She said she's less concerned about whether the Liberals' plan will actually end all homelessness, compared to whether it will do good for the people who are sleeping on the streets right now.

"In a situation where we have seen so much stigmatizing language, so much demonizing language, so much emphasis on getting these people somewhere that's out of sight, to talk about this in terms of community and care, that in itself is actually quite important."

World.title: Scientists race to discover and protect what lives in the ocean
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Scientists say not knowing what lives in our oceans is holding back efforts to protect them. Because of that, many are racing to discover and document the wild and diverse species in marine environments that are often hard for humans to access.

Ocean Census, a global collaboration of scientists and non-profit organizations, estimates that scientists have documented less than 10 per cent of some 2.2 million fish, marine mammals, shellfish, plankton, squid, jellyfish and other species that live in our oceans.

"It's very difficult to protect what you don't know," said Michelle Taylor, head of science at Ocean Census.

A sea cucumber with horned appendages, nicknamed Loki, and a bright red-orange coral with fans of slender branches are among 57 new species announced and identified in October from an Ocean Census expedition off Argentina last year.

This new sea cucumber species was nicknamed Loki because of its prominent horned appendages, reminiscent of the god in Norse mythology. It was found in the Mar del Plata submarine canyon off Argentina. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)

A striking, bright red-orange octocoral was photographed nearly 2,000 metres below the surface of the ocean in Argentina's Mar del Plata canyon. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)

A landmark UN biodiversity agreement in 2022 committed to protecting 30 per cent of the world's land, water and marine areas by 2030 , but has been falling short on ocean protection , with just 12 per cent of oceans (compared to 27 per cent of lands) set to be protected by 2030.

Canada has so far protected 15.5 per cent of its oceans, according to the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society (CPAWS).

Claire Goodwin, a research scientist at Huntsman Marine Science Centre in St. Andrew's, N.B., said the goal is to protect areas with high biodiversity.

"But if you're not surveying some of your marine life and you don't know what's living there, you can't say which those biodiverse areas are."

A cone jelly captured by the remotely operated vehicle SuBastian off the coast of Argentina. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)

Sponges that eat meat, provide housing

The problem is that even within Canada, many areas are difficult to explore. Goodwin was part of an expedition in the Saguenay Fjord in Quebec in 2023.

On its steep walls, where only one species of sponge had previously been recorded, her team discovered 20 or 30 sponge species, including some new to science.

Carnivorous sponges were found in Quebec's Saguenay Fjord in 2023. (Claire Goodwin/HMSC)

Among them were carnivorous sponges that trap shrimp with glass, velcro-like appendages to engulf and digest slowly, "which was really exciting," said Goodwin, since most sponges are passive filter feeders.

Goodwin says sponges have important roles in the ecosystems — as food for sea stars, homes for some worms and a place to lay eggs for some fish. Sponges in Canadian waters can also grow to half the size of an adult human.

Claire Goodwin collects sponges in the Bay of Fundy off the coast of New Brunswick. (Torben Brydges/Fisheries and Oceans Canada)

The sea slug Dendronotus yrjargul was recorded on a recent expedition led by the Innu Nation. It was the first time the species has been found off the coast of Canada. (Claire Goodwin/HMSC/Innu Nation)

Now Goodwin is working with the Innu Nation in Labrador to survey uncharted waters in their territory. "We literally don't know what the seabed's going to be like, let alone what's going to be living on it."

Climate change impacts and solutions

The race is on to find out as the ocean warms rapidly , and climate change shifts where species are found.

Already, Goodwin says, some species have completely disappeared from regions where they were once common. She points to basket stars, "really cool sea stars that have branching arms," which were once common around St. Andrew's, but haven't been seen there since a rapid warming around 2016.

A basket star, Gorgonocephalus arcticus, is seen in the Saguenay Fjord. The species used to be common in the Bay of Fundy but seems to have disappeared due to climate change. (Claire Goodwin/HMSC)

Loïc Jacquemot, a postdoctoral researcher at Université du Québec à Rimouski, said in many areas, we don't even have much of a baseline from which to compare changes.

He's currently surveying Baffin Bay off the coast of Nunavut using a technique called eDNA, which identifies species from DNA shed into the water by organisms' skin, poop and tissues. That way, they can be surveyed without actually seeing or catching them — all you need is a water sample.

Loïc Jacquemot samples water for eDNA in B.C.'s coastal fjords. (Submitted by Loïc Jacquemot)

He said species adapted to colder waters are expected to move into a smaller and smaller area "because, of course, they cannot go much more north," while warmer water species may expand their range.

That can have big impacts on things like the food chain — including fish and shellfish humans eat — and on the way carbon is moved around the ocean by zooplankton species that migrate each day between the depths and the surface.

"It's important for the climate because all these changes impact the way carbon is stored in the ocean," Jacquemot said.

This tiny copepod is one of 20 new species identified by the Ocean Census in October. These organisms are among the zooplankton that move carbon between the surface and depths of the ocean. (The Nippon Foundation-Nekton Ocean Census/Schmidt Ocean Institute)

Photosynthetic algae called diatoms from fjords in Greenland. Diatoms are important for capturing carbon dioxide in the oceans. (Submitted by Loïc Jacquemot)

The carbon stored by the ocean and its species is known as blue carbon. So far it includes 30 per cent of carbon dioxide generated by humans, along with 90 per cent of the excess heat trapped by climate change, said a recent UN report , which warned that the ocean's ability to absorb more CO2 and heat is weakening.

Meanwhile, coral reefs, known as biodiversity hotspots with the ability to store huge amounts of carbon , are one of the ecosystems most threatened by climate change .

The impact of the ocean and its species on climate change are at the forefront of this year's UN climate summit, COP31, underway in Antalya, Turkey. Protecting marine ecosystems and "unlocking blue carbon for climate resilience" is one of 10 items on the meeting's " action agenda ."

This week at COP31, former U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and groups representing island states pushed for a strong reference to oceans in next year's global "stocktake" of climate policies, supported by the European Union and African countries.

This grenadier fish was observed with parasitic copepods attached to its head during a 2025 Ocean Census expedition off Montagu Island near Antarctica. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)

This marine worm, Harmothoe imbricata, was found off Canada's Atlantic coast. (Christy Carr/HMSC)

For the 'biogeochemical functioning of our planet'

Taylor with Ocean Census said marine ecosystems are important for humans — even people who live far from the sea, not just for producing food and medicines, but also on a bigger scale. "You know, it's part of the biogeochemical functioning of our planet. We're very reliant on it, whether we realize it or not."

Taylor, Goodwin and Jacquemot all hope that by sharing with people the amazing diversity of life in the ocean, they can help people appreciate the importance of saving it.

"When we show people pictures and videos of what's underwater, they're always amazed by what we actually have down there," Goodwin said.

Michelle Taylor, head of science for Ocean Census, checks out views from the cameras on the ROV SuBastian during a mission to catalogue deep sea species. (Paul Satchell)

Taylor describes them as an incredible diversity of "wild looking creatures" and says for some of them "you wouldn't believe they were of this planet."

She said she's very worried about coral reefs especially, but "you have to have the attitude that there are solutions to this." In the meantime, she added, "we need to find as many species as we can, so we can understand diversity on this planet before it is lost."

This is part of a series of articles highlighting the work of scientists looking at disappearing groups of species you may not have thought much about. It's a chance to get to know them and how they impact our lives, and find out what can be done to keep them around.

World.title: It started with a lobster supper. Now it's an East Coast institution
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Standing shoulder-to-shoulder on the edge of a picturesque Nova Scotia cove, thousands of roaring fans watched the sun melt into a sky brushed with amber and blue, eagerly awaiting rocker Matt Mays to strike his first chord.

The outdoor festival took place just outside the Shore Club, a historic music venue and lobster supper hall in the tiny community of Hubbards that has endured for 90 years and draws visitors from across the globe.

After playing inside the wooden building every summer for decades, Mays admitted he initially worried whether its signature “magic” would follow him outdoors. It did.

“It's one of those places on earth that all the vibes are,” Mays said in a new CBC documentary about the club.

“It's a very spiritual event for myself … and if it's spiritual, that means it's just bigger than anything.”

The outdoor shows at the Shore Club represent yet another evolution in the story of how a quaint venue in a rural South Shore hamlet at the end of a winding road became a world-famous Maritime institution.

WATCH | How one family built their legacy on lobster dinners and live music: For 80 years, East Coast musicians and fans have revered this venue | Duration closed caption 22:24 For more than 80 years, The Shore Club in Hubbards, N.S., has served up classic lobster suppers and legendary live music to fans worldwide. In a new CBC documentary, Aly Thomson and Dave Irish show how the Harnish family turned a rural dance hall into a Maritime icon.

Each summer, the family-run business draws thousands to its classic lobster suppers, electric concerts, camping under lofty pines and basking on its private beach.

The venue has gained a reputation among big Canadian artists and music fans for its distinct atmosphere and long-standing traditions.

Its unique Maritime esthetic has drawn the likes of Kentucky Fried Chicken founder Colonel Sanders, Mariah Carey, and then-Prince Charles and Princess Diana.

But the club is always evolving, while staying true to its roots. It’s a balancing act the Harnish family, which operates the club, has done for nine decades.

Still, its allure isn’t something they can put their finger on.

“At any given night in this room, we'll have people from almost every continent on earth in here.... You realize this is a really unique and fun and amazing place to be,” said Luke Harnish, sitting in the club’s dining hall and dance floor next to his father, Rhys Harnish.

"Dad and I looked at each other dumbfounded many times this summer, just like, why does this work?"

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: De la Espriella replaces director of earthquake reconstruction fund as scandals mount
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked the director of the Miracle Fund, which was to reconstruct the parts of Colombia destroyed by an earthquake in August, over excessive wages and hardly any progress.

De la Espriella decided to sack the director, befriended businessman Jaime Andres Uribe, after the opposition revealed he had given himself a COP39.4 million ($11.9 thousand) salary.

The labor cost of the 26 Miracle Fund staff was COP765.5 million ($231.2 thousand), revealed opposition Senator Kamelia Zuluaga (Pact0 Historico), who had filed an open information request.

The fund additionally estimated it needed an annual COP8.9 billion ($2.7 million) for the 130 people that were supposed to be hired.

The president responded on Twitter, claiming that “the salaries that have been announced for the Milagro Fund are NOT in line with my austerity policy. I DO NOT APPROVE THEM! I have ordered that this absurdity be reversed immediately.”

Hours later, De la Espriella said he accepted the resignation of Uribe and said that former Housing Minister Luis Felipe Henao would assume the leadership of the reconstruction effort.

Henao became controversial in 2020 when a photo appeared of him and late drug trafficker José Hernandez, a.k.a. “El Ñeñe,” who allegedly helped finance the campaign of former President Ivan Duque.

Henao’s wife, Luz Stella Murgas, was recently appointed director of business association ANDI.

The government’s response to the earthquake has been fiercely criticized as it has failed to effectively begin reconstruction efforts in western Colombia, where the 7.4M earthquake destroyed more than a 100,000 homes an much of the regional economy.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Why Brazil?
World.content:
A sky that doesn`t charge to dream.

By Dany Cesario

HAVANA TIMES – Ever since I arrived in Brazil, there is one question I get asked repeatedly: “Why do so many Cubans come here?”

And every time I hear it, I think the question should be different: What is happening in Cuba that makes so many people decide to seek a different life?

The island is deteriorating, hardships are mounting, and people are wearing themselves out trying to get ahead. Yet the leaders’ worn-out rhetoric never changes, as if repeating the same slogans could feed a family, rebuild a country in ruins, or restore hope to those who have spent far too long waiting for change.

It outrages me that people are expected to make sacrifices without seeing them translate into a decent life. That expressing a different opinion becomes a problem, and that deciding one’s own future comes up against so many barriers.

Despite everything, there are still those who continue to justify this reality, as if defending a political narrative were more important than acknowledging the suffering of those who live it.

All of this makes me think of my mother and so many Cubans like her.

I wonder how many more years they will have to wait to live with the peace of mind they deserve. How many more promises will they have to hear before they can simply live, without worrying every day about what they will put on the table?

I’m not talking about privileges. I’m talking about rights: the right to live with dignity, to express what we think, and to make decisions about our own lives.

No government should take ownership of a people’s future or demand gratitude for what it is obligated to provide.

That is why Brazil, like any other country, does not have to be perfect for us Cubans to find what we have lacked for years: freedom, opportunities to grow, and the possibility of forging our own path without arbitrary restrictions.

It is not enough to talk about the homeland when the present is suffocating us and forcing us to pack our bags.

If we must emigrate to prosper, and if we have to seek new horizons to live with dignity, then the failure is not that of the people. It is the failure of a political system that has forced them to leave.

El destino comienza donde aprendemos a seguir..

Read more from the diary of Dany Cesario.
