World.title: Costa Rica Banks Pay as Little as 436 Colones per Dollar – Here’s How to Get More
World.content:
If you are changing dollars into colones, where you do it matters more than ever. With the dollar at a record low, Costa Rica’s banks closed Friday buying dollars for between ₡436 and ₡440 each, according to Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) data compiled by El Observador. On $1,000, the gap between the best and worst of those rates is ₡4,000, or about $9.

The dollar closed Friday at a weighted average of ₡446.10 on Monex, the foreign exchange market run by the BCCR, a new record low and the lowest level since Monex began operating in 2006. It was the eighth straight session of declines and broke the previous record of ₡446.80, set on Sept. 17. The dollar has lost 10.3% of its value against the Costa Rican currency so far this year, according to El Observador.

Bank counter rates, as reported to the BCCR on Friday, varied by up to ₡4 per dollar. Banco Cathay offered the most, buying dollars at ₡440 and selling them at ₡452.50. Banco Nacional and BAC bought at ₡439 and sold at ₡453. Banco de Costa Rica (BCR) and Banco Popular bought at ₡438 and sold at ₡452. BCT paid the least, buying at ₡436 and selling at ₡454. The BCCR’s official reference rate in effect for the weekend is ₡442.56 for buying and ₡448.34 for selling.

Every bank pays less than the market rate when you sell it dollars. At BCT’s ₡436, changing $1,000 brings in ₡10,100 less than the Monex average, about $23. For a retiree converting a $2,000 monthly pension, choosing the best counter rate over the worst is worth about ₡8,000 a month. Changing money twice costs even more. At Banco Nacional’s rates, converting dollars to colones and back again loses ₡14 on every dollar, or roughly $31 on $1,000.

The BCCR publishes the buying and selling rate of every bank and exchange house each business day on its website, so you can compare before you go. Rates posted on Friday afternoon generally carry through the weekend, but they will move again when Monex reopens on Monday. If you already bank in Costa Rica, ask whether your bank applies a different rate to conversions made through online banking than at the teller window.

If you are paying with a foreign card, choose colones when a card terminal or ATM offers to charge you in dollars instead. That on-the-spot conversion, known as dynamic currency conversion, usually uses a less favorable rate than your card network applies. Shops, restaurants and tour operators that accept cash dollars set their own exchange rate, so it is worth checking it against the bank rate before you pay.

The Central Bank has been buying heavily without stopping the slide. On Friday it bought $41.8 million, or 84.8% of the $49.3 million traded on Monex, including $32.3 million in purchases meant to stabilize the market, according to El Observador. Its stabilization purchases total $1.39 billion so far in 2026, with no stabilization sales recorded. Specialists have said the dollar’s decline tends to deepen toward the end of the year, particularly in November, as companies pay year-end aguinaldo bonuses and taxes in colones.

For residents whose income arrives in dollars, including retirees, remote workers and landlords who charge rent in dollars, the slide has meant a steady loss of purchasing power. By early November, each $1,000 bought 46,810 fewer colones than in January, and the weak dollar has also hit businesses that earn in foreign currency, from exporters to Costa Rica’s medical tourism industry. With no sign yet that the slide is ending, the few colones you gain by shopping around for a rate are among the only savings within your control.

World.title: Costa Rica Moves to Demolish Narco Airstrips Without a Conviction
World.content:
Costa Rican authorities could destroy clandestine airstrips used by criminal groups without waiting for a final court ruling, under a bill that cleared a key legislative committee this week with unanimous support.

The Security and Narcotrafficking Committee approved the bill on Thursday. It is titled the Law to Sanction and Disable Clandestine and Unauthorized Airstrips and Allow the Confiscation of Assets Linked to Illicit Activities. The bill now goes to the full Legislative Assembly for a first-round vote and is not yet law.

President Laura Fernández submitted the measure in June as one of six bills in her administration’s package against organized crime. It is the fourth of the six to clear the committee. Under the bill, the Civil Aviation Directorate (DGAC) would declare an airstrip, airfield or helipad clandestine or illegal through a reasoned administrative resolution. Owners, tenants and administrators would first get a 10-business-day hearing to present evidence.

Once that resolution is final, the Public Security Ministry’s Air Surveillance Service could disable, demolish or destroy the site, with help from other agencies and municipalities. The rules would cover facilities used for drug trafficking, money laundering, human trafficking and organized crime.

Prosecutors could also ask a criminal judge to freeze the property in the National Registry, which would block its sale, donation, transfer or mortgage while the measure is in force. Machinery, vehicles and aircraft used to build or operate the strips could be seized and later permanently forfeited. The Costa Rican Drug Institute (ICD) would administer them.

The bill raises the prison sentence for building, enabling, facilitating or allowing a clandestine airstrip from the current three to eight years to five to 10 years. Owners, tenants or administrators who rebuild, rehabilitate or reuse a strip that authorities have already closed or destroyed would face 10 to 15 years.

Fines for operating aircraft at unauthorized facilities would double, from 20 to 40 base salaries. Deputy Kattia Calvo of the governing Pueblo Soberano party said changes were added to guarantee due process, including a way for property owners to present evidence of their innocence. Social Christian Unity Party deputy Abril Gordienko backed the bill, noting that clandestine strips can also enable crimes beyond drug trafficking.

Frente Amplio caucus leader José María Villalta said it was the first bill the committee had discussed that could truly hit organized crime, because it targets the assets criminal groups use to operate. He also raised procedural concerns. He warned that a separate bill on tourist airparks could create conflicting rules on air surveillance.

Costa Rica already allows the Air Surveillance Service to identify, declare illegal and disable clandestine strips under Law 9902, in force since 2020. According to the new bill’s statement of purpose, that law has no specific tools to act on the assets used to build or maintain the strips.

How many strips exist is unclear because they are built to go unnoticed. Fernández has said there are close to 200. The Public Security Ministry’s last official figure, from 2020, put the number of identified unauthorized strips at more than 140, and at least 20 were reported destroyed between the law’s entry into force and the end of 2024.

Some legal analysts have questioned whether the property freeze adds much to existing organized crime and registry security laws. They have also warned that a landowner may not know a strip is operating on their land. The bill now awaits a first-round vote in the full Assembly.

World.title: Italian Wanted in 2021 Santa Cruz Killing Extradited to France
World.content:
Costa Rica extradited two men to France on Thursday afternoon. One of them is an Italian national investigated in connection with the 2021 shooting death of a French citizen in Santa Cruz, Guanacaste. The Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) identified the men as Gianni Marco Basile, 68, and Iván Javier Pablot Martínez, 48, a Colombian-born naturalized Costa Rican.

French authorities want them in separate cases. Basile is sought on suspicion of aggravated homicide and extortion, and Pablot on international drug trafficking charges. Agents from the OIJ’s Special Tactical Response Service (SERT) escorted both men from La Reforma prison to Juan Santamaría International Airport in Alajuela. There they were handed to French officials and flown on a commercial flight to Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris.

INTERPOL’s National Central Bureau in San José coordinated the transfer, and the Public Prosecutor’s Office directed the case. Attorney General Carlo Díaz said the extraditions are part of the international judicial cooperation mechanisms through which Costa Rica responds to requests from other countries.

According to the OIJ, Basile is investigated for his alleged role in the killing of Pierre Claude Gazel, a French citizen who died on Oct. 5, 2021. The agency said Gazel was shot in front of his home in Santa Cruz at around 6:40 a.m., and the gunman fled on a motorcycle with another person.

The OIJ said French investigators identified prior conflicts and communications between Basile and Gazel. Because the victim was French, authorities in France chose to prosecute the case there. A judicial authority in Paris issued an international arrest warrant for Basile on Feb. 14, 2025.

OIJ INTERPOL agents tracked Basile for about two months before finding that he lived in Escazú, west of San José. They arrested him on Nov. 7, 2025, while he was driving in Curridabat. A criminal court in San José’s Third Judicial Circuit authorized his extradition on June 3, 2026. Pablot was detained in September 2025 by OIJ agents who specialize in organized crime. French authorities allege he belonged to a network that shipped drugs from Colombia to France and other European countries.

The case dates to Nov. 22, 2011, when French customs officers in Marseille arrested two Colombians carrying 29 kilograms (64 pounds) of cocaine. Investigators found the group allegedly used a company that sold wooden houses as cover for moving drugs into Europe. French authorities linked Pablot to the group, where he allegedly worked with a man known as “El Viejo.”

Case documents cited in local reports indicate that a criminal court in Marseille sentenced Pablot to nine years in prison on drug trafficking charges. A San José criminal court authorized his extradition on in April and an appeals court later upheld the decision. The OIJ described Pablot’s case as one of the first extradition proceedings coordinated with France over international drug trafficking. A second man detained with Pablot and named in the same French case, Hamilton Fernando Restrepo Osorio, has not yet been extradited.

Both cases now pass to the French courts. The transfers add to a growing number of extraditions out of Costa Rica this year, as the country handles more requests from abroad tied to violent crime and drug trafficking.

World.title: The Local Pharmacy and the Surprises of Costa Rica Life
World.content:
Your local neighborhood pharmacy is a one-stop-for-all-your-health-needs institution. Last year, a law passed requiring a doctor’s prescription for many types of antibiotics and other stronger drugs. Before that, you could self-medicate with your choice of uppers, downers, painkillers and plain old antibiotics if you knew which pharmacy to frequent.

I knew a guy who walked into one with the word ‘clonazepam’ written on a piece of paper and told the person at the counter that he was a truck driver in the states, and this was prescribed it for his insomnia, and wouldn’t you know it, he was suffering from the same sleep issue here and could anyone help? They could. A few minutes after a brief consultation with the pharmacist, he walked out with a bottle of high potency valium.

My first experience with a pharmacy took place in a back room. I knew I wasn’t in the US anymore when the pharmacist led me behind the counter, closed the door, instructed me to drop my trousers, and injected me in the thigh with a shot of epinephrine ( better known as adrenaline).

The reason for the shot was that I had been hit with asthma so severe that every breath sounded like I had just tried to run to the top of Chirripo. I’d spent a sleepless Saturday night seated in a rocking chair as I was unable to breathe lying down. It was rainy season and I was living in a half finished cabina that provided little protection from the elements. A tropical front had arrived, the rain came down in torrents, wind howled off the nearby Fila Tinamastes, and I was no match for the elements.

Sunday morning I was driven to a pharmacy half an hour away. Every shallow wheezing breath felt like it could be the last. The jab of the pharmacist’s needle brought instant relief. I had received this same injection as a teen, for the same reason. There it was done by a doctor, and I still remembered the doctor’s instruction to remain seated for several minutes after the injection as there is risk of a sudden drop in blood pressure.

The pharmacist here gave me no such instruction. He was not a medical doctor after all, just a guy who could measure out the proper dosage and give an injection. I stayed put in the back room, puzzling the pharmacist. Many pharmacies now have a doctor on duty during business hours, in order to write the antibiotic or clonazepam prescription that is no longer available over the counter. Still, I am always surprised by what is available without a doctor.

A while back I pinched a nerve in my upper back and the pain ran from my neck down to the fingers on my left hand. I was about to leave for a visit stateside and needed relief. My stepson is an RN in the local hospital and he gave me a list for purchase from the pharmacy. I bought a syringe and several ampules of painkiller. My stepson injected me at home. No doctor or prescription necessary.

There remain smaller mom and pop pharmacies in Costa Rica that don’t have a doctor on duty but will prescribe medication based on your symptoms. They are worth finding if you trust your self-diagnoses and don’t feel the need for a middleman with MD after the last name. And those back rooms? They are still open if an injection is necessary.

World.title: Costa Rica Falls 2-0 to Ecuador in Quito as the Bryan Ruiz Era Begins
World.content:
Costa Rica opened the Bryan Ruiz era with a 2-0 loss to Ecuador on Friday night in Quito. The team finished the friendly with 10 men and lost a defender to a knee injury, four days before it faces Argentina. Jordy Caicedo put Ecuador ahead in the first half. Moisés Caicedo, the Chelsea midfielder and Ecuador captain, sealed it from the penalty spot late in the second half at Estadio Olímpico Atahualpa, which sits about 2,850 meters (9,350 feet) above sea level.

The result gave Argentine coach Marcelo Gallardo his first win in charge of Ecuador. It was Ruiz’s first match as Costa Rica’s permanent head coach. The former national team captain won both of his games as interim coach, against Nicaragua and Haiti in the Concacaf Nations League, before the Costa Rican Football Federation gave him the job.

Costa Rica set the early tempo. The visitors pressed high and won the ball back quickly in the opening minutes. Striker Manfred Ugalde, back with the squad after serving a suspension, forced a save from Ecuador goalkeeper Hernán Galíndez around the ninth minute. Ecuador struck midway through the half. Jordy Caicedo, who plays for Argentine club Huracán, ran onto a long ball from Piero Hincapié. He went around goalkeeper Patrick Sequeira and finished with his left foot for his fifth international goal.

Costa Rica came closest to an equalizer early in the second half. Andrey Soto shot after a pass from Carlos Mora, and Ecuador defender Jackson Porozo cleared the ball off the line. Ruiz made four changes shortly before the hour mark. Alexis Gamboa, Celso Borges, Josimar Méndez and Kenyel Michel came on for Francisco Calvo, Roan Wilson, Soto and Josimar Alcócer. The changes quickly turned costly.

Gamboa went down after a collision with Ecuador’s John Yeboah a few minutes after coming on and was carried off on a stretcher. The federation said he has a left knee injury and will return to Costa Rica on Saturday for further tests, which rules him out against Argentina. Diego Mesén replaced Gamboa around the 65th minute in his first appearance for the national team. He was sent off a few minutes later for a foul on Jordy Caicedo.

Playing a man down at altitude, Costa Rica could not hold on. Ecuador was awarded a penalty for a foul on Yeboah in the box, and Moisés Caicedo converted with less than 10 minutes left. Ruiz said after the match that he left Quito satisfied with what he saw. He said many of the things the coaching staff asked for were carried out and the team showed personality, and he called the result secondary to what the squad learned. He also acknowledged that the game became an uphill battle and said the team’s style of play still needs fine-tuning.

Gallardo said Ecuador grew into the match after an uncomfortable start and called it a constructive performance. He added that the win was a good way to reconnect with the home crowd. The loss extended Costa Rica’s winless run against Ecuador, which dates back to 1992. Ecuador has now won six straight meetings, including a 3-0 win at the 2006 World Cup in Germany and a 3-1 friendly win in Chester, Pennsylvania, in June 2023.

Costa Rica plays Argentina, the 2026 World Cup runner-up, on Tuesday, Nov. 17, at Estadio Mario Alberto Kempes in Córdoba. It is the team’s last match of the year. The federation tried to call up Kendall Waston as cover, but Saprissa said the veteran defender is still recovering from an injury and will not travel.

For a team rebuilding after missing this year’s World Cup, the night in Quito showed what Ruiz has to work with. There were early signs of the aggressive approach he wants, but also how quickly a thin squad can come apart. Tuesday’s game against the world’s runner-up will show how much of that can be fixed in four days.

World.title: Monteverde Went From 25 Dry Days a Year to Nearly 120, BBC Reports
World.content:
Costa Rica’s best known cloud forest is in the international spotlight this week after the BBC published a lengthy feature on Monteverde, reporting that the clouds that define the forest are pulling away from it and changing the life inside. The piece appeared on November 12 on BBC Future, the British broadcaster’s science and environment section. It was written by journalist Jocelyn Timperley, who reported from the Children’s Eternal Rainforest and other reserves around Monteverde.

The central message will be familiar to anyone who has followed the science here. The BBC reports that the fog bank that once sat on the forest almost year-round is rising with warmer temperatures, leaving the canopy exposed to sun and dry air for much of the dry season.

It leans on the long running records of Alan Pounds, resident scientist at the Monteverde Cloud Forest Biological Preserve, who has counted the days when neither rain nor mist reaches his gauge. There were about 25 a year in the 1970s. His latest figures, which the BBC describes as preliminary, put the recent average near 119.

Much of the feature is devoted to the epiphytes, the orchids, mosses, bromeliads and ferns that cover Monteverde’s trees and drink directly from the mist. The BBC follows ecologists Nalini Nadkarni of the University of Utah and Sybil Gotsch of the University of Kentucky, along with Costa Rican scientist Elenter Cubero Campos, whose experiments are designed to show what the forest loses as those hanging gardens dry out.

The feature also revisits the golden toad, the Monteverde species that vanished after 1989 and is widely cited as one of the first extinctions linked to a warming climate. It also describes the newcomers now arriving from the lowlands, including toucans, terciopelo snakes and bats that were once kept out by the cold.

Local voices get a share of the space. The BBC speaks with members of the Monteverde Institute, the Costa Rican Conservation Foundation and the community group CorClima about tree planting, biological corridors and whether ecotourism, long credited with saving the forest from cattle pasture, is approaching its limits as new hotels go up.

Little of this is new to Costa Rica as reseasrchers here have reported on Monteverde’s rising dry day count for years. What is different is the scale of the audience. Monteverde is one of our signature protected areas and a place known by name around the world, and a prominent BBC feature puts its troubles in front of millions of readers and potential donors.

That attention cuts both ways. Coverage of this kind can bring research funding and support for conservation groups working on the mountain. It can also change how the world sees a place whose identity is built on mist and dripping moss. For now the forest remains green, the quetzals still nest and the reserves are open. But the BBC’s reporting makes plain that the scientists who know Monteverde best believe it is becoming a different kind of forest, and that the rest of the world is now watching it happen.

World.title: Blocked Estuary May Explain Playa Langosta Fish Die-Off
World.content:
Sand blocking an estuary’s connection to the ocean, combined with reduced freshwater flow during a period of little rain, may explain the mass fish deaths at Playa Langosta, according to National University (UNA) biologist Teresita Ulate. Ulate said the interruption of water exchange between the mangrove and the sea could have reduced the oxygen available to aquatic animals. Her assessment offers a possible explanation, but the cause has not been confirmed.

The deaths occurred at the San Francisco Estuary in Playa Langosta. The Ministry of Environment and Energy (MINAE) opened an investigation after images showed dead fish, rays and other animals along the shoreline and in the water, including two bull sharks found dead in the estuary.

The ministry said the analysis, led by the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC), would examine the blocked outlet, water quality and possible effects of El Niño, including warmer Pacific waters and changing coastal conditions. Authorities cautioned that assigning a cause before a technical evaluation would be premature.

Ulate explained that reduced rainfall meant less freshwater was reaching the mangrove while accumulated sand restricted its connection to the sea. She said El Niño had contributed to that drop in rainfall, part of the dry conditions now straining water supplies across Guanacaste, and that the episode could have been anticipated given the lower rain forecast.

Decomposing organic matter can add pressure because bacteria consume oxygen as they break it down, leaving less available for fish. Ulate said water testing she carried out in the San Francisco mangrove in June had already found low oxygen levels, which she described as a warning sign for the ecosystem. She added that daily monitoring would be needed to produce precise data.

The animals were reported dead on Nov. 4. Local lifeguards urged people not to collect or eat them because they were decomposing, and asked residents to stay away from the estuary, warning that the loss of fish could draw crocodiles closer to shore. The environment ministry also asked residents not to alter the estuary’s mouth without authorization.

Eduardo Vargas, director of the Tamarindo Integral Development Association, said strong seasonal tides had carried sand from other stretches of coast and sealed the opening. He said residents initially tried to clear it with shovels before bringing in heavy machinery, that the work had the necessary permits and that subsequent heavy rain helped widen the opening.

Vargas described the reopening as a stopgap rather than a fix, saying a lasting solution would require managing the mangrove from the surrounding watershed. Restoring that connection does not establish what killed the animals. Ulate cautioned that human activity could not yet be ruled out as a contributing factor and that SINAC’s analysis would be needed to better understand the episode.

World.title: US Ground Stop Canceled 15 Costa Rica Flights. Here’s What to Expect Today
World.content:
Updated Saturday afternoon with the cause of the outage, Saturday’s cancellations and when flights should be back to normal.

The nationwide US ground stop that froze flights on Friday afternoon is over, but if you are flying between Costa Rica and the United States this weekend, you may still feel it. Fifteen flights were canceled on Friday at Costa Rica’s two main international airports, 10 at Juan Santamaría International Airport and five at Guanacaste Airport in Liberia, and US airlines were still canceling thousands of flights early Saturday as planes and crews worked their way back into position.

The backlog should clear soon. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said on Saturday he expected air travel to return to normal levels by Sunday. Saturday was still rough, with more than 5,000 US flights canceled, according to FlightAware, more than the FAA had forecast. If you fly Sunday or later, your flight is much more likely to run as scheduled, but check it before you leave for the airport anyway.

Aeris, which runs the airport outside San José, said 23 flights there were affected on Friday, 12 departures and 11 arrivals. Six departures and four arrivals were canceled. The other 13 flights were moved to overnight and early Saturday morning slots.

The Federal Aviation Administration lifted the order at about 8 p.m. Eastern time on Friday, or 7 p.m. in Costa Rica, after more than four hours. That made it the second-longest nationwide ground stop on record, behind the shutdown that followed the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. When it began, it was only the third nationwide US ground stop ever.

Aeris said operations will return to normal gradually, depending on each airline’s schedule. Guanacaste Airport in Liberia canceled five departures on Friday, flights to Dallas, Toronto and Ottawa carrying 473 passengers, who were left waiting for new itineraries. Airport officials there had said on Friday afternoon that 23 flights were scheduled for Saturday.

The knock-on effects are what matter today. The flight-tracking service FlightAware counted more than 9,100 cancellations and more than 24,500 delays in the United States on Friday, and more than 3,000 additional cancellations by early Saturday. Many US airlines fly a plane into Costa Rica and send the same jet straight back, so a canceled flight in Miami, Houston or Atlanta can mean a canceled departure here.

Check your flight in your airline’s app before you leave for the airport. App and text alerts usually update before departure boards do. Copa Airlines said the US disruption could cause delays and cancellations on its flights to and from the United States and asked passengers to confirm their status on its website or app. United and JetBlue both said they would cancel most of their remaining Friday night flights, a fresh strain for JetBlue’s Costa Rica routes.

If your flight was canceled or you want to move your trip, look for a travel waiver on your airline’s website. American and other US airlines said they would change tickets affected by the outage with no fee and no fare difference, which is often faster than waiting in a rebooking line. If you decide not to travel at all, US rules entitle you to a cash refund, even when the cause is out of the airline’s control. Airlines do not have to cover hotels or meals in that case, so keep your receipts if your travel insurance covers delays.

If you are connecting through a US hub, rebook through the airline that sold you the ticket rather than each carrier separately. And if you are heading north, remember that every passenger flying to the United States must now sign a new form, which can slow check-in on a day when lines are already long.

US officials said the outage was not a cyberattack. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Saturday that it began while contractor L3Harris Technologies was switching telecommunications lines from copper wire to fiber at a remote FAA site. When one router was switched over, he said, it flooded other routers in the air traffic control network with more than 1,000 connection attempts about every five seconds, disrupting radio communications and radar feeds at the Air Route Traffic Control Centers, the facilities that guide planes between airports. The FAA has not yet determined the root cause. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no evidence of a hostile attack. Duffy said he had asked Congress on Thursday for $30.1 billion to modernize the air traffic control system.

The disruption was the second to hit air travel at Juan Santamaría airport in less than a month, after a power failure affected its control tower in October. Costa Rica relies on US gateways for much of its air traffic, and the busy high season is just weeks away, so even a few hours of trouble in US airspace can strand travelers here for a day or more.

World.title: International News: Small Island nations demand urgent Climate action at UN summit
World.content:
International News: Small Island nations demand urgent Climate action at UN summit

By Zoila Palma: Leaders of small island nations are calling for urgent global action to address climate change, warning that rising sea levels and increasingly severe weather events threaten the survival of their countries.

The appeal was made Thursday during the United Nations climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, where world leaders are discussing ways to reduce emissions and support vulnerable nations.

Seychelles Vice President Alix Sebastien Pillay said climate change is already causing millions of dollars in damage to his country, a 115-island archipelago in the Indian Ocean, despite its minimal contribution to global warming. He urged governments to move beyond discussions and strengthen funding mechanisms to help vulnerable countries recover from climate-related disasters without accumulating unsustainable debt.

A report released during the conference by the independent Climate Action Tracker warned that global progress in reducing warming has stalled over the past five years. It found that even if countries fulfill their existing climate commitments, global temperatures could rise by approximately 2.6 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels by the end of the century, exceeding the 1.5-degree target established under the 2015 Paris Agreement.

Leaders from vulnerable countries also highlighted the growing financial and human costs of climate disasters. Niue Prime Minister Dalton Tagelagi warned that unusually high Pacific Ocean temperatures signal worsening conditions, while Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called for greater international cooperation and financing, noting that no country can confront the climate crisis alone. Climate activist Greta Thunberg also criticized world leaders for failing to take sufficient action.

Meanwhile, the United Kingdom announced the appointment of Madeleine Alessandri as its first special envoy for climate security risks, citing concerns that environmental damage could threaten food supplies, increase migration and contribute to conflict.

World.title: International News: Pope Leo celebrates mass before 500,000 faithful in former Peruvian Diocese
World.content:
International News: Pope Leo celebrates mass before 500,000 faithful in former Peruvian Diocese

By Zoila Palma: An estimated 500,000 people gathered on Friday, November 13, to attend a Mass celebrated by Pope Leo in Chiclayo, Peru, where he previously served as bishop for eight years.

The large outdoor celebration took place at the Pampas de Pimentel grounds, drawing pilgrims from across Peru and abroad for the pontiff’s return to the northern city.

Vatican figures cited by EWTN News Español placed attendance at approximately half a million people, despite temperatures reaching 90 degrees Fahrenheit.

Worshippers began arriving on Thursday night, with many spending hours waiting to secure a place at the celebration.

During his homily, Pope Leo expressed his joy at returning to the community where he served from 2015 to 2023, before Pope Francis called him to Rome for new responsibilities at the Vatican. “What a joy to return to Chiclayo! It is a blessing for me to be with you again,” he told the congregation.

The pontiff also thanked the faithful for their affection, support and prayers, particularly as he continues recovering from recent medical difficulties. Representatives of the Diocese of Chiclayo welcomed his return and recognized his eight years of service to the local Catholic community.

In his message, Pope Leo emphasized that sharing the Catholic faith should go beyond religious teaching and be demonstrated through personal example, solidarity and commitment to helping those in need. He also highlighted the importance of respecting freedom of conscience while warning against religious indifference, materialism and selfishness.

The Mass formed part of the Pope’s visit to Peru, the final stop on his South American tour, which began on November 6 and also included Uruguay and Argentina.

World.title: International News: Powerful El Niño could bring flooding risks across parts of North America
World.content:
International News: Powerful El Niño could bring flooding risks across parts of North America

By Zoila Palma: A developing El Niño phenomenon is continuing to strengthen and could significantly influence weather patterns across North America during the 2026-2027 autumn and winter seasons, BBC reports.

The event is already showing signs of becoming one of the strongest recorded, with the United States National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) reporting a strong-to-very strong El Niño is likely to persist through early 2027.

El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon that develops when trade winds over the Pacific Ocean weaken or reverse, allowing warmer ocean waters to shift eastward.

This releases additional heat into the atmosphere and influences global weather patterns, affecting rainfall, temperatures and storm activity in different regions.

NOAA’s November 12 assessment indicated approximately a 60% chance that the event could reach historic strength, exceeding previous El Niño events recorded since 1950 under one measurement.

For the United States, forecasts suggest increased rainfall across much of California, the Southwest, Central and Southern Plains, the Southeast and parts of the eastern seaboard. Florida and other southeastern states could experience particularly wet conditions, raising concerns about flooding. California may also face increased risks of heavy rainfall, flooding and mudslides, particularly in areas affected by previous wildfires. However, the intensity and location of rainfall will vary.

Meanwhile, warmer-than-average winter temperatures are expected across parts of Alaska, the western United States and northern regions, while below-average precipitation is forecast for areas including the Northern Rockies and parts of the Great Lakes.

El Niño can also influence snowfall patterns, increasing the possibility of heavier snowfall in some southern mountain ranges while reducing snow chances in certain northern areas. Scientists are also monitoring possible disruptions to the stratospheric polar vortex, which can sometimes allow Arctic air to move farther south.

World.title: Belizean Pride: British Royal Army Medical Service welcomes Cayo-native Indira Greig
World.content:
Belizean Pride: British Royal Army Medical Service welcomes Cayo-native Indira Greig

By Zoila Palma: Indira Greig from San Ignacio, Cayo District, has completed basic military training in the United Kingdom and officially joined the British Army’s Royal Army Medical Service (RAMS). Private Indira Greig marked the milestone after successfully completing her training at the Army Training Centre (ATC) Pirbright.

Pte Greig proudly marched off the parade square during a ceremony celebrating the completion of her basic training.

The Royal Army Medical Service is a specialist corps established on November 15, 2024, providing medical, nursing and dental support to British Army personnel during both peacetime and military operations.

Her achievement was celebrated by family members, including her father, Robert Greig, his partner, Susan, and her brother, Gunner Gordon Greig, who serves with the Royal Artillery.

Her grandparents also travelled all the way from Belize to witness the special occasion.

Several members of the British Army were present to welcome Greig into the medical corps, including Sergeant J. Tablada of 1 Medical Regiment and Belizean Network Ambassador Warrant Officer Class One (Regimental Sergeant Major) Heredia.

The milestone marks an important step in Greig’s military career and a proud moment for her family, community and country.

World.title: International News: France sees 5th consecutive Saturday of nationwide protests
World.content:
International News: France sees 5th consecutive Saturday of nationwide protests

By Zoila Palma: Today, thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across France marking the fifth consecutive weekend of nationwide protests.

The demonstrations brought together members of the Yellow Vest movement, students, education unions and other advocacy groups expressing frustration over the rising cost of living, education funding, child protection and proposed changes to police powers, euronews reports.

In Paris, demonstrators gathered at Place de la République before marching toward Place de la Nation. According to France’s Interior Ministry, approximately 106,000 people participated in demonstrations nationwide, including 24,000 in Paris.

Organizers, however, estimated the turnout at 200,000, with nearly 100,000 in the capital. The turnout was lower than the previous weekend, when authorities recorded 146,000 demonstrators nationwide.

Protesters also opposed a proposed police bill that would provide officers and gendarmes with additional legal protection when using firearms in the line of duty. Supporters argue that the measure would protect law enforcement officers from automatically being presumed guilty when using their weapons, while critics have described it as a “license to kill,” warning that it could weaken accountability for alleged police violence.

Demonstrators also called for better protection of children and teenagers and improved funding for public education.

The protests come after more than a month of school blockades and demonstrations over economic and social concerns.

World.title: Mopan Technical High School wins Gold at ExpoCiencias Nuevo León 2026 in Mexico
World.content:
Mopan Technical High School wins Gold at ExpoCiencias Nuevo León 2026 in Mexico

By Zoila Palma: Mopan Technical High School has made history after securing first-place Gold award at ExpoCiencias Nuevo León 2026 in Monterrey, Mexico.

The school’s delegation proudly represented Belize as the only participating school from the country, earning top honours in the Social Sciences category for its project titled “Supporting Multilingual Learners!”

The achievement marks the first time Mopan Technical High School has secured a first-place award at an international competition.

Students Karoly and Jasiely were recognized for their dedication, creativity and hard work in developing the project, which earned them international recognition and brought home the gold medal for Belize.

The school also credited the achievement to the guidance of their coach, Marcelo Torres, and mentors Casiana Sagastume and Karen Figueroa.

Appreciation was also extended to the school’s administration, staff, wider school community and sponsors whose support helped make the international participation possible.

Mopan Technical High School celebrated the victory as more than just a medal, highlighting the importance of investing in young people and creating opportunities for students to showcase their talents internationally.

Mopan Tech says that the achievement is a proud moment for Benque Viejo del Carmen and Belize, as its students made their mark on the international stage.

World.title: Belize’s Maya-led Climate adaptation project highlighted at COP31 in Türkiye
World.content:
Belize’s Maya-led Climate adaptation project highlighted at COP31 in Türkiye

By Zoila Palma: Belize’s Indigenous leadership took centre stage on November 11 during the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye.

The Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (CCCCC) and Belize’s Julian Cho Society hosted a side event at the CARICOM Pavilion titled “Project Q’anil: A Maya-Led Pathway to Green Climate Fund Adaptation Finance,” highlighting the importance of placing Indigenous communities at the centre of climate adaptation efforts.

The discussion explored Maya principles, including “Aj ral Ch’och” (people of the land), “Loq’la Tzuul Taq’a,” which recognizes the sacred relationship between the land, forests, animals and the spirit world, and “Komonil,” which emphasizes mutual support, collective work and commitment.

The Julian Cho Society works to advance Indigenous rights and environmental conservation in southern Belize. The event highlighted how traditional knowledge, community leadership and partnerships can help Indigenous communities access climate financing and develop solutions that reflect their needs and priorities.

Elishah St. Luce, Social Inclusion and Gender Specialist at the CCCCC, emphasized the importance of ensuring that Maya communities lead efforts shaping their future. “It is our responsibility to take the future the Maya people have dreamt and place that in a project ensuring that the Maya-led aspect dominates,” she stated.

COP31 is being held from November 9 to 20, 2026, bringing together world leaders, governments, Indigenous representatives and climate advocates to advance global climate action.

World.title: Belize brings Kulcha to International stage in Mexico
World.content:
Belize brings Kulcha to International stage in Mexico

By Zoila Palma: The Mopan Technical High School delegation brought a taste of Belizean culture to the international stage during ExpoCiencias 2026 in Monterrey, Nuevo León, Mexico.

Beyond showcasing scientific knowledge and innovation, the international science fair also provided an opportunity for participating countries to celebrate their cultural identities, traditions and talents.

During a cultural presentation, Belize was represented through a dance celebrating Creole culture, accompanied by music from Belizean cultural icon Leela Vernon. The performance highlighted Belize’s rich cultural heritage and gave international audiences an opportunity to experience a piece of the country’s music and traditions.

Among those participating were students Karoly and Jasiely, alongside Mopan Technical High School Principal Katie Jones, who also made a special appearance in the cultural presentation. The delegation proudly showcased their talents and represented Belize with enthusiasm and national pride.

Mopan Tech noted that experiences such as ExpoCiencias go beyond classroom learning by encouraging cultural exchange, building friendships and allowing students to discover different perspectives.

From sharing scientific innovations to celebrating Belizean culture, the Mopan delegation continues to represent the country in Monterrey, Mexico.

World.title: Road woes deepen
World.content:
Traffic, including a tour bus, is seen manoeuvring the Shettlewood to Mackfield main road in the vicinity of Chester Castle, Hanover, last Friday. Photo: Garfield Robinson

Tourism stakeholders in Treasure Beach have expressed concern over the deteriorating main road linking the south coast community to Montego Bay through eastern Hanover and southern St James, warning that its deplorable state is already triggering booking cancellations and threatening business ahead of the crucial winter tourist season.

Meanwhile, residents and business operators along the Anchovy-Shettlewood and Mackfield main roads, which traverse southern St James and eastern Hanover, are cautiously welcoming repair work that began last week, but are questioning how long the improvements will last.
