World.title: GLOBSEC report: In Bulgaria, more people name Russia a strategic partner than a security threat
World.content:
In Bulgaria, more people name Russia a strategic partner than a security threat, 51 per cent against 35 per cent, according to the GLOBSEC Trends 2026: The Reality Check report, released on November 13.

The report refers to polling done in mid-May in 14 countries: Czechia, Estonia, France, Germany, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Ukraine, the UK, the US and Bulgaria.

Bulgaria is the only country surveyed where Russia tops the list of strategic partners.

Just 35 per cent see Russia as a threat, fewer than anywhere else, while more say the same of the US.

Asked about what Russia does rather than what it is, concern rises: 56 per cent see Russian sabotage or disinformation as a risk, but this is the lowest of any surveyed country.

Perception of Russia as a key strategic partner varies widely across the 14 surveyed countries, with three outliers: Bulgaria, Slovakia, and Hungary.

“In Bulgaria, Russia is often viewed through historical liberation narratives, the memory of Russian intervention against Ottoman rule sustaining a degree of popular sympathy with few equivalents in the region,” the report said.

“That narrative has been reinforced by a political environment in which pro-Russian parties won elections, blocked reform coalitions, or opposed weapons transfers to Ukraine,” it said.

The report said that recent crises had prompted diversification that sharply reduced European dependence on Russian supplies, but public opinion remains split between principle and price.

While 62 per cent agree that European countries should stop purchasing Russian energy given the risk of political pressure, 49 per cent would still permit their own country to buy from Russia if energy costs ran high – rising to 75 per ceent in Bulgaria, 66 per cent in Hungary and 63 per cent in Slovakia.

Were a referendum on Nato membership to be held now, 57 per cent of Bulgarians would vote to stay in the Alliance – however, this is the lowest among the countries surveyed.

Bulgarians are the most susceptible to Russian propaganda and believe Russian narratives about the war in Ukraine, it emerges from the report. Bulgaria is the only country where only 51 per cent of people believe that Russia is responsible for the war and invaded Ukraine.

A full 65 per cent of Bulgarians believe that Ukrainian authorities have repressed Russian-speaking minorities, and this is sufficient justification for the Russian invasion. Fifty-eight per cent of Bulgarians believe another thesis used by the Kremlin, that the Europeans and Americans provoked Russia and are responsible for the war.



According to GLOBSEC, Slovakia and Hungary are the other countries where the Kremlin’s claims justifying the Russian invasion are most widely spread. The report says that in Bulgaria the acceptance of the Kremlin’s explanations for the war is most pronounced.



These results are also consistent with previous GLOBSEC studies, which reported a widespread spread of manipulative narratives in Bulgaria, the report said.

Bulgaria is also in last place in terms of support for continued European aid to Ukraine regardless of US actions (40 per cent). In terms of Nato military aid to Ukraine, Bulgaria is second to last (36 per cent), followed only by Hungary (33 per cent).

Furthermore, only 39 per cent of Bulgarians believe that Ukraine’s fight against Russia is important for the future security of their own country. This is again the lowest score in the survey.

On issues related to defence and the army, Bulgarians have conflicting positions. Seventy-one per cent want the return of compulsory military service, and 66 per cent say they would defend their country if attacked.

Meanwhile, however, less than half of Bulgarians (49 per cent) trust their own army. Bulgaria is in 13th place (20 per cent) in terms of the country’s sense of preparedness in the event of a major crisis or war. Only Slovakia is behind Bulgaria, with 19 per cent.

Sixty-five per cent of respondents agree that Bulgaria should increase its defence spending. However, support is cut by almost half when the increase has to be financed through cuts in social or healthcare spending. Only 34 per cent of Bulgarians would support higher military spending under such conditions.

Bulgaria records the weakest support for EU membership, with only 53 per cent potentially voting to stay. Yet, 59 per cent see economic benefits in membership, and seven in 10 want the EU to build its own defence alongside Nato and an EU army. The data hints that respondents in Bulgaria appear to value what the EU delivers more than belonging to it, the report said.

Around one in four respondents in Hungary and Bulgaria perceive China among their most important strategic partners.

“In Bulgaria, the driver appears more political than economic: limited attention to China as a strategic rival, influence advancing through media and local academic and business partnerships, public opinion inclined to view China as a partner rather than a threat,” the report said.

World.title: EU to mobilise billions of euro for AI Gigafactories, Europe’s tech sovereignty
World.content:
Seven Gigafactories are in the planning, and about 30 billion euro is being mobilised for them, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said after EU leaders held on November 13 their first-ever AI Summit.

The seven Gigafactories “will provide the computing capacities our startups need to build the most advanced AI models,” Von der Leyen told a news conference after the informal European Council meeting.

More computing capacity will also be key for Europe to play a role in the development of frontier models, frontier AI, she said.

For Europe’s tech sovereignty, massive investments will be required, Von der Leyen said.

“At least 500 billion euro according to our own estimates,” she said.

“We have done very well in creating a vibrant start-up ecosystem. Europe is creating more tech start-ups than the US, but many of these start-ups fail to receive the necessary support to scale,” Von der Leyen said.

“That is why we have created the Scaleup Europe fund which has been a great success from the outset. What is missing now are the large investments in chips, compute and frontier AI.”

“Therefore, we need to complete our Savings and Investment Union, and attract private investment. And of course, our next European budget must also reflect this ambition,” she said.

She said that the meeting had seen a shared will to put forward ideas for funding for Tech sovereignty financing.

“I will follow up with an ambitious proposal,” Von der Leyen said.

Europe leads in AI adoption, she said.

In 2025, 37 per cent of EU businesses used AI on average in the EU. Looking at specific member states, Finland is “outstanding”, with 66 per cent of businesses using AI already – almost double than the US, Von der Leyen said.

“We want to continue this trend and accelerate the use of AI – move AI from the screen to the real world,” she said.

“That is why, earlier this year, I appointed Jim Snabe as Special Envoy for Industrial Artificial Intelligence.”

“We are focusing work on five sectors where AI can have the biggest value and impact. In each sector, we will deliver a vision coupled with concrete actions. The first part of this work will come out in two weeks,” Von der Leyen said.

European Council President António Costa told the news conference: “AI is the most important technology of our time”.

Europe must make the most of its benefits, from higher productivity to better public services, Costa said.

“We must also manage the risks effectively. To do that, we must help set global standards and responsible global governance to make AI safe and human-centric,” he said.

“Europe has real strengths: we have skilled talent, world class research and a dynamic start up scene.

Now is the time to translate them into real advantages,” Costs said.

“That will depend on the choices we make. Above all: on how much public and private investment we can mobilise to develop our own competitive AI models, on our capacity to secure value chains and reduce dangerous dependencies, and on our access to affordable and clean energy sources.”

“At the same time, we need to ensure effective adoption of AI in our economy to reap its productivity gains. We are already acting,” he said.

Initiatives like the Savings and Investments Union and the so called “28th regime” will help, Costa said.

“But the volumes of funding that we need to catch up with our global peers require significant extra efforts. The next European long-term Budget, in particular the new European Competitiveness Fund, will play a decisive role,” he said.

Clear oversight for managing the risks and challenges of AI is a pre-condition for public trust,” Costa said: “Without trust, AI strategy cannot succeed”.

The European Union is the first region in the world with an AI governance framework, he said.

“And we can use our experience to shape global standards. For that, the European Union must be active where this debate is taking place: in the G7, in the G20, supporting the efforts of the upcoming UK presidency, and in the United Nations.”

“We also have to reflect on the impact of AI on our labour markets and globally on our society, especially on the sustainability of our social model,” Costa said.

“That is why we want to make AI and its impacts on societies the central theme of our Social Summit in 2027, where we will mark 10 years of the European pillar of social rights, together with our social partners,” he said.

On November 12, the European Parliament adopted – by 405 votes to 133 with 60 abstentions – a resolution calling for parliamentary scrutiny and regulation of the impact of artificial intelligence on EU democratic processes, institutional balance, and fundamental rights.

According to the resolution, MEPs recognise AI’s transformative potential in supporting EU lawmaking but emphasise that AI use within the EU institutions must remain human-centred, subject to human oversight, and aligned with EU values.

AI can assist with evidence-based policymaking, and the simplification and evaluation of EU law, MEPs argue, but must never replace human political responsibility or result in purely automated political decisions.

They say European AI tools should be prioritised, particularly within EU institutions. To this end, the text says that the EU should scale up “European technology” and ensure strategic autonomy across the AI value chain.

Technologies with global security and societal implications require an international agreement, modelled on nuclear non-proliferation, with the EU taking a leading role. Safeguards must be built alongside AI, but without unnecessarily hampering innovation or competitiveness.

Artificial intelligence increasingly shapes political communication, electoral processes, public discourse and decision-making.

MEPs therefore called for a systematic parliamentary assessment of risks as well as opportunities of AI and for a reform of the European electoral law. The Charter of Fundamental Rights should include new rights, such as the protection of personal identity and likeness and algorithmic transparency, they say.

The report proposes a budget-neutral administrative unit – the “European Parliament AI observatory” – to support the work of Parliament committees in tasks such as ex post evaluation of AI-related legislation and analysis of AI’s impact on the Union’s institutional balance and democratic processes.

The rapporteur on the resolution, Manolis Kefalogiannis, said: “AI does not progress linearly. It advances in leaps, and Europe must take the lead in shaping it. To paraphrase Abraham Lincoln: By humans, for humans, with humans. So that AI does not become the last invention that humans will ever need to create.”

(Photo via Von der Leyen’s page on X)

World.title: Bulgarian economy grew by 0.6% in Q3 2026 – flash estimate
World.content:
Bulgaria’s economy grew by 0.6 per cent in the third quarter of the year, the National Statistical Institute (NSI) said in a flash estimate on November 13. In real terms, gross domestic product (GDP) in Bulgaria in July-September was 35.51 billion euro.

Year-on-year, the economic growth in the third quarter was 2.5 per cent. NSI is due to announce preliminary growth figures for the quarter on December 4.

The flash estimate’s seasonally-adjusted data showed domestic consumption increase by 1.4 per cent during the third quarter, and it was 6.3 per cent higher on an annual basis. Gross fixed capital formation shrank by 0.8 per cent in July-September, and was 0.5 per cent lower compared to the third quarter of 2025.

Exports fell by four per cent compared to the second quarter of the year, and were 5.5 per cent lower compared to the third quarter of last year, while imports shrank by 4.8 per cent on a quarterly basis and were down one per cent year-on-year.

The country recorded a trade surplus of 357.2 million euro in the third quarter, the equivalent of one per cent of GDP, NSI said.

World.title: Defence Minister: MiG-29s and F-16s will guard Bulgaria’s skies ‘on rotational basis’ in 2027
World.content:
Bulgarian skies will be guarded on a rotational basis by MiG-29s and F-16 fighter jets in 2027, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told a November 13 news conference about the defence budget for next year.

Stoyanov did not explain what is meant by rotation, but he said that in 2027, F-16s will only be on duty during the day because they are not certified and prepared for night flights.

He made it clear that the military will continue to rely on the nearly 40-year-old Soviet MiG-29 fighter jets, without it being clear how many of them are still operational, where spare parts will be obtained, and where they will be repaired and tested for safety.

At the same time, Stoyanov spoke of problems surrounding the use of the new US-made F-16 fighter jets. Bulgaria has already acquired eight of them and is waiting for another eight, which will probably arrive in Bulgaria in 2029, a delay from the initial schedule.

The first eight F-16s will also be modified. For example, they must be equipped with the new AN/ALQ-254(V)1 Viper Shield electronic warfare suite.

This is a mandatory electronic warfare package because it is related to the survival of the F-16 against modern radars and electronic threats. Stoyanov said that the US had given an assurance that the Viper Shield systems would be delivered and installed in 2027.

In addition, according to Stoyanov, the already trained Bulgarian pilots are prepared for air-to-air mode, not air-to-ground, that is, they cannot hit ground targets.

The repair of the engines, as well as the repair of maintenance units for the MiG-29 aircraft , is to be ensured.

“There is no way we can continue to fulfill our functional obligations, including our obligations to Nato structures, without the MiG-29 aircraft,” Stoyanov said.

There are also two new projects included in the new budget. They are related to the maintenance of the F-16. One is specifically for the maintenance of the F-16, and the second project is for the acquisition of additional missile armament for the aircraft.

As to when the F-16s can do duty fulltime, Stoyanov said that this could happen when the Viper Shield systems are received. But he added that the necessary pilots must also be available.

The draft budget of the Defence Ministry for 2027 envisages expenditures amounting to 2.23 per cent of gross domestic product.

The total planned finance for defence spending amounts to 3.151 billion euro, which is an increase of 17 per cent compared with 2026.

“The largest increase is in capital expenditures – from 868 million euro this year to over 1.223 billion euro next year,” Stoyanov said. This represents 40.83 per cent of the ministry’s budget budget.

“This is a budget for accelerated modernisation. With Nato’s requirement for a share of capital expenditures above 20 per cent, we exceed 40 per cent,” he said.

Stoyanov said that Bulgaria is working on many projects, both under the SAFE loan mechanism and from the Bulgarian budget.

This includes the acquisition of seven new three-coordinate (3D) radars , a coastal anti-ship missile system from the United States , French Caesar self-propelled artillery systems (SAU), German Iris ground-based air defence systems, 155 mm shells, vehicles, multiple launch rocket systems, drones.

The budget envisages purchasing six firefighting aircraft.

“We are working on the implementation of a project to acquire up to six firefighting aircraft. If the procedure passes without appeals, there is a possibility that the first two will be delivered by the end of 2027, after which the procedure for their absorption will begin,” Stoyanov said.

Stoyanov said that new projects will also be launched with national funds, including modernisation of the avionics of the C-27J Spartan transport aircraft and maintenance of the MiG-29.

It is also planned to acquire new small arms, unmanned aerial systems and space-based platforms; for reconnaissance and surveillance of land and sea targets, strike and FPV drones.

Personnel costs are maintained, with an additional four million euro to compensate for the increase in the minimum wage.

Military personnel will welcome the new year with frozen salaries, due to the freezing for the second time of the automatic increase tied to the average salary. ” If we increase salaries, we have to cut capital expenditures , ” Dimitar Stoyanov said recently.

To fill the shortage in the Bulgarian military, a target of 27.5 million euros from the central budget has been earmarked for the appointment of new military personnel.

At the same time, the resources saved from the dismissal of over 400 employees in the Ministry’s administration this year are being redirected to positions in the military formations.

Stoyanov hopes to recruit at least 1000 new military personnel in 2027, but he made it clear that he is not very optimistic.

The military itself admits that in some units there is even a 25 per cent shortage of personnel, with the situation being the worst in the army.

The Defence Ministry has tried to patch things up with initiatives such as “Be a Soldier” and with changes in the law to introduce so-called voluntary service, but in practice there has been little positive result and the personnel gap remains.

(Archive photo of Bulgarian Air Force Mig-29s, a Spartan and F-16s: Defence Ministry)

World.title: Opposition parties slam PM Radev over ‘reservations’ on Dublin declaration on European security
World.content:
In statements on November 13, opposition parties slammed Bulgarian Prime Minister Roumen Radev over Bulgaria’s position to support “with reservations” France’s initiative on key principles of European security, presented in Dublin.

While some media reports said that Bulgaria was alone among EU countries in not signing the declaration, the website of the President of France showed Bulgaria among the signatories, and the Bulgarian government information service said that the country had supported it, with reservations about the preamble.

Daniel Mitov, an MP for Boiko Borissov’s opposition coalition GERB-UDF and a former foreign minister, said that Bulgaria continues to pursue an unclear foreign policy.

“It was not clear again what he (Radev) signed, what he did not sign and with what reservations,” Mitov said.

“We have Schrödinger’s foreign policy again – we are both there and not there. They never explained what these reservations are,” he said.

“Obviously, Prime Minister Radev is not talking to Bulgarian citizens through such explanations. He is talking to his masters in the Kremlin and giving them a signal that he is actually defending their interests in European formats,” Mitov said.

Borissov said: “Did we sign the declaration or didn’t we? I didn’t understand! German media says we didn’t, the Elysee Palace says we did”.

Ivailo Mirchev, co-leader of opposition coalition Democratic Bulgaria, said: “This is yet another ‘hybrid’ position from Bulgaria—we have joined, yet we haven’t joined”.

“Mr. Radev is clearly afraid of Russia. We ought to treat our partners as a true ally would,” Mirchev said.

Radev, speaking on November 13, said that Bulgaria supported the declaration with reservations only regarding the preamble.

“And we support the declaration in its working part, where we have clearly expressed principles for joint efforts to counter organized crime, terrorism, hybrid attacks, the production and distribution of drugs, and countering illegal immigration,” Radev said.

“But we also take into account that negotiations are currently underway, finally at a high diplomatic level, for a peaceful solution to the war in Ukraine. It is here that we think that the language of common European documents should reflect the dynamics of these political processes, especially when it comes to negotiations,” he said.

“That is why we also expressed reservations about the preamble of the declaration, so that these formulations correspond to these dynamics. So that we can have a broader scope of dialogue and not exclude peaceful solutions in their entirety.”

Radev said that in the earlier versions, there was a formulation about the importance of the negotiations in Abu Dhabi “and that we should support them, then that disappeared, dropped out”.

“We insist on having such a text, to take it into account and not to narrow the field for dialogue and the options for finding a solution. We supported this declaration with reservations only in the preamble. What we have reservations about – these are the formulations in light of the negotiations that have already begun. This is an adopted document by Bulgaria and we welcome it, my reservations to the preamble are recorded.”

Regarding Bulgaria’s position on a new EU loan for Ukraine, Radev said: “Our position is clear – we support all efforts for peace”.

“I do not accept the imposition of the position for peace from a position of force, because we saw a year and a half ago, when I stated it, that this will only lead to more victims, more destruction and an even greater escalation of the conflict, which is already a risk not only for Europe, but for the entire world,” he said .

“We must take into account that Bulgaria, unlike other EU member states, is the country with the largest historical community in Ukraine. And we are deeply concerned by the fact that Bulgarians continue to die in this war every day,” Radev said.

“And that is why we want peace to be restored as quickly as possible. The task of our government is to help our compatriots in Ukraine live in peace as soon as possible, but also to have access to education, healthcare, electricity, and heating during this transitional period. And this will not be solved by investing in military means.”

Radev again referred to Bulgaria being in an excessive deficit procedure, as he has before when speaking about assistance for Ukraine.

“We are in an excessive deficit procedure. We have problems with the reserves in the state. And we have no way in this situation to provide financial resources, but in no case do we hinder the decisions of other member states,” he said.

“Whoever decides to help and invest financial resources in whatever they decide. So we are not blocking anyone in this situation,” Radev said.

“We are ready to talk about mechanisms that will guarantee that these funds will not go to weapons, but to humanitarian activities, to support with electricity, to medical activities, and this is very important for us – we want to see mechanisms that will target these funds, if we invest such as a guarantor, to go specifically to our community. It is compactly expressed in several regions of Ukraine,” he said.

(Photo: government.bg)

World.title: The Place in Croatia Where a Doctor Once Prescribed Wine
World.content:
November the 14th, 2026 – There’s a beautiful house in Croatia that looks as if it’s rising from the sea, and the doctor who lived there used to prescribe both aristocrats and prisoners wine there.

The beautiful Brijuni islands are an unusual Istrian archipelago. They were once a favourite destination of European aristocracy and the place where Josip Broz Tito hosted statesmen from around the world. Ivana Vasarevic reports for Putni kofer that on Veliki Brijun specifically, right next to the harbour where tourist boats dock, there’s a particularly interesting building. It looks as if it is rising right out of the sea, it’s over 120 years old, and for decades a doctor lived there who took care of the health of the island’s guests. It’s known as the Boat House (Kuća za brodice) and it is at the heart of a story that takes us back to the era when the Brijuni islands were one of the most elegant resorts on the entire Adriatic coast.

THE ONLY COMPLETELY PRESERVED ART NOUVEAU BUILDING ON VELIKI BRIJUN

Johann SUHM

It all began back at the end of the 19th century, when the Austrian industrialist Paul Kupelwieser purchased Brijuni and decided to turn the area into a luxury tourist destination. That’s when the Boothaus, or Boat House, was also constructed. In 1901, Kupelwieser engaged the young Viennese architect Eduard Kramer, a pupil of the famous Otto Wagner, to design an apartment above the existing boat storage. The building was completed in 1902 and is considered the only completely preserved Art Nouveau building on Veliki Brijun. The ground floor of the House boasts four large arches facing the sea and once served for storing boats. Above it is the residential floor with a spacious balcony and an elegant wrought-iron railing, while on the land side a winding staircase leads to the former apartment. It is also worth noting that the attractive Boat House was the first building of civil purpose on the island built using reinforced concrete.

DOCTOR OTTO LENZ EVEN PRESCRIBED WINE WITH IRON TO HIS PATIENTS

From 1903 to 1938, it was the home and workplace of doctor Otto Lenz, who settled on Brijuni with his wife and son. His task was to take care of the health of the resort’s guests, and in the house he set up a surgery and a well-equipped pharmacy. He received patients every day from 10 to 12 o’clock. Among them were distinguished and wealthy visitors to Brijuni, but also convicts from the prison in Koper who worked on the construction of the island’s hotels.

In Lenz’s pharmacy one could obtain tonic syrups and preparations against headache, rheumatism, colds, fainting and seasickness, and the doctor also prescribed wine with iron to his patients! This preparation was used to stimulate the appetite, strengthen the nerves and improve the blood count. The original glass bottles for medicines, found during diving and cleaning of the Brijuni harbour, are today exhibited precisely in the Boat House.

THE LENZ COUPLE LEFT THE BRIJUNI ARCHIPELAGO IN 1938 AND MOVED TO OPATIJA

Thanks to the notes of the doctor’s wife Maria, who in 1956 handed over her memories to the archive of the Brijuni Administration, it was possible to reconstruct the former purpose of the rooms. Thus we know that their house had a kitchen, bedroom, salon, maid’s room and waiting room. Maria was a musician, so music was also an important part of the family’s everyday life. An interactive museum exhibition has been arranged in the house where you can listen to music from that time, and as you pass through the former kitchen, the sounds of dishes can be heard that evoke the everyday life of the Lenz family. The Boat House was their home for more than three decades. The couple eventually left the archipelago in 1938 and moved to Opatija on the mainland.

World.title: What Can Croatia Do to Slow the Warming of the Adriatic Sea?
World.content:
November the 15th, 2026 – Croatia should be deeply concerned about the warming of the Adriatic Sea, but what can actually be done about it right now? Quite a lot, as it happens.

The Mediterranean is one of the world’s hot spots when it comes to damaging climate change, and the Adriatic in particular is among the seas where average and extreme surface temperatures are rising the fastest. Nenad Jaric Dauenhaur reports for Index that the surface of the world’s oceans has warmed by about 1 °C since the end of the 19th century. In the southern Adriatic specifically, the warming trend of the upper 20 metres of the sea has, in places, reached about 3 °C per century. The Adriatic is a semi-enclosed sea, and its shallow north is particularly sensitive to warming. But changes are also visible in the depths. A study published this autumn showed that the acceleration of warming of deep waters is particularly pronounced in the southern Adriatic.

The consequences are also felt on land, or in the air. The air in the Mediterranean has been warming faster than the global average since the 1980s. At the beginning of the 2020s the average air temperature in the region was about 1.5 °C higher than in the pre-industrial period. Heat waves are becoming more frequent and more intense, the risk of droughts and fires is rising, and extreme heat increases mortality, especially among the elderly. Droughts in turn reduce water reserves and threaten agriculture.

the limits of coastal protection

Nicolas Entrup, director of international relations at the organisation OceanCare, revealed that the coast can be protected from floods and sea-level rise, which is a matter of adaptation, but that such measures will not stop the main cause, which is warming. “We must do everything to limit its scale, and we can only do that if we reduce emissions faster,” he adds.

extensive economic damage

According to an estimate by the World Bank, damage from climate change in Croatia from 1980 to 2021 averaged around 0.7 percent of GDP annually, with tourism, agriculture and forestry being the most affected. Croatia, Entrup says, can introduce some measures immediately, and can achieve a greater effect if it manages to actually agree on some common rules with its neighbours. This is where OceanCare comes into the picture. OceanCare is a Swiss non-governmental organisation that deals with the protection of marine species, underwater noise, plastic pollution and the impact of fishing on the sea. It has special consultative status with the UN Economic and Social Council, is accredited for UN climate negotiations, and this year co-organised a discussion on the de-carbonisation of the Mediterranean in the European Parliament.

Mediterranean countries agreed in 2025 on a common framework for adaptation to climate change, but emissions in the region, according to OceanCare, continue to rise. Ahead of the UN climate conference COP31, which is being held from 9 to 20 November in Antalya, Turkey, the organisation called on them to draw up a joint emissions reduction plan within the framework of the Barcelona Convention. It would be the first such plan within any of the world’s conventions on regional seas.

According to an analysis by the Basque Centre for Climate Change prepared for OceanCare, if emissions remain at the current level, the Mediterranean will by 2035 already have exhausted its share of the remaining global carbon budget. That budget represents the total amount of CO₂ that the world can still emit while aiming to keep long-term global warming below 2 °C relative to the pre-industrial period. The analysis estimates that from 2030 to 2050 emissions should be reduced by around six percent per year. Earlier cuts would ease the pressure after 2030.

croatia will have the opportunity to make history in 2027, but will it take it?

OceanCare is calling for countries to start reducing emissions immediately, to stop exploration of new oil and gas deposits at sea, and to fairly share the remaining carbon budget. Entrup stresses that Turkey and the countries of North Africa must also participate in the agreement. He sees an opportunity at the meeting of the parties to the Barcelona Convention in Croatia in December 2027. “Croatia will then have the opportunity to make history,” he emphasises.

immediate measures that can be taken in croatia

One measure that states, according to Entrup, could introduce immediately is mandatory slowing of vessels. “Just like when you drive a car, the faster you go, the more fuel you use. When a ship sails more slowly, it emits fewer greenhouse gases and pollutants and creates less underwater noise. Slower sailing also reduces the risk of collisions with endangered whales. Even one or two knots less can significantly reduce emissions if the measure is applied to a large number of ships,” Entrup claims. Limits could differ according to vessel category, while common rules for the entire Mediterranean should ensure equal conditions for all shipowners.

Shipowners must also know which fuels they will be able to count on before investing millions in new ships. The International Maritime Organisation has set a goal of net-zero emissions around 2050, with intermediate targets for 2030 and 2040, but has postponed the adoption of concrete measures. “Nobody wants to risk such an investment if they do not know what conditions will apply in ten or fifteen years,” Entrup says. Among the countries that oppose a faster abandonment of fossil fuels, the USA, Russia and Iran particularly stand out.

are there any good examples?

Colder seas often abound in plankton and fish, especially where the mixing of water brings nutrients from the depths to the surface. Warmer seas can mean less fish and a different composition of catches, Entrup warns.

“Tropical species can displace native ones, and among the newcomers in the eastern Mediterranean there are also poisonous species. Intensive fishing further burdens the sea,” he warns. As an example of a measure that has proven useful, Entrup cites the Jabuka Pit between Croatia and Italy. There, in 2017, certain forms of fishing were restricted in order to allow the recovery of populations of hake, Norway lobster and other species.

“When you protect an area, the fish stocks can recover. Fishermen see that in their nets,” he says. OceanCare is calling for a ban on bottom trawling, starting with protected marine areas. Dragging heavy nets along the bottom damages habitats and consumes a lot of fuel, and the organisation also warns of the possible release of carbon from the sediment.

what could croatia do, and how can the eu remain competitive?

Entrup proposes that Croatia gradually phase out existing oil and gas exploitation at sea and stop issuing new permits. As examples of countries that have stopped new exploration he cites France, Portugal and Spain. OceanCare warns that seismic surveys, among other things, create strong underwater noise that can harm marine animals over a large area, because noise is transmitted more strongly through water than through air. Asked how the EU specifically can remain competitive while the USA wants to expand drilling and Russia relies significantly on energy exports, Entrup replies that it is precisely dependence on fossil fuel imports that endangers Europe and exposes it to price spikes. As examples he cites the Russian war against Ukraine and the war involving Iran. In the transition to sun and wind he sees an opportunity for greater energy security and new jobs.

renewable energy and the plague of data centres

In addition to investment in renewable sources, Entrup also advocates more efficient equipment and incentives for energy saving. “If production from renewable sources grows, but total consumption grows at the same rate, the share of renewables will not increase,” he says.

Asked about plans for a huge data centre in Topusko in Croatia, he said he does not know the details of the project, but that powering it with additional quantities of gas would be contrary to the energy transition. The cost of delaying emissions reductions is already visible, Entrup says, from summer fires in Spain, Greece and France to coastal damage and water shortages that affect agriculture. “We are already feeling the consequences now. What will it be like in ten years if warming continues? We need to act together, as neighbours. We are all in the same boat,” he concluded.

World.title: Austria Claims Croatian Police Beats Migrants
World.content:
November the 15th, 2026 – Austria has claimed that Croatian police have been beating migrants. Interior Minister Davor Božinović has since responded.

Deputy Prime Minister and Interior Minister Davor Božinović stated that the Croatian police have no information that would confirm claims about the alleged beating of migrants by Croatian police officers. Index reports that he also said that they have not received any official information on the matter from the competent authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

“We learned about these allegations from the media and the police immediately took steps to check whether they have any information about this incident. We do not have such data, nor have we received any official notification from the Bosnian authorities, primarily the police, with whom we are in constant contact,” Božinović said.

constant migratory pressure

He emphasised that migratory pressures on the Croatian border have not stopped and that the police prevent an average of up to 90 people every day from attempting to enter Croatia illegally. In doing so, they act in accordance with national and international regulations.

“The Croatian police protect the Croatian and external border of the European Union 24 hours a day. The migratory wave has not subsided, and our police officers prevent illegal entries on a daily basis, while consistently respecting the law,” the minister stressed. Božinović also warned of the problem of violence among migrant groups in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He stated that the latest information they received from the Bosnian police related to armed criminal groups within the migrant population.

are there armed criminal groups among the migrants?

“The Croatian police have been warned about the possibility of them crossing onto our territory, which has not happened. The Bosnian police later found automatic weapons and pistols in their improvised shelters,” he said. He emphasised that there are known patterns of violence by criminal groups against migrants, but that these circumstances cannot automatically be linked to the specific case. “I am not claiming that this happened in this case because we do not yet have established facts. However, we know that such patterns of violence exist and that is why we are very carefully monitoring the security situation on the border,” he said.

Božinović stated that the Croatian police will continue to decisively combat migrant smuggling and protect the Croatian and external border of the European Union, while consistently respecting the law.

World.title: The Disappearing Homeland – A Crowdfunding Campaign
World.content:
November the 15th, 2026 – Podravina-based geographer Vedran Šikić and film director Vedran Štefan have joined forces to tell the story of 37 villages with fewer than 50 residents in the documentary film Disappearing Homeland.

After two years of filming, more than 25 interviews with local residents, and over 20 hours of recorded footage, the film is entering the final stage of production. A crowdfunding campaign has been launched on the Bona Fides Invest platform to complete the film, with a fundraising target of €15,000.

The village of Srdinac, not far from Koprivnica. Beside an old, abandoned house, of which only crumbling walls and an old gate remain, a shepherd tends to a flock of sheep. It is a scene that can still be found in Podravina’s villages, but one that many people would no longer even stop to notice. For Vedran Šikić, a geography professor from Koprivnica, this particular scene was one of the first things that inspired him to take a closer look at the villages of Podravina.

As he cycled through the villages of Podravina, Šikić gradually began to discover just how little we know about places that are, in fact, right on our doorstep. His friends, for example, had often never even heard of certain villages located just a few kilometres from Koprivnica. They knew even less about how many people still lived there, how they lived, and what was happening to places that had once been much more vibrant.

This realisation gave rise to the Disappearing Homeland project, followed by the documentary film of the same name, which seeks to capture life in small Podravina settlements before their residents, homes, and memories become nothing more than entries in historical records. After two years of work, filming has been completed, and the filmmakers are now facing the demanding final stage of production, which requires additional funding.

37 villages, less than 1,000 residents

The selection criteria were straightforward: all villages with fewer than 50 residents according to the 2021 population census, located within a 20-kilometre radius, measured as the crow flies, of Koprivnica. Since official census figures do not always fully reflect the actual situation in the smallest settlements, Šikić also verified the data directly in the field by speaking with local residents.

In the end, he included 37 villages. The smallest is Mali Botinovac, which today has just six residents.

The scale of demographic change becomes particularly evident when comparing past and present figures. Around thirty years ago, all 37 villages together had more than 2,500 residents. Today, that number has fallen to fewer than 1,000.

Most villages are now predominantly inhabited by older people, and their age structure is particularly unfavourable. Nevertheless, there are exceptions showing that the future of rural settlements is not equally uncertain everywhere. In Vojvodinec, for example, more than 30% of the population is under the age of 19, considerably above the Croatian average of less than 20%.

“Some villages have a future, but unfortunately, there aren’t many of them,” Šikić points out.

The reasons why young people leave are complex. A lack of infrastructure, poor transport connections, and inadequate internet access are just some of the problems. In certain villages, the internet connection is, as he puts it, “catastrophic”. The vast majority of working-age residents are still engaged in agriculture, but even this activity can no longer ensure the demographic renewal of villages on its own.

the asphalt ends at the village sign

The first phase of the project consisted of cycling trips through the villages. These journeys allowed Šikić to meet people, earn their trust, and document scenes that would later become part of the film’s story.

One such moment took place in Kostadinovac. “The asphalt road reaches the village sign, and then there’s nothing. It’s tragically comical. And it’s still the same today,” he recalls.

Yet alongside the shortcomings in infrastructure, it was the people who left a lasting impression on him. In Pobrđani Vojakovački, during one of his most demanding cycling routes, the local hosts immediately offered him homemade food to help him regain his strength. Later, those same people treated the film crew on several occasions during filming.

A particularly touching encounter took place with an elderly woman in Velika Branjska. Speaking about her neighbours from nearby Mala Branjska, and visibly moved while discussing the project, she pointed out with tears in her eyes that she is an Orthodox Christian and that the best people in the world are her neighbours from Zagorje.

Her testimony also reveals a lesser-known dimension of Podravina’s villages, connected with the history of migration and the shared lives of people from different backgrounds and religious traditions. Part of the local population consists of descendants of settlers from Hrvatsko Zagorje who, both before and after the Second World War, driven by poverty and overcrowding in their homeland, moved to Podravina in search of work as domestic servants and day labourers. In some settlements, Catholic and Orthodox families lived side by side for decades, building communities in which mutual respect, good neighbourly relations, and everyday solidarity mattered more than their differences.

It is precisely these encounters that give the project its particular value. Disappearing Homeland is not simply about documenting empty houses and demographic statistics, but also about recording human relationships, shared history, and ways of life that have shaped this region.

Gaining the trust of interviewees was not difficult. Šikić had met most of them during his cycling trips, and the residents were pleased that someone was showing an interest in their small villages. Nobody refused to speak in front of the camera, resulting in more than 25 interviews.

two vedrans, and the story that became a film

A documentary film was not the original idea. Šikić initially considered publishing a monograph, but over time he concluded that a film would be a more effective way of bringing the story to a wider audience.

His collaboration with film director Vedran Štefan of the production company TETRABOT Ltd. began following one of Šikić’s presentations about the project. Together, they concluded that making a documentary was a natural next step in the research.

Over the two years of filming, the villages changed somewhat. In some, the population declined; in others, new residents arrived, while certain settlements gained paved roads, playgrounds, or water supply infrastructure. Nevertheless, these remain small improvements compared with the long-term demographic trends.

The film material comprises more than 20 hours of footage, interviews, and scenes from everyday life. It is from this material that the final story of the 37 villages, their residents, their past, and their possible future will take shape.

agro-tourism: untapped potential waiting for better days…

The economic dimension of the project is particularly interesting. Disappearing Homeland is not only about demographic decline, but also about the untapped opportunities offered by rural areas.

The Podravina region has relatively fertile soil, arable land, forests, and a diverse landscape. On one side are the Drava River lowlands and the river itself, while on the other are the hills of Bilogora and the foothills of Kalnik.

Most of the land surrounding the villages included in the project is still cultivated, although some areas remain unused. Farmers interviewed by the film crew pointed to difficulties in consolidating agricultural holdings, which makes it harder to expand production.

Several villages are home to a number of family farms engaged in dairy farming. However, they face problems related to labour shortages and an ageing population. Increasingly, young people are reluctant to pursue this type of work.

The tourism perspective is also interesting. Despite the natural beauty of the area and its proximity to Koprivnica, there are only three holiday homes across all 37 villages, all located in a single settlement, Segovina.

“Perfect for holiday homes,” says Šikić, describing a landscape that, with adequate infrastructure and entrepreneurial initiative, could attract significantly more visitors.

However, potential alone is not enough. Without good transport connections, communal infrastructure, reliable internet access, and favourable conditions for business development, it is difficult to expect new residents and investments to arrive.

Šikić believes that the future of some villages may not resemble the way they were lived in fifty years ago, but that rural areas can take on a new role. He envisions a kind of “Village 2.0” model, in which older residents connected with agriculture would live alongside younger families or individuals seeking peace, nature, and a better quality of life, while working in a town just 15 to 30 minutes away by car.

crowdfunding as a way to complete the film

The filming has so far received financial support from the City of Koprivnica, the Municipalities of Rasinja, Novigrad Podravski, and Legrad, as well as the company Hartmann.

The City of Koprivnica provided funding through its annual public call for cultural projects, while the other partners supported the project through donations. In this way, slightly less than €15,000 was raised. However, completing the film to full professional standards requires between €60,000 and €70,000. The production company has therefore also invested some of its own funds to ensure the highest possible quality of filming.

After the project failed to secure funding through the public call of the Croatian Audiovisual Centre, the filmmakers had to find an alternative way to obtain the resources needed to complete production. They decided to turn to crowdfunding, a form of collective financing in which a large number of individuals and organisations contribute smaller individual amounts towards achieving a shared goal.

The campaign is being conducted on the Bona Fides Invest crowdfunding platform, with the aim of raising an additional €15,000.

The funds raised will be used to engage the film professionals whose expertise is essential to completing the documentary. Most importantly, a film editor will need to review and process more than 20 hours of footage and shape it into the final cinematic narrative. A composer will prepare the music in collaboration with KUD Rudarice, while a sound designer will process the recorded audio and create the final sound mix.

The production also requires the creation of graphics and animations of historical maps featured in the film, final colour grading, and preparation of the documentary for screening in cinemas, on television, and on online platforms.

supporters become guardians of their homeland

The crowdfunding campaign is open to everyone who wishes to support the project, regardless of whether they live in Podravina, have family roots in one of the villages featured in the film, or are simply interested in preserving Croatia’s rural heritage.

Contributions start at €10, and supporters are assigned to different categories depending on the amount they contribute. These include Donors, Friends of the Village, Friends of the Homeland, Guardians of the Village, Guardians of the Homeland, and Guardians of Heritage. Those making larger contributions can also become sponsors of an individual village or the entire homeland.

The names of supporters will appear in the film’s end credits in accordance with their selected contribution category. Particularly interesting is the opportunity to sponsor a specific village, symbolically connecting a financial contribution with a place the supporter wishes to help preserve from oblivion.

Contributions can be made by credit or debit card, KEKS Pay, Aircash, cryptocurrency, or through a general payment slip, online banking, or mobile banking.

According to the figures published during the campaign, the public response has been encouraging. The project’s Facebook page has attracted approximately 4,700 followers and more than 2.3 million views. Support has come from the authors’ friends and acquaintances, active followers of the page, as well as residents of the villages featured in the film.

Šikić openly admits that one particular aspect of the campaign is especially difficult for him.

“We are sorry that people from the very areas we are filming have to finance this documentary. We wanted to make this film for them and their region, without them having to financially support the project.”

He had hoped that the necessary funding could be secured through larger sponsorships and donations, for example from major companies in the region for which many residents of these villages had worked for many years. Nevertheless, the very fact that local people are supporting the project shows how much they care about having their stories documented and preserved.

a record for future generations

The plan is to complete the film in the spring of 2027, followed by festival distribution and efforts to secure screenings on television and online platforms. No concrete acquisition agreements have been made so far, as the filmmakers have focused most of their energy on fundraising and completing production.

They are particularly excited about the possibility of organising free outdoor screenings in several of the villages featured in the film during the summer of 2027. They hope to secure support from local tourist boards and other partners who could assist with the technical and logistical arrangements. A photography exhibition has also been scheduled for the spring of 2027, while a monograph is being considered as a possible continuation of the project.

Nevertheless, the film’s greatest value may not lie in its initial screenings, but in what will remain long after them. Šikić makes no secret of the fact that some villages may no longer be capable of demographic recovery. Those with fewer than 20 residents, and especially those with fewer than ten, could disappear completely over the coming decades.



This is precisely why the film also has an important archival dimension. Its creators want to produce a high-quality documentary that will remain valuable 50 or even 100 years from now, when some of these villages may no longer exist.

“One of the purposes of the film is to record these places forever, while they are still here,” Šikić emphasises.

Although he often encountered pessimistic reflections from older residents who remember the time when the villages were full of life, the film’s conclusion nevertheless carries a message of hope. He believes that rural areas possess values that contemporary society fails to recognise sufficiently.

“As a society, we have too little respect for nature, agriculture, and the people who put food on our tables,” he warns.

He hopes the film will encourage viewers, as well as decision-makers, to become better acquainted with the region, explore its historical, recreational, and tourism opportunities, and recognise its uniqueness and the value of preserving it. A village does not have to remain forever as it was fifty years ago, but it should not disappear simply because we have failed to recognise its value and the opportunities it still holds.

At the end of the conversation, Šikić shares the words of an elderly local resident, which perhaps best summarise the entire story:

“Once, the village fed the town, and today the town feeds the village. Think about whether this is realistic and sustainable in the long term for the village itself and for agriculture.”

how you can support the disappearing homeland

The crowdfunding campaign to complete the documentary is being conducted on the Bona Fides Invest platform. The goal is to raise €15,000, with contributions starting at €10. Depending on the amount contributed, supporters will be included in the corresponding acknowledgement category in the film’s end credits, with the additional opportunity to sponsor an individual village. Every contribution helps preserve the stories of 37 Podravina villages, their residents, and their way of life for future generations.

World.title: Advent Zagreb 2026: Festive Cheer, Cultural Highlights, and a Packed Calendar
World.content:
November the 14th, 2026 – It’s that time of year again! Advent Zagreb 2026 is just around the corner, promising a programme packed with festive cheer and a very full calendar.

The most wonderful time of the year is knocking at the door. Advent in Zagreb, which is considered one of the best in Europe, starts on the 28th of November and lasts until the 7th of January.

The multi-award-winning Advent Zagreb once again brings a rich cultural, entertainment and food programme, which, along with New Year’s events, will take place from the 28th of November 2026 to the 7th of January 2027. Organised by the City of Zagreb, the Zagreb Tourist Board (TZGZ) and numerous institutional and private partners, the programme will officially kick off with the traditional lighting of the first Advent candle on Ban Jelačić Square, after which the other locations will open.

zagreb’s progression as a festive city delight

Boska i Kreso/TZGZ

Director of TZGZ, Martina Bienenfeld, stated that “Advent Zagreb has grown into one of the most recognisable Advent events in Europe, and this year’s edition brings new cultural content and more strongly connects city locations into a unique holiday experience. We pay special attention to culture and programmes for children and families. Among this year’s novelties intended for the youngest, I’d highlight LumiLicious on Mažuranac, which starts on the 6th of December, the feast of St Nicholas. Novelties are also The Magic Within on Marulić Square and the festive decoration of the Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts, whose ceremonial openings are planned for the 18th of December. Together with the new arrangement of the space in front of the Croatian National Theatre, these contents will connect the locations of the Green Horseshoe into a unique Advent promenade. In this way we enrich the Advent offer and open new possibilities for exploring the city, while at the same time putting Zagreb’s historical spaces, architecture and cultural heritage in the foreground.

The international recognisability of Advent Zagreb is also confirmed by this year’s awards and recommendations from world media. We are particularly pleased that Zagreb has been declared the best European destination for a Christmas city break in the selection of the European Best Destinations organisation, while the prestigious Time Out ranked it first on its list of the best European destinations for a winter city break in 2026, highlighting its attractiveness for family travel. Such recognitions have significant promotional value because they strengthen Zagreb’s international visibility, encourage interest in coming and contribute to its positioning on key source markets. In this context we continue with intensive promotional activities on 17 international markets, including targeted campaigns at stations of the London Underground and the Milan metro, as well as long-standing cooperation with Croatia Airlines and HŽ Passenger Transport.

Julien Duval/TZGZ

I believe that Advent Zagreb will once again achieve good tourist results this year and further strengthen Zagreb’s position as an attractive year-round destination. At the same time, we do not measure its success exclusively by tourist indicators, but also by the quality of the experience it provides to visitors and our fellow citizens. Precisely in this balance between tourist attractiveness and value for the local community we see the foundation of its long-term development and sustainability.”

The entire programme, detailed schedules of all events and current information can be found here, and we’ll also bring you descriptions of each below.

what’s on this festive season for europe’s best advent?

Julien Duval/TZGZ

What we’ve been waiting for all year finally starts on the last weekend of November. Zagreb has won a new title – it is the best Christmas city-break destination 2026 according to European Best Destinations. Along with well-known attractions such as the Ice Park, Advent on Zrinjevac, Fuliranje and numerous other events, there are also novelties for the youngest on Mažuranac, and the entire Upper Town, as well as the Green Horseshoe of the Lower Town, become a unique Advent promenade. Run with Santa Claus, dance or skate in the parks, sing on the tram or just stop and enjoy.

if you’re the musical type…

Samir Ceric Kovacevic/TZGZ

Advent concerts of the Zagreb Soloists

Museum of the City of Zagreb, on the 3rd, 6th, 10th and 13th of December at 18:00

The Zagreb Soloists continue the tradition of Advent concerts at the Museum of the City of Zagreb. At each of the four concerts the Zagreb Soloists will be joined by a young musician.

Advent concerts of the Zagreb Chamber Orchestra

Church of St Joseph, Journalists’ House

Advent concerts of the Zagreb Chamber Orchestra in the city’s historical spaces. The Church of St Joseph is the location of the first concert on the 29th of November, followed by three more at the Journalists’ House on the 5th 13th and 19th of December with performances by renowned Croatian and international soloists.

Advent concerts of the Chamber Choir “Ivan Filipović” – Zagreb Voices

Church of St John the Baptist 29 Nov, Basilica of St Anthony of Padua on the 13th of December, the Church of St Francis of Assisi on the 29th of December

Concerts of the Chamber Choir “Ivan Filipović” – Zagreb Voices bring a combination of classical music, choral compositions and Croatian traditional Advent and Christmas songs. Contemporary choral arrangements of Croatian musical heritage are performed for the first time.

Music in St Mark’s Church

St Mark’s Church, on the 13th 20th and 24th of December (Midnight Mass)

Advent tradition, performances of classical and sacred music that echo within the historical walls of the Church of St Mark. Admission is free.

Advent with the Opera of the Croatian National Theatre in Zagreb

Republic of Croatia Square, balcony of the CNT, the 5th of December at 17:30 and the 7th of December at 19:00

From the balcony of the Zagreb CNT, young soloists accompanied by piano perform opera and Advent compositions. Two half-hour concerts for residents and guests alike will fill the space in front of the theatre with holiday melodies.

seasonal music

Boska i Kreso/TZGZ

From Christmas balconies to Zagreb

Balcony at the Stone Gate, balcony at Tkalčićeva 33, balcony of the CNT



Christmas melodies from Zagreb balconies performed by the six-member brass ensemble Ad gloriam brass. A unique musical experience of European flair and classical music, film themes and Christmas songs.

Festival of Advent and Christmas songs

Society of University Teachers and Other Scientists, Greek Catholic Co-Cathedral of Sts Cyril and Methodius, Church of St Peter the Apostle, Church of St Mark, Church of St Blaise, Stone Gate, terrace of Cravaticum – the Tie Museum



The Festival of Advent and Christmas songs brings festive concerts of Advent-Christmas music of different genres and eras. From classical to klapa and holiday pop songs at the 11th edition of the festival at six city locations. A children’s concert will also be held as part of the festival.

Zagreb Advent postcards

Oktogon, Neboder, Baković Sisters Passage



The vocal quartet Vox in the heart of Zagreb performs Advent compositions from Croatian and world musical heritage. With pop-up concerts, short performances without prior announcement, they will surprise random passers-by with the musical magic of Advent.

Advent under the lantern

Lotrščak Tower



Join the lamp-lighter and singers every Wednesday, Thursday and Friday until Christmas Eve at Lotrščak Tower. Light the gas lamps while singing kolende at Advent under the lantern in the Upper Town.

Advent symphony of the city

Radićeva – Tomićeva – Stone Gate – Bloody Bridge – Mažuranić Square



An Advent walk through Zagreb accompanied by Christmas songs performed by the Musical-Artistic Atelier Kralj. The Advent symphony of the city from 19:00 to 20:30 at various locations in the heart of Zagreb.

Musical control – Zagreb promenade

Ljubljanica depot, Zrinjevac Park



The Musical Control of the Zagreb ZET Orchestra on Saturday morning will surprise passengers at selected locations in the city. The ride starts at 10:00 from Ljubljanica and ends in Zrinjevac Park.

‘Flash mob’ on the tram

Zagreb trams



Surprise flash-mob concerts on Zagreb trams are a Christmas tradition. Sing along with the choir during the ride through the Lower Town.

single day events

Samir Ceric Kovacevic/TZGZ

Advent Run

Zagreb streets, 6th of December at 12:00



Zagreb Advent Run, a costume race for the whole family through the city, again has a humanitarian character this year. It is run as part of the Croatian national campaign for early detection of high cholesterol and blood pressure. You can choose to run five or ten kilometres.

Broadcast of the ballet The Nutcracker

Republic of Croatia Square, in front of the CNT, on the 19th of December 2026 at 18:00



Broadcast of the most performed classical ballet in the world in front of the Croatian National Theatre on 19 December from 18:00. The beloved Nutcracker in the ambitious version of the famous Russian ballet dancer Rudolf Nureyev.

Choirs on Christmas Eve – Midday Advent Melodies

Ban Josip Jelačić Square, 24th of December at 11:00



This year again on Ban Jelačić Square Zagreb choirs bring Christmas magic with a joint performance of fairy-tale evergreens. Enjoy the harmonious polyphony of the choirs accompanied by guitar and piano.

workshops and activities

Ernest Mazarekic/TZGZ

Christmas story at the Ethnographic Museum

Mažuranić Square 14



The Christmas programme at the Ethnographic Museum brings an exhibition of Pannonian nativity scenes from Burgenland and an exhibition dedicated to 30 years of exhibiting Croatian Christmas nativity scenes in Rome and the Vatican. You can also make your own Christmas nativity scenes from cornhusks and wool.

Advent at the Museum of the City of Zagreb

Opatička 20



The Advent programme of the Museum of the City of Zagreb brings an exhibition of Advent cards and objects “Christmas Story”, tours “Forgotten Holidays” and creative workshops for making Advent wreaths. For children there are theatre performances on the occasion of the feast of St Nicholas, and for quiz lovers a special edition of KviZG.

Advent at the Croatian Natural History Museum

Demetrova 1



The Croatian Natural History Museum uniquely connects science, art, music and entertainment. There are lectures and projections about the secrets of the universe, interactive scientific and creative workshops, as well as theatre performances and Advent concerts in the museum atrium.

Advent in the Crafts Passage

Ilica 49



A Christmas fairy tale at the Croatian Crafts Matrix in Ilica. There are hand-made souvenirs and appropriate workshops by the greatest masters. All accompanied by concerts of Christmas songs on the gallery of the Croatian Crafts Matrix.

for the kids

Samir Ceric Kovacevic/TZGZ

Teatrino klincolino

Antun, Ivan and Vladimir Mažuranić Square



The children’s puppet theatre at this year’s Advent performs more than thirty performances of popular and lesser-known children’s stories. Creative puppets perform on Mažuranić Square.

Living Christmas nativity scene

Opatovina Park, 19th to the 23rd of December, 26th to the 30th of December, 1st and the 6th of January

Traditional staging of the living nativity scene at Opatovina. Young people from the Cenacolo Community designed the entire performance themselves and perform it with the help of parents and friends. Performances are held at 16:00, 17:00 and 19:00.

The Magic Within

Marko Marulić Square



The projection runs from the 18th of December to the 1st of January on the building of the Croatian State Archives, which turns into a stylised Christmas house. Together with the neighbouring buildings of FKIT and PMF it will create a visual whole of recognisable architecture.

Very Merry Square

Ban Josip Jelačić Square



The Christmas tree on Ban Jelačić Square is the central symbol of the Christmas holidays in the city. Surrounded by snow-covered pines and sparkling lights, the Square becomes a real winter fairy tale with Manduševac as the most beautiful Advent wreath.

LumiLicious

Antun, Ivan and Vladimir Mažuranić Square from the 6th of December to the 1st of January



Mažuranac comes alive with Christmas magic. Walk through snowy pine forests and discover a world of imagination among oversized Christmas decorations. There are LUMI and LICI, an interactive audiovisual installation that invites children to bring two cute digital characters to life.

HNK – Layers of Christmas

Republic of Croatia Square



This Advent the building of the Croatian National Theatre will be wrapped in Christmas attire. Republic of Croatia Square becomes a glowing forest which is absolutely perfect for photos.

Let It Glow

Flower Square (Cvjetni trg)

The popular Flower Square, through lavish decorations, sparkling installations and interactive elements, combines the charm of old Zagreb with a modern Christmas atmosphere. A special photo point is the perfect place for unforgettable holiday moments.

Advent Open House Zagreb

9th and and the 16th of December

Advent Open House Zagreb opens the doors of normally inaccessible, most attractive architectural works in the city centre with expert guidance in Croatian and English. The festival encourages reflection on the values of the city. Click here to register.

Bells in the Oktogon

Oktogon, from the 13th to the 29th of December

In Zagreb’s Oktogon you will find a sound installation of 24 bells that every full hour perform an atmospheric version of the composition “Imagine”.

Polar Worlds

Grič Tunnel

A true polar dream in the Grič Tunnel – new scenes inspired by glaciers and crystal formations that transform it into an imaginary landscape of polar worlds. Experience the Grič Tunnel in a new edition.

Moon Garden

King Béla IV Park

Step into the magical Moon Garden in King Béla IV Park. Make a special wish on the Moon with an unforgettable view of the city.

Winter Nocturne

Grič Park, Strossmayer Promenade

Winter Nocturne brings a winter atmosphere to Grič Park, inspired by the stars and Chopin’s nocturnes. The benches are free throughout Advent.

Bells and Bell Towers of Croatia: Symphony of Peace and Togetherness

Palace of the Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts (HAZU), Nikola Šubić Zrinski Square 11

Saša Šekoranja presents drawings and video installations of bell towers from all over Croatia in the HAZU Palace. Their sounds create a unique Advent symphony of togetherness, love and holiday joy.

ADVENT IN HOTELS

Julien Duval/TZGZ

Hilton Hotels

Hilton Hotels: DoubleTree, Garden Inn, Canopy



Festive decorations, a warm atmosphere, signature cocktails and special offers at Hilton Hotels Zagreb.

Hotel Jägerhorn

Ilica 14



A small but idyllic Advent is hidden in the passage of Hotel Jägerhorn, the oldest in the city.

Advent Bachata Congress

Hotel Diplomat, Zrinjevac



An international dance congress from the 11th to the 14th of December gathers hundreds of bachata and salsa dancers from all over the world. Free dance programme on Zrinjevac on the 13th of December from 16:00 to 19:00.

Fuliranje

Hotel Esplanade



The Fuliranje – Christmas Station is a new edition of the popular Zagreb Advent project. The Oleander terrace of Hotel Esplanade turns into a unique Christmas destination. There is an impressive covered and heated greenhouse, a Christmas living room that in the evening turns into a large Christmas Disco Club.

LOCATIONS IN THE CITY CENTRE

Julien Duval/TZGZ

EU Advent

European Square



EU Advent on European Square brings a new theme – The City that Loves. Through performances by female vocalists, DJ programmes and stand-up evenings, European Square becomes a place of meetings, music, laughter, tastes and togetherness.

Baš Naš Vremeplov

Ban Josip Jelačić Square

January, Ban Josip Jelačić Square will beecome a place where the past and the present meet until January the 7th, 2027. Baš Naš Vremeplov (Our Time Machine) invites all generations to gather in the very heart of Zagreb.

Advent on Zrinjevac

Zrinjevac Park



Thousands of sparkling lights, music from the pavilion, the scents of winter delicacies and charming Advent houses – Zrinjevac once again opens the doors to the most beautiful holiday moments! This year it becomes a magical poetry promenade. Verses of Croatian poets about love, Christmas and Zagreb come to life among the century-old plane trees.

Fuliranje

Strossmayer Square



Until the 7th of January, Fuliranje on Josip Juraj Strossmayer Square brings an open-air winter living room. Creative workshops, children’s and family programmes, musical performances, theatrical and educational content, as well as top gastronomic offerings.

Ice Park

King Tomislav Square



In the heart of Zagreb, against the magnificent backdrop of the Art Pavilion and the glow of thousands of lights, the Ice Park once again becomes a favourite place for winter gatherings. From the first steps on the ice to evening get-togethers with music and favourite winter delicacies. The most beautiful outdoor winter stage is once again adorned by the Nutcracker on Ice performance.

Caffe de Matoš – Advent in the Upper Town

Strossmayer Promenade and Gradec Plateau



On Strossmayer Promenade, Caffe de Matoš offers a daily musical programme of young bands in cooperation with the Music House. A photo point with the best view of Zagreb. On the nearby Gradec Plateau, Caffe de Matoš revives the spirit of old Zagreb in a special holiday edition. Thousands of lanterns, red houses and a magical forest, with an unforgettable view of illuminated Zagreb.

The Great ZbiGatsby on Stross

Strossmayer Promenade – west



On Zagreb’s most romantic promenade, feel a touch of old Zagreb. Tak imam te rad – The Great ZbiGatsby on Stross brings the warmth of holiday gatherings with the charm and elegance of the 1920s and 1930s.
