World.title: Azerbaijan rejects claims that Soyudlu residents to be evacuated for gold mining
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 15. The dissemination by a YouTube channel operated from France and specializing in the systematic spread of disinformation against Azerbaijan of completely unfounded claims that the village of Soyudlu in the Gadabay district and nearby settlements will be evacuated to make way for gold mining is another attempt to manipulate public opinion.

This was stated in a statement by the Media and Broadcasting Council of the Republic of Azerbaijan.

The statement noted that presenting fabricated and rumor-based information in the aforementioned material as a decision adopted at the state level is part of a multi-stage disinformation campaign aimed at causing panic among the population, undermining public trust in government institutions, and heightening tensions in society.

"Previously, this channel has also specialized in systematically spreading disinformation and manipulative content targeting our country.

An official appeal has been sent to the relevant platform regarding this matter, and we are confident that the company will promptly review the appeal and take the necessary steps to prevent the spread of the aforementioned disinformation on its platforms," the statement said.

World.title: Wells Fargo declares dividends on six series of preferred stock
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 15. US banking group Wells Fargo & Company has declared quarterly cash dividends on six series of its preferred stock, with payments scheduled for December 15, 2026.

According to the company's announcement, the dividends will be paid to shareholders registered as of the close of business on November 30, 2026.

The declared dividend on the 7.50% Series L preferred stock amounts to $18.75 per share. For the 5.625% Series Y series, the dividend is $351.56 per preferred share, equivalent to $0.35156 per depositary share.

Wells Fargo also declared dividends of $296.88 per preferred share for its 4.75% Series Z stock, $293.75 for the 4.70% Series AA series, $273.44 for the 4.375% Series CC series and $265.63 for the 4.25% Series DD series. These amounts correspond to $0.29688, $0.29375, $0.27344 and $0.26563 per respective depositary share.

Each depositary share of Series Y, Z, AA, CC and DD represents a 1/1,000 interest in the corresponding preferred share, which has a liquidation preference of $25,000. Series L has a liquidation preference of $1,000 per share.

All six series carry noncumulative perpetual dividend terms and are listed on the New York Stock Exchange.

Wells Fargo & Company is a leading diversified financial services company founded in 1852 by Henry Wells and William G. Fargo. Headquartered in San Francisco, California, and led by CEO Charles W. Scharf, it ranks as the fourth-largest bank in the United States by assets, with approximately $2.3 trillion in total assets, and placed No. 38 on Fortune’s 2026 ranking of America’s largest corporations.

The company provides a wide range of banking, investment, mortgage, and consumer and commercial finance products and services to individuals, businesses, and institutions, primarily in the U.S. and in select international markets.

Its operations span four reportable segments: Consumer Banking and Lending, Commercial Banking, Corporate and Investment Banking, and Wealth & Investment Management.

World.title: Azerbaijan participates in NATO Charity Bazaar
World.content:
Photo: Mission of the Republic of Azerbaijan to NATO

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 15. The latest “NATO Charity Bazaar” was held at NATO Headquarters. As is customary, the Representation of the Republic of Azerbaijan to NATO, as well as the Military Representation of the Azerbaijani Armed Forces to the NATO Military Committee, took an active part in the event.

This was reported by the Representation of Azerbaijan to NATO.

According to the statement, the charity bazaar, which brought together around 40 countries, featured a stand showcasing Azerbaijani national products and traditional cuisine, with the sponsorship of Hyatt Regency Baku.

The event was attended by senior officials from NATO's International Staff and International Military Staff, ambassadors and military representatives of Allied and partner countries accredited to the Alliance, as well as other guests.

The stand featuring Azerbaijani national products and the rich variety of traditional Azerbaijani dishes attracted considerable interest from visitors.

World.title: Alleged Chinese spy left Megaspeed last year, company says
World.content:
Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International says Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whose relationship with former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang sparked US national security concerns, left the company last year.

Megaspeed, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, also announced an internal investigation led by outside lawyers.

The company said it ran a "legitimate and lawful business" and was aware of media reports containing claims about its business, supply chain and global operations "that are not supported by verifiable evidence".

It did not address specific allegations.

"The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation," it said in an emailed statement.

Jensen Huang (centre) admitted to having an affair with Megaspeed's Alice Huang. (Supplied: NetThunder/LinkedIn)

Alice Huang "left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company," the statement said.

" Megaspeed does not comment on Ms Huang's personal and private matters. "

A customer and cloud partner of Nvidia, Megaspeed has faced scrutiny in recent months, including from US authorities, over allegations that it circumvented US export restrictions to route large quantities of advanced chips to Chinese companies.

Last December, it said there was "no evidence" of illicit chip transfers.

China's spy networks in view With all eyes on the Nvidia sex scandal, questions are being asked about China's vast and complex spy networks.

Singapore's government said last week it initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in February 2025, including possible "false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers".

Authorities also investigated Alice Huang, whom the government identified as Megaspeed's then-chief executive, chairperson and one of its key controllers.

Singapore authorities questioned her and withheld her passport last year. They later concluded there was insufficient evidence that she had committed a crime, despite suspecting she had provided "inaccurate" information to downplay her role at the company.

An earlier New York Times report suggested US officials believed Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited to potentially influence Nvidia to make its advanced chips more available to China.

As scrutiny intensified and reports of her romantic relationship with Jensen Huang gained attention, Nvidia announced on Thursday that he was stepping down as chief executive.

Nvidia's chips are widely used to develop AI models. (Reuters: Ann Wang)

US Attorney General Todd Blanche said, however, that the Justice Department had not concluded whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy.

Asked whether she was a spy, President Donald Trump said: "I don't know if that's been determined yet."

Australian links to firm in Nvidia scandal The Australian subsidiary of the firm at the centre of the alleged Nvidia spy scandal lists a newsagent worker as it sole director.

Beijing rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated.

The Associated Press has been unable to reach Alice Huang for comment.

Megaspeed began as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer and was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International.

It adopted its current name in March 2023, when all its shares were transferred to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. Alice Huang is also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le.

By November 2023, she was no longer listed as a Megaspeed director, and all her shares had been transferred to an entity owned by Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan.

Despite those public records, short seller Culper Research cited a Megaspeed employee in a report released this May as saying Alice Huang was "actually still our boss" and remained involved in daily operations.

The company's finances have also attracted attention. Singapore corporate records show its total assets rose roughly 90-fold from the end of 2023 to 2024, reaching almost $US3 billion ($4.4 billion).

World.title: Live: Wallabies and Scotland locked in tight tussle, hosts lead
World.content:
You'd never have picked it... (Getty Images)

It's been a big weekend of rugby in the Nations Championship...

And it's not been a great one for the southern hemisphere, all things considered.

Here's the run down.

France edge South Africa in classic

One of the all time great Test matches was played at a break-neck speed (Getty Images)

France and South Africa played out on the game of the year on Friday night local time at a raucous Stade de France, with Les Bleus running out winners 21-19 in a genuine thriller. Odds on a repeat in the final in two weeks time are shortening by the hour...

Want an indication as to how furious a pace that match was contested at? Check out the final seconds in this clip - especially one of the all-time great tackles by Louis Bielle-Biarrey on Jesse Kriel.

Hook that crowd noise into the veins of every French player and they'll never lose a Test again. Astonishing.

Wales stun All Blacks

Wales will be talking about this one for a generation (Getty Images)

On Saturday, Wales pulled off the shock of the year, ending a 53-year drought against the All Blacks to win 35-28 in front of a dazed and confused Cardiff crowd, who are probably still in the cities bars and clubs toasting the most unlikely of successes.

England crush Japan

Five of the best for Will (Getty Images)

England dealt a thumping of epic proportions to their former coach, Eddie Jones, thrashing Japan 78-15 at Twickenham. Of the 13 tries England scored, five came via Will Joseph, a record-equalling haul for the man winning his second Test cap — the first of which was given to him by Jones...

Ireland labour to win over Fiji

Incredibly, McNabney once had a promising future in equestrianism (Getty Images)

Ireland overcame a spirited Fijian side 43-15, rousing themselves after a very sluggish start to win in Dublin. Special mention to Ulster debutant James McNabney, who came on, made a bullocking run down the middle of the pitch, got to within a hair's breadth of the try line, before a swinging arm from Inoke Ravuiwasa knocked him clean out. Pretty eventful debut.

Pumas tame Italy in Genoa

You're doing it wrong, lads (Getty Images)

Only Argentina held up the end of the southern hemisphere, edging past winless Italy 19-14 in Genoa. I have nothing smart or clever to say about this one.

World.title: Speed kills as New Zealand fall flat in World Cup final fizzer
World.content:
In the lead up to the World Cup final, the match seemed to have all the makings of a classic but nobody must have told New Zealand.

Australia's dominance through their 32-12 victory at Lang Park was built on speed and precision as the Kangaroos cruised home to bury the Kiwis under a mountain of errors.

It turned the final into a fizzer. After all the anticipation and hype, New Zealand let themselves down badly, totally failing to meet the moment while the Kangaroos saved their best for last.

RLWC finals live The Kangaroos are Rugby League world champions for a 13th time after defeating New Zealand 32-12 in the final at Lang Park. Follow live.

They played like champions and Australia were ruthless in punishing the Kiwis for their lapses, perhaps because they had plenty of practice at it.

Jamayne Isaako's kick off going out on the full and Liam Martin scoring the fastest try in World Cup final history after just 88 seconds before New Zealand had touched the ball, turned out to be the tone setter.

After steadying with some fine opening exchanges where both teams gave as good as they got, it proved to be the aberration as the Kiwis fell into a death spiral from which they never escaped.

From the 15th minute to the 35th minute, New Zealand completed just one set. Errors came thick and fast and there were so many of them — lost balls in contact, passes that went awry, fumbles under the high ball and stone dead drops that wouldn't have looked out of place at park footy.

They dug their own grave, but only after dropping the shovel first.

Meanwhile, the Kangaroos, through Cameron Munster and Harry Grant, seized control of the match like it was their birthright.

Jacob Preston was excellent, as was the Lang Park specialist Bradman Best. But it was the Melbourne duo who decided this game as they ran the show with an experts touch.

Grant used misdirection around the ruck to open up spaces while Munster marshalled the backline magnificently.

Cameron Munster was magnificent for Australia. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris )

He might be wearing the number six jersey, but make no mistake, Munster is the chief organiser of this team and through this tournament he has played his best football in some time.

He has a madcap reputation that he plays up but don't be fooled. Munster can always go back to the wild stuff if he has to, But he also knows how to turn the screws on a battling opponent as tightly as anyone.

With Tom Dearden and Reece Walsh in tow, the Aussies upped the pace until New Zealand were gasping for air. And on a night where Brisbane's humidity made it feel like you were living inside someone's armpit, the need for oxygen became an enemy.

It played towards Australia's strengths, which is the quickness and versatility of their spine, while robbing New Zealand of any opportunity to get their vaunted forward pack into the game.

Bradman Best was immense with the Kangaroos in total control. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris )

All that power and size just made it hard for them to move and some of their most important players left their best football at home.

Erin Clark looked more like the fringe first grader of his Gold Coast days than the two-time defending Dally M lock of the year that he's become at the Warriors while Kodi Nikorima and Briton Nikora were targeted mercilessly until they cracked.

They will forever count this night as one of the most disappointing of their careers.

It's not because they lost — there is never any shame in suffering defeat against Australia — but because they did not get near the limits of their abilities.

Chances like this do not come along often. This will likely be the last World Cup for players like Joseph Tapine, James Fisher-Harris and Jahrome Hughes and the team missed a real shot at taking home the trophy.

An aging New Zealand side will undergo major changes before the next World Cup. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

They have a side capable of being the best, and that's a blessing. But if you can't access those capabilities when they matter most, it becomes a curse.

By contrast, Australia seemingly always find a way to do it. And it's not just through players like Munster, Walsh and Grant, all of whom have been consistently brilliant through the tournament.

Kotoni Staggs, a controversial selection at right centre, had his best game since he was dropped from the New South Wales Origin side while Tino Fa'asuamaleaui went a big way towards restoring the forward pack's reputation.

That reputation took a bit of a hit early in the tournament and Australia were clearly listening.

It was one of several criticisms Walsh mentioned in his post-match interview with Channel 7, where he said Australia had proved people wrong with their victory.

Martin had a similar line, saying there were plenty of doubters throughout the World Cup.

Regardless of whether you believe that or not — Australia were the bookies favourite the whole way through the tournament — it's clear the Kangaroos believed it and the power of that belief was on full show.

It helped them put in a performance that was, to a man, worthy of a World Cup final.

They have conquered their enemies, real or imagined, by playing their best when it mattered most.

That sounds simple, but that's not the same as being easy. Just ask New Zealand.

World.title: Jordan sentences three men to death over deadly church attack
World.content:
Israeli forces have killed a top commander of the militant Hamas group in an overnight air strike on southern Gaza, officials said on Sunday.

Meanwhile, Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed that it struck a radar system at an American helicopter base in Bahrain.

The US military command did not immediately comment on the claim.

Jordan sentenced three men to death for a deadly shooting at a Greek Orthodox Church in the city of Karak last month, state-run Al Mamlaka TV said.

In Yemen, health authorities with the Iran-backed Houthi rebels said an air strike on Sanaa wounded two women and two children, and blamed Saudi Arabia for the attack, without offering evidence.

Gunmen opened fire inside a church in Jordan's Karak region in October. (Reuters)

Iran says it hit an American radar system in Bahrain

Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said two tankers were on fire after striking naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, according to a statement carried by Iranian state media.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed early on Sunday that it struck a radar system at an American helicopter base in Bahrain, the state-run IRNA news agency reported.

The development comes after CENTCOM said on Friday that it intercepted two Iranian drones headed toward Bahrain and denied Iran's claim at the time that it had struck a US early-warning radar system there.

Bahrain's military said on Sunday that its air defence systems had intercepted a number of Iranian projectiles before they reached their targets.

Measuring Israel's expansion across the Middle East ABC analysis reveals the extent of Israel's expansion on four fronts: Lebanon, the West Bank, Gaza and Syria.

Earlier Sunday, Bahrain's Interior Ministry issued two nationwide alerts warning of a threat, the first such alerts since September. It did not specify the nature of the threat or say whether anything had been hit.

"Iran continues its systematic hostile approach through its sinful attacks targeting the Kingdom of Bahrain," the statement added.

Israel says it killed a top Hamas commander in Gaza

Israel said it killed a top Hamas commander in an air strike on southern Gaza.

A Hamas statement confirmed the killing of Samir Mahmoud Hassan Abu Younis, commander of the group's Rafah Brigade, and said a funeral would be held for him later in the day.

The Israeli military said Abu Younis was killed in a strike just after midnight on Saturday.

It said he had been working to build up Hamas and directing plans "to advance and carry out terror attacks".

The aftermath of Israeli strikes and gunfire in Gaza City in September. (Reuters: Dawoud Abu Alkas)

Two months earlier, his predecessor was killed in an Israeli strike.

Jordan sentences three men to death over deadly church attack

Jordan's State Security Court on Sunday sentenced three men to death for a deadly shooting at a Greek Orthodox Church in the city of Karak last month, state-run Al Mamlaka TV said.

The men were charged with "carrying out terrorist acts".

The October 23 attack was one of the deadliest on Jordan's Christian minority in decades, with nine people killed and dozens more wounded.

The attackers targeted mourners attending a funeral at a church in Karak.

The three defendants, identified by authorities as two brothers and their brother-in-law, were arrested three days after the attack following a shootout with security forces in Karak.

Jordanian authorities described the men as followers of an extremist ideology but said they were not affiliated with an organised group.

No group claimed responsibility for the attack.

Yemen's Houthis say air strike wounds four

Houthi health officials say an air strike on Sanaa, Yemen's capital, wounded two women and two children.

US diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes The United States has ordered non-essential US embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia.

The strike hit a residential neighbourhood in north-eastern Sanaa early on Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said in a statement, without providing further details or saying what was hit in the strike.

It said the wounded were taken to the Muayyad Hospital for treatment.

Ministry spokesman Anees al-Asbahi blamed Saudi Arabia for the strike.

There was no immediate comment from the kingdom.

A Saudi military spokesman, meanwhile, said air defence systems intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis early on Sunday toward Riyadh, the Saudi capital.

Two drones were also shot down over the Saudi oil-rich Eastern Region, said the spokesman, Major General Turki al-Maliki.

The air strike in Sanaa and the missile and drone attacks in Saudi Arabia were the latest in a month-long escalation between the Houthis and the kingdom that has seen a return of fighting in Yemen's civil war after more than four years of ceasefire.

World.title: Volume of illegal tobacco shrinks after years of rapid growth
World.content:
The government says its crackdown on organised crime and at the borders has seen Australia's illicit tobacco market shrink for the first time in years.

New figures from the Illicit Tobacco and E-cigarette Commissioner (ITEC) show that after five years of rapid growth, an average 22.6 per cent increase each year, there's been a fall from last year's peak of 5,972 tonnes.

ITEC estimates the total volume of black market tobacco has dropped to 5,893 tonnes and could be as low as 4,453 tonnes.

Legal cigarette sales jump after crackdown Calls to Quitline more than doubled in the days after major tobacco black market enforcement operations in Queensland, suggesting the crackdown may encourage some smokers to quit.

An exact figure is hard to determine given the market's illicit nature but ITEC argues the inclusion of several datasets this year, including the Australian Health Insitute of Welfare data released every two years, has lead to a narrower and more accurate range.

The government attributes the shrinkage to stronger enforcement, larger seizures and better coordination between federal, state and territory agencies.

Julian Hill says the government crackdown is reversing years of illicit tobacco growth. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Assistant Minister for Customs Julian Hill has argued that the crackdown, as well as public health measures to curb demand, was "reversing years of growth".

"Every illicit cigarette seized, every store closed and every network disrupted sends the same message to criminals: we know who you are, we know how you operate, and we're coming after you and your profits," he said.

However, record seizures by Australian Border Force officers, including 730 tonnes in the first three months of this financial year, call into question the scale of the market.

Up to four in five nicotine products now smoked in Australia are illegal, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

Coordination model praised internationally

The National Disruption Group, comprised of 31 federal, state and territory agencies, has coordinated more than 600 operations nationwide since it was established last October.

It has led to the seizure of 24 million illicit cigarettes and 3.6 tonnes of loose-leaf tobacco.

It represents more than $45 million in evaded tobacco duty, while on-the-ground operations have led to the closure of 1,300 stores.

International cooperation has also played an integral role in creating sustained pressure to disrupt criminal networks, with 340 referrals from foreign partners resulting in tobacco and vape seizures.

The New Zealand Customs assistant comptroller of intelligence and investigations, Terry Brown, said the multi-agency model was helping shape New Zealand's enforcement response to illicit tobacco.

"The challenges posed by illicit tobacco are increasingly transnational, and effective responses require equally connected enforcement partnerships," he said.

Vaping levels drop Vaping and smoking rates are on the decline, but a shift to other nicotine products could represent an increase in average use.

"By sharing intelligence, insights and operational experience, our agencies are enhancing our collective ability to identify, disrupt and deter the criminal networks that profit from illicit trade across our region."

The approach has garnered praise from Australia's neighbours but domestically, both the Coalition and One Nation have instead proposed slashing the tobacco excise by 80 per cent and 75 per cent respectively.

The opposition has also suggested legalising and taxing vape and nicotine pouch alternatives, helping to regulate their content.

The ABS found illicit nicotine product consumption, including e-cigarettes, vapes and loose-leaf tobacco, jumped from 12 per cent in 2017 to 80 per cent in 2025.

However, Labor has warned that the Coalition's pitch risks undermining the progress made, with daily smoking rates having fallen to a record low of 5.8 per cent and vaping rates on the decline.

World.title: Perth man charged with murder after rural shooting death
World.content:
Police have charged a 38-year-old man with murder after a 44-year-old man was shot dead at a rural property in Perth's south, triggering a major security operation.

The 38-year-old man, from Mount Richon, who was taken into custody on Saturday, will appear before the Armadale Magistrates Court on Monday. Police say the two men were known to each other.

Police swarmed an orchard in Keysbrook after a serious incident. (ABC News)

Heavily armed police swarmed the Hilltop Orchard property in Keysbrook, about 70 kilometres south-east of the CBD, after the incident.

The victim's partner — a woman in her 40s — and her young son were inside the residence at the time of the shooting, but managed to flee to a neighbour's house where they called emergency services.

Police said detectives had found three firearms inside the residence.

"These firearms remain the subject of ongoing investigations," the police said in a statement.

The property was cordoned off as police contained the incident. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

Major police search

On Saturday, dramatic aerial footage showed officers systematically searching multiple structures, including a house, shipping containers and tin sheds, to ensure there was no ongoing threat to the community.

The 38-year-old man was found sitting in a vehicle at the property and was apprehended without incident, Detective Senior Sergeant Stephen Cleal said.

Two officers stood guard over the man who was placed inside a police vehicle. (ABC News)

Police said they do not believe the man in custody was a licensed firearms holder.

An aerial view of the property, which includes an orchard. (ABC News)

"What has occurred in this house is tragic to say the least, and my thoughts go out to the family and friends who knew the deceased," Detective Senior Sergeant Cleal said on Saturday.

At least eight police vehicles, forensics officers and three St John ambulance crews were sent to the scene.

World.title: Homophobic graffiti sprayed on Sydney MP's office under investigation
World.content:
Homophobic graffiti sprayed on the outside walls and windows of Sydney MP Alex Greenwich's office is under investigation by NSW Police.

Mr Greenwich told the ABC that the vandalism was unprecedented.

"I've got lots of written threats, phone abuse, social media, but never anything like this," he said.

Alex Greenwich says he has never experienced this level of attack before. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

Reports of the attack at the Oxford Street premises in the inner-east Sydney suburb of Surry Hills were received by police on Sunday at about 12pm.

"A crime scene has been established, and investigators are reviewing CCTV and conducting inquiries to identify the people involved," police said in a statement.

In a post on social media, Mr Greenwich said the incident was "deeply distressing" for both his staff and himself.

"No-one should face this kind of hatred in their workplace, especially on the 9th anniversary of Australia’s marriage equality YES vote," the post said.

"If the intention was to intimidate me, it has had the opposite effect. I’m more determined than ever to make Sydney and NSW safer, fairer and more equal for our community."

The incident has been condemned as "vile". (Supplied)

Allegra Spender, the federal member for Wentworth, condemned the incident as "vile", saying she was "disgusted and appalled".

"There is no place for homophobia or hate in our community, and certainly not in Australian politics," she said.

"Words matter, and this kind of attack is designed to intimidate and harm."

She added that her electorate was "sending you all our love and support".

Focus on violence against politicians

The vandalism comes after growing awareness and discussion on violence against politicians, after the shocking car attack on Victorian Independent MP Helen Haines, which led to both her legs being amputated.

NSW MP Jodie Harrison told the ABC last month that the attack on Ms Haines had resurfaced memories of nine years ago when two envelopes containing death threats were slipped under the door.

Threats to MPs linked to political debate AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett on the correlation between heated moments of political discourse and the number of threats reported against politicians.

"It made me feel physically sick," she said.

"One of the downsides of public life is that people who might not like us know that we can actually easily be found, because we're public people."

Recently, AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC's Insider programme that there was a direct link between inflammatory political discourse and threats against parliamentarians.

"It does have a direct correlation to what we see in terms of threats and abuse, and sometimes it's very immediate," she said.

"I would challenge any Australian to read some of these threats and some of the abuse that is reported to us from federal parliamentarians and for anyone to argue that that is free speech or political discourse."

Police are urging anyone with information to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or Surry Hills Police Area Command.

World.title: Jillaroos' World Cup win is more of the same old story
World.content:
Right from the start, the women's Rugby League World Cup final was yet another version of the same old story.

Australia's 34-10 win over New Zealand was the latest procession for the Jillaroos, who cruised to victory on the back of a brilliant and brutal beginning from which the Kiwi Ferns never recovered.

Against the second-best team in the world, the Jillaroos still looked several classes above. By the time New Zealand completed its first set it was already down 12-0.

Rugby League World Cup finals live: Look back on all the action in our blog.

Jillaroos win Rugby League World Cup A dominant first-half performance and a Jaime Chapman hat-trick has fired the Jillaroos to a 34-10 victory over New Zealand in the Rugby League World Cup final.

The Australians fell short of beating the clock in the first half but with a 34-6 lead at the break they went pretty close.

Jess Skinner's side has the greatest collection of talent the women's game has ever seen and it was typified by the likes of Jamie Chapman and Jess Sergis, who both turned one-out runs into long range tries.

Chapman was particularly exceptional. Her first-half hat-trick displayed the full dimensions of her athleticism: the strength of her first try, the graceful finish for her second and the speed she showed for her third earned her player-of-the-match honours.

A repeat of the 2022 final, which Australia won by 50, looked to be on the cards before a meandering second half in the thick Brisbane humidity and by the end, the match was falling over the line.

It was far from their greatest performance but the Jillaroos are the kind of team who would be good enough on a bad day and New Zealand, like everyone else who's run into the Jillaroos through this World Cup, was helpless to stop what was coming.

You might as well ask them to stop the tide coming in or stop the sun rising in the morning.

The Kiwi Ferns did a better job of it in the second half but the contest was already gone. Winning the second half is little consolation if it's a World Cup final and what long felt inevitable came to pass when Isabelle Kelly lifted the trophy.

Australia was way too good for New Zealand right from the start. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

This victory and that inevitability is both a measure of how far the game has come and a reminder of the cost of that progress.

Through the development of the NRLW, Australia is so much better than everyone else that its dominance threatens the international game as a spectacle.

Australia has so many players who can light up a match. Chapman's speed, power and finishing abilities, Jessie Southwell's kicking game and Olivia Kernick's cunning and strength are all rugby league joys to behold.

But it always adds up to the same thing. We always end up in the same place and if the journey always has the same ending it makes it harder to follow it through to the end.

It has made this tournament a slog and there is no way out of it either, not for a while yet.

There is no end in sight to Australia's dominance. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Samoa and Fiji both have improvement in them and New Zealand will get better as the Warriors settle back into the NRLW, but the depth of Australia's talent is near bottomless.

For any other nation, losing a player like Millie Elliott to retirement would be a hammer blow that leaves behind an enormous space to fill.

But the only problem for Australia will be choosing between the excellent options at their disposal.

Sarah Togatuki, fresh off making the Dally M team of the year, can't make this side. Neither can Cronulla's Ellie Johnston or Tigers signing Rima Butler.

For any other nation, they'd be automatic selections every single time. For Australia, they must wait their turn.

Couple that with the fact that the best football is still ahead of someone like Jesse Southwell, a World Cup winner at 21, and this era of Australian domination has no end in sight.

They are not a big fish in a small pond; they are a leviathan in a bathtub and even as they crush all comers, they keep growing.

World.title: Labor talks health, Coalition crime as both parties play in safe spaces
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Labor talks health, Coalition crime as both parties play in safe spaces Kieran Rooney, Angus Delaney and Patrick Hatch November 16, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Labor and the Coalition have pivoted to their respective policy strengths in launching their election campaigns, with Premier Ben Carroll promising $1.2 billion for hospital wait lists while Jess Wilson pledged new stalking penalties six years after the murder of Melbourne woman Celeste Manno. Carroll sought to inspire the Labor faithful to action in the face of dire polling, at a campaign launch in Moonee Ponds on Sunday, as a quarter of staff in party headquarters are sent out to assist local campaigns. Jess Wilson and Ben Carroll at their respective campaign launches on Sunday. The Age Wilson and senior Liberals received rock star welcomes from party faithful at Olympic Park, whereas the mood at the Labor launch was less buoyant. But senior Liberals said the Coalition couldn’t afford to get ahead of itself, and warned of a close election. At the Labor event, Carroll promised $1.17 billion to deliver an extra 100,000 planned surgeries over the next four years, and $195 million for 500,000 more specialist appointments that facilitate these surgeries.



He sought to contrast the policy, which is for the public health system, with the Coalition’s $1.27 billion pledge to pay the private sector to deliver another 25,000 surgeries a year. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Coalition’s flagship health policy hit by $880 million budget shortfall The Age revealed in October that the Coalition’s promise to fund its surgery commitment by winding up the state-owned investment company Breakthrough Victoria fell $880 million short of what the party had anticipated. Carroll argued his scheme was $100 million cheaper than the Coalition’s plan and that the money was better spent going to the public system. His wife, Fiona Rothville, sought to reinforce this message as she introduced the premier to the stage at Moonee Ponds.



She started by sharing the complications she experienced when pregnant with the couple’s daughter. Madeleine was underweight and spent a month in hospital after she was born. “Ben is a rock. I was in hospital in a wheelchair and didn’t see Madeleine for days. I didn’t worry. I knew he was there for Madeleine,” Rothville said. Carroll and wife Fiona Rothville and their daughter, Madeleine, earlier this month. Jason South Carroll, who emerged after this story to cheers from those in the room, said his family had needed the public system because the private sector couldn’t always handle complex specialist requirements like theirs. “Those doctors saved my family,” he said.



The mood in the room at Kellaway Avenue Neighbourhood Centre in Moonee Ponds was positive, but not as rapturous as Labor campaign events in previous election years. The latest Resolve Political Monitor shows Labor is headed for defeat with a primary vote of 20 per cent, compared to 30 per cent for the Coalition and 23 per cent for One Nation. Robyn Baillieu takes a selfie with her husband Ted (right) and another former Victorian premier, Jeff Kennett, at the Liberals’ event. Luis Enrique Ascui Carroll on Sunday accused the Coalition of acting like it had already won the election and not revealing enough detail about its policies, including costings. Labor national secretary Paul Erickson on Friday night gave a pep talk to staff at the Victorian campaign headquarters, which included party officials from interstate who are in Melbourne to inform their own approach to contests against One Nation.



One-quarter of staff at Labor headquarters have been sent to local campaigns as the centralised operation scales down. Early voting opens on Wednesday. Over the weekend, Labor made nearly $3 billion in commitments in education and health, and accused the Coalition of preparing to cut these areas, where voters typically rate Labor higher. Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles at Sunday’s Labor launch. Louis Trerise Wilson has focused on the Coalition’s strength of crime and community safety. On Monday, she will announce a suite of reforms to stalking laws, including a trial of round-the-clock monitoring of high-risk stalkers.



The use of GPS tracking will attempt to prevent stalkers entering exclusion zones around their victims’ homes and workplaces. The reforms will also enable non-family violence stalking victims access to the same courtroom protections as victims of family violence. This would include allowing stalking victims to tender pre-recorded evidence, and prevent perpetrators from cross-examining victims. The policy is named in recognition of Celeste Manno, a 23-year-old Melbourne woman who was stabbed to death by an obsessed colleague who broke into her family home six years ago. Celeste Manno (centre), her mother Aggie Di Mauro (left) and killer Luay Sako. AAP, Supplied Manno’s killer became infatuated with her, prompting Manno and her mother to report their concerns to police and take out an interim invervention order against him.



After her murder, Labor ordered a review by the Victorian Law Reform Commission, which in July 2021 made 46 recommendations, but most were never acted on. Manno’s mother, Aggie Di Mauro, has repeatedly criticised the lack of progress, and told the Herald Sun earlier this year that Labor was “doing nothing … it’s absolutely disgusting”. Related Article Updated

Courts ‘It’s outrageous’: Devastated mum of Celeste Manno furious as daughter’s killer avoids life sentence On Sunday, Wilson said Manno’s case clearly identified that regardless of who a victim was being stalked by, they deserved the same legal protections. “Celeste Manno should still be here today,” Wilson said. “Her death exposed gaps in our justice system that must be addressed.” The Coalition is promising to implement all 46 recommendations from the review, introduce mandatory specialist stalking training for police, toughen laws against digital stalking, introduce perpetrator behaviour change programs, and improve victim support for regional and rural Victorians.



Related Article Victorian election After 12 years, crime may bring Labor undone. How have rising rates affected your suburb? Former Liberal leader Brad Battin introduced Wilson to the launch as the “next premier of Victoria”, and all published polling suggests he will be proven right. But Wilson and state president Brian Loughnane urged the room to take nothing for granted. “Make no mistake, this election will be close,” Wilson said. “There is much that is unusual about this election, and with that comes great risk.” Loughnane, who took up the role as state president at the request of Wilson and others, said the Liberals need a historic swing to win.



“This is a very complex election, much more so than the public commentary and the polls would suggest,” he said. Without mentioning One Nation, Wilson acknowledged the anger in the electorate and positioned the Liberal Party as the solution, not Pauline Hanson. Liberal state president Brian Loughnane on Sunday. Getty Images “They are right to be frustrated,” Wilson said of voters. “They are right to be angry.” But she added that while “anger and frustration are good at identifying problems ... we need more than that”. “We need solutions.”





The surprise speaker at the Liberal event was Samantha Byrne, the party’s candidate for the seat of Niddrie, who is working to unseat the premier. Internally, the Liberals believe Carroll’s seat is vulnerable, and Byrne said voters in her electorate felt taken for granted by Labor. “I think it’s time to give Ben Carroll and Labor the wake-up call they deserve,” she said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Everyone wrote us off’: Historic night as Kangaroos, Jillaroos beat Kiwis to make it four in a row
World.content:
Brisbane: We should have known this was going to be Australia’s night from the actual kick-off.

There was so much excitement about New Zealand heading into Sunday night’s World Cup final.

There were plenty of black jerseys walking the muggy streets of Brisbane in the afternoon, a lot of buzz when the players performed the haka, and the comfort that they had newly-crowned Golden Boot winner Kalyn Ponga calling the shots at the back.

But Jamayne Isaako sent the kick-off far too deep, the Kangaroos received a penalty, marched down field and scored a try via Liam Martin.

Rugby league fans have spent the past month working out whether this could finally be the year the Australians lost the World Cup.

Could it be Tonga? Maybe Samoa? New Zealand had the forward pack and Ponga and arguably should have won the Cup opener against the Kangaroos.

But when it mattered most, the class rose to the top and the men wearing green and gold won the Cup for a fourth straight time, triumphing 32-12.

Liam Martin and Jack Bostock both scored two tries each in Australia’s World Cup triumph. Getty Images

Martin finished with a double. Isaah Yeo, 100 days after rupturing his pec against the New Zealand Warriors, was inspirational in the middle. You can only imagine the sense of satisfaction when he lifted the trophy in the middle of Suncorp Stadium. He never once gave up on returning to the field from such a serious injury, and had this final forever in the back of his mind.

Jack Bostock bagged a double, Tom Trbojevic got across the line for his ninth Cup try, and Bradman Best did his stocks no harm with a try, a try-saver on Jahrome Hughes, and an excellent pass for Bostock’s final four-pointer.

Throw in the magic of Reece Walsh, the unpredictability of Cam Munster, a bone-jarring tackle from Jacob Preston on Naufahu Whyte, and the craftiness of Harry Grant, we should have all known Australia were never going to get rolled.

They are rugby league’s equivalent of almighty racehorse Winx. We keep trying to convince ourselves they are about to get rolled, but they do not know how.

The longer the tournament went, the better Australia got. Kevin Walters never panicked, and the coach was always on the money.

Like Yeo, Walters thoroughly deserves to head to England to take up the head coaching role with St Helens knowing he bows out a winner. He wanted this as much as his skipper.

James Tedesco, who was overlooked for Walsh for most of the tournament, will forever appreciate Walters putting him on late when the match was won, and full well knowing this was probably going to be the last time he pulled on the Roos’ colours.

The Kangaroos congratulate Moses Leota at fulltime following the World Cup final in Brisbane. Getty Images

New Zealand were excellent most of this tournament, but their errors were punished most of the night. They came up with too many errors, and Australia knew what to do with the invites.

Losing Casey McLean to a delayed concussion at half-time did not hurt their cause, but it also did not cost them the win.

New Zealand and the rest of the rugby league nations need to wait another four years for their special day.

World.title: I have schizophrenia. There are no monsters under my bed.  I’m a person, not a headline
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsPsychology Opinion I have schizophrenia. There are no monsters under my bed. I’m a person, not a headline Heidi Everett Contributor November 15, 2026 — 8:00pm

November 15, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Every day I buy myself a coffee. It reminds me I am an adult, despite all the things convincing me, and perhaps society, otherwise. I work hard to remind myself I’m actually OK. The world is not falling apart because of my existence and there are no monsters under my bed. Buying a coffee is a way to remind myself I am an adult human, not just a diagnosis. Photograph by Chris Hopkins Then out of nowhere, I get another reminder: I am bad. As I’m waiting for my coffee, I glance down at the newspaper stand and there in big, bold shouty letters is my health condition linked to a shockingly violent crime. Instead of leaving the cafe sipping my freshly brewed coffee, I become a walking headline.



I was diagnosed with schizophrenia at 23. My version was schizoaffective, which usually involves hallucinations or delusions and mood changes. (There are at least seven subtypes). When I was young, I was bullied by classmates and teachers alike and the fictional world of Narnia became my happy place. As I got older, magical friends were displaced by people more interested in how I’d believe anything I was told. My skills living in other worlds became a form of survival. While I was still a teenager, the streets became a familiar place and that’s where I was later scraped up and put into a public psych ward full of human suffering. The diagnosis I got for the rest of my life was based on a set of questions asked by a male psychiatrist I’d only just met (in a suit and bow tie no less). Did I hear voices? Did I see things nobody else did? Did I want to die? I answered yes to everything – I wanted to tell him my “voices” were jazz singers, opera sopranos and orchestras, but lacked the ability to respond beyond yes or no. There were no long conversations about the difficult times, places and people I’d already lived through. Twenty minutes later, I became Schizophrenia. No longer Heidi Everett – artist, wannabe park ranger and Michael J. Fox’s wife. Just Schizophrenia.



Related Article Haines attack Dezi Freeman and Helen Haines’ alleged attacker needed mental health help before attacks. None came One of the hallmarks of my condition is psychosis. Its Greek and Latin etymology means “abnormal condition of the soul”. But these days, anything with “psych” in the title equates to “mind” alone. And just like my doctor’s report, that label is all over the headlines again. I categorically condemn the actions of all people who hurt other people. Sadly, when psychosis is a factor in someone doing something inconceivably awful, it’s me and my friends with schizophrenia who are implicated. Our diagnosis is the explainer. My schizy community is enduring another round of shame because the latest research indicates we are to blame. So we decide it’s better to not play tennis today, meet for coffee or go for that job interview. Reading these headlines I can see why people might be fearful of psychosis. Mental health is complex, yet a whole community of disabled people bear the shame. The stigma does the driving, but we pay the toll. In the 20th century, the medical model sought to cure, treat or prevent health conditions. But in the early 2000s, the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities said, “You know what, let’s try improving the environments we all share to reduce the disabling element of health conditions.” I learnt Auslan as part of the move towards a more inclusive society, and we’re all pretty good with guide dogs and ramps now. But this social model doesn’t seem to extend to accommodating people with psychosocial conditions such as schizophrenia.



The mental health system, led by psychiatry, still reigns supreme and psychosis is the problem; not social attitudes, practices or infrastructure that cause or enhance it. The social model of disability has moved on from deficit language and attitudes. So, I refer to my disability as “complex mental health” rather than using my clinical diagnosis. For me, a flare-up happens when the stresses of life become too much. These can be both mundane – starting a job, too much admin, lack of accessible public transport – and extraordinary things like homelessness or grief. Psychosis can happen when both categories get lots of ticks. Related Article Opinion

Homelessness Every night, I walk the city’s streets. For someone like me, it’s safer to keep moving Heidi Everett Contributor I have a posse of familiar people I trust and I talk to them regularly. But I don’t have any faith left in our mental health system. It has surpassed its capacity for stress management and is now in its own state of psychosis. The biggest barrier to people asking for help is the fact there’s no one around to ask. I’d love it if Australia had a Triple Zero option for mental health emergencies, staffed by crisis teams, carers, First Nations and lived expertise peers. It’d be far more practical to have someone rock up in sneakers (perhaps with a Labrador and a tennis ball) than police with Tasers and handcuffs.



People with conditions such as schizophrenia aren’t only mentally ill – we are creative geniuses who have developed some remarkable coping mechanisms to survive brutal social abuses. Headlines don’t fill the void in public understanding or reduce violence. The UN states that framing mental health conditions as a social burden undermines equal rights, inclusion and access to care. It’s our right to go through the day not feeling ashamed, frightened or stigmatised by a health condition. We need to start having dignified dialogue with people with lived experience of complex mental health, and systems to make sure we have a society built on conversations, not left reeling from a headline. If you or anyone you know needs support, contact Kids Helpline on 1800 551 800, Lifeline on 131 114 or Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636. Heidi Everett is an artist, writer and mental health advocate. World.title: New data points to major inflection point in the fight against illegal tobacco
World.content:
PoliticsFederalTobacco New data points to major inflection point in the fight against illegal tobacco Paul Sakkal November 15, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australia’s lucrative illicit tobacco market may finally be shrinking after years of rampant criminality including homicides and more than 300 firebombings that turned cigarette taxes into a frontline political issue. New federal data suggests the black market has contracted by between 79 tonnes and 1400 tonnes over the past year. The drop points to the success of tighter border enforcement, alongside aggressive store closures in NSW and Queensland. Victoria has been a laggard, only beginning to close shops in September, long after other states. A closure notice on the front door of a tobacco store in Docklands, Melbourne, where authorities have started to crack down. Paul Rovere Because the black market is difficult to measure, the estimate spans a wide range. It was developed by combining wastewater testing for combustible nicotine with the best available measure of household use, being Australian Institute of Health and Welfare data released earlier this year. The illicit tobacco commission, which compiled the data, believes it shows the crackdown has yielded results.



“Just 12 months into scaled-up enforcement … the data is encouraging, including record seizures at the border,” assistant minister for customs Julian Hill said. “As other states and territories follow South Australia and Queensland’s lead and dial up shop closures, we want to see a bigger impact on the illicit market.” The Coalition and One Nation have been calling for drastic cuts in the tobacco excise to strip profits from criminal networks. NSW Labor Premier Chris Minns has also been calling to wind back taxes that have pushed legal cigarettes above $50 a pack, compared with the $10-$20 price for illegal ones. But Labor has stuck to its view that narrowing the profit margin for criminals is not the right approach and would lead to higher smoking rates. Instead, it has put renewed effort into intercepting cargo at the border and pushing state governments to clamp down on dodgy tobacconists. The scourge of illegal tobacco has caused particular damage in the streets of Melbourne, where an underworld gang controlled by the notorious Kaz Hamad orchestrated a wave of violence to control the booming market.



Federal data shows seizures of tobacco at the border are up 50 per cent on the same time last year. Interceptions of vapes have increased by nearly 20 per cent. Annual spending on illegal tobacco is estimated at $8.5 billion, more than on ecstasy, heroin, cannabis and cocaine combined. Researchers from University of Sydney and Deakin University argued before the new data release that an enforcement-only response to the illicit market would fail in the same way as the war on drugs. Public health lecturer Edward Jegasothy and associate professor in criminology James Martin used an article in The Conversation to say that “the world’s highest tobacco taxes” handed control of the market to criminals. Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics states illicit sources of tobacco grew from about 12 per cent to as high as 80 per cent as legal prices rose. Gangs, the researchers argued, factored in the cost of seizures and arrests of lower-level criminals and easily replaced jailed operatives with a steady supply of willing mules.



“What the government has not yet done is examine highly regressive tobacco taxation and its rejection of reduced harm alternatives. It should evaluate whether they are fit for purpose, ethically or practically,” the researchers wrote. “The division is … not partisan but jurisdictional, with the Commonwealth collecting the excise while the states are left with the mess. “Until that happens, the response to each failure of prohibition will be more prohibition.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: This school’s black and red blazers are more than a uniform. They’re a passport to a prestigious network
World.content:
In its 148 years, Xavier has produced a Queensland premier, a lord mayor of Melbourne, and 18 federal and state MPs. Schoolboys who enter the exclusive Kew Catholic school’s gates are “Xaverians for life”.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Walking into Xavier College – with its Great Hall, its 250-space underground temperature-controlled car park, 600-strong rotating art collection, lush sporting ovals and view of the city skyline – feels less like entering a school and more like gaining access to Melbourne’s upper echelons. And that’s just for a visitor. For the boys who enter the Kew college’s gates, the black and red blazer is a passport that will gain them entry to an exclusive network that can open doors throughout their lives – in business, politics and sport. Xavier is exclusive and prestigious, with annual fees above $44,000 for every secondary year level. For that fee, families gain access to not only great facilities and teaching, but to one of the largest alumni communities in Australia, according to Xavier. Xavier College rector Father Chris Middleton with students in front of the school’s chapel. Simon Schluter But enrolments at the Catholic boys’ school have been declining for more than a decade. The decline has occurred alongside the cost-of-living crisis and changing demographics, and as most boys’ schools battle the general perception that single-sex schools can breed hypermasculine culture.





And at the end of last year, former Xavier student Tom Silvagni, the son of AFL legend Stephen Silvagni, was convicted of two counts of rape. Interim principal Lee MacMaster, who is about to retire after 46 years as an educator, said the news of Silvagni’s conviction, which Silvagni is appealing, sent reverberations through the whole school. “Things like this should never happen,” he said. MacMaster said the school had strong relationships with girls’ schools, there were female staff in senior roles, and a no-tolerance approach was taken to misogyny. “What we’re trying to educate our boys is there’s something much bigger than yourself,” he said. In its 148 years, Xavier has produced a Queensland premier, a lord mayor of Melbourne, and 18 federal and state members of parliament – including former leader of the federal opposition Bill Shorten and federal member for Wannon Dan Tehan. Tehan, who graduated in 1985, said Xavier taught him not to take things at face value but to prosecute, interrogate and always seek the truth.



Tehan said he also gained a group of lifelong friends. “That is to me what a great education should be about,” he said. Celebrity chef Adam D’Sylva and his son Javier at Xavier College. Luis Enrique Ascui Xavier alumni include 16 graduates who have been knighted, two Rhodes Scholars and a High Court judge. There have also been 62 OAM recipients and a United Nations special rapporteur. Celebrity chef Adam D’Sylva, who has appeared on MasterChef and Snack Masters and is the owner of newly hatted restaurant Decca, is among the famous alumni. “Once you go to Xavier, you are a Xaverian for life,” said D’Sylva. “What Xavier gave me, aside from the academic side, it gave me the feeling that you can be invincible, you can do anything and be anything you want in life.” He said his teenage daughter jokingly calls his network of Xavier friends a cult.



“But it’s a really good cult,” he said. Academically, Xavier achieved a median VCE study score of 33 in 2025, above the state average of 30, yet it wasn’t among the state’s top-performing schools last year. But as a founding member of the Associated Public Schools of Victoria (APS Sport), Xavier’s sporting teams are among the state’s most competitive. While Xavier doesn’t offer standalone sports scholarships, the school has produced more than 149 AFL players, 17 Olympians and a Paralympian. Head of sports Michael Wilson said sporting scouts often visit games, and AFL teams use the school’s football oval. He said the school had replicated a professional sporting environment on campus where they could. “We put GPS units on our footballs so we can track the distances they run, ice baths after class, world-class gym with gym instructors; it’s a unique opportunity for our boys to taste-test what they are going into,” Wilson said.

World.title: Labor talks health, Coalition crime as both parties play in safe spaces
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Labor talks health, Coalition crime as both parties play in safe spaces Kieran Rooney, Angus Delaney and Patrick Hatch November 16, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Labor and the Coalition have pivoted to their respective policy strengths in launching their election campaigns, with Premier Ben Carroll promising $1.2 billion for hospital wait lists while Jess Wilson pledged new stalking penalties six years after the murder of Melbourne woman Celeste Manno. Carroll sought to inspire the Labor faithful to action in the face of dire polling, at a campaign launch in Moonee Ponds on Sunday, as a quarter of staff in party headquarters are sent out to assist local campaigns. Jess Wilson and Ben Carroll at their respective campaign launches on Sunday. The Age Wilson and senior Liberals received rock star welcomes from party faithful at Olympic Park, whereas the mood at the Labor launch was less buoyant. But senior Liberals said the Coalition couldn’t afford to get ahead of itself, and warned of a close election. At the Labor event, Carroll promised $1.17 billion to deliver an extra 100,000 planned surgeries over the next four years, and $195 million for 500,000 more specialist appointments that facilitate these surgeries.



He sought to contrast the policy, which is for the public health system, with the Coalition’s $1.27 billion pledge to pay the private sector to deliver another 25,000 surgeries a year. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Coalition’s flagship health policy hit by $880 million budget shortfall The Age revealed in October that the Coalition’s promise to fund its surgery commitment by winding up the state-owned investment company Breakthrough Victoria fell $880 million short of what the party had anticipated. Carroll argued his scheme was $100 million cheaper than the Coalition’s plan and that the money was better spent going to the public system. His wife, Fiona Rothville, sought to reinforce this message as she introduced the premier to the stage at Moonee Ponds.



She started by sharing the complications she experienced when pregnant with the couple’s daughter. Madeleine was underweight and spent a month in hospital after she was born. “Ben is a rock. I was in hospital in a wheelchair and didn’t see Madeleine for days. I didn’t worry. I knew he was there for Madeleine,” Rothville said. Carroll and wife Fiona Rothville and their daughter, Madeleine, earlier this month. Jason South Carroll, who emerged after this story to cheers from those in the room, said his family had needed the public system because the private sector couldn’t always handle complex specialist requirements like theirs. “Those doctors saved my family,” he said.



The mood in the room at Kellaway Avenue Neighbourhood Centre in Moonee Ponds was positive, but not as rapturous as Labor campaign events in previous election years. The latest Resolve Political Monitor shows Labor is headed for defeat with a primary vote of 20 per cent, compared to 30 per cent for the Coalition and 23 per cent for One Nation. Robyn Baillieu takes a selfie with her husband Ted (right) and another former Victorian premier, Jeff Kennett, at the Liberals’ event. Luis Enrique Ascui Carroll on Sunday accused the Coalition of acting like it had already won the election and not revealing enough detail about its policies, including costings. Labor national secretary Paul Erickson on Friday night gave a pep talk to staff at the Victorian campaign headquarters, which included party officials from interstate who are in Melbourne to inform their own approach to contests against One Nation.



One-quarter of staff at Labor headquarters have been sent to local campaigns as the centralised operation scales down. Early voting opens on Wednesday. Over the weekend, Labor made nearly $3 billion in commitments in education and health, and accused the Coalition of preparing to cut these areas, where voters typically rate Labor higher. Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles at Sunday’s Labor launch. Louis Trerise Wilson has focused on the Coalition’s strength of crime and community safety. On Monday, she will announce a suite of reforms to stalking laws, including a trial of round-the-clock monitoring of high-risk stalkers.



The use of GPS tracking will attempt to prevent stalkers entering exclusion zones around their victims’ homes and workplaces. The reforms will also enable non-family violence stalking victims access to the same courtroom protections as victims of family violence. This would include allowing stalking victims to tender pre-recorded evidence, and prevent perpetrators from cross-examining victims. The policy is named in recognition of Celeste Manno, a 23-year-old Melbourne woman who was stabbed to death by an obsessed colleague who broke into her family home six years ago. Celeste Manno (centre), her mother Aggie Di Mauro (left) and killer Luay Sako. AAP, Supplied Manno’s killer became infatuated with her, prompting Manno and her mother to report their concerns to police and take out an interim invervention order against him.



After her murder, Labor ordered a review by the Victorian Law Reform Commission, which in July 2021 made 46 recommendations, but most were never acted on. Manno’s mother, Aggie Di Mauro, has repeatedly criticised the lack of progress, and told the Herald Sun earlier this year that Labor was “doing nothing … it’s absolutely disgusting”. Related Article Updated

Courts ‘It’s outrageous’: Devastated mum of Celeste Manno furious as daughter’s killer avoids life sentence On Sunday, Wilson said Manno’s case clearly identified that regardless of who a victim was being stalked by, they deserved the same legal protections. “Celeste Manno should still be here today,” Wilson said. “Her death exposed gaps in our justice system that must be addressed.” The Coalition is promising to implement all 46 recommendations from the review, introduce mandatory specialist stalking training for police, toughen laws against digital stalking, introduce perpetrator behaviour change programs, and improve victim support for regional and rural Victorians.



Related Article Victorian election After 12 years, crime may bring Labor undone. How have rising rates affected your suburb? Former Liberal leader Brad Battin introduced Wilson to the launch as the “next premier of Victoria”, and all published polling suggests he will be proven right. But Wilson and state president Brian Loughnane urged the room to take nothing for granted. “Make no mistake, this election will be close,” Wilson said. “There is much that is unusual about this election, and with that comes great risk.” Loughnane, who took up the role as state president at the request of Wilson and others, said the Liberals need a historic swing to win.



“This is a very complex election, much more so than the public commentary and the polls would suggest,” he said. Without mentioning One Nation, Wilson acknowledged the anger in the electorate and positioned the Liberal Party as the solution, not Pauline Hanson. Liberal state president Brian Loughnane on Sunday. Getty Images “They are right to be frustrated,” Wilson said of voters. “They are right to be angry.” But she added that while “anger and frustration are good at identifying problems ... we need more than that”. “We need solutions.”





The surprise speaker at the Liberal event was Samantha Byrne, the party’s candidate for the seat of Niddrie, who is working to unseat the premier. Internally, the Liberals believe Carroll’s seat is vulnerable, and Byrne said voters in her electorate felt taken for granted by Labor. “I think it’s time to give Ben Carroll and Labor the wake-up call they deserve,” she said. World.title: ‘Everyone wrote us off’: Historic night as Kangaroos, Jillaroos beat Kiwis to make it four in a row
World.content:
Brisbane: We should have known this was going to be Australia’s night from the actual kick-off.

There was so much excitement about New Zealand heading into Sunday night’s World Cup final.

There were plenty of black jerseys walking the muggy streets of Brisbane in the afternoon, a lot of buzz when the players performed the haka, and the comfort that they had newly-crowned Golden Boot winner Kalyn Ponga calling the shots at the back.

But Jamayne Isaako sent the kick-off far too deep, the Kangaroos received a penalty, marched down field and scored a try via Liam Martin.

Rugby league fans have spent the past month working out whether this could finally be the year the Australians lost the World Cup.

Could it be Tonga? Maybe Samoa? New Zealand had the forward pack and Ponga and arguably should have won the Cup opener against the Kangaroos.

But when it mattered most, the class rose to the top and the men wearing green and gold won the Cup for a fourth straight time, triumphing 32-12.

Liam Martin and Jack Bostock both scored two tries each in Australia’s World Cup triumph. Getty Images

Martin finished with a double. Isaah Yeo, 100 days after rupturing his pec against the New Zealand Warriors, was inspirational in the middle. You can only imagine the sense of satisfaction when he lifted the trophy in the middle of Suncorp Stadium. He never once gave up on returning to the field from such a serious injury, and had this final forever in the back of his mind.

Jack Bostock bagged a double, Tom Trbojevic got across the line for his ninth Cup try, and Bradman Best did his stocks no harm with a try, a try-saver on Jahrome Hughes, and an excellent pass for Bostock’s final four-pointer.

Throw in the magic of Reece Walsh, the unpredictability of Cam Munster, a bone-jarring tackle from Jacob Preston on Naufahu Whyte, and the craftiness of Harry Grant, we should have all known Australia were never going to get rolled.

They are rugby league’s equivalent of almighty racehorse Winx. We keep trying to convince ourselves they are about to get rolled, but they do not know how.

The longer the tournament went, the better Australia got. Kevin Walters never panicked, and the coach was always on the money.

Like Yeo, Walters thoroughly deserves to head to England to take up the head coaching role with St Helens knowing he bows out a winner. He wanted this as much as his skipper.

James Tedesco, who was overlooked for Walsh for most of the tournament, will forever appreciate Walters putting him on late when the match was won, and full well knowing this was probably going to be the last time he pulled on the Roos’ colours.

The Kangaroos congratulate Moses Leota at fulltime following the World Cup final in Brisbane. Getty Images

New Zealand were excellent most of this tournament, but their errors were punished most of the night. They came up with too many errors, and Australia knew what to do with the invites.

Losing Casey McLean to a delayed concussion at half-time did not hurt their cause, but it also did not cost them the win.

New Zealand and the rest of the rugby league nations need to wait another four years for their special day.

World.content:

Terry Wooldridge of Mona Vale is another fan of the Australia Hotel’s Sportsman’s Bar (C8): “It served icy cold beers but the most notable fact was it was the birthplace of the Leprechaun Rugby Club in the early 1970s, which played in the Sydney Subbies comp for several years. Are there any old Leprechauns out there?”

“When shopping in Sydney as a young adult in the 1950s, I always felt a sense of pride if I was among those shoppers carrying bags with the distinctive black and white houndstooth pattern indicating a purchase from David Jones (C8),” recalls Christine Perrott of Armidale. “Is there an equivalent today? Perhaps a handbag by a certain designer? However, that’s not quite the same, is it?”

In an effort to move on from all this David Jones chat (C8), we’ve turned to Dan Aspinall of St Ives: “I’ve never been too fashionable, and not much of a shopper. But when I arrived in Sydney in the early 2000s, I found my retail nirvana. A quick trip to Gowings and I could get a pair of Aussie-made Blundstones, a flat white while having a haircut, secret Santa presents for the new workplace colleagues and a kayak! Puts the middle aisle at Aldi to shame. I’ve still not fully recovered from the closure, although I did enjoy dinner at its new incarnation, Gowings Bar & Grill, recently. I did like the DJs food court 20 years ago, but not enough kayaks to make a lasting impression.”

“While ‘articulate buses’ (C8) are all very well, I prefer the polite, relaxed ride that comes with a ‘courtesy bus’,” says Alan Marel of North Curl Curl.

Peter Russell of Coogee wonders if “ginger-nut biscuits (C8) have to be thinner in Queensland because of weaker teeth due to no fluoridation of water supplies in many council areas?”
