World.title: Big announcements come in twos for Richard Pratt’s granddaughter
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCBD Big announcements come in twos for Richard Pratt’s granddaughter Fiona Byrne November 15, 2026 — 8:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

After tying the knot in Melbourne’s society wedding of the year in early 2025 at the billionaire Pratt family’s Raheen estate in Kew, Bella Falk, granddaughter of late business titan Richard Pratt, and her husband, Jose, are expecting their first child. Falk, the daughter of packaging magnates Raphael and Fiona Geminder, shared her happy news with friends and family last week. Bella Falk at her Strange Luxury pop-up store in Armadale. But it was not the only reveal for the business-minded former model that day, with the news coinciding with the launch of her Strange Luxury pop-up store in upmarket Armadale. After coming up with the idea for Strange Luxury in 2019 while living in Los Angeles, Falk launched the skincare brand in 2024 with one product, the Barrier Balance Cream. She has thoughtfully expanded it into a complete range over the past two years.



Falk’s parents; her sisters Georgia, founder of the Gem bathroom essentials range, and Sammy; her aunt Heloise; cousins Milly and Jacob; and, of course, husband Jose were at the event, and in what should come as no surprise, she has sought wise advice from her family on business matters. “I’m incredibly lucky to be surrounded by such brilliant minds in my family,” Falk told us. “We are all very close, so I’m constantly seeking their advice and leaning on them every step of the way. “One of the strongest values my family has instilled in me is the importance of hard work. Nothing comes without hard work, dedication and persistence. It’s something I have grown up with and a value I will definitely pass down to my own children one day.” Bella and Jose Falk in January 2024. Instagram/@bellafalk_ As for Strange Luxury, it’s all about doing fewer things better and with a personal touch. Falk was on site each day at the pop-up, which wrapped on Sunday, and is across every aspect of her growing business.



“Creating something meaningful takes a lot of time,” she said. Hughesy and his F-bombs primed for home-town crowd When lobby group Get Ahead launched its campaign against the Albanese government’s changes to capital gains tax and treatment of trusts in Sydney last week, it was described as a night of “F-bombs and finfluencers” by the Fin Review, with Dave Hughes adding the celebrity factor. It sounded like quite the night, and it was fortunate that there was not a swear jar for speakers given Hughesy alone reportedly let fly with the F-word 19 times during his impassioned turn on the microphone. Dave Hughes and Nahji Chu at the Sydney launch of the Get Ahead campaign. Oscar Colman



Well, stand by to drag out the swear jar, Melbourne, because our turn is coming. The Get Ahead outfit, headed by Wilson Asset Management founder Geoff Wilson, is holding its Melbourne launch in South Yarra next Sunday, with the state and federal government’s chief comedian-turned-antagonist, Hughes, expected to be on the bill for his home-town launch. When we checked in with him at the weekend, Hughesy confirmed he would “most likely” be there. Tax, trusts and punchlines – it’s going to be a hot ticket. CBD hears business leader Ruslan Kogan, footy champion-turned-fund manager Chris Judd and restaurateur Chris Lucas are also expected to attend. Get Ahead has some pretty well-known names attached, with its board including Wilson, restaurateur Nahji Chu, investor Gabriel Radzyminski, Luxury Escapes founder Adam Schwab and SugarMamma founder Canna Campbell. The campaign spokesman is Tom Humphries. Humphries has a bit on his plate at the moment, being a City of Stonnington councillor and enthusiastic pothole spotter on social media.



Playing a straight bat Talk about timing, as Melbourne breakfast radio king Ross Stevenson kicked off his annual Love Letter To Music lunch in Richmond on Friday, which included the 3AW star detailing prizes up for grabs in a raffle, the latest chapter in Australian cricket’s Sandpapergate scandal was playing out. Around the same time as Stevenson was welcoming guests, Australian captain Pat Cummins was in Sydney in the midst of slamming his former teammate Usman Khawaja’s claims that everyone on the national team knew about the ball tampering that was going on in 2018. From left: Phil Ceberano, Simon Madden, Denis Walter, Jane Kennedy and Myf Warhurst at Ross Stevenson’s 2026 Love Letter To Music Lunch. Fiona Byrne Khawaja had inflamed the festering sore in Australian cricket that Sandpapergate remains by putting forward his take on the scandal in his new memoir, Sabr. He was part of the squad when the notorious sandpaper incident occurred.



Back to the raffle: naturally, in a room full of people interested in news, there was great interest in one of the prizes on offer at Stevenson’s lunch – a cricket bat signed by the Australian cricket team. Signatures including those of Khawaja, Cummins, Dave Warner and Steve Smith. Timing! Russel Howcroft with the raffle prize. Fiona Byrne This year’s sold-out Love Letter to Music, hosted by Stevenson and his AW co-host Russel Howcroft at the Corner Hotel in Richmond, featured odes to the power of music from casting director and author Jane Kennedy, musician Phil Ceberano, 3AW’s Denis Walter, Spicks and Specks panellist Myf Warhurst and former Essendon champion Simon Madden, who described himself as “a pretend guitarist and a bloke who can’t sing”. Turns out Madden can hold a note and can work a crowd. He had no lack of support getting the guests to join him on his pub versions of Daryl Braithwaite’s cover of The Horses and The Angels’ Am I Ever Gonna See Your Face Again – with the unredacted ad lib chorus, of course. Theatre drama



There was some added drama at the early afternoon performance of One Flew Over The Cuckoo’s Nest on Sunday: the show briefly stopped towards the end of act one after a woman in the audience suffered a medical emergency. The stalls of the Athenaeum Theatre were briefly evacuated and an ambulance was called. Jason Donovan stars in One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest. Matt Crockett Ambulance Victoria said the woman was taken to St Vincent’s Hospital. The show resumed after a short break. One Flew Over The Cuckoo’s Nest stars Jason Donovan and Nadine Garner and is in preview performance mode. The show’s gala opening night is on Tuesday.

World.title: I have schizophrenia. There are no monsters under my bed.  I’m a person, not a headline
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsPsychology Opinion I have schizophrenia. There are no monsters under my bed. I’m a person, not a headline Heidi Everett Contributor November 15, 2026 — 8:00pm

Every day I buy myself a coffee. It reminds me I am an adult, despite all the things convincing me, and perhaps society, otherwise. I work hard to remind myself I’m actually OK. The world is not falling apart because of my existence and there are no monsters under my bed. Buying a coffee is a way to remind myself I am an adult human, not just a diagnosis. Photograph by Chris Hopkins Then out of nowhere, I get another reminder: I am bad. As I’m waiting for my coffee, I glance down at the newspaper stand and there in big, bold shouty letters is my health condition linked to a shockingly violent crime. Instead of leaving the cafe sipping my freshly brewed coffee, I become a walking headline.



I was diagnosed with schizophrenia at 23. My version was schizoaffective, which usually involves hallucinations or delusions and mood changes. (There are at least seven subtypes). When I was young, I was bullied by classmates and teachers alike and the fictional world of Narnia became my happy place. As I got older, magical friends were displaced by people more interested in how I’d believe anything I was told. My skills living in other worlds became a form of survival. While I was still a teenager, the streets became a familiar place and that’s where I was later scraped up and put into a public psych ward full of human suffering. The diagnosis I got for the rest of my life was based on a set of questions asked by a male psychiatrist I’d only just met (in a suit and bow tie no less). Did I hear voices? Did I see things nobody else did? Did I want to die? I answered yes to everything – I wanted to tell him my “voices” were jazz singers, opera sopranos and orchestras, but lacked the ability to respond beyond yes or no. There were no long conversations about the difficult times, places and people I’d already lived through. Twenty minutes later, I became Schizophrenia. No longer Heidi Everett – artist, wannabe park ranger and Michael J. Fox’s wife. Just Schizophrenia.



Related Article Haines attack Dezi Freeman and Helen Haines’ alleged attacker needed mental health help before attacks. None came One of the hallmarks of my condition is psychosis. Its Greek and Latin etymology means “abnormal condition of the soul”. But these days, anything with “psych” in the title equates to “mind” alone. And just like my doctor’s report, that label is all over the headlines again. I categorically condemn the actions of all people who hurt other people. Sadly, when psychosis is a factor in someone doing something inconceivably awful, it’s me and my friends with schizophrenia who are implicated. Our diagnosis is the explainer. My schizy community is enduring another round of shame because the latest research indicates we are to blame. So we decide it’s better to not play tennis today, meet for coffee or go for that job interview. Reading these headlines I can see why people might be fearful of psychosis. Mental health is complex, yet a whole community of disabled people bear the shame. The stigma does the driving, but we pay the toll. In the 20th century, the medical model sought to cure, treat or prevent health conditions. But in the early 2000s, the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities said, “You know what, let’s try improving the environments we all share to reduce the disabling element of health conditions.” I learnt Auslan as part of the move towards a more inclusive society, and we’re all pretty good with guide dogs and ramps now. But this social model doesn’t seem to extend to accommodating people with psychosocial conditions such as schizophrenia.



The mental health system, led by psychiatry, still reigns supreme and psychosis is the problem; not social attitudes, practices or infrastructure that cause or enhance it. The social model of disability has moved on from deficit language and attitudes. So, I refer to my disability as “complex mental health” rather than using my clinical diagnosis. For me, a flare-up happens when the stresses of life become too much. These can be both mundane – starting a job, too much admin, lack of accessible public transport – and extraordinary things like homelessness or grief. Psychosis can happen when both categories get lots of ticks. Related Article Opinion

Homelessness Every night, I walk the city’s streets. For someone like me, it’s safer to keep moving Heidi Everett Contributor I have a posse of familiar people I trust and I talk to them regularly. But I don’t have any faith left in our mental health system. It has surpassed its capacity for stress management and is now in its own state of psychosis. The biggest barrier to people asking for help is the fact there’s no one around to ask. I’d love it if Australia had a Triple Zero option for mental health emergencies, staffed by crisis teams, carers, First Nations and lived expertise peers. It’d be far more practical to have someone rock up in sneakers (perhaps with a Labrador and a tennis ball) than police with Tasers and handcuffs.



People with conditions such as schizophrenia aren’t only mentally ill – we are creative geniuses who have developed some remarkable coping mechanisms to survive brutal social abuses. Headlines don’t fill the void in public understanding or reduce violence. The UN states that framing mental health conditions as a social burden undermines equal rights, inclusion and access to care. It’s our right to go through the day not feeling ashamed, frightened or stigmatised by a health condition. We need to start having dignified dialogue with people with lived experience of complex mental health, and systems to make sure we have a society built on conversations, not left reeling from a headline. If you or anyone you know needs support, contact Kids Helpline on 1800 551 800, Lifeline on 131 114 or Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636. Heidi Everett is an artist, writer and mental health advocate. World.title: AI overlords: we were warned
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters AI overlords: we were warned November 15, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Badiucao To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE Can someone please explain the thinking behind AI? It doesn’t make sense to me. Qantas unloads staff thanks to AI, forgetting to refund taxpayer-subsidised billions. Canva unloads staff thanks to AI, as does NAB, and on it goes.

So, when AI eventually steals everyone’s copyright, worker rights and jobs, how do we buy goods without income? We will all need a universal basic income (UBI) that the tech bros promote.

How will this be funded without the taxes from a nation of now-unemployed people. Will Elon pay us all a wage?

A bit of research explains that ‘in order to fund a UBI, significant bureaucratic and taxation reform will be needed’ and ‘the implementation of the UBI will require holistic tax and welfare reform’, but we can’t even tax our own gas companies now, and many big corporations pay no tax at all.

It seems that the amount of rejigging needed for the transfer of misallocated capital to pay a UBI is the same amount of rejigging we’ve always needed (but never done) to force big players to pay their tax dues and stop offshoring businesses that were built here in Australia from the bounty of our common wealth.

But a nobbled, soon to be taxpayer-less government isn’t going to be able to rejig anything.

Maree Coote, Port Melbourne AI efficiency should start at the top

It is said that job cuts enabled by reliance on AI make companies more efficient, reduce duplication and speed up decision making.

Isn’t that what very highly paid executives claim they do? Seems to me that AI job replacement should start at that level.

Gerry Lonergan, Reservoir



What’s in a name?

Nvidia by name, invidious by nature.

Catherine Healy, Brighton Putting humanity’s future in hands of few

If we were offered an investment opportunity promising untold upside potential but also significant risk of becoming worthless, some might invest a small amount of “gambling money” but most would reject such odds.

In a very important article, James Massola reveals that this is the bet, with even greater consequences, that humanity is taking with AI (“Pacific jewel is in the grip of an AI fever dream – deranged but oh so real”, 13/11).

Sure, AI can do great things, but there is a 10 to 50 per cent chance it will also kill us – within just a few years.

This is the pessimistic view from AI safety experts, confirmed by the Australian government’s intelligence community. Have we become so inured, distracted, dismissive or disinterested in the dangers facing humanity, that we will allow just two political leaders and a handful of technical egomaniacs, cheered on by big business, to place this bet on our behalf? As with climate change, we have been warned.

Peter Thomson, Brunswick Hope my super fund avoids the AI bubble

AMP chief economist Shane Oliver is quoted as saying that companies such as AI computer chip manufacturer Nvidia ″⁣are so big that it is impossible for Australia’s superannuation funds not to be exposed to them″⁣ (14/11).

Australians currently pay around $50 billion a year in super management fees. I would have hoped that for that stunning outlay we would get some actual management and not simply be ″⁣exposed″⁣ to all available investment options. In the case of massive AI companies, data centre hyperscalers, and the world’s biggest chip manufacturer, it is abundantly clear that they are likely to become the most spectacular investment bubble the world has ever seen. I hope my super fund is avoiding them like the plague.

Richard Barnes, Fairfield Watch this space

As I watch footage of various billionaires sending their spaceships skyward, I can’t help but wonder; what are they sending up there, and what right do they have to do this? We know about satellites (and, hard as it is to believe, Elon Musk’s apparent control over their capabilities, which can impact the progress of wars, no less), but what else are they sending up there? Weapons? How can this be allowed?

Do we have no say in this? What input do all those countries without a space program have? Surely, it is not just a case of the richest countries having first dip at populating or industrialising space? When you have expansionists like Musk, Bezos and others of that ilk sending up whatever they want, we should all be very worried. We must set up an international body to control this with representation from all countries.

Trevor Holland, Lower Plenty THE FORUM



Not apathy, alienation

Sussan Ley’s reflection on voter apathy (“The most dangerous of all emotions has hit voters, and who can blame them”, 14/11) identifies a serious problem while avoiding an uncomfortable question: what responsibility do longstanding political leaders bear for creating it?

After years in parliament and senior ministerial office, Ley owes readers more than sympathetic accounts of disappointed voters. Which policies failed? Which decisions would she now reverse? What prevented her from addressing these concerns while exercising power?

Her diagnosis also confuses apathy with alienation. Young people rejecting established parties may care deeply about politics. Families avoiding political arguments may be exhausted by disagreement, rather than indifferent. Indeed, her celebration of a youthful electoral surge complicates her warning that younger voters are vacating the field.

Ley is right that an equal vote does not guarantee an equal voice. But “authentic engagement” is inadequate unless listening changes decisions.

A young worker priced out of housing needs practical reform, with its costs and trade-offs honestly explained.

Democracy will regain confidence when leaders deliver results and accept responsibility for failure. Former leaders can contribute by explaining how the system disappointed voters, including their own part in that story.

Empathy matters. So does accountability.

Sam Salcman, Caulfield South Review data centres

We read that every council across Victoria is calling for a state parliamentary inquiry into data centres and a pause on all new approvals until stronger safeguards are established. Furthermore, a fast-track system sends applications directly to the planning minister that strips us residents of appeal rights.

On the verge of an election and with the Municipal Association of Victoria calling for a moratorium on the rapid expansion of data centres, it’s surely not too much to ask that the state government shows it has the capacity and the gumption to establish a robust framework that respects communities, the environment, and prevents, where possible, the worst of risks to our climate.

Cynthia Pilli, Doncaster East Brutal cost of density

Thirteen years ago, I bought a small apartment in Richmond in a quiet cul-de-sac with a large green space and many mature native trees which were home to lots of kookaburras and magpies.

Twelve months ago, work began on our green space to build 500 apartments. Our green space is now concrete. There are problems with water leakage and power outages. All the trees were wood chipped in two days and the birdlife has disappeared.

They work on the site for at least 50 hours a week. The noise is exhausting and depressing, and there is at least another year to go. The people who have somewhere else to go have gone. This happy community has been ruined. The general mood is now one of sadness and resignation.

Louise Ryan, Richmond It’s trust, not density

The finding that voters prefer Melbourne to grow outwards and around the CBD rather than through suburban activity centres should surprise nobody.

For years, governments have promised that higher-density housing would be supported by better transport, infrastructure and services. Residents have learnt to be sceptical.

As a town planner, I know Melbourne cannot afford to sprawl forever. Equally, communities cannot be expected to support significant growth without confidence that the supporting infrastructure will follow.

The problem is not density. The problem is trust. Until governments get that right, voters will continue looking for alternatives.

Stephen O’Brien, Doncaster Heights Rue the day

I am dismayed by the number of people who feel they have little or no choice in the forthcoming elections. Despite our history of people fighting long and hard for the right to vote, some are considering voting informal, or for frivolous parties, such as ‘I am voting to avoid the fine’.

Others appear to feel that there are only three parties and do not even consider other options. Admittedly, it is difficult when some of the options are single issue parties, or a choice between two competing socialist parties, or a deliberately misleading party, such as the ‘Free Palestine Party’, which we are told was created in order to attract progressive or pro-Palestine voters and redirect their upper-house preferences towards conservative parties such as One Nation.

Then there are the Greens, who have gone off on tangents and alienated people, but have serious policies on environment, health, education and increasing wealth disparity. Let’s make informed choices. If we make bad decisions through carelessness or indifference, we will have the next four years to regret it.

Rita Thorpe, Coburg



My fine, your pothole

I’ve received two ridiculous parking fines in the past week and a half, probably in an effort to improve the budget bottom line. Why doesn’t the government just ask me to pay for fixing the pothole at the end of my street? I would gladly chip in.

Benjamin Levy, Caulfield North Women’s work reduced

Every day, we hear about job losses across Australia. David Jones is closing stores, while banks and Qantas are outsourcing administrative jobs overseas. What do these job losses have in common? Many are in female-dominated sectors.

Yet, when jobs are threatened in traditionally male-dominated industries such as mining and manufacturing, the political response is often dramatically different. The Coalition and One Nation warn of economic decline, while media coverage highlights the devastating impact on workers, families and regional communities.

Why is there not the same political outrage or media attention when women lose their jobs?

Job losses in female-dominated sectors are too often presented as necessary business restructuring or improvements in efficiency, rather than as a social and economic crisis affecting real people.

Women’s employment is not secondary to men’s. In today’s cost-of-living crisis, losing a job can be financially devastating, particularly for single-parent households and families relying on two incomes.

Every lost job represents a person, a family and potentially a community under financial pressure, regardless of whether the worker is employed in a mine, a factory, a department store or an office.

Rosmarie Speidel, Clifton Hill Regime change needed

Friday’s reports of yet another air strike by Israel on a hospital in Gaza, reportedly killing a doctor and injuring medical staff and patients, fills me with continuing dismay. Israel claims, without providing any supporting evidence, that the hospital was sheltering a Hamas militant, yet none of those killed or injured were other than medical staff or patients.

The cessation of American financial and military aid to Israel coupled with Trump’s exit from the political stage, cannot come soon enough.

Michael Kennedy, Pipers Creek CA’s correct call

Cameron Bancroft’s sandpaper ball tampering was undeniable due to the relatively immediate film and material evidence. The next Test match was only days away. Surely, Cricket Australia had no option but to take strong action as soon as possible to show the cricket world it viewed such action as a serious breach of rules, and to prevent its recurrence.

Cricket Australia’s punishment of coach, captain and vice captain was the right thing. To his credit, Steve Smith has all along accepted his responsibility as captain. I have yet to hear either Usman Khawaja or close friend David Warner acknowledge the latter’s share of responsibility as vice captain.

Jennifer Gerrand, Carlton North Under the bus. Really?

David Warner says the current Australian men’s cricket skipper, Pat Cummins, has “thrown Usman Khawaja under the bus” at the “sandpapergate” press conference on Friday. Am I missing something? Khawaja could have briefed Cummins and the CA management prior to the book release as journalists sometimes do before publishing a controversial story – offering a right of reply opportunity – even an edit or rewrite after discussion.

As it stands, if you have zero interest in cricket, you know Khawaja has released a book – and it’s seemingly singular topic of sandpapergate.

Justin O’Halloran, Clifton Hill



AND ANOTHER THING Victorian election

Here’s an idea: how about whoever wins the Victorian election concentrates on building up regional housing and commerce instead of ugly, high-rise buildings in already overcrowded city areas.

Robyn Williams, Sale Why don’t Labor and LNP just form a coalition and then everyone would be happy?

Keith Lawson, Melbourne Hasn’t anyone heard of the Greens? Surely, if you can’t bring yourself to vote ALP, Liberal or One Nation then that’s the obvious option.

Jules Rolfe, Aireys Inlet Help! I am drowning in the sea of election promises. Whatever gets delivered may be a bonus. Perhaps, AI could keep a spreadsheet of promises and subsequent deliveries. If ever.

Helena Kilingerova, Vermont



She may not be on the ballot, but a vote for One Nation is a vote for Gina Rinehart!

Kyle Matheson, Mont Albert One Nation’s election mantra is ″⁣Let’s take Victoria back″⁣. I thought the aim of political parties was to take the state forward.

Ross Corben, Knoxfield Furthermore

Re US flights grounded. Obviously, must’ve been Obama’s fault.

Bob Speed, Trafalgar Your correspondent (Letters, 14/11) suggests four tasks for AI, but should realise that achieving world peace, ending poverty and solving climate change are all easy compared with getting an AFL flag for Essendon.

Ray Pilbeam, Camberwell Cricket

Women’s cricket may not have quite the same ‘brawny biff’ as the men’s, but it is still good to watch ″⁣fair dinkum cricket″⁣, minus the theatrics the men’s seems to attract

Tris Raouf, Hadfield



Re sandpapergate. As the late Queen informed us, ″⁣some recollections may vary″⁣.

Russell Kidd, Carnegie What a mess the sandpapergate saga has become. Sadly, so many of us seem to be taking sides. Perhaps, at this stage, we might do better to adopt the Ted Lasso approach: “be curious but not judgemental”.

Terry Kelly, Coburg The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Kiwis crushed by Kangaroos in Rugby League World Cup final
World.content:
The Australian empire rolls on.

After the Jillaroos decimated the Kiwi Ferns earlier in the evening, the Kangaroos backed it up with their own emphatic victory, crushing the Kiwis 32-12 in Brisbane to complete a clean sweep of the World Cup titles.

It was an error-riddled effort from the New Zealanders, the Kangaroos ruthlessly punishing them with six tries to two for a fourth title on the trot.

The signs were ominous from kick off, as Jamayne Isaako sent it sailing over the dead ball line to concede a penalty inside the opening seconds.

The Aussies cashed in on the early chance, Liam Martin going in for the opener with just one minute on the clock, the fastest try in a RLWC final.

Erin Clark is tackled in the final of the 2026 Rugby League World Cup between NZ and Australia at Suncorp Stadium. Andrew Cornaga/www.photosport.nz

Try-scoring machine Casey McLean struck back for the Kiwis on the back of a bit of razzle dazzle, Kodi Nikorima with the final basketball style offload for his centre to score an eighth at the tournament, and tie things up.

But the Kangaroos clicked right back into gear with two quick tries to Jack Bostock and Bradman Best to re-establish a comfortable 12-point buffer.

Mistakes continued to kill the Kiwis, Naufahu Whyte having the ball stripped from his grasp, Martin bashing his way over from the turnover for his second just before half-time, the Kangaroos taking a 24-6 lead into the sheds.

The carnage continued on the other side, Reece Walsh dancing and jinking through Kiwis left clutching at air, floating an offload to Tom Trbojevic to drive another nail in the coffin.

Australia claim their fourth title on the trot. Andrew Cornaga/www.photosport.nz

There were some signs of life after Ronaldo Mulitalo went soaring into the skies to bring down a Jahrome Hughes bomb, only to be denied by the bunker for an offside.

The consolation would come courtesy of Isaiah Papali'i, latching onto a Nikorima grubber but the Kiwis appeared resigned to defeat.

That defeat would be cemented with Bostock's second, slick hands through the backs sealing the title.

Once again, Australia stands alone atop the international rugby league mountain, with the rest of the world not even in sight of the summit.

World.title: Australia dispatch Kiwi Ferns to retain Rugby League World Cup women's crown
World.content:
The queens of rugby league have extended their reign to four successive World Cups, delivering another ruthless reminder of the gulf that exists between the champions and their rivals.

The Jillaroos cantered to a fourth title on the trot, crushing the Kiwi Ferns 34-10 in Brisbane.

It was a clinic in attacking efficiency, the Jillaroos showcasing their class in a flawless first half, before taking the foot off the gas somewhat in the second with the title already firmly secured.

Up by 32 points at half-time, the Kiwi Ferns simply had no answers for the rampant Australians, their 18-year wait for a World Cup to continue.

What was once a rivalry dominated by the women in black has become increasingly one-sided, Australia now just one win away form squaring the overall head to head ledger which once read 15-3 in favour of the Ferns.

Superstar Jamie Chapman cut capers in the Kiwi Ferns defence, as the Aussies took metres at will.

The would have one hand on the trophy after only twenty minutes as the defending champs raced out to a 24-0 lead.

Chapman struck twice, Shaylee Bent and Jessica Sergis also dotting down to put Australia firmly in control.

Finally getting some decent possession, the Ferns hit back with their one and only try of the half through Shannon Mato on the back of a a deft ball out of dummy half from Ashleigh Quinlan, reducing the margin to three converted tries.

But any hopes of a miracle were crushed when Chapman once again ripped the Ferns line wide open, sprinting 50 metres away to finish a first half hat-trick.

Tamika Upton drove the nail in further right on the brink of the break with a sixth try, for a commanding 34-6 half-time lead.

After the 35-minute scoring blitz, the second would remarkably be scoreless right up until the 70th.

New Zealand managed to end things in style as Mackenzie Wiki got over for a consolation right on the siren, the only points produced in the second spell.

But this was Australia's afternoon, the dynasty showing no signs of slowing.

World.title: NZ Nurses Organisation claim Auckland hospital patients unable to vote
World.content:
The NZ Nurses Organisation is surveying its members at two Auckland hospitals to determine the extent to which patients missed out on voting in the general election.

Delegate Sophie Tomes said the Electoral Commission had mobile voting teams at North Shore and Middlemore Hospitals only on the day before the election.

She claimed at least 12 North Shore patients were unable to vote, because they were bed-ridden.

"Our patients have been denied democracy," Tomes said. "We have confirmed that at least 12 patients at North Shore were unable to vote, including five from the Elective Surgery Centre, four from Ward 4 and three from Ward 15.

"These patients were bedridden and unable to get to the mobile voting team. They have been denied their democratic right.

"NZNO members reported voting for them personally was more challenging than previous elections, with long queues on the Friday also preventing busy nurses from having their say."

Tomes said union delegates had previously urged the Electoral Commission to make the mobile voting teams available on election day, but the patients were denied their democratic right.

"We work with hospitals directly, and the type of service we provide will depend on what works for them and the space available," said the Electoral Commission. "For example, we had a mobile team at Middlemore Hospital all day Friday, 6 November, to issue takeaway votes to patients in the wards.

"Patients were able to request a takeaway vote from the ward staff, who would record their details and pass it on to our team to prepare a takeaway vote. Our team returned on election day, as well, to pick up completed votes.

World.title: NZ First still considering MP Michael Laws' future in the party
World.content:
New Zealand First are yet to give an update on MP Michael Laws' future in the party - after promising to do so following the election.

Laws was reprimanded by the party only a few days before election day for comments he made about Opportunity Party MP Kayla Kingdon-Bebb mocking her demeanour and appearance, describing her as "rather severe-looking" and making sexual remarks while broadcasting on his online talkshow.

Laws apologised for those remarks, which were panned by Kingdon-Bebb and her party, National Leader Christopher Luxon and Laws' leader Winston Peters who told RNZ they were "simply unacceptable".

Laws was initially reprimanded by Peters, who said there could be further consequences after the election when the party had time to meet.

"The board can't meet as well, and so as a consequence, we have to defer it until after the election when we can deal with it properly."

"Properly and soberly," Peters told RNZ at the time.

However, more than a week on from election day, a spokesperson for the party confirmed to RNZ there was no update on Laws' future in the party as yet.

Laws made it back into Parliament following the election after being ranked sixth on the party list.

World.title: 'Flood' of weka sightings in Dunedin becomes a trickle
World.content:
Weka look likely to disappear from Dunedin again, despite a breeding pair making their home in a northern suburb last year.

They used to live in the area - Otago Peninsula's iconic Hereweka translates to 'catch the weka' - but they were wiped out along the east coast of the South Island and now the nearest populations live a few hundred kilometres away.

Retired ornithologist Bruce McKinlay started to record weka sightings in the city over the last five years, after receiving credible reports.

"In February, March 2025, there was a real flood of them," he said.

McKinlay recorded about 76 sightings by September last year.

Audio player for " Weka sightings spark debate over possible Dunedin return " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/environment/2607793%2Fflood-of-weka-sightings-in-dunedin-becomes-a-trickle

Weka sightings spark debate over possible Dunedin return Morning Report Download MP3 3m

There were three clearly different groups of weka - a breeding pair in Normanby that had three broods of chicks, one at Seconds Beach at St Clair and one on the Otago Peninsula, he said.

Then the reporting unexpectedly stopped.

The last sighting of the St Clair weka was in October last year and reports of the Normanby weka stopped from about March, he said.

Only the weka on the peninsula remained.

"Weka, no matter how confident or bolshy you think they look, are susceptible to predation," he said.

Stories from iwi suggested weka were an important seasonal food in the area before European settlement and hapū would travel to harvest weka at the right time, he said.

A trail camera photo of a weka on the Otago Peninsula. Supplied/Supplied/Fiona Morrison, Otago Peninsula Biodiversity Group

They were vulnerable to environmental changes, and the introduction of mustelids, cats and dogs.

McKinlay said people had to be involved in the return of weka to Dunedin, as it was too far for weka to walk.

He urged people not to bring weka into the area, although acknowledged the curious birds could have become stowaways.

"If you're going to think it's fun to bring a weka home, you are condemning it to eventually die," he said. "If we wanted weka back in Dunedin, it will take quite a lot of effort and co-ordination."

McKinlay believed the decision should not be taken lightly, and was not risk free to weka or other native species.

Weka were a known predator of sooty shearwater and the one on the peninsula lived near the colony at Sandfly Bay.

"If you've got one precious taonga like the sooty shearwater and you've got another one that eats it, which one do you actually want?

"How do you actually make these choices to actually accommodate a predator within your landscape?"

Weka are slowly disappearing from Dunedin. Tess Brunton/RNZ

McKinlay encouraged anyone who spotted a weka in Dunedin to log it with the DOC Hotline 0800 362 468.

He has reached out to previous weka spotters, but none of them reported further sightings.

McKinlay recorded their absences, saying it was part of their story in the city and painted a picture of how vulnerable weka were, if their arrival was not managed properly.

"One of the problems with this sort of work is the absence of records really doesn't attract people's attentions as much as the positive," he said.

World.title: Nations Championship: Fiji remain winless after Irish loss
World.content:
The Flying Fijians' losing run in the Nations Championship continued in Dublin, as they were hammered 43-15-by Ireland.

In the Nations Cup, Tonga could not hold out Georgia, losing 55-31 in Tbilisi, while Samoa grabbed their second consecutive win on the road, beating Portugal 36-5 in Lisbon.

For Fiji, costly errors - including the inability to win their own lineout throws, conceding the scrum battles and losing the ball when in possession - continued to plague their campaign.

The loss means the Pacific Islanders have lost all five of their championship matches so far, with just one more game to go for them in the series.

Match commentators said it was a tale of what might have been once again for the islanders, just like they had done in the last five championship matches they have played so far this year.

Although they stayed in the contest in the first 40 minutes, their inability to keep the basics right worked against them, as Ireland took advantage and piled the points on in the second 40 minutes to keep their record against Fiji at home safe.

Ireland managed to score seven tries, two each to wingers Tommy O'Brien and Robert Baloucoune. Other tryscorers were Ronan Kelleher, Andrew Porter and Nick Timoney.

Flyhalf Sam Prendergast added six points from three successful conversions, while replacement Ciaran Frawley also got a kick through for two points.

Fiji managed only two tries to captain Peceli Yato and Josua Tuisova, while flyhalf Ben Volavola added five points through a conversion and a successful penalty kick.

New head coach Jake White has had just one victory with the side, since taking over last month, that coming against Japan in a one-off international.

He has now had two setbacks, losing to France last weekend and today's beating by the Irish at the Aviva Stadium.

White's disappointment in the coaching box was caught on television during the game and he told the media his Fiji side "did Ireland a favour".

"Let me put it that way, because I think Ireland deep down know that, if they play like that against South Africa, they're going to be up against it."

Ireland led 17-15 at halftime.

Ireland started well

The hosts started the game well, with O'Brien claiming the first try of the game in the eighth minute. Prendergast kicked the conversion for the 7-0 advantage.

Eight minutes later, halfback Jamison Gibson-Park went over the Fiji line, after he picked up from the base of the scrum five metres out, but referee Agnus Gardner and the TV match official ruled that out, after replays showed Gibson-Park had lost the ball over the line.

The Flying Fijians did not let go of their hold on the Irish lead and that resulted in Tuisova's try in the 18th minute.

'The Bus' ran onto a Frank Lomani pass off a lineout win close to the Irish line, bulldozed his way through the defensive wall and planted the ball firmly for his try. Volavola missed the conversion attempt.

Then in the 22nd minute, captain Yato, who was getting some assistance with his knee inside the Irish 22-metre zone, stood up to take a pass from Jiuta Wainiqolo, who had broken free from the Irish grasp, to dive over and put the visitors ahead 12-7 on the scoreboard.

However, Baloucoune was on hand to score a double from out wide, running into free space both times, after the Irish had sucked the Fijian defence in to create overlaps on the flanks.

Volavola slotted in a late penalty, after the hooter had sounded for halftime, keeping Fiji in the game, as the two teams ran off for the break.

Irish domination

A disappointing second-half performance from the Flying Fijians saw Ireland take control.

The islanders failed to score any points after the break, as the Irish rallied to score 26 unanswered points and keep their hopes of topping the Nations Championship northern hemisphere standings alive.

Two early knock-ons from Fiji - one unforced from a lineout maul - gave the possession back to Ireland early.

Four minutes after the restart, the hosts drove a lineout maul towards the Fijian line and hooker Kellaher was over in the corner.

Replacement prop Inoke Ravuiwasa was yellow-carded for a swinging arm tackle nine minutes later and the Irish extended their lead with Potter going over.

O'Brien had his second for the match, when he chased a Prendergast grubber kick, and then Timoney crashed through under the crossbar for his try with three minutes remaining, as Ireland clocked off with another good win.

Tonga second best

Meanwhile, in the Nations Cup, Georgia marked their 300th international match with a fifth straight win to be crowned Pool B champions with a round to spare.

They defeated Tonga 55-31, their biggest win over the Friendly Islanders to date.

Captain Theo McFarland scored two tries for Manu Samoa against Portugal. Supplied/World Rugby

The bonus-point success was rapturously received by the home crowd, as the Lelos outscored their opponents by eight tries to five in a fiery clash.

Georgia captain Davit Niniashvili, who played outstandingly during the game, said it was great to have won against Tonga and create a bit of history.

"It feels good," he said. "We prepared for this and knew Tonga are big boys.

"The second half was good and, when we have this support behind us, it gives us even more energy, so I hope they will keep coming to support us."

Tonga captain Ben Tameifuna said they gave Georgia the opportunities, which their hosts successfully converted into points.

"You can't give easy ball to a team like Georgia, especially with the set-piece they have," he said. "I'm definitely proud of the team and I feel like we are definitely heading in the right direction, but congratulations to Georgia."

Tameifuna put Tonga ahead with a close-range score early, but they lost Patrick Pellegrini to the sinbin for a deliberate knock-on.

Georgia scored twice in six minutes through Vano Karkadze, after they took advantage of the one-man advantage.

His first was an easy close-range finish and he repeated the trick for his second try with a similar effort, before scrumhalf Vasil Lobzhanidze added a third home score.

Tonga cut the hosts' lead, when flanker Semisi Paea claimed their second try, following a superb maul.

Georgia led 22-14 at halftime, but lost Akaki Tabutsadze to a yellow card after the second half resumed, and winger John Tapueluelu collected a stunning offload from full-back Taniela Filimone to run in from the corner to score for Tonga.

Georgia came back strong with three more tries, while Tonga responded with tries to Veikoso Poloniati and Lotu Inisi.

The 'Ikale Tahi also had Fetuli Paea sin-binned late.

Samoa victorious in Lisbon

Samoa showed their class to comfortably dispatch Portugal 36-5 in an impressive bonus-point victory at Estadio do Restelo.

The visitors surged into a commanding 24-0 lead over Os Lobos in the Portuguese capital.

Tries from Peter Umaga-Jensen, captain Theo McFarland, Niko Jones and Latrell Ah Kiong put them in total control at the break in the first-ever test match between the sides.

Portugal hit back through Domingos Cabral, but Samoa added further late scores through McFarland and Miracle Faiilagi in the second spell to win the contest.

Manu Samoa kept with the same side that beat Zimbabwe so impressively last weekend.

They led in the sixth minute, when former Hurricanes centre Umaga-Jensen brilliantly burst through midfield to score, before captain McFarland added a second with a pick-and-go try.

Then Jones, son of All Blacks and Manu Samoa legend Sir Michael, got into the act with a similar close-range effort, as the islanders found top gear early.

Ah Kiong, who scored a hattrick against Zimbabwe seven days previously, added Samoa's fourth, when he raced clear from halfway, after intercepting an errant Portugal pass.

World.title: Five charged after police uncover drug lab in Avondale
World.content:
Five people are due to appear in court on Monday, after police were led to a clandestine drug laboratory in the Auckland suburb of Avondale.

Detective Senior Sergeant Anthony Darville says officers received a report of a person with a firearm on St Jude Street just before 6pm Saturday.

The police Eagle helicopter guided armed officers to a property, where equipment associated with a clan lab was found.

Three women aged 39, 43 and 53, and a 57-year-old man were charged with possessing equipment with intent and further charges have not been ruled out.

World.title: New study shows what does and doesn't work for ADHD kids
World.content:
A new study says giving kids with ADHD extra time for tasks and more frequent breaks while in class may not affect their behaviour.

Researchers from Florida International University got more than 200 primary school children at summer camps in the US to switch between taking and not taking medication and different classroom environments.

The study, published in the Jama Pediatrics medical journal found medication improved the kids' rule-following and test results but the adaptations in the classroom, including extended time for tasks, frequent breaks, using a standing desk and having a low distraction space, didn't affect their behaviour or achievement.

University of Auckland development neuropsychology expert Professor Karen Waldie said the study came as no surprise to those who work with children with ADHD and do research in the area.

"Procrastination and time blindness are one of the key symptoms of ADHD. The main reason for the benefits of medication and behavioural therapy comes down to the brain chemical dopamine and the reward system of the brain.

"Stimulant medication such as Ritalin works to increase dopamine in the prefrontal cortex and this helps those with ADHD focus on the task at hand: right now."

Waldie said the study found that medication and behaviour therapy improved academic productivity and rule-following behaviour in the classroom, but accommodations such as extended time on tasks had no effect.

"Another thing that works in a similar way as stimulant meds is a hard deadline and quick consequences of actions - so basically people with ADHD work very well under pressure, which gives them a dopamine reward hit, and do less well when there is time available to perform a task like a test or when there is a distant or inconsequential reward."

Consultant clinical psychologist and honorary senior lecturer at University of Auckland's Te Ara Hāro Centre for Infant, Child and Adolescent Mental Health, Dr Melanie Woodfield, said the study is an important signal from a carefully designed experiment, but needs testing in the real world.

"Positive behaviour supports, medication, or both, are known to improve academic performance and decrease challenging behaviour for many children with ADHD."

Woodfield said the study leaned towards strict control, excluding children with low IQ or autism alongside ADHD, and taking place in a specialist American summer camp treatment classroom, where staff even counted the ratio of teacher praise to commands, to ensure it was 3:1.

"That's quite far removed from a messy, complex, real world classroom with fewer resources, stretched teachers, and children with higher needs. The authors themselves recommend the study now needs to be repeated in real- world classrooms, where they expect the effects would be weaker.

"Ideally, we should also acknowledge that some accommodations do work for some children, some of the time," Woodfield said.

"However, this research suggests that a blanket, Oprah-style giveaway 'You get extra time! And you get extra time' may not return reliable dividends, compared to behavioural approaches and/or medication."

Clinical psychologist Giselle Bahr said there's been no specific research about what happens when children with ADHD are offered structured classroom changes, and while the study showed they did not make a difference to behaviour in this instance, it was food for thought.

"It's like, of course it would make sense to give a child more time if they're struggling, but it looks like it's not as simple as that," she said.

"What we already know is that behavioural strategies help children and they don't have any adverse effects, there's no risks associated with them. We already know that methylphenidate changes children's behaviour in the short term, but over the long term it leads to worse outcomes."

However, Waldie did not agree and said she had not seen that supported in scientific literature.

Bahr said the study had not been done in a normal classroom setting, but at a summer camp during one-hour class periods, and the adjustments were randomised.

"The rest of the hours of the day they were doing fun activities and the classes were small. They only had 15 to 18 students in them and there were two adults in each of those classrooms. It's not an exact match with how a classroom generally run, so we have to be careful about what we extrapolate from that.

"It doesn't look like they matched a child's kind of need for what's going to help them learn better in a classroom, they just kind of trailed these adaptations."

She said the researchers, Fabiano and Pelham, had authored papers about children and ADHD for decades and said behavioural interventions remained an important, low-risk strategy for supporting children with ADHD.

"Some of their previous work looked at the best order for interventions. They found that starting with behavioural strategies was more effective than starting with medication. Also, that ADHD medication made things worse for children in the long term, even if it produced improvements in the short-term."

Bahr said ADHD medication came with serious risks, including reduced growth, a risk of psychotic symptoms, and cardiovascular problems.

Waldie said the only well-established effect would potentially be with appetite, however research on that aspect was conducted with fast-acting mythylphenidate before the slow-release medication was available.

Waldie said methylphenidate was the most-studied pediatric medication, with evidence showing it reduced rates of mortality, accidents, and self-medication.

Waldie was interested in understanding the study's findings in relation to the dopamine system in a person with ADHD, procrastination and the need to go down to the wire before panic set in.

"That's when the ADHD person tends to excel, it's like a light flipping, that's when things get done," Waldie said.

Bahr said the findings challenged the common-sense assumptions that adaptations like extra time or low distraction spaces would always improve outcomes, but more research was needed to determine how classroom adjustments could benefit kids with ADHD.

Study details: The study evaluated the single and combined effects of academic accommodations, behaviour therapy, and stimulant medication (methylphenidate, 0.3mg/kg).

The academic accommodations were: extended time on tasks, frequent breaks during task, a low-distraction workspace with the option of using noise-cancelling headphones, and the ability to stand at the desk. A general classroom setting was compared with a classroom with enhanced behaviour interventions including a daily report card with contingent rewards, and lots of praise.

Results: 255 children with a mean age of 8 years and 8 months, took part in the study. 201 (79%) of the children were male, and 235 (84%) completed the study.

World.title: Shark attack hero breaks through for Iron Series win
World.content:
An emotional Charlie Verco has described his journey from a shark-attack rescue to a maiden Iron Series win as a "roller coaster".

Five months after saving Leah Stewart at Coogee Beach, Verco claimed the third round of the series by prevailing in a sprint finish in Sunday's race at Thirroul Beach.

In June, the 25-year-old paddled towards the danger and pulled the unconscious woman from the surf.

This shark attack hero believes Olympic inclusion could save lives The top seed in this year's Iron Series, who made headlines by helping save a shark attack victim earlier this year at Coogee, says having surf life saving in the Brisbane Olympic Games would help raise the profile of the sport.

After 12 days in a critical condition in hospital and a series of surgeries to amputate her arm, Stewart woke from an induced coma and was reunited with her daughter.

"Being able to manage the ups and downs of it, like the stressful rescue with Leah — I'm so happy that she was able to be alright," Verco said.

"It meant that I was able to keep focused on what I love, which is the sport.

"But realistically, we all do this sport as part of surf lifesaving. It certainly doesn't feel like we were doing a race like that.

"It feels like we're all just really wanting to win and compete against each other.

"But I like that we have the skills to be able to go and help people when they need it."

Verco beat home Ethan Callaghan and Henry Simpson in a breakthrough victory, which comes after the 25-year-old had entered this year's Iron Series as the top seed following the legendary Ali Day's retirement.

"It is a step up to try and put yourself at the front of the race as opposed to just being happy that you're here," Verco said.

"And for so long that was my goal, was just to get here. It's all about confidence.

"I've spent a long time doing races trying to get myself comfortable being at the front and setting my own pace, and I think that definitely helps."

Naomi Scott took out the women's event, with the Northcliffe athlete pipping Emma Woods in a sprint up the beach.

Before the Iron Series heads to Newcastle in January, Scott will travel to South Africa next week to defend her global Ironwoman title at the world lifesaving championships.

World.title: Chapman hat-trick fires Jillaroos to Rugby League World Cup glory
World.content:
The Jillaroos have defended their Rugby League World Cup title, dominating New Zealand 34-10 in the tournament decider at Lang Park.

The victory was all but assured after a commanding first half, with winger Jaime Chapman crossing for a hat-trick in sweltering Brisbane heat.

The win saw Australia claim a fourth-straight crown in the fifth-consecutive final featuring the Trans-Tasman rivals.

Rugby League World Cup finals live: Look back on all the action in our blog.

Chapman, whose treble brought her World Cup tally to 13, told ABC Sport it was a dream afternoon for her side.

"I feel over the moon. There's no better feeling than winning a World Cup on your turf, against the Kiwis as well.

"We knew it was coming. It was a really hard, tough game in this heat and super proud of our team and proud of our girls."

Chapman scored a stunning treble in sweltering Brisbane heat. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Lessons seemingly learnt from a lethargic start to their semifinal win over Fiji, the Jillaroos were dominant from the first minute in the tournament decider.

It took Chapman just two minutes to score the first try of the day by breaking wide, stutter stepping and rampaging through the New Zealand defence, allowing for the recalled Jesse Southwell to nail a difficult conversion.

A spectacular dive and one-handed putdown saw Chapman cross for her second in the 14th minute, before the winger put on the afterburners to complete her treble with a scintillating breakaway effort.

By half-time, Australia had run in six tries to the Kiwi Ferns' one, with Shaylee Best, Jess Sergis and Tamika Upton having also registered four-pointers, and Southwell having nailed all but one of the conversions.

Sergis's effort came after a breathtaking breakaway, while Upton completed some neat interplay with Abbi Church to compound New Zealand's misery in the shadows of half-time.

Shannon Mato's 23rd-minute converted effort was the Kiwi Ferns' only contribution to a 34-6 half-time scoreline.

Only a try-saving tackle prevented the Jillaroos from going further ahead five minutes after the break, but the Australians struggled for any cut through in an energy-sapping second half in which the still taxing conditions restricted the quality of play.

New Zealand winger Mackenzie Wiki was denied a late score thanks to a try-saving Isabelle Kelly tackle, but proceeded to find the only points of the second period by diving over with the full-time siren seconds from sounding.

Their 4-0 second-half scoreline meant the Kiwi Ferns went the entire tournament without conceding a point after half-time.

World.title: After tragically losing a mate, Herbert is helping businesses with his shirt
World.content:
Golfer Lucas Herbert has returned to Australia on a mission to use his platform to help those struggling in the tough economic climate.

Herbert has played in this week's NSW Open at the Hunter Valley, finishing in a tie for third.

But Herbert, fresh off the collapse of LIV Golf, entered this week's tournament without something synonymous with professional sport: sponsorships.

The end of LIV Golf brought an end to many commercial arrangements Herbert had, meaning he entered this week's NSW Open with his clothing as a blank canvas.

But Herbert decided he wanted to use his platform to help, following the tragic death of a mate earlier this year.

The 30-year-old from Bendigo put a call out to small businesses in the lead-up to the tournament, offering to promote them on his clothing.

He said small business owners were doing it tough, and said he wanted to help out.

He told golf journalist Tom Hobbs earlier this week that he was inspired to help small Australian businesses following the passing of a friend.

"Just seeing local business getting destroyed over here makes me sad," he said.

"One of my good friends took his own life in January because he was a small business owner and couldn't take the pressures of working 60 hours a week to keep the lights on any longer.
