"I thought it would be better than coming home wearing blank hats and clothes."

A mental health charity, electrical and a lawn care business were among the sponsors Herbert carried on his clothing this week.

Herbert will also be part of the Australian Open and Australian PGA Championship during this golf season.

World.title: Aussies crashes to record ODI loss against England after top order collapse
World.content:
Australia's top-order batters have crashed spectacularly as England romped to a record 135-run win to level their one-day international series 1-1.

England opener Tom Banton clubbed 121 runs from 99 balls as the tourists posted 6-355 — their highest ODI total in Australia — after being sent in at Adelaide Oval on Sunday.

The hosts were bowled out for 220 in 44.3 overs as England achieved its biggest winning runs margin in an ODI in Australia.

Australia's run chase started horribly with three batters — Travis Head (7), Cooper Connolly (0) and captain Mitchell Marsh (2) — caught at slip in a six-ball span.

The rapid-fire dismissals left the hosts reeling at 3-13 after 3.2 overs as England set course to level the series ahead of Wednesday's decider in Hobart.

It could have been worse for the Australians, who were 4-29 before England dropped two regulation catching chances from the bats of Matthew Renshaw, on 27, and Cameron Green, on 7.

The reprieves allowed Renshaw (63 from 74 balls) and Green to pause the rot with a 98-run partnership.

Green top-scored with 64 from 82 balls but the early damage inflicted chiefly by England paceman Gus Atkinson, who snared 3-22 from his initial seven overs, was irreparable.

Atkinson finished with 4-28 from 10 overs, his best ODI figures, and Sam Curran (2-38) and spinner Liam Dawson (2-41) also claimed multiple wickets.

Earlier, Banton, Jordan Cox (67 from 49 balls), Joe Root (62 from 68) and Will Jacks (54 not out from 40) dominated.

Banton and Root took control with a 137-run partnership from 136 balls for the second wicket, taking England to a powerful position of 1-156 in the 28th over.

Somerset batter Banton, 28, reached his second ODI ton from 86 balls before Cox and Jacks combined for a 102-run stand in less than 12 overs as England accelerated to an imposing total.

Tom Banton led from the front as England posted 6-355 in its innings. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Mark Brake)

Paceman Xavier Bartlett (3-72 from 10 overs) was the only Australian to take multiple wickets before a crowd of 31,412, the fifth-highest ODI attendance at Adelaide Oval.

Australia rested paceman Mahli Beardman, two days after his stunning one-day international debut of 6-24 in a seven-wicket win in Perth.

Beardman was replaced by Riley Meredith, who was punished in taking 1-75 from 10 overs.

Bartlett, Meredith, Spencer Johnson (1-61 from eight overs) and Jack Edwards (0-73 from nine) all conceded more than seven runs per over.

AAP

World.title: Aussie quick says 'everyone knew' about sandpaper, as Warner doubles down
World.content:
Former Australian cricketer Chadd Sayers, who played his lone Test after Sandpapergate on the infamous 2018 South African tour, has said he is comfortable stating he believed everyone in the team knew about ball-tampering.

The notorious Cape Town Test match, where Cameron Bancroft was filmed using sandpaper on the cricket ball, was thrust into the spotlight this week after Usman Khawaja in his memoir, Sabr, claimed ball-tampering was commonplace and the entire team needed to take responsibility.

The memoir has caused a rift in Australian cricket.

David Warner, who was suspended with Cameron Bancroft and then-captain Steve Smith over the incident, backed Khawaja's account in Sabr, saying it was "100 per cent accurate".

Meanwhile, Test captain Pat Cummins, who was part of the infamous 2018 side, held a 70-minute press conference on Friday, again denying he had any knowledge of sandpaper being used and claiming Khawaja had been "casual" with people's lives and reputations.

Sayers, who was part of the Australian touring squad in 2018, said ahead of Australia's second ODI against England in Adelaide on Sunday that he was comfortable saying every member of the team knew sandpaper was being used.

"I'm comfortable saying where I'm sitting now that everyone knew what was going on [in South Africa in 2018]," Sayers said on the SEN broadcast.

"It [sandpaper] was used in two Test matches and there were discussions in change rooms … I'm not taking sides; it's just my recollection of what took place."

Sayers also said there was a meeting held in the wake of the team being caught with sandpaper, which lasted between 60 and 90 minutes.

Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball during the Test match in Cape Town, with an investigation determining he, Smith and vice-captain Warner were responsible for the ball tampering.

The trio was suspended, while the bowlers in that Test have always denied knowledge that sandpaper was being used on the ball.

In his memoir, Khawaja claimed he knew sandpaper was being used on the ball and told Bancroft to be careful.

Khawaja also said ball-tampering was commonplace in cricket.

Test captain Pat Cummins, who was part of the infamous 2018 side, held a 70-minute press conference on Friday, again denying he had any knowledge of sandpaper being used and claiming Khawaja had been "casual" with people's lives and reputations.

Cummins hits out at Khawaja Australian Test cricket captain Pat Cummins rubbishes Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering claims in a long and passionate press conference.

"When he says 'we all knew', if by that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100 per cent wrong," Cummins said on Friday.

"I've said that consistently for the last eight years; I did not know that was happening.

"But I think Usman actually says things that are far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper; that's complete and utter nonsense.

"I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out Usman admitted that he told Cam [Bancroft] to be careful when using sandpaper. That's not the Usman that I know. It's not the Usman that has been part of the team that's helped rebuild the Australian cricket culture over the last eight years, and the Usman that would have stopped that from happening there and then.

"Usman's a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations. In his book Ussie's been casual with my [life] and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket. I support his right to tell a story, 100 per cent. I'm really glad he feels like he can, but we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."

Warner doubles down on Cricket Australia on social media

David Warner has hit out at Cricket Australia as Sandpapergate continues to dominate headlines. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

David Warner has made another statement on social media, claiming he was not aware of all the facts before taking the brunt of punishment for Sandpapergate.

On Saturday, Warner accused Cricket Australia of a potential cover-up by claiming he believed the bowlers were not interviewed by the organisation about the incident.

Cape Town inquiry spoke to all Aussie bowlers, ABC understands Sources connected to the Australian bowling group say they all spoke to investigators as part of the inquiry into Cape Town ball tampering, which runs counter to claims by David Warner.

"As far as I am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," he wrote on Instagram.

"If that's correct then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?

"It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning … ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea.

"That stinks of a cover-up."

Multiple media outlets, including ABC Sport, have reported the bowlers were interviewed by Cricket Australia.

On Sunday, Warner then doubled down on his criticism of Cricket Australia and supported his previous post.

Loading Instagram content

"Just to clarify 'As far as I am aware' was the POINT," he wrote.

"I was never told the bowlers had been interviewed or provided statements.

"That information would've been pretty useful when I was forced to make decisions back in 2018.

"Why weren't we given all the evidence by CA?"

World.title: Kangaroos dominate Kiwis to win fourth straight Rugby League World Cup
World.content:
The Kangaroos are rugby league world champions for a 13th time after defeating New Zealand 32-12 in the men's final at Lang Park.

Australia claimed the men's and women's titles, both for the fourth straight time, after the Jillaroos took down the Kiwi Ferns 34-10 in the earlier women's decider in searing heat.

Both Australian sides dominated from the opening whistle almost literally, with hat-trick hero Jaime Chapman scoring her first after just two minutes and five seconds.

It was the fastest try in a World Cup final until a couple of hours later when Jamayne Isaako's opening kick-off went dead on the full and Liam Martin cross just 80 seconds into the game.

The Kangaroos scored four tries in the first half against an error-riddled Kiwis side, who were well below their best all night.

Tom Trbojevic extended Australia's half-time 24-6 lead just after the break, ensuring any New Zealand comeback never gathered any steam.

The victory had already been confirmed long before player of the match Jack Bostock scored his second try of the night in the 77th minute to cap the 20-point win for Kevin Walters's side.

Look back at all the action from both games in our live blog below.

World.title: How Swim GP may have given a glimpse of the future of para-sport
World.content:
Swim GP's made for TV, all-action racing format has proven a hit with swimmers and spectators alike.

But the biggest benefit may well be the innovations that placed para-swimmers front and centre of the competition at the Melbourne Sports and Aquatics Centre.

In front of a sold-out crowd, four teams: Kraken, Wahoo, King Tide and Tsunami, competed in a variety of races ranging from skins events through to mystery medley relays.

Times are not important. It's all about who touches the wall first.

"It is an opportunity for our athletes, our Paralympic team and our Olympic team, to come together and really showcase what they do," Swimming Australia Paralympic head coach Mel Tantrum said ahead of Saturday's evening events.

"This is about building the brand, building the profile of the athletes, swimming in prime time in preparation for the next six years."

The Melbourne Sports and Aquatic Centre was sold-out for day two. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Swim GP is not a new idea, and indeed has built on the concepts reintroduced at last year's Australia vs the World in Brisbane.

However, crucially, Swim GP has seen para-swimmers take a leading role.

Swimming Australia chief executive Rob Woodhouse told ABC Sport that involving the para-swimmers "was one of the most important factors" and a "no-brainer" in Swim GP's planning for a couple of reasons.

"Both our head coaches, Mel Tantrum and Rohan Taylor, they absolutely want a packed stadium for our trials, ideally Sydney next year, but particularly the Olympic/Paralympic trials in '28 in Chandler, one of the reasons being, for the Olympics, SoFi Stadium, with 40,000 screaming Americans and Long Beach for the Paralympics," Woodhouse said.

"Some of those [para-]athletes do have sensory issues, so for them to have some experience coming out to all of that noise and those bright lights, the flashing lights and all those sorts of things is really, really important.

"So there's quite an important benefit from Swim GP for those para-athletes that do have to deal with those things to get more accustomed to a noisy venue, to a bright flashy venue and things like that.

"[Also] that aspirational view that these athletes can provide, whether they're para-athletes or able-bodied athletes, to the young kids at home, and there's a lot of kids with various disabilities that don't have opportunities to get into a pool or to even just get involved in the other sports. So, just being able to showcase our amazing para-athletes and what they do is a really critical factor."

A big atmosphere is vital for Australia's swimmers to prepare for LA Olympic Games in 2028. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Tantrum agreed, saying integrating the two programs was vital.

"Swimming Australia is really inclusive in terms of the parity between Olympic and Paralympic programs and making sure our swimmers across both programs are really profiled and really supported," Tantrum said.

"The athletes are loving being part of a bigger team. Those sort of innovative, creative competitions make the athletes feel they're part of an elite team.

"It's not just para, it's not separate, it's part of being the Australian Dolphins swim team and both programs coming together.

"The athletes are fully integrated team members. They don't sit separately. They've got the same uniform, same bleachers, same team meetings.

"And I think that's, for the athletes, it's a chance for them to really showcase their athleticism.

"It's not about, oh, you're a para-athlete, it's about elite swimming at its best.

"The world's best swimmers are here in the pool. And yeah, whether you're Olympic or Paralympic, you know, able-bodied or have a disability, it doesn't matter. You're an elite athlete first and you're here to perform."

New tech bringing para-sport into the mainstream

Victoria Belando Nicholson (right) was a member of the King Tide team. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

One of the biggest challenges in para-sport when there are a limited number of athletes, is integrating multiple classifications and how to accurately, and fairly, ensure a level playing field.

In a standard multi-class meet, swimmers with varied impairments all start their races at the same time, with the winner determined by how close a swimmer gets to the world record in their particular classification.

That's all well and good but, for spectators, it can get confusing as to who as actually won because the winner does not always touch the wall first.

Swim GP gets around this by having a staggered start, with lights on the blocks for each swimmer.

The time-gap is determined based on a swimmer's season best in a particular distance and should result in a blanket finish — far more appealing for spectators.

"I think it's a really good idea to then see everyone come up towards each other and finish pretty closely," Paralympic legend Lakeisha Patterson told ABC Sport.

"It makes it an exciting race, I think, towards the end.

"I think for an event that isn't preparing for a world champs or a major international meet, this is really good for fans to see how multi-class swimming works."

Lakeisha Patterson said she was nervous before her race, perhaps made more so when Ben Hance literally ripped the shirt off his back when walking out. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Patterson competed in, and won, Saturday night's opening race, a multi-class, mixed 100m event where each swimmer swam a different stroke, with Patterson unusually swimming butterfly, which she noted "definitely" won't be on her program for next year's world championships.

Perhaps she should reconsider. Patterson, who is classified as an S9 swimmer, swam a PB to blitz the field, although the other three swimmers; Tim Hodge (S9), Ben Hance (S14) and Keira Stephens (S10), were far closer together.

"It doesn't matter what their classification is and, in some cases, what their gender is," Tantrum explained.

"It's some new tech that we're trialling for the first time on the block so that athletes, no matter what their class or their gender, they can race together.

"With this [Swim GP] format, it's basically who touches the wall first is the winner.

"These staggered starts and close finals make the crowd get right into it. It makes it exciting if someone's got a 20-second stagger to catch up on in 100 metres. It makes for exciting racing, and the crowd really got into that last night and you could feel the crowd lift.

"That's what swimming should be, right? It should be exciting."

The future of para-sport?

Lakeisha Patterson (right) and Rowan Crothers (second right) were key members of Team Tsunami. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Patterson noted that giving para-swimmers the same platform was crucial for the development of the sport.

"I think it's incredibly important to showcase that our athletes aren't just here for participation," she said.

"We are athletes showcasing what is possible, and I think Australia is leading the way in that inclusion space and how we can involve our entire team.

"Leading into Brisbane we can really build on that and hopefully have all of Australia behind us, and showing to the people watching at home that they may have a space in Paralympic sport as well."

Fully integrated competitions remain a rarity for para and able-bodied sporting events, the Commonwealth Games being a notable exception.

Given the success of this format, Tantrum said that innovations like the staggered starts seen in Swim GP could inspire more innovation elsewhere, perhaps even adding more athletes to future Commonwealth Games fields.

"If we could influence Commonwealth Games Federation … we could potentially have a greater number of athletes and a greater number of classes competing together," Tantrum said.

"We left a number of athletes at home [from the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games] because they simply didn't have events for those classes.

"So something that is more of a multi-class format for Commonwealth Games would be a great innovation to at least consider.

What should the future of para sport look like? Birmingham 2022 celebrated the largest para sport program in history, but there's still a large gap between wealthy and developing nations. What should integration look like?

"There's potential there that we could make this more integrated, fun, with exciting finishes and more athletes involved from Australia."

Perhaps even other sports could take note?

"Our immediate purpose is to showcase swimming," Tantrum said.

"But you know, if we can lead other sports and things like track and field to follow a similar format, where the para-athletes are standing alongside their Olympic athlete colleagues?

"You know, it's humans, right? It's human story, it's humans doing the best that they can do.

"If other sports such as athletics or cycling, want to come in and do what we're doing, if we're the trailblazers of that space, we'd love others to join in as well."

World.title: Swimming stars tipped for big 2027 despite illness, injury hiccups
World.content:
Battered by illness and injury, a trio of Australian Olympic swimming stars are being backed to be ready for Los Angeles Games.

Between them, Kaylee McKeown, Mollie O'Callaghan and Kyle Chalmers have won 11 Olympic gold medals.

McKeown returned to competition over the weekend at the inaugural Swim GP in Melbourne, having not raced since last year because of glandular fever.

Chalmers was poolside at the event, in the midst of a six-week break from swimming as he manages long-term back problems.

O'Callaghan, who nursed back and shoulder injuries through the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, was a late withdrawal from the Swim GP because of a skin infection.

McKeown said the one positive of her illness was that it had happened this year, not next.

Australian swimming head coach Rohan Taylor echoed that sentiment about the three stars in the context of the four-year Olympic cycle.

Mollie O'Callaghan missed competing at Swim GP due to an infection. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

"No-one will remember what happens in 2026 [in terms of injury or illness]. You can't worry about that now," Taylor told AAP.

"You have to get them right, you have to remember their talent won't go anywhere.

"It's about getting them healthy and then letting the fitness build. We know they can race and we just have to get ourselves to the arena fit and healthy, then we will be right."

McKeown made a successful return to racing at the Swim GP and Taylor was pleased with the backstroke queen's progress after the illness knocked her flat.

"I live on the Sunshine Coast, so I get to see it up close and see the progression," Taylor said.

"It's really good to see her back racing. She's such a competitor.

"She just looked back to her normal self, competitive, focused when the race was on, but enjoying herself.

"She just has to build momentum back."

McKeown gave a glimpse of her blistering backstroke speed on Saturday night, storming home after the staggered start to beat Ella Ramsay's breaststroke in the 50m skins champions race.

It was her first racing since the world championships in July last year.

Kaylee McKeown is one of Australian swimming's biggest stars. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"I've been doing some pretty solid sessions, but it's hard to come into these races — not racing all year — and then my body just hasn't recovered as quickly as it would," McKeown said.

"It's good, nice practice and gives a bit of confidence that I'm still swimming well.

"It's great there are no times, which takes the pressure off. It's just about racing."

As McKeown notes, glandular fever affects people differently and in her case, "it just really knocked me flat".

So competing for the Tsunami team at the Swim GP, with nothing riding on the results, was an ideal stepping stone as McKeown looks to next year's world championships and then the 2028 Olympics.

"It's really good fun and I'm glad we can race in this format," she said.

"It's taken a long time to build back and then I have to build to where I was, which is even more of a gap.

"I'm lucky it was this year and not next year, when it counts, so it's a blessing in disguise. I've had some nice time at home."

Swim GP is a points-based competition in a 25m pool, with no official times recorded and a variety of relay and individual race formats.

The Wahoo team, lead by Meg Harris and Sam Short, dominated the two-night Swim GP and comfortably won on 222 points.

McKeown's Tsunami were next on 173, ahead of Kraken (170) and KingTide (149).

AAP

Tech.title: LG’s budget-friendly B6E OLED TV is up to 50 percent off this weekend
Tech.content:
LG’s B6E was already one of the most affordable OLED TVs you could buy, but it’s an even better deal now that it’s included as part of Best Buy’s latest doorbuster event. Now through the end of today, November 15th, the 55-inch model is 50 percent off, dropping it to an all-time low of $699.99 ($700 off) at Best Buy. If you want a larger 4K set, the 65- and 77-inch models are also discounted, dropping them to $999.99 ($900 off) and $1,499.99 ($1,200 off), respectively.

Although it’s not as bright as LG’s pricier C6, the B6E still delivers the excellent contrast and deep blacks OLEDs are often praised for. It’s nearly identical to the standard B6, except it comes with a simpler remote that lacks the motion controls and voice features found on LG’s Magic Remote. It supports Dolby Vision and HDR10 for more lifelike colors and detail in bright and dark scenes, along with Dolby Atmos for more immersive audio. And with Apple AirPlay and Google Cast built in, you can easily stream content from your phone or tablet and access a variety of streaming apps, including Netflix, HBO Max, and YouTube via LG’s webOS platform.

The B6 also offers a lot of features gamers will appreciate. It has a 120Hz refresh rate for modern gaming consoles, which is still plenty fast even if it doesn’t rival the 165Hz refresh rate on the C6. It also offers variable refresh rate support — including Nvidia G-Sync and AMD FreeSync Premium — to help minimize screen tearing. You also get a zippy Alpha 8 Gen 3 AI processor and four HDMI 2.1 ports, making it easy to connect multiple consoles. It may lack some of the more advanced features found on LG’s more premium OLED TVs, but at 50 percent off, the B6 is a great option if you want the benefits of OLED without spending a fortune.

Tech.title: The Sony Aibo was a robot revolution dressed like a dog
Tech.content:
In the 1990s, Sony was absolutely convinced that we were on the precipice of a robot takeover. Pretty soon, the company decided, we’d all be living among countless humanoid robots. Some would be our coworkers; others would be our friends; and at least one would be our pet. And “pet” was exactly what Sony was going for when it created the Aibo. It was supposed to be part of the family.

On this episode of Version History, we go back in time and tell the story of the Aibo. David Pierce is joined by The Verge’s Victoria Song and Jennifer Pattison Tuohy, and together they discuss the origins of this remarkable robot dog, and its impressive success and longevity. They also try to figure out why Aibo had such an effect on its owners, what Sony got right (and wrong) about robots, and whether the idea of a robo-pet will ever be a global phenomenon.

This is the first episode of the sixth season of Version History. We’re back! This season is all about pets: gadgets that are pets, gadgets for your pets, and one gadget called pet. Tech.title: An overview of Jensen Huang’s messy days
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on Jensen Huang’s resignation and the fallout from Nvidia’s leadership crisis, follow Terrence O’Brien. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

On October 29th, The New York Times reported that Nvidia co-founder and showman CEO Jensen Huang appeared to be the target of a Chinese spy plot. Any major tech CEO potentially being compromised by the Chinese government is concerning — especially Jensen Huang. “If you could draw the network diagram of the entire US AI ecosystem, Nvidia would be at the center of that,” Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, previously told The Verge. “If you could draw the diagram of the entire Nvidia ecosystem, a single man is standing at the heart of all of that.”

The Times reported that Jensen Huang had developed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. Alice Huang had been on the American government’s radar for some time, perhaps as early as 2024. Her company was investigated by the US Commerce Department over suspicions it was illegally smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China in violation of US government trade restrictions. Singapore authorities confiscated her passport back in June of 2025, eventually barring her from the country, after she reportedly gave “inaccurate information” to police. And perhaps more concerningly, some US officials believed she was passing information, possibly about Nvidia’s designs or the White House’s deliberations over trade restrictions, directly back to Beijing.

This made her relationship with Jensen Huang concerning for multiple reasons. Nvidia’s chips are considered crucial to America’s AI superiority and a matter of national security by the White House. The government has restricted the sale of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China since the Biden administration. But Jensen Huang has routinely pushed to loosen those trade restrictions. Meanwhile, he had gotten quite cozy with President Trump, once even putting him on speakerphone on-stage at the All-In Summit.

Then last week, things escalated quickly.

On Friday, November 6th, the Times reported that Alice Huang was specifically recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO. Though, there is some disagreement among US intelligence officials over the strength of evidence tying Alice Huang to Beijing. While the paper did not confirm it at the time, rumors suggested the “close relationship” between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang was romantic in nature.

On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair, but did not name the Megaspeed exec and alleged Chinese spy specifically. Nvidia’s board announced that it was launching an investigation into its CEO shortly after.

Many believed that Jensen Huang would survive the scandal. His company’s importance to America’s booming AI industry and his crucial role at the company seemed to make him nearly untouchable. He was, after all, the only CEO the company had ever known with no clear and obvious succession plan in place, and he sat atop an unusual corporate structure with around 60 direct reports. (These numbers are slightly outdated, but according to the Harvard Business Review, 10 to 20 is far more common among Fortune 500 companies, and Tim Cook reportedly had 17 in 2015, which was deemed “a lot” by Business Insider.)

Then on Wednesday, November 11th, The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had a second affair — this one with one of his direct reports, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care. Whether that was the last straw or if they were afraid it would be merely the tip of the iceberg, the board was ready to push Jensen Huang out, according to reports circulating that evening. According to Bloomberg, he had accepted his fate Wednesday evening reportedly looking “broken and shattered” and telling people, “I’m a piece of shit.”

On Thursday, November 12th, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO of Nvidia.

How it’s going

CFO Colette Kress was immediately named interim CEO, and acknowledged to employees that this has been an “extraordinarily difficult period.” Harvey Jones was also named the first board chair in the company’s history, already signaling there would be some changes to the corporate structure. In a memo to employees, Jones said the company would “search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates.”

But the destabilizing impact was immediate. Nvidia’s stock closed at an all-time high of $239.24 on October 6th. It closed at $162.85 on November 13th. It’s hard to overstate the importance of Nvidia to the US’s AI arms race with China, and the industry in general. The company has invested $99 billion in various AI labs, startups, and neo clouds. Plus has announced plans to mobilize over $500 billion in financing for building out AI data centers and other infrastructure.

Even before Jensen Huang had resigned, Nvidia was already facing a shareholder lawsuit claiming the company had deceived investors. Jensen Huang and the company’s spokespeople insisted that the relationship with Alice Huang and Megaspeed was “completely normal and not unusual.” Only days later, Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair that raised “national security concerns” without naming anyone specifically. According to Reuters, Jensen Huang misled several Nvidia leaders, “including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld” about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang.

Some even speculated that Jensen Huang was the victim of a vast conspiracy, whether that was a coup by some faction within Nvidia, or perhaps the goal of China all along had simply been to chase him from the CEO chair.

By Thursday night, Reuters reported a third affair, this one also with an Nvidia employee, though no further information has emerged.

What happens next

First and foremost for Nvidia, it must find a new CEO. It’s possible that Kress eventually ceases to be “interim” CEO, but other names, including Apple’s hardware chief Johny Srouji, have also been rumored. (Donald Trump believes they should hire Tim Cook, but to call that unlikely would be an understatement.)

It’s also possible that Nvidia will undergo a dramatic reorganization. Whoever takes over as CEO is unlikely to keep the 60 direct reports of Jensen Huang. With a first-ever board chair in Jones, it’s also possible that the board of directors will play a larger role in the company going forward.

The board’s investigation into Jensen Huang that began on November 8th is ongoing. The scandal is likely to drag on for some time. With the possibility that Jensen Huang will have to testify before Congress, the company may choose to be proactive about disclosing any additional information publicly.

The incoming Democratic majority is expected to come down harder on Silicon Valley than the current Republican Congress. While it’s unclear just how far the new House and Senate will go in trying to rein in the tech industry and its billionaire leaders, it’s possible it will try to make an example of Nvidia as an early act of strength. If Nvidia is found to have been turning a blind eye to companies like Megaspeed, which are suspected of funneling advanced chips to China, it could face civil or criminal penalties. And it seems increasingly likely that stricter trade restrictions will be implemented on Nvidia’s chips, which could increase tensions with China in an already costly trade war.

There is a possibility that Jensen Huang could face criminal charges. In May, he claimed that Nvidia had “zero percent” market share in China due to stringent export restrictions. But shortly after, Culper Research published a report claiming that in reality over 20 percent of the company’s 2026 compute revenue was from China, though that number has not been independently verified. The report cited “illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries” as the primary source of those revenues. Among the largest of those intermediaries, according to Culper Research, was Megaspeed, which Nvidia repeatedly vouched for to the US government.

If proof is established that the CEO was knowingly helping Megaspeed or any other companies to illegally divert restricted chips to China, he could face criminal charges. And, as The Verge’s Elizabeth Lopatto put it, “under a functioning legal system, [he] could actually go to jail.”

There is the chance that members of the current administration are also tied up in this scandal, as it’s unclear how much the White House knew and when.

Considering Nvidia’s sizable investments, borrowing to build data centers, and the importance of its hardware, there are tons of open questions about how this impacts not just the AI industry, but the American economy as a whole. Nvidia is essentially propping up a large part of the tech industry and, if money stops flowing out of its coffers, it could drag a lot of other companies down with it.

There are also open questions about how this impacts the American public’s perception of the AI industry. The new Democratic majority was elected in part by campaigning against AI companies and the explosion of data center buildout across the country. That one of its more prominent CEOs is now embroiled in a spying scandal and multiple extramarital affairs probably isn’t going to endear the industry to the public.

By the way

Megaspeed was the largest buyer of Nvidia chips in Southeast Asia, but when Singaporean newspaper The Straits Times visited its office in October of 2025, it found “no signs of activity.”

Megaspeed is just one of multiple companies that Nvidia has been approved to sell chips with suspicious offices. The New York Times described New Matrix’s headquarters as “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.”

Jensen Huang’s connections to Super Micro are also under scrutiny. Earlier this year, one of its founders , an employee, and a contractor for the company were indicted by the Justice Department for conspiring to violate American export controls and divert Nvidia chips to China.

Read this

While a lot has changed, it’s still worth reading the Times ’ first big report from October 29th that lays the groundwork for the eventual deluge of international intrigue and infidelity that ultimately led to Jensen Huang’s downfall.

The New York Times paints a fascinating portrait of Alice Huang who now finds herself at the center of an international espionage scandal.

The Decoder interview with Kyle Chan , a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, digs into what China hoped to get out of Jensen Huang.

Tech.title: Watch SpaceX successfully execute the first ‘chopstick’ catch of Starship
Tech.content:
After aborting a planned catch of Starship Flight 15’s booster, SpaceX successfully captured Starship with its “Mechazilla” launch and catch tower for the first time. The company has performed ‘ chopstick ’ catches of its boosters before, but this is the first time the maneuver has successfully been executed on the Starship vehicle itself.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call that “success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I’d say it’s more likely than not that this succeeds next flight.” While not a complete success, in that the company was unable to recover the entire launch vehicle, it still stands as a milestone for the Starship program. And, since it has previously caught boosters on previous launches, there is reason to believe the failure today was not an insurmountable obstacle. SpaceX is still trying to determine what caused the booster to abort its landing and detonate over the Gulf of Mexico.

Tech.title: Magic: The Gathering is getting a Netflix animated series. For real this time.

is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

“It’s really happening. I promise. For real.” Those are the first words from Roy Graham, Head of Story at Magic: The Gathering, in a video posted yesterday announcing Planeswalker, the animated series heading to Netflix in 2027.

An animated Magic: The Gathering series was first teased back in 2019 with Joe and Anthony Russo at the helm. But that fell apart. In 2024, Netflix announced it still planned to make a series based on the game, but it decided to rework it from the ground up.

Now fans are finally getting their first glimpse of the show, which will be called Planeswalker. According to the sneak peek, because each plane exists in its own pocket universe, it will have a unique design, animation, and filmmaking style.

According to a synopsis of the show shared with IGN, Planeswalker will focus on Chandra Nalaar, a “volatile pyromancer hunted for her gifts, and haunted by her past.” Storyline details beyond that are vague, other than mentioning an “insidious force” that Chandra and other Planeswalkers will team up to confront “to prevent a cataclysmic war that threatens to consume their very existence.”

Tech.title: Work to replace old copper wire led to the FAA’s ground stop
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

At a press conference today, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that Friday’s nationwide ground stop ordered by the FAA was related to work replacing outdated copper wire with a fiber optic line at a “remote FAA facility.” The secretary said that this was “routine maintenance,” rather than the result of a major modernization effort. He told reporters that it was “such an old wire that it was being discontinued, meaning that line was going to get shut down,” necessitating the upgrade.

What wasn’t clear, according to Secretary Duffy, was the root cause of the problem. He said that it could have been faulty hardware, a misconfigured router, or “incompetence” on the part of contractor L3Harris. Regardless, what followed was the newly installed router “flooding” other routers in the Air Traffic Control system. Duffy said that there were “over 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” causing disruption to radar feeds and communication with planes.

Secretary Duffy also took the opportunity to call on additional funding from Congress for modernizing the Air Traffic Control system, and to tout the work the FAA has done so far. “We are building, we are building safely, but we are building fast,” he said, but said that Congress had only given him a “partial payment” to complete the necessary work.

In a statement posted to their site, L3Harris said:

L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA. With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel. L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.

Update November 14th: Added a statement from L3Harris.
