Tech.title: New Species of Giant Fungus Discovered in China Grows up to 20 Inches Tall
Tech.content:
Sometimes new species evade detection because they’re tiny and thus easy to miss—not this giant fungus. Shaped like a hand reaching out of the ground, this new species of fungus was discovered deep in the forest in China’s Yunnan Province. A research team from the Kunming Institute of Botany, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, reported it as a new species they named Dianjunus rex.

The name comes from the region’s ancient Dian Kingdom and the Chinese pronunciation of the word “fungus.” D. rex is a type of Ascomycete, which is the largest phylum of fungi with over 64,000 known species, and among them, this new fungus produces the largest masses of mushroom recorded. Unlike what we typically think of as a “mushroom,” Ascomycetes don’t form caps and stems but produce structures called fruiting bodies, which release spores to reproduce. And growing up to 20 inches and weighting nearly five pounds, D. rex’s are huge.

Within the Ascomycetes, the giant fungus constitutes an entirely new biological family (the broader classification of genus and species), meaning that it has no close relatives—at least that we know of. While 6,000 fungal species have been documented in Yunnan, mycologists believe the province known for its biological diversity could easily harbor 100,000

“The discovery illustrates how much fungus biodiversity remains to be discovered in East Asian forests,” Indunil C. Senanayake, an associate professor at the Kunming Institute of Botany and the lead author of the paper, said in a press release.

Senanayake and his research team conducted surveys in the Nanban tropical rainforest, where they came across large, whitish fruiting bodies growing in the soil near the roots of dying trees. They documented and collected fungi growing in a wide variety of shapes like cylinders, spindles, and cupped palms. The fruiting bodies appeared to develop finger-like branches upon maturity. They found that the above-ground portions are covered with white, powdery fibers that turn dark yellow as the fungi mature while the portions buried in the soil are black and smooth.

Tech.title: Xbox Game Pass Subscribers Can Play Football Manager, Warhammer Survivors and More Now
Tech.content:
On Tuesday, Nov. 3, Microsoft announced the games it’s adding to its Xbox Game Pass service in the first half of November. However, Rockstar Games is preparing to release Grand Theft Auto 6 on Nov. 19, so that game will likely take up a lot of your playtime from then on. That still leaves plenty of time to give these upcoming Game Pass titles a shot. I’m particularly excited about Warhammer Survivors. I enjoyed Vampire Survivors, and can’t wait to play as Fo’Baran, the chaplain of my beloved Salamanders from Warhammer 40K.

Xbox Game Pass, a CNET Editors’ Choice award winner, offers a wide selection of games you can play on your Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, Xbox One and PC or mobile device for as little as $10 a month. With a higher-tier Game Pass Ultimate subscription ($23 per month), you can access hundreds of games, including new ones on release day, each month.

Here are all the games Microsoft is adding to Xbox Game Pass soon.

More from CNET

Escape Academy 2: Back 2 School

Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Class is back in session in this puzzle game. This sequel to the award-winning Escape Academy brings you more puzzles to solve and a series-first open-world format. That makes the campus one big puzzle room filled with secrets, traps and more. If you get stuck, you can always chill with your friends and enjoy student life away from the classroom. The choice is yours.

Warhammer Survivors

Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Poncle, the creator of the indie hit Vampire Survivors, teamed up with Auroch Digital to let you bring your favorite Warhammer primarchs and champions into bullet-heaven action. Each character has their own special ability to help you defeat waves of enemies. Every stage is a new arena full of enemies and secrets to uncover. So grab your chainsword and whirlwind axes, because there are pixelated enemies to destroy.

Football Manager 2027 Console

Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Get ready for the most immersive matchday experience yet in the latest installment of the long-running Football Manager series. You’ll shape your club and define your team’s style, and you can get lost in the wider football universe thanks to smart news and events that mirror the drama of the football calendar.

These other games are also coming to Xbox Game Pass

In addition to the titles above, Xbox is also adding these games to Game Pass soon:

Xbox Game Pass Essential gets new games too

Game Pass Essential costs $10 a month and offers access to a relatively small library of games compared with Game Pass Premium and Ultimate. While Microsoft doesn’t regularly add many games to Essential’s library, it did add eight titles to this Game Pass tier on Nov. 15. So Essential subscribers can play these games now.

Games that left Xbox Game Pass

While Microsoft added several games to Game Pass, it also removed over a dozen games on Nov. 15. So you’ll have to buy these games separately if you still need to complete your main campaign or any side quests now.

For more, here’s our Xbox Game Pass review and other titles you can play on the service. You can also read our recent review of the Xbox Nano Controller.

Tech.title: No, the World Won’t Shut Down on Nov. 17. What the Blackout Rumors Get Wrong
Tech.content:
As global conspiracy theories go, this is a juicy one.

On Tuesday, Nov. 17, at around 2:20 p.m. ET, the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the Federal Communications Commission are planning a test of the Emergency Alert System. That’s when all hell is supposed to break loose. At least, that’s what you might believe if you only rely on social media.

Coming just days after an abrupt and disruptive government-ordered shutdown of air travel in the US and technical issues that caused an unwelcome outage of widely used Microsoft workplace software, the test will be happening in an atmosphere of heightened anxiety.

More from CNET

Videos across Facebook, Instagram and TikTok have floated the theory that this emergency test signals a catastrophe is coming, potentially stemming from a cyberattack or a digital disruption that could knock out electricity, internet and other services. Many have started scrambling to buy emergency supplies, pointing to the need for a 90-day stockpile of food, water, cash and essential medicines in case hackers wipe out bank accounts and shut down the web.

Similar rumors have spread globally, as the governments of France, the UK and Canada have put renewed attention on the importance of households being able to survive a potential weather-related crisis or technological disaster.

How extreme have the conspiracy theories gotten? Some have cited a 2023 Simpsons episode as proof, which referenced a massive Nov. 17 blackout in Lisa’s future, even though it didn’t mention a year.

For Gen Xers and Boomers, this panic could feel familiar. Leading up to the year 2000, there were fears that a potential computer-related disaster, known as Y2K, would cause widespread chaos and disruption, based on the belief that older digital systems couldn’t handle the calendar change. The new year ended with only minor glitches, thanks to a significant global effort to update computer systems to avoid the bug.

Before we delve into the suspicions, let’s start with a bit of debunking: CNET spoke with multiple experts in disaster preparedness and cyberattacks, who all cautioned against letting our guard down. But remember that no federal agency or institution has mentioned a blackout. Unless hackers decide to take advantage of the hysteria already generated, there’s no reason to think Nov. 17 is any riskier than any other date.

Richard Mariano, a protective intelligence expert at Kronus Intelligence, who spent nearly three decades with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, said that people share all sorts of things that get picked up and go viral. “Then it creates panic where panic is not necessary,” he said.

Mariano said too many people are spreading fear rather than seeking the truth. “On every one of these social media posts that is suspect or has some form of conspiratorial edge to them: source it, source it, source it.”

What is happening on Nov. 17?

Next week’s nationwide Emergency Alert System, or EAS, is similar to the public tests Americans have experienced since 1963, when the Emergency Broadcast System replaced an older radio-based warning system called CONELRAD. In 1997, the Emergency Broadcast System was replaced by the EAS, part of FEMA’s Integrated Public Alert and Warning System, which broadcasts emergency alerts to any wireless device in the country, including phones, radios and televisions. The system was designed for the president to communicate with US households within 10 minutes of a national emergency.

The Nov. 17 test will consist of a nationwide EAS message issued by FEMA, noting that no public action is required. The test will include standard alert tones to support accessibility for those who are deaf or hard of hearing and should last about a minute. This time around, wireless emergency alerts will not be triggered on mobile phones, so don’t expect a notification on your cellphone. After the alert, programming should resume as normal on TV, radio and other broadcast channels.

Many equate the emergency system with threats of nuclear war, but it could also be used to alert people to a major weather event, a national cyberattack or even AMBER alerts at the local level (without a presidential message). So it’s natural there might be some anxiety.

“With this event simulating an activation of an emergency notification system, it would be a logical next step to worry about what happens if something bad happens during that test,” said Robby Winchester, chief global professional services officer at SpecterOps, a Virginia-based security company,

But, all in all, these system tests are routine. Local stations conduct a weekly test, and federal law requires a nationwide EAS test every three years. In addition to helping people get used to responding to alerts, the tests also allow the government to identify potential technical or operational issues it needs to fix before an actual emergency alert.



FEMA has a backup date of Dec. 3 in case it can’t perform it on Nov. 17 — which could happen if the agency is dealing with a real emergency or if there are technical issues. Representatives from the FCC and FEMA did not respond to a request for comment.

Why are blackout rumors spreading?

Another factor that helped spark conspiracy theories was a Pentagon order requiring military bases to stock enough supplies for 90 days without outside support. Dubbed “Fortress America,” the initiative memo (PDF) was released in late September but got more attention as the November date approached.

The timing of that memo coincided with the UK launching a campaign on Oct. 22 called Be Ready, urging citizens to keep enough supplies (PDF) such as water, food, medical kits and pet products to last at least three days. Other countries, including Japan, Sweden and about a dozen more, are also urging citizens to prepare for emergencies.

Still, the blackout rumor isn’t solely driven by government communications. Heightened global instability over the past few months has also played a major role. Just in the last month, the Federal Aviation Administration called a nationwide ground stop on all departing flights; a major Microsoft Outlook outage kept millions of people from working; PHP vulnerabilities exposed websites to hacking; and cyberattacks have targeted supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe.

On the financial side, Nvidia’s CEO scandal led to a stock plunge and fears of an AI bust, while Paraguay just experienced a major digital bank collapse that froze millions of accounts. The ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine have sparked national security concerns, and floods in Nepal and fires in Indonesia demonstrate the increased dangers of climate change.

Though there’s never been a nationwide power outage in the US (several regional outages have been triggered by overloaded lines and software bugs), The New York Times reports that there’s still no comprehensive plan for what to do if the country goes completely dark.

All the online chatter surrounding Nov. 17 has raised concerns that warnings of a potential cyberattack might inadvertently trigger one.

Winchester said that even though there’s no specific information indicating an imminent crisis, “it is common for attackers to use current events of all types to help with achieving successful attacks.” The upside? If people are being spurred by government notices and their anxiety over global instability to prepare emergency supplies, it could actually help in the event of a real threat or disaster.

How to prepare for a disruption (on any date)

Regardless of whether you buy into the Nov. 17 conspiracy theories, it doesn’t hurt to have some supplies at the ready, which could be useful in the event of a digital disruption or weather event, even if it doesn’t involve nuclear weapons or hackers.

“We live in a world where there are many threats to our communities, our families and ourselves,” said Philip Farina, chief advisor for Risky Business and a federal law enforcement veteran. “Understanding the basics of self-reliance is important. Even preparing for a residential fire, which is very common, can help to save lives and protect us better.”

You don’t need to buy enough for 90 days off the grid (and most of us can’t afford that), but it’s recommended that families have at least three days’ worth of food and supplies. Some of the basics listed on Ready.gov’s Build a Kit page include:

A gallon of water per person per day

Several days’ worth of nonperishable food

A battery-powered or hand-crank radio to keep up with alerts

A flashlight

A first-aid kit

Batteries

A cellphone with a backup battery

Optional: Pet supplies, sleeping bags, cash, a fire extinguisher and books or games for children

While warnings from governments can spark panic and distrust, they can be beneficial at a time when we’re so reliant on the internet and cell service, which can be easily disrupted. Mariano said it’s worth being prepared in the “old-fashioned ways.”

Tech.title: Before Grand Theft Auto 6, CNET Staff Relive Their Favorite GTA Moments
Tech.content:
Rockstar Games is set to release Grand Theft Auto 6 on Thursday, Nov. 19, with both PlayStation and Xbox saying it’s the most preordered game in the history of either platform’s digital storefront. Given the 13 years of buildup and hype surrounding the game, that’s perhaps not surprising.

Though the series has evolved over time, Grand Theft Auto has been a pop culture behemoth since its inception in 1997, thanks to its biting satire, complex storylines and cinematic gameplay.

CJ and Big Smoke’s train chase

Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas is still my favorite GTA game. Rockstar Games

I have so many memories of playing Grand Theft Auto games at an age some might call “too young.” I’d go over a friend’s house and we’d boot up Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas on his PlayStation 2 and do whatever we wanted. It wasn’t until later that I found out there were missions to accomplish. And the funniest part for me was failing the mission Wrong Side of the Tracks in San Andreas. The character Big Smoke would utter the iconic line, “All we had to do was follow the damn train, CJ!” That line is funny, goofy and a good reminder that beneath the guns and violence, these are inherently silly, unserious games.

– Zachary McAuliffe, senior writer

Cockney coppers in London

Yes, this is a real Grand Theft Auto entry, a semisequel to the original Grand Theft Auto, released in 1999. Rockstar

I still quote the policemen from GTA London 1969 who yell, “Stop right there! Oi!” My friends and I in college would play it hotseat-style on my ancient laptop, and the cockney coppers became a meme (or “banter” as we called it back then, onions hanging from our belts as was the fashion).

– Nick Hide, managing copy editor

Video game dance moves

Ready to boogie the night away. Rockstar Games

I’ll say walking out of Blockbuster with a copy of GTA: Vice City as a teen whose most hard-core games before that were maybe Twisted Metal and Shivers 2 made me feel like a rock star. Tearing across the city, blowing red lights and running over onlookers was an absolute thrill, especially since my friends and I didn’t even have our learner’s permits yet.

The moment that sticks with me the most, however, was the infamous private dance scene in the Pole Position mission. I was playing over a long weekend at my best friend’s house, taking turns at the wheel, when we finally got to the scandalous part we’d read about on the internet. But instead of titillated, she and I were reduced to fits of giggles as the pixelated private dancer blockily gyrated on screen. And – sorry to our parents – after regaining composure, we immediately got to copying the unsultry choreo and teaching it to our friends. These moves would be busted out at the most opportune moments, even when we got old enough to go to real clubs. Sadly, it’s never earned us as much as a free drink.

– Faith Chihil, social producer

Postgraduation stress relief

Nothing says blowing off steam like blowing up a few cars. Rockstar

When GTA 5 came out in 2013, I had just graduated from college, moved back home with my parents and had no idea what to do with my life. So I waited several hours in line at my local GameStop, along with hundreds of other people, to be the first to get the game. I rushed back home and played for an irresponsible amount of time. There was something comforting about having an entire world to explore when I felt stuck in my own. Mostly, though, I made life worse for the people of Los Santos. My degree wasn’t opening many doors, but carjacking was.

– Nelson Aguilar, writer



Grand Theft Auto 5’s huge map

GTA 5 featured a huge map, but GTA 6 promises an even larger one. Rockstar Games

Forget the explosion-packed heists or the bullet-riddled car chases around city streets; my favorite GTA moment is when I discovered just how vast the GTA 5 map was and how much of it I could explore on foot. Or by helicopter.

GTA 5’s map was considered massive when it launched, and while I thoroughly enjoyed playing through the game’s actual storylines, I spent just as much time (if not more) simply seeing what’s out there beyond the expected play zones.

The GTA 6 map is apparently at least twice the size of that of GTA 5, and I’m super hyped to settle into hour after hour of serene exploration of a whole new landscape.

– Andrew Lanxon, editor at large

For more on GTA 6, here’s what we know about the game and how to prep your console for the massive file size.

Tech.title: Meet the Custom-Built Machine That Has Folded the iPhone Duo Nearly 500,000 Times
Tech.content:
We’re now nearly halfway through November, and CNET’s lab continues to work overtime testing Apple’s first folding phone, the $1,999 iPhone Duo. We purchased this model of the Duo more than three weeks ago, and since then, its only job has been to bend and flatten.

How many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? On Friday, Nov. 13, we passed 450,000 folds, and there was also an interesting change in the phone’s behavior.

I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations in our lab in Louisville, Kentucky. My team and I designed and built a proprietary machine to test foldable phones like Apple’s and its Samsung rival, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which we’ve also started testing). I’ve worked on the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone.

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

My team of engineers and testing experts has been watching the iPhone Duo open and close over and over for the past three weeks to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

Product Quiz

Powered by Digioh

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube weekdays from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

The Samsung Galaxy Note 8 above, in the same machine, lasted more than 260,000 folds before we swapped it out for the Duo. Matthew Murray/CNET

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

How CNET’s Fold-a-Phone tests foldable phones like the iPhone Duo

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

Matthew Murray/CNET

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

Tech.title: I Let My Apple Watch Eavesdrop on My Conversations for 2 Weeks
Tech.content:
We’ve long suspected that our devices are listening to us, but what about when we invite them to do it? That’s what testing Audio Intelligence has felt like on the Apple Watch. But despite how disturbing it may sound to have your smartwatch listening and taking notes of your entire day, the reality has been a lot more mundane.

Along with the general sensor, processor, and battery upgrades, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 introduced Audio Intelligence, a new set of features that allows the watch to listen in on conversations.

Siri Recap generates summaries of what you’ve discussed throughout the day, while Live Rewind gives you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of audio in case you missed something.

It’s similar functionality as AI-powered recording pins like Plaud or Amazon’s Bee, but within the context of your smartwatch and without the additional cost or subscription.

And it’s completely optional. You have to first opt-in to the features to activate them, then choose to turn the feature you want on whenever you want to start using it. Then you can leave it on all day, set it on a schedule or toggle it manually whenever you need it. If you’re like me and forget that it’s on, you get reminders that it’s still listening or to check your recaps.

The fact that you have so much control over whether you use it and how much helped ease the creepy factor for me, but there’s still everyone else to consider.

Beyond a barely audible chime when I double-click the Digital Crown to activate Live Rewind, there’s no way to alert others that the feature is in use and that whoever’s in earshot is inadvertently getting roped into my little experiment as well. Other wearables like smart glasses have an indicator light on the front to alert spectators when they’re recording video.

Apple has built-in privacy safeguards for the audio, how it’s processed and then deleted. I’ve broken all that down in a separate Audio Intelligence FAQ. This is about what it’s like to use it in the wild.

I’ve been testing Audio Intelligence in the WatchOS 27.3 (and iOS) public beta for two weeks. Because this isn’t the final version (Apple says it will release publicly later this year), consider this a sneak preview.

Live Rewind on the Apple Watch generates a transcription of what was said during the last 15 seconds. Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Live Rewind: Late to the trigger

Let’s get Live Rewind out of the way because there’s not a lot to say about it. Whether from a lack of muscle memory (or usefulness), I’ve had to go out of my way to remember the feature exists.

I figured it’d come in handy for those “come again?” moments during conversations, but the reality is that it’s just easier to ask someone to repeat what they said than remember to double-press the Digital Crown at just the right moment. I can see it being more useful when you’re listening to a presentation or other event.

Fifteen seconds go by a lot faster than I expect and by the time I realize something might be worth revisiting, the person has moved on with the conversation. I either missed what I intended to get or just captured the silence after.

Siri Recap can be toggled on or off manually from the Control Center. Apple

Siri Recap: Good at meetings, bad at life

Siri Recap has been more useful, though it’s still hit-or-miss. The feature gives you high-level summaries of what it heard — it doesn’t provide a transcript to review, and it doesn’t identify who said what. It shines brightest during dedicated meetings when there’s a single conversation to follow rather than a jumble of unrelated discussions.

One success story: I was moderating the chat for our iPhone Duo live folding test on YouTube while Matthew Murray, CNET’s lab director, answered viewer questions on the stream.

I thought I’d caught the gist of what he was saying, but the typing must’ve distracted me more than I realized because I was pleasantly surprised to learn some interesting facts that I’d missed in the Siri Recap, like “Opening a phone 20 times daily over 10 years equals 73,000 folds” or that the “machine runs approximately 22,560 cycles every 24 hours”.

But Siri’s batting average wasn’t always that good, which made it challenging to trust the notes. During a conversation with another mom about car-pool logistics, Siri Recap pulled out action items, like who I was picking up and at what time, which I appreciated, but the information wasn’t accurate. Not only had Siri gotten the names of the kids wrong, it also had me picking up the wrong kid. Clearly, the mental load of figuring out after-school logistics is challenging even for Siri.

Siri can’t handle the messy conversations (and TV shows)

Where things get interesting (and occasionally hilarious) is how Siri discerns what constitutes a conversation and how many topics belong in a single recap.

Siri is generally good at accurately labeling what conversations are about: “Parent-teacher conferences,” “Car-pool logistics,” “Folding phone durability testing.” But rather than keeping them separate, as it should, it sometimes conflates two or even three completely unrelated conversations into a single recap.

I encountered bullet points summarizing a serious conversation with a friend about a medical condition alongside notes about a chaotic (albeit funny) exploding apple cider incident with my kids. The two conversations happened within the same two-hour window, but they were by no means back-to-back.

Siri’s version:

Details about medical condition

Entire case of apple cider ruined after repeated warnings to stop shaking

No more apple cider will be brought into the house

Any remaining stickiness on the floor results in no iPad on the plane

It’s a good thing Siri Recap leaves out tone and volume cause that last bullet would’ve been in ALL CAPS.

What it did decide was worthy of a standalone recap was a discussion about wedding plans during an episode of Nobody Wants This on Netflix. To be fair, this would’ve absolutely warranted a recap if I’d been discussing my own wedding plans; however, the fact that the “conversation” happened at midnight should’ve tipped off Siri that this was a late-night binge session and not an actual conversation needing to be recapped.

Rather than coming away better informed about the important conversations I’d had throughout the day, I came away feeling validated by the sheer chaos of it all. The constant whiplash of being pulled in a dozen different directions — bouncing between work, kids, gossip and the occasional sticky beverage crisis — was real and now immortalized (until the recap automatically expires if you don’t choose to save it).

A case for manually enabling Siri Recap during meetings

For now, while novel, neither Siri Recap nor Live Rewind is reason enough to buy (or avoid) the Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. They’re two of our top-rated smartwatches for their fitness, health and other smart features. Audio Intelligence is either an added bonus (it’s free) or something you can ignore altogether.

But if you do decide to venture into this brave new world of AI notetakers, my suggestion would be to use Siri Recap intentionally rather than leaving it running all day.

Turn it on before a work meeting, a doctor’s appointment or another conversation where you might want a few notes to jog your memory later. Just make sure everyone involved knows it’s enabled and is comfortable with it, and that you’re not relying on it for crucial information.

If the stakes are high, have a backup — whether that’s your own notes or a recording — lest you risk coming home with the wrong kid.

Tech.title: Which Earbuds Are Best for Voice Calling? Check Out the Pair That Won My Latest Test
Tech.content:
In the past, I’ve typically produced a couple of videos highlighting my top headphones and earbuds of the year. In 2026, we’re wrapping things up a bit differently with our Holiday Office Hours from the Labs video series.

Instead of just talking about my favorites, I recently tested the voice-calling performance of some of this year’s best earbuds alongside a set of budget buds. Plus, my colleagues Jada Jones from ZDNET and Eric Zeman from PCMag drop their own top holiday picks for headphones and earbuds.



Each premium pair of earbuds I selected for my test has earned a CNET Editors’ Choice award. They include Apple’s AirPods Pro 3, Sennheiser’s Momentum True Wireless 5 and Anker’s Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro. I also threw the $27 JLab Go Pods ANC into the mix to see how a pair of truly budget wireless earbuds would compare. (Spoiler: They weren’t great, but they performed better than I expected.)

Tech.title: Razer’s Wild $1,000 Gaming Chair Has Six Motors, Built-In Speakers and RGB Lighting
Tech.content:
There are different levels of gaming immersion when it comes to haptics. On one side, you have controller haptics, which provide a bit of stimulation in games. You might feel a nice little rumble from explosions or gunshots and maybe a bit of vibration to give you some feedback while driving off-road.

On the other side, you have Razer’s two new gaming chairs, the $1,000 Soma Pro and the $570 Soma Sense HD Haptics, which feature some serious motors to really shake your spine. Both incorporate Razer Sensa HD Haptics, which the company first debuted as part of Project Esther back in 2024. The chair also has THX Spatial Audio support and Razer Chroma RGB lighting built in.

This isn’t an entirely new line for Razer. The Soma series is one the company has been working on for some years now. The Soma Chroma was the first wireless RGB gaming chair announced this summer for $499. Now Razer is rounding out its gaming chair lineup.

More from CNET

How immersive are these chairs?

Razer

Both chairs come with six haptic motor actuators built into each seat, unlike the $300 Razer Freyja, which was essentially a wired cushion you placed on top of your existing chair and plugged in. I actually owned the Freyja, and while it worked OK for some games, for a lot of others I tried it with, it just used a generic rumble without really customizing things. It was also very uncomfortable to sit on long-term. Plus, I didn’t like the feeling of being tethered to a cable and ended up getting rid of it. A built-in wireless option, like these new chairs, seems like a much better solution to me.

Both new chairs deliver “multizone feedback” via Razer Sensa HD Haptics, and Razer says they should match the intensity, direction, and distance of in-game events. For example, an explosion off to the side will feel different from one that’s up close to you. So this isn’t just a generic rumble that applies to every situation; it’s customized based on the gameplay.

Razer lists more than 100 PC games that support integrated Sensa HD Haptics, including Battlefield 6, Borderlands 4, Marvel Rivals and S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Heart of Chornobyl. For everything else, the chairs use Audio-to-Haptics via Razer Synapse, converting audio into vibration, so the effect also works with games without native support, as well as with movies and music.

In theory, this should allow the feature to work on anything that supports controller vibration, but a Razer representative did not immediately respond to a request for clarification. On the Soma Pro, you can dial the overall intensity up or down in Synapse or adjust each of the six motor zones individually.

Razer

It’s worth noting that, unlike the Freyja, both chairs are wireless, though that doesn’t mean they’re completely untethered since Razer hasn’t managed to break the laws of energy yet. Each chair draws power over a single USB-C connection, from either a wall outlet or a compatible power bank, to preserve what Razer calls a wireless-aesthetic setup.

A power bank isn’t included in the box, so budget for one if you want the cable-free look. (You’ll also need a power adapter if you don’t have one handy, as the company doesn’t provide one.) That’s a downside because my LiberNovo Omni chair, which comes with adjustable lumbar support, a motorized spine, and even a massager setting, shipped with a rechargeable 2,200-mAh power bank.

Both Soma chairs carry a three-year warranty on mechanisms and moving parts and a two-year warranty on electronic parts.

Soma Sensa HD vs. Soma Pro

Razer

Both Soma chairs share the same hardware, at least where you rest your backside. There’s a built-in lumbar arch intended to encourage a neutral sitting position, a dual-density cold-cured foam seat cushion with a softer top layer over a firmer core and a backrest that reclines up to 132 degrees. Both have a steel frame and are rated for people up to 331 pounds. Razer lists the Soma Pro for people 5 feet, 5 inches to 6 feet, 6 inches tall, and the Sensa model for people who are 5 feet, 3 inches to 6 feet, 6 inches.

For $1,000, the Soma Pro offers sound and light in addition to haptics. Built-in speakers deliver THX Spatial Audio directly from the chair. Yes, that’s right: You don’t need computer speakers — they’re right behind your head now. You can use them on their own or pair them with front speakers to widen the soundstage, with the chair effectively handling the rear of the setup. It is the same idea Razer has used with Razer Clio headrest speakers before, now integrated rather than clipped on.

The Pro is also the only model in the line with Razer Chroma RGB. The reactive lighting uses 16.8 million colors, responds to on-screen action in more than 300 integrated games and syncs with the rest of a Razer setup via Synapse. While I love a good light show, this isn’t really meant for the person seated in the chair. It seems designed for streamers and people watching you since it doesn’t look like you can really see the light show unless you take your eyes off the stream.

The Pro also gets the line’s most adjustable fit — 4D armrests, a magnetic head cushion and a frog tilt mechanism — on a powder-coated aluminum alloy wheelbase.

The controls are on a built-in panel that switches between Razer HyperSpeed Wireless (2.4 GHz) for PC and Bluetooth LE for mobile, with a companion Razer Furniture app on the Pro for adjusting haptics, audio and lighting from a phone. The controls are a nice alternative to using Razer’s annoyingly overlapping and often invasive Synapse and Chroma software.

Price and availability

The $570 Soma Sensa HD Haptics chair keeps the same six-actuator haptic system and drops the speakers and the RGB. That makes it $71 more than the lighting-only Soma Chroma ($499), and $430 less than the Soma Pro ($1,000). If you already have a headset or speakers, which I’d assume you do as a gamer who’s considering a product like this, the Soma Sensa HD Haptics gets you most of the key features without the unnecessary extras.

Tech.title: Live Now! The iPhone Duo Hinge Is Showing First Signs of Wear After 451K Folds in Our Machine
Tech.content:
After three weeks and over 451,000 folds in our custom Fold-A-Phone machine, Apple’s iPhone Duo is showing its first signs of wearing out its hinge. We’ve been endurance testing Apple’s $1,999 foldable phone since Oct. 23, with the intention of seeing how far the Duo’s first-gen hinge can hold up. But as of Friday, the Duo is beginning to have issues with fully opening in our machine.



CNET Lab Director Matthew Murray will go over these changes on today’s 1 p.m. ET livestream on our YouTube channel, which you can watch embedded above. Our robust in-house machine has been opening and closing the foldable phone around 20,000 times per day to simulate years of wear and tear on the hinge from our CNET Labs location in Louisville, Kentucky.

Product Quiz

Powered by Digioh

The livestream isn’t just for watching a phone open and close — you’ll also be able to chat with CNET editors who will be available to answer your iPhone Duo questions live in the chat. Will Apple’s first foldable live up to the likes of the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold? Will its neat opening animation remain slick over thousands of folds? Join us and find out.

Apple’s iPhone Duo is starting to show noticeable wear on its hinge after 451,944 folds. Matthew Murray/CNET

This long-term test will join our iPhone Duo review, which provides a snapshot of what it’s like to be among the first to use Apple’s first foldable phone. If you’re sold on it, check out the best iPhone Duo deals. And if you want to compare even further, you can check out our roundup of the best foldable phones currently available if you want help deciding between the Duo and other folding and flip-style phones from Samsung, Motorola and Google.
